en: Commentary on the Abhidharmakośa-śāstra, Scroll Two, Composed by the Śramaṇa Fa-bao.
Chapter One: Analysis of the Elements (Dhātunirdeśa), Part Two.
Treatise:
Furthermore, as for "up to how many are indeterminate," the following constitutes the second major section of the text, consisting of nineteen verses.
This is the analytical classification of the eighteen *dhātus* according to their meanings.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Because within the *dhātus*, the faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are fully manifested."
Since the categories and meanings of the various doors are easily understood, we shall now briefly analyze them by way of the eighteen *dhātus*.
By this, the categories and meanings of the *skandhas* and *āyatanas* are also established. This single verse analyzes [the subject] through three doors.
First the question is posed,
then the answer is given in verse.
This passage is the question.
In the verse, the first line refers to "with vision" (sadarśana);
the second line refers to "with resistance" (sapratigha);
and the latter two lines refer to the three natures (trividha). These may be understood according to the text.
The Commentary states: "Up to the point where it says 'the rest are not seen,' this is the prose explanation.
The verse is divided into three sections according to three gates."
This first explanation [states that it] has visibility (*sanidarśana*). Both the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Nyāyānusāra* provide two explanations.
The *Nyāyānusāra*, in its fourth chapter, asks:
"Why is this said to be 'with visibility'?"
This is due to two reasons.
First, because this form is invariably accompanied by vision, it is called "visible."
Because form and the eye arise simultaneously,
they are like companions;
this is the second [reason].
This form is called "visible" because it can be pointed out;
it can be indicated as being here or there,
just like an object of cognition.
Some say: This visible form is called "visible" (sanidarśana) because an image can appear within mirrors and the like, and it can be pointed out, just as one might point to "this" or "that.
However, it cannot be said that sound is "visible" on the grounds that it possesses echoes and the like, for if it were so, [the definition] would lead to the absurd conclusion that sound is visible.
Because they do not arise simultaneously, the *Vibhāṣā* is in agreement.
This treatise, however, adopts only the second [position], because it can demonstrate the distinction between "this" and "that. By this principle, it is inferred that others are without vision.
Excluding form (*rūpa*), the remaining seventeen [bases] cannot be manifested; this distinction is called "invisible" (*anidarśana*).
According to the *Nyāyānusāra*, the three aforementioned meanings constitute "invisible."
Because this treatise is concise, there is only a single commentary. The treatise says:
Thus has been explained [the section] up to "because of the difference in the objects of perception."
The second [section] explains "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*).
First, the conclusion of the citation establishes the heading;
subsequently, the explanation follows according to that heading.
This is the beginning of the treatise.
Regarding "obstructive resistance" (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*), it extends up to "or two [substances] mutually obstruct each other."
This is the second explanation.
Within this explanation there are eight parts;
this passage is the first, explaining obstructive resistance (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*).
The five faculties and the five objects do not arise when obstructed by their own or other locations.
This is the meaning of "obstructive resistance" (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*): it is like the reaching of a hand or the mutual obstruction of two forms.
This is an explanation by way of citing a concrete instance;
it is analogous to the case of a hand and a stone.
All other ten material dharmas are likewise so,
like tiles, wood, and the like.
Treatise:
Regarding "resistance through the object" up to the objects such as form;
this is the second explanation of resistance through the object.
The text contains two parts:
first, the demonstration of the essence;
second, the citation of evidence to establish the conclusion.
This is the beginning of the text. Regarding the twelve bases (*dhātu*):

they consist of the six sense faculties (*indriya*) and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). As for "a portion of the dharma-base (*dharmadhātu*) consisting of all phenomena that possess an object": these are mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).
Regarding "objects such as form" (*rūpādi-viṣaya*): [this refers to the remaining objects].
That is to say, because the six sense organs, the six consciousnesses,
and so forth possess functional capacity within respect to objects such as visible forms,
they are termed "objects" (viṣaya).
That which possesses resistance in this context is termed "impediment" (sapratigha).
Thus, the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states that [the definition] applies until the exclusion of the aforementioned characteristics.
The second [section] cites scriptural authority.
The *Prajñapti-śāstra* is one of the six auxiliary treatises (*ṣatpādābhidharma*), composed by Mahākātyāyanīputra. The four lines may be understood as follows: "This obstruction..."
This is the meaning of "seeing form.
"Obstruction" (*pratigha*) is another name for its opposite;
that is to say, it is called "obstructive" (*sapratigha*) with respect to the form that is seen. *Piśāca*.
In the language of Tang, this refers to the "blood-and-flesh-eating ghost.
Formerly known as the *piśāca* ghost, the *śiṃśumāra* belongs to the class of animals (*tiryagyoni*).
Their shape is like that of a walled palace;
the smallest are twenty feet long,
while the largest reach a length of one hundred feet.
"These are called 'obstruction by way of object' (*ālambana-pratighāta*).
This is the summary verse (*uddāna*). Now, the commentary (*bhāṣya*):
Regarding the resistance of the object (*ālambana-pratighāta*):
up to its own respective object. This is the third explanation of the resistance of the object.
The mind and mental factors encounter obstruction when meeting their own respective objects.
It is called "resistance by way of an object.
In the treatise,
what further distinction is there between the objective field (*viṣaya*) and the object of cognition (*ālambana*)?
The fourth section distinguishes the differences.
First, the question;
second, the answer.
This is the question. The treatise states:
"If one reaches those phenomena, they are termed the 'object-condition' (ālambana)."
Answer: If this [consciousness] possesses efficacy toward those dharmas,
the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Just as when a person possesses superior capacity regarding something,
they say that thing is their own domain.
The commentary states:
A phenomenon that possesses an object has the functional capacity to engage its own object through seeing, hearing, and so forth; this is called an "object-field" (*viṣaya*).
Mind and mental factors grasp an object and arise [in dependence upon it]; this is called an "objective referent" (*ālambana*). This is the distinction between mind and mental factors.
When the mind arises by apprehending an object, the mental factors (caitta) share the same name as "having an object" (sālambana).

Because they do not function toward those respective objects or toward other objects, they are called "possessing resistance" (sapratigha). They differ in their functional capacities for grasping images and maintaining them.
Mind and mental factors are designated by the alternative term "object" (*viṣaya*).
Because they do not function with respect to other objects when directed toward a specific one—transcending that particular object—they are called "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*).
This refers to their distinction. There are four interpretations held by some: first, it is said:

Regarding "resistance" (*pratigha*), there are two types: resistance as an object-domain (*viṣaya-pratigha*) and resistance as an obstruction (*āvaraṇa-pratigha*). Resistance as an object-domain refers to the capacity [of a sense organ] to encounter its object; it does not necessarily require the actual exercise of that function. For example, the eyes of those who possess the "homogeneous class" (*sabhāga*) are called "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*) because they have the capacity to encounter their objects.
Resistance as an obstruction means that one must grasp the objective domain and then arise to reach the present moment.
The first explanation states that when the function of grasping an object arises upon the presence of a condition, and fails to arise in its absence, it is termed "resistant" (sapratigha).
The second explanation defines "resistance regarding the objective sphere" (viṣayapratighāta) as the function of obstructing the apprehension of an object.

The third interpretation: that which is "obstructive with respect to the object" (*ālambana-pratighāta*) is so called from the perspective of the meaning of obstructing the function of grasping the fruit; that which is "obstructive with respect to the objective sphere" (*viṣaya-pratighāta*) is so called from the perspective of the meaning of obstructing the function [itself].

The fourth interpretation: that which is "obstructive with respect to the objective sphere" (*viṣaya-pratighāta*) is so called from the perspective of the function of obstructing the grasping of the object.

"The function of obstructing the objective sphere is called 'resistance with respect to the object' (*ālambana-pratighāta*). To examine these four interpretations, none of them accord with the intent of the treatise.
The treatise asks:
"Why are the eye and so forth said to be 'possessing resistance' (*sapratigha*)?"
The fifth [section] explains the term "with resistance" (sāpattika).
First, the question;
subsequently, the answer.
This text poses the question.
The treatise responds that because [the term] does not apply to others beyond those [specific cases],
it is excluded from them.
The answer is twofold;
this is the former response. That is to say, it clarifies whether [the object] is a *viṣaya* (objective field) or a *ālambana* (supporting object).
Among form and the other [sense objects], that which is designated as "possessing resistance" (sapratigha) is that which obstructs the eye and so forth,
such that the mind and its concomitants do not arise with respect to other [objects];
this is the meaning of "possessing resistance."
Treatise:
Alternatively, "obstructing" refers to the fact that [the mind] proceeds until it reaches a state of harmonious integration;
this is the second explanation.
This refers to the subject that cognizes and the object that is cognized; when these—
the objective sphere and its corresponding object—
conjoin and arise together, it is termed "possessing resistance" (sapratigha).
Neither of these constitutes an obstructive substance that obstructs the acquisition of results and so forth.
One should know that within this treatise, up until the point where it says "the rest are non-obstructive" (*apratigha*),
the sixth verse of the assembly explains that being "without superior obstruction" (*an-ūrdhva-pratigha*) is what is meant by "non-obstructive."
Treatise:
If a phenomenon (*dharma*) is an object-impediment (*viṣayapratighāta*), it belongs to the fourth category;
this is the numerical analysis of the seventh [set of] phrases. There are two parts within the text.
First, the fourfold permutation regarding objective spheres (*ālambana*) and resistance (*pratighāta*).

Second, the permutation regarding objective spheres and objects of cognition (*ālambana*), which follows the subsequent clause; this is the first [of the two]. The first clause is: that which is an objective sphere with resistance, but not resistant.
The second phrase refers to that which is an obstacle but not an object;
the third phrase is the combination of both;
and the fourth phrase is the negation of both.
All may be understood.
Treatise:

If a phenomenon is an object that possesses resistance (*sapratigha*) and reaches the five faculties, such as the eye, this is the second "subsequent clause" (*anuloma-paścādvākya*). This is a case where a broad question is answered with a subsequent clause that is narrower in scope.
If that which is an object of cognition (*ālambana*) were necessarily characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*), it would follow that because it is an object of cognition,
its nature as an obstruction (*āvaraṇa*) would be unrelated [to the subject];
therefore, these two terms cannot be combined into a compound.
Treatise:
Herein, the Venerable [Vasubandhu] accepts this point up to here.
The eighth [section] describes the tenets of the Sautrāntika school. Kumāralāta.
This is known as Śrīlāta.
He was a patriarch of the Sautrāntika school,
who composed works such as the *Upamānasaṃgraha* (The Garland of Similes) and the *Mūḍhasaṃgraha* (The Garland of Fools) within that tradition.
Within this [text] there is the following verse,
which clarifies the existence of resistance (*sapratigha*) and differs from the Sarvāstivāda school: "In this place, where the mind intends to arise..."
This means that when the mind arises toward a blue color or the like, it is obstructed by another so as not to arise;
that is, being hindered by something else, the mind cannot arise toward the blue color. One should know that this is what constitutes "resistance" (sapratigha).
Regarding the "obstructive" (*sapratigha*): this is the opposite of the aforementioned "non-obstructive.
The Sarvāstivādins maintain that it is precisely upon the blue [color] that the designation "obstructive" arises. This is what is accepted [by them].
The Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) approves of this Sautrāntika tenet.
The treatise says:
Thus has it been explained up to [the point where] it is therefore called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
The third section is the analysis of the three natures.
This passage contains two parts:
first, the explanation of the eight elements (*dhātu*).
The second [section] explains the ten realms; this is the opening of that text.
That is to say, among the ten material realms, with the exception of the two realms of visible form and sound, the remaining eight cannot be designated as either wholesome or unwholesome.
Therefore, it is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
There are two explanations for "indeterminate," and this is the first.
The treatise further states that [this] "attainment" (*prāpti*) should be exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The refutation of alternative views is as can be understood from the text.
[End of] Treatise.
The remaining ten elements (dhātus) up to the [dharma-element] are termed indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
This is the second explanation of the ten elements. The text consists of three sections:
first, the explanation of the seven mental elements (*citta-dhātu*).
Second, the explanation of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). Third, the explanation of the two elements of visible form (*rūpadhātu*) and sound (*śabdadhātu*).
This is the beginning of that section. The seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) are called wholesome when they are associated with wholesome states such as non-attachment (*alobha*).
That which is associated with the three unwholesome roots, such as greed and so forth, is called unwholesome;
that which is not associated with those two is called indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Thus says the Treatise.
If the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) is [any other] than these, it is called indeterminate (avyākṛta).
This is the second explanation of the dharma-element.
If it consists of non-greed and so forth...

These are wholesome by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*). Those associated with mental factors such as perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*), which are themselves wholesome by intrinsic nature, are called wholesome by association (*samprayoga-kuśala*).
This includes unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*), the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of dharmas, and acquisition (*prāpti*).

These two, being the co-arising of the wholesome, are also called "wholesome. Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), being an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), is also called "wholesome" because it is the ultimate good (*paramārtha-kuśala*). Thus, within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*)...
There are four kinds of wholesomeness: that of intrinsic nature, that of association, that of origination, and that of the ultimate.
These four kinds of wholesomeness will be explained in detail later.
Treatise:
The elements of visible form and sound that extend to others are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
This is the third explanation of visible form and sound.
Among these two, there is only that which is wholesome or unwholesome by way of motivation (*samutthāna*). [Abhidharmakośabhāṣya] states:
Having already explained that wholesome meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) belong to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
the second verse-line clarifies their affiliation with the three realms (*dhātu*).
This passage consists of three parts.
First, the introduction;
second, the verse;
third, the commentary.
This is the beginning of the text. In the verse, the first line clarifies the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
the next two lines clarify the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
and the final line clarifies the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The Commentary states: "Up to 'endowed with the eighteen [dharmas]' is the second long prose explanation. This explanation of the three realms is divided into three sections.
This first section explains that which is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). "Bound" (*baddha*) means being attached to or dependent upon.
This refers to the meaning of being bound.

Before analyzing the number of dharmas, we first explain the meaning of "bound" (*saṃyukta*). Dharmas bound by the craving and other afflictions of the desire realm are called "bound to the desire realm. These consist of the four elements of the nose, tongue, odor, and taste in their entirety.
A portion of the remaining fourteen elements belongs to the desire realm;
it is by virtue of this that the desire realm possesses all eighteen elements.
Treatise:

Because that which is bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu) reaches the point of having no object of perception (anālambana), this is the second explanation of the realm of form. There are two parts within this text.
This consists of two parts: first, distinguishing the number of dharmas;
second, analysis through question and answer.
This is the beginning of that [second part]. Because there is no nutriment of physical food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), there are no objective spheres of odor (*gandha*) or taste (*rasa*).
Because there is no object, there is no nose-consciousness or tongue-consciousness.
Treatise: If that were so, it would follow [that they exist] because they have the nature of substantial food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
The second section consists of questions and answers concerning distinctions.
Fragrance and flavor are of the nature of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Since there is no edible food in the higher realms, the objects of fragrance and flavor do not exist there.
If that were so, the tactile element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) would also lack the nature of substantial food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). [Response:
The tactile objects present there are not of the nature of substantial food.
Answer: There is tangibility in the form realm that is not edible food.
Treatise.

If that were so, it would follow as a difficulty that the same should apply to the categories of odor and taste. The sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) is of the nature of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*);
however, in the higher realms, there is tangibility that is not edible food.
Odor and taste are of the nature of edible food [only in the desire realm].
Question: In the higher realms, there is fragrance, yet taste is not of the nature of substantial nutriment (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*). Answer:
Fragrance and taste are present because they reach [the senses] even apart from food; it is not the case that touch is absent. Question: Apart from food, fragrance and taste have no further utility.
In the higher realms, there is neither the fragrance nor the taste of solid food; however,
tangible objects (spraṣṭavya) exist apart from solid food and possess utility,
specifically the functions of sustaining the sense faculties and serving as clothing and so forth.
Therefore, although there is no edible food in the form realm, there is still the element of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*).
According to other masters in the treatise:
The statement that [these] do not exist there because they have reached [that state] is a mistaken interpretation.

"Dwelling here" refers to dwelling in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Regarding those who, relying on the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and attainments (*samāpatti*), see forms and hear sounds while accompanied by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*):
This refers to one whose body is in the desire realm,
who attains the supernormal powers of the divine eye and ear to see forms and hear sounds;
at the time of entering meditative concentration, there arises a state accompanied by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
The superior object of touch benefits the body;
because these three factors are present together during the causal stage,
they likewise follow one another into the resultant state.
Fragrance and taste are not like this;
therefore, they do not exist there. Thus says the treatise.
If that were so, it would be difficult [to maintain] because they would be useless upon reaching there. Since edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) does not exist there,
and since the two objects of fragrance and flavor are useless, they do not exist there.
The nose and tongue have no function regarding non-dual objects;
therefore, they should not exist there.
Treatise.
It is not so; [the faculties] reach and adorn the body.
Answer: To say they are useless is not the case, for the tongue gives rise to speech.
The nose adorns the body;
because it serves a useful purpose, all [beings] possess it.
Treatise.
If it is for the purpose of adorning the body, what need is there for two organs?
This is the objection. [The response is: The bases of the two organs consist of the two objects—visible form and tangibility—which serve to give rise to speech and to adorn the body.

If only the two objects—visible form and tangibility—are required for speech and for the adornment of the body, what is the use of the two faculties? [The treatise says: The term "only" (but) serves to exclude other objects. Since visible form and tangibility are sufficient for the purpose of speech and for the adornment of the body, what need is there for the two faculties? [The opponent] asks: Why are the two faculties unnecessary? For it is by means of visible form that one speaks, and it is by means of tangibility that one adorns the body. Therefore, these two alone should suffice. What further use is there for the two faculties? What is the purpose of establishing them? This is the meaning. [The author] replies: It is not so. Why? Because they serve as the basis for the faculties of sight and touch. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be manifest. Moreover, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be apprehended. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be established. Why? Because the two objects are established based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is established; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is established. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be perceived. Why? Because the two objects are perceived based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is perceived; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is perceived. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be known. Why? Because the two objects are known based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is known; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is known. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be experienced. Why? Because the two objects are experienced based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is experienced; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is experienced. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be manifested. Why? Because the two objects are manifested based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is manifested; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is manifested. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be distinguished. Why? Because the two objects are distinguished based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is distinguished; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is distinguished. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be differentiated. Why? Because the two objects are differentiated based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is differentiated; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is differentiated. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be determined. Why? Because the two objects are determined based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is determined; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is determined. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be established as distinct. Why? Because the two objects are established as distinct based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is established as distinct; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is established as distinct. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be established as separate. Why? Because the two objects are established as separate based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is established as separate; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is established as separate. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be established as individual. Why? Because the two objects are established as individual based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is established as individual; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is established as individual. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be established as unique. Why? Because the two objects are established as unique based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is established as unique; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is established as unique. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be established as specific. Why? Because the two objects are established as specific based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is established as specific; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is established as specific. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be established as particular. Why? Because the two objects are established as particular based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is established as particular; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is established as particular. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be established as distinct entities. Why? Because the two objects are established as distinct entities based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is established as a distinct entity; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is established as a distinct entity. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be established as different natures. Why? Because the two objects are established as different natures based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is established as a different nature; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is established as a different nature. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be established as diverse characteristics. Why? Because the two objects are established as diverse characteristics based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is established as a diverse characteristic; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is established as a diverse characteristic. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be established as manifold aspects. Why? Because the two objects are established as manifold aspects based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is established as a manifold aspect; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is established as a manifold aspect. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be established as various modes. Why? Because the two objects are established as various modes based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is established as a various mode; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is established as a various mode. Therefore, the two faculties must necessarily exist. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the two faculties did not exist, the two objects would not be established as distinct functions. Why? Because the two objects are established as distinct functions based upon the two faculties. Just as when the eye faculty exists, the object of visible form is established as a distinct function; and when the body faculty exists, the object of tangibility is established as a distinct function. Therefore, one knows that they are not the primary elements (*mahābhūta*); and since they are not perceived by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) as form, sound, and so forth, one knows that form and the rest are not the four great elements. Thus, it is certain that the reasoning stated by them is not correct.
This concludes the treatise.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says, "up to the invisible and impinging."
The second section refutes [the opponent's position] by citing a sutra.
This passage contains four parts:

Second, explaining the intent of the sūtra;

fourth, resolving those objections.
This is the first point of this text. In the Sūtra, it is taught that the five faculties and four objects are all exclusively derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Regarding the element of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*), it is taught that it contains the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as well as derived matter.
This establishes that the four great elements (mahābhūta) are exclusively the creators [of derived matter] and are not themselves [the derived matter of] form and so forth.
Treatise:
Thus, in the sutras, it is stated that they are all not the great elements.
The second [section] explains the intent of the sutra;
it may be understood according to the text.

"If that were so... and so forth, as explained at length.

This is the third objection, citing a sūtra from outside [the Abhidharma]. The sūtra says: "Within the mass of flesh that is the eye, whatever is internal, having the nature of solidity, belonging to the category of the solid," and so on.
Therefore, it is known that the eye and so forth are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Treatise.
That statement does not entail the fault of contradiction;
this is the fourth resolution of objections.
The text contains two parts.
First, a sūtra cited in the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*;
second, the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*.
This is the former. That [sūtra] states that within the mass of flesh of the eye faculty, there is solidity and so forth.
It does not mean that solidity and so forth are themselves the eye-faculty;
thus, there is no contradiction or error in the treatise.
Because the *Garbha-avakrānti-sūtra* extends up to the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
This refers to the *Garbha-avakrānti-sūtra*. That sutra speaks of the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*), namely:
the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), space (*ākāśa*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
This is for the purpose of establishing the fundamental nature of the person (*pudgala*). The person is not limited to this alone,
as there are also the six objects and the mental factors (*caitta*).
This is known because that sutra also speaks of the six bases of contact, such as form and so forth.
[Treatise]
Furthermore, because all mental factors (caitta) depend upon the mind (citta) as their basis,
this constitutes a counter-objection: if it is argued that the four great elements (mahābhūta) are themselves formless (arūpa) and so forth according to the Sūtra,
then it would follow that mental factors are also non-existent, since the Sūtra speaks of the element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu).
Furthermore, one should not maintain that mental factors (*caitta*) are identical to the mind (*citta*),
because the Sūtra states that mental factors such as perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) depend upon the mind.
If feeling, perception, and so forth were themselves the mind, [they could not be said to depend upon it].
Why does the Sūtra state that mental factors (caitta) depend upon the mind (citta)?
The Śāstra further states that the Sūtra also speaks of "a mind possessed of greed" (sarāga-citta) and so forth.
This further cites scriptural evidence:
since it is stated that there is "greed," the mind itself cannot be greed.

By this, as previously stated, the meaning of the distinctions is established;
this is the conclusion.
The treatise having thus explained [the matter] up to the point that it does not reach the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*),
the second major section explains the accumulation (*saṃcita*) and so forth.
This may be understood according to the text.
Treatise:
Having thus explained up to how much is designated [as "cuttable"],
the seventh section, consisting of one verse, analyzes the three categories of that which cuts, that which is cut, and so forth.
The summary verse provides the answer;
it may be understood according to the text.
The treatise says: "At this point, the name for this phenomenon is 'cutting' (*chidya*)."
This is the explanation.
Within the text there are three parts.
First, the explanation of the "cutter" and the "cuttable."

The first part of this passage consists of two types of compound analysis: the *dvandva* (copulative) explaining that which is burned and that which weighs, and the *tatpuruṣa* (determinative) explaining that which burns and that which is weighed.
This text is divided into two sections: the first clarifies that which cuts and that which is cut.
Second, the clarification of "neither":
this is the beginning of the passage. It refers to the four external elements, excluding sound.
When wood and fuel are combined,
they constitute that which cuts and that which is cut.
What phenomenon is designated as "cutting"?
Because the axe separates the wood into two distinct parts that arise successively,
it is called "that which cuts. [Abhidharmakośa] Bhāṣya.
The physical sense organs, such as the eye, extend as far as their radiance, like that of a jewel;

this explains why the five organs are both [material] and non-material. Since there are no organs apart from the body’s limbs and joints, they cannot be divided into two parts, and thus they are not subject to being severed.
Because it is like the light of jewels and so forth, it cannot cut. The treatise states:
because that which can cut reaches [the object] without continuity.

The response consists of two verses and three expositions;
this is the beginning of that text.
