This is the answer provided by the verse.
The commentary says: "Because up until that point there is no distinct nature [of the factors]."
This explains the verse. As for the statement "the five internal [bases]," it refers to the five faculties,
namely the eye and so forth.
There are those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and those that are nurtured (*aupacayika*);
since these exclude the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*), they are not mentioned [here].
Because there is no distinct nature.
The treatise states that this is said because [the result] arises from a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
This explains that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
There are four parts to the text;
this is the first explanation: "that which is produced by the cause of maturation."
To say that the cause is named "maturation" (*vipāka*) while the fruit is named "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) is an example of the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound.
Because it is produced by a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), it is called "born of ripening" (*vipākaja*).
By omitting the two characters *yin-so* (cause-produced), it is termed "born of ripening.
The meaning of the analogy is thus understandable.
This merely explains the reason why the name of the fruit is "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*),
but does not state the reason why the name of the cause is "maturation cause" (*vipāka-hetu*).
[End of] Treatise.
Alternatively, the karma that has been performed reaches the stage called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*);
this is the second explanation.
In this explanation, the cause is termed "maturation."
This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
That which is maturation (*vipāka*) is itself the cause, thus it is called the "maturation cause" (*vipāka-hetu*);
that which is the fruit is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
This is an explanation based on the possessive compound (*tatpuruṣa*). The treatise states:
"That which is called 'ripening' (*vipāka*) is so named because the fruit obtained by it reaches [its completion]."
This is the third explanation.
Herein, the fruit is indeterminate (avyākṛta),
while the cause is either wholesome (kuśala) or unwholesome (akuśala).
That which is of a different category from its cause is called "distinct" (*visadṛśa*).
Furthermore, that which is what is matured is called "maturation" (*vipāka*).
Maturation itself as it arises is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
The treatise states: "Or, regarding the cause, it refers to karma previously created."
The fourth is the possessive compound (*tatpuruṣa*).
It is called the "ripening cause" (*vipāka-hetu*) because it possesses the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*);
that which arises from that ripening cause is called "born of ripening" (*vipākaja*).
This is an analysis based on possessive relation (*ṣaṣṭhī-vigraha*). There are four interpretations in the *Nyāyapraveśa*.

Three interpretations are the same as this treatise; the third interpretation not found in this treatise is an analysis based on that which is of a different category from the cause (*hetu*) yet is what is ripened (*vipacyate*).
Another interpretation states:
it is called "vipāka" (ripening) because it matures apart from its cause;
it is called "vipākaja" (born of ripening) because the essence of ripening arises. The commentary explains:
Therefore, the term "ripening from maturation" (*vipākaja*) is explained by way of its dissociation from the cause.
"Dissociation from the cause" means that the cause has already ceased and a long period of time has elapsed before the maturation arises.
This is precisely what is meant by the term "ripening" (vipāka) as applied to the fruit.
For the treatise states: "Because it ripens apart from its cause, it is called 'maturation' (vipāka);
because its substance arises [from that], it is called 'born of maturation' (vipākaja)."
This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Master Tai states:
"That eye which is a maturation (*vipāka*) is called 'born of maturation' (*vipākaja*) because it is produced from a cause that is maturation."
Just as a carriage drawn by oxen is called an "ox-cart" because the intermediate term [drawn by] has been omitted,
so too it is simply called "born of maturation" (vipākaja).
The term "ripening cause" (*vipāka-hetu*) mentioned here is general;
the following three meanings are specific. Second, when the karma that has been performed reaches the time of attaining its fruit, it possesses the power to transform and mature.
It is called "vipāka" (maturation) because it is different from the time when it was not yet matured.
Since the fruit arises from that maturation, it is named after its cause as "vipākaja" (born of maturation). Thirdly, the fruit obtained is neutral (avyākṛta).
Because of these wholesome and unwholesome causes,
the results are of a different category from the causes;
nevertheless, they are so called because they are what has ripened therefrom.
The fruit is called *vipāka* (maturation).
Because the cause receives its name from the fruit, it is called the maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*).

Because the fruit arises from maturation, it is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*). Alternatively, because the name of the fruit is metaphorically applied to the cause, the cause is called "maturation."
Just as the name "cause" is metaphorically applied to the fruit,
the third cause is called "maturation" (vipāka) by way of the name of its fruit;
the fourth cause has the name of the fruit metaphorically applied to it.
The cause is called "ripening" (*vipāka*).

The former [designation] is named according to its derivative characteristics, while the latter is a provisional designation; thus, there is a difference between them. Now, let us examine this in detail.
They follow one another;
it is provisionally established that both are *bahuvrīhi* compounds,
and no difference is seen between them.
Furthermore, there is a difference between the general and the specific.
The general [classification] is combined at the very beginning,
or it is placed at the very end.
For what reason is correct reasoning (*yukti*) presented as the second explanation? Some interpret the first [explanation] as follows:
regarding the term "maturation" (*vipāka*), "differentiation" (*vi*) refers to the cause and "ripening" (*pāka*) refers to the fruit; or alternatively, "differentiation" refers to the fruit.
Maturation occurs either in the cause or it pervades both cause and fruit;
maturation occurs in the fruit or it occurs in the cause; or maturation pervades both cause and fruit.
Dissimilarity occurs either in the cause.
Either in the fruit or as maturation;
either in the cause or as maturation;
or both as cause and fruit, it is common to both cause and fruit as maturation.
Such a complex [exposition] does not yet constitute a definitive commentary on the meaning. The treatise states:
"From the support of food and drink up to the protection of the inner city."
"Śeṣa" means nourishment (*āpyāyana*).
According to this treatise, there are three types: first, food and drink (*āhāra*); [the other two follow].
Second, sleep; third, meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
According to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, brahmacarya is added.
This treatise does not accept [that position]; it refutes it, saying:
"This merely lacks [the specific quality], but it is not a distinct hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*), just as an outer wall serves to protect an inner city."
Retribution (vipāka) is necessarily accompanied by nurturance (aupacayika); however, there are instances of nurturance that lack retribution, such as the divine eye of Aniruddha.
In the case of Aniruddha, his physical eye had already been lost.
According to the *Nyāyānusāra*,
there are those that are nurtured and distinct from those born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
such as the divine eye and divine ear acquired through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*).
According to this principle, when one in the desire realm cultivates and attains the divine eye, ear, and so forth,
these are all exclusively of the nature of nurtured growth (*aupacayika*);
they do not possess the nature of maturation (*vipāka*) belonging to their own level.
To cause the small to grow large and to nourish the exhausted until they are fat is called "nourishment" (*puṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is explained that because they grow by means of being nourished,
they are named "nourishment."

Because it is nourished and grows, it follows the explanation given for the *pudgala* (person). Question: Regarding external insentient objects, why is it not said that they possess growth through nourishment (*puṣṭi*), as is the case with grains, wheat, and so forth?
Answer: Growth through nourishment is explained in contrast to *vipāka* (maturation).
Because there is maturation within, it is said that there is nourishment;
because there is no maturation externally, it is not said to be nourishment.
This is because the power of nourishment prevents maturation. Question: If there is maturation, it is then said to be nourishment.

Question: Since the mind and mental factors also possess maturation (*vipāka*), why is it not said that they possess nourishment (*aupacayika*)? Answer: Material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) can be described as being made fat through nourishment;
however, mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) are formless.
Regarding how they are nurtured (*aupacayika*), from the perspective of their specific characteristics, there are also nurtured sounds.
Because the treatise states that sound has *niṣyanda* (outflow) and extends up to being "subject to the will" (*vaśavarti*),
it is explained that sound belongs exclusively to two categories.
Because food and so forth nourish and sustain [the body], there is "nourishment" (aupacayika).
Because there is "outflow" (naiṣyandika) apart from nourishment, there is a distinct "outflow.
The material phenomena of maturation (vipākaja) arise once and then continue in a succession.
Sound is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*) because it arises according to desire;
it is not real because it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
and it is not momentary (*kṣaṇika*) because it arises from a cause of similar type (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Treatise:
If that were so, one would not attain the mark of the Brahma-voice.
External objection: Since one attains the Brahma-voice by abandoning coarse and evil speech, [how can it be said that it is not attained through that cause?]
How is it that sound is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*)?
The treatise states: Some say that sound belongs to the category of contact-conditions, being produced by the striking of an impact.
This is the first explanation: Although one attains the Brahma-like voice as a result of abandoning harsh speech,
that voice itself is not a karmic maturation (*vipāka*),
because it belongs to the third transmission.
The treatise states that sound arises only when it reaches [the ear];
this is the second interpretation. The treatise says:
If that were so, it would contradict correct reasoning that bodily sensation reaches [the object]. Some say:
"The Master's refutation of the first teacher is erroneous."
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"For what reason is the sound-element (*śabdadhātu*) not born of maturation (*vipākaja*)?
Because it is repeatedly interrupted and then arises again."
Matter born of maturation (*vipākaja*) does not possess such a quality;
it does not arise according to one's desire, for the fruit of maturation is not produced at will.

Sound, however, arises according to desire, and therefore it is not maturation. [Objection: Is it not as stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*: "Because he has well cultivated the avoidance of coarse and evil speech, he attains the mark of a Great Man consisting of a Brahma-like voice"? Although this is produced by karma, it is not maturation.
Because sound arises in the third transmission;
that is to say, from those karmas,
the primary elements (mahābhūta) are produced.

If sound is produced by the striking of conditions derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), then bodily sensation (*kāyikī-vedanā*)—being produced by the primary elements generated by karma—should not be considered a maturation (*vipāka*). This objection is not valid.
Not all bodily sensations are caused by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), nor are they all produced by the primary elements generated by karma;
furthermore, not all of them are maturation (*vipāka*). Nevertheless, bodily sensations can also be caused by primary elements that are not produced by karma.
Furthermore, because it arises without depending on the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
That is to say, the arising of bodily sensation requires conditions such as the body, attention, and body-consciousness;
by virtue of this, it also arises depending on external primary elements.
It is not necessary to wait for a "great birth" induced by karma;

this does not contradict reason, and thus it is categorized as a maturation (*vipāka*). If one maintains that the sound-element (*śabda-dhātu*) is produced from maturation, [it is likewise consistent].
In this way, the sound-element (śabdadhātu) would arise solely from the primary elements (mahābhūta) and solely from the maturation-born (vipākaja) primary elements;
it would not escape the faults previously mentioned. If one were to say that the sound-element is not born of maturation, [the same fault would apply].

Thus, it is not contradictory to reason that the sound-element (*śabdadhātu*) arises solely from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), whether those elements are caused by maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) or are non-maturation elements.
Furthermore, there is no fault as previously stated. Therefore, one should distinguish the sound-element in this way: it is not experienced by any bodily sensation (*kāyavijñapti*).
Regarding the claim that "only the internal primary elements (mahābhūta) are maturation (vipāka)," it is not the case that only maturation primary elements serve as causes;
furthermore, this does not entail the logical fallacy of contradicting reason as that [opposing] view does.
Therefore, the principles of the analogy are fundamentally inconsistent. Now, examining the intent of the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*:
the maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*) and others necessarily possess a support (*āśraya*) and an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) before they can arise.
Since [feeling] arises based on great elements that are not themselves maturation,
why is bodily feeling— which is maturation— not itself considered maturation? Furthermore,
if it were to arise based on maturation [great elements], it could not arise at all.
"There would then be no maturation-feelings (vipāka-vedanā) of the body at all.
Since you admit that they do exist, would it not follow that body-feelings arise based upon and conditioned by [the mind]? Thus say other masters.
Since sound is not a maturation (vipāka), how could it be produced by the great elements (mahābhūta) that are maturations?
Therefore, one must admit that sound belongs to the fourth or fifth stage of transmission.
It is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
That is to say, from the maturation primary elements produced by karma,
the nourishment (*aupacayika*) primary elements are successively generated.
Furthermore, it is said that these [great elements] further produce homogeneous great elements (*niṣyanda-mahābhūta*),
and that the nourishing great elements (*puṣṭi-mahābhūta*) produce nourishing sounds,
while the homogeneous great elements produce homogeneous sounds; this explanation is unreasonable.
Is it not just as when a wholesome or unwholesome sound is produced from neutral primary elements (*mahābhūta*),
or when that which is non-appropriated is produced from that which is appropriated,
or when that which belongs to the domain of the body produces that which belongs to the domain of the ear?
Thus, what contradiction is there in [the claim] that something may arise from great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are resultant (*vipākaja*) while being itself non-resultant?
Therefore, that [previous] explanation is certainly irrational. Regarding this correct reasoning, some who follow the *Abhidharmakośa* master offer the following refutation:
If you say that bodily sensation arises from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and thus, because it does not arise from what is not a primary element,
it is universally of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*), whereas sound arises only from the primary elements; [then this is incorrect].
If it does not pertain to maturation (*vipāka*),

then matter (*rūpa*) would also arise solely from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and thus should likewise not pertain to maturation. If you say that bodily sensation arises from primary elements that are maturational, nurtured (*aupacayika*), or of uniform outflow (*naiṣyandika*), [then the same applies to matter].

Regarding that which is common to both [the cause and the effect] and is of the nature of maturation (vipāka): you yourself must also admit that sound arises from these three [causes]; therefore, it should be common to both and of the nature of maturation.
If you say that bodily sensation arises from the great elements of maturation (*vipāka*),
it is not the case that all such sensations are exclusively maturational, for some are also associated with the wholesome or the unwholesome.
Nor do I maintain that all bodily sensations arise solely from the great elements of maturation.
All of these are maturations (*vipāka*), and they also pertain to both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Now, in this context, the refutation is based on the premise that bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*) is a maturation.

It is difficult to maintain that what arises from the primary elements produced by karma is itself [karmic]. If you argue that sound is not a maturation because it belongs to the third transmission, this third transmission does not constitute a definitive proof.
It is like the experience of bodily sensation born of maturation (*vipāka*),
because it belongs to the third transmission;
thus, sound is maturation.
It is as with the experience of pleasant and unpleasant bodily sensations;
because it belongs to the third transmission,
sound is not a result of maturation (vipāka).
I point out your error regarding indeterminacy: you claim that because bodily sensation is indeterminate, it must therefore be a maturation (*vipāka*).
Is this not merely empty talk? Thus, the word "therefore" does not belong to the third logical sequence.
The former master having refuted the latter master, the latter then re-establishes his position; yet, upon close examination, this refutation has not grasped the [former's] intended meaning.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā* (Treatise on Right Reasoning) offers a defense for the third transmission, stating:
"Is it not just as when wholesome or unwholesome sounds are produced from neutral (*avyākṛta*) primary elements (*mahābhūta*)?"
From that which is appropriated, there arises that which is non-appropriated;
from the objective field of the body, there arises the objective field of the ear.
Likewise, from the great elements of maturation, there arise those that are non-maturation.

What contradiction is there? If one were to refute this as a master of the *Abhidharmakośa*, [the position would be that] in reality, there is no fixed rule regarding the relationship between the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
This sound produced by the primary elements of maturation (*vipākaja*)— [...is not subject to such a restriction.]
Since it is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*), what is it?
If it were nurtured growth (*aupacayika*),
then logically it should consist of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) produced by that growth.
If these were outflows (*niṣyanda*), they should logically be composed of the great elements that are themselves outflows.
What reason is there for them to be composed of the great elements of maturation (*vipāka*)? Upon examining the intent of this explanation, it does not fully accord with reason.
Who says that the ripening primary elements (vipāka-mahābhūta) produce the sound of growth (aupacayika)? Furthermore, to examine the intent of the treatise:
the *Nyāyānusāra* refutes the latter master, while the *Abhidharmakośa* refutes both masters.
Since the *Nyāya* (Correct Principle) school preserves the views of the former masters, it offers its defense after those former masters;

since the *Abhidharmakośa* refutes both masters, it presents its critique later, following the second [master]. Furthermore, the critique regarding bodily sensation primarily refutes the former master while also incidentally addressing the latter.
This is because one wishes to maintain that sound is distinct from the maturation [of karma].

However, the intention of the *Nyāyānusāra* is that all great elements— whether of maturation (*vipāka*), nourishment (*aupacayika*), or outflow (*naiṣyandika*)— are capable of producing sound, and not merely those of maturation.
This refers to the production of sound through striking, not to the sense of "creation. Venerable sirs,
many take this treatise to preserve the interpretation of later masters,
who regard "striking and producing" as the sense of "creation."
In neither case can the underlying intention be maintained.
If you claim that the later master’s view is correct, why is it that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of maturation (*vipāka*) do not produce sound when they strike one another,
whereas only the great elements of outflow (*niṣyanda*) produce sound when they strike?
This contradicts the *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 127, which states:
“The critique says:
Generally speaking, this sound is produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of all bodily parts; that which is produced by the primary elements pervading the entire body [is also included].”
This refers to the primary elements (mahābhūta) at the throat and around the navel.
It does not mean that the primary elements throughout the entire body produce the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) and so forth;
rather, it means that there are further primary elements throughout the entire body that produce sound.
If sound were produced by the same great elements that produce derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*),
there would be the fault of one cause producing multiple forms of matter. As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*,
this continues until it is clearly observed [in experience].
Because these involve the tossing and moving of the entire body; according to the treatise,
since the whole body is tossed and moved.
For what reason do the *vipāka* and *aupacayika* [great elements] not vibrate?
And if they were to vibrate, why would no sound be produced by their mutual impact?
It must be that the *naiṣyandika* great elements are transmitted [to produce it].
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 90, states:
"Question: How is it that the sound-element (*śabda-dhātu*) is always possessed?
Some offer this explanation:"
The coming together and separation of the great elements necessarily produces the sphere of sound.
If sentient beings reside within the desire or form realms, sound is constantly produced because the great elements are always present. [Critique: This is said.
He should not speak thus:
if the four great elements necessarily always produce sound,
by which great elements is this produced sound constituted?
If it were produced from these very same [elements],
then many resistant forms would arise from a single set of the four great elements. If, on the other hand,
you say it is produced from others...
Furthermore, the remaining four great elements would necessarily produce sound as well;
in this way, there would be the fault of an infinite regress.
One should state it thus:
Within the bodies of sentient beings born in the desire and form realms,
many of the four great elements exist within a single body;
when they strike against one another, sound is produced.
When there is no mutual striking, sound does not arise.
Although the sound-element (śabda-dhātu) necessarily exists within a single body, it is not the case that all parts of the body simultaneously emit sound.
[End of] the treatise. Based on this, for what reason would there be no maturation (vipāka) or nourishment (puṣṭi) when there is no mutual striking?
It must necessarily involve the transmission of the great elements (mahābhūta) that are of the nature of outflow (niṣyanda).
Furthermore, this proves that the view that sound is produced by the striking of conditions does not constitute the meaning of "creation" (kṛtaka).
Therefore, it is known that the position of the second master contradicts the correct doctrine of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Because this is refuted by the *Nyāyānusāra* and not established [therein],
the position of the first master does not contradict the *Mahāvibhāṣā*; however,
since the intention of the author of the treatise (*śāstrakāra*) does not accept it, both masters are equally refuted.
Because it is admitted that sound is born of maturation (*vipākaja*), and because most masters say that sound belongs to the third transmission— namely,
that it is produced by the great elements (*mahābhūta*) which are themselves born of maturation, nurtured (*aupacayika*), or of uniform outflow (*naiṣyandika*)— this too is unreasonable.
If the "producing agent" is designated as the third factor,
then the production of other resultant forms and so forth is likewise from the primary elements born of karma.
The great elements (mahābhūta) that produce derived matter (upādāyarūpa) and so forth are also the third [category],
and thus they should not be considered maturation (vipāka). Furthermore, if the great elements were maturation, [the following would occur].
Regarding that which produces sound:
these great elements (mahābhūta) that produce sound,
if they were to exist as a continuum within the body like other types of resultant matter (vipākaja-rūpa), [would lead to the following consequence].

If it were the case that sound is absent while the primary elements (mahābhūta) exist, this would contradict the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 132, which asks: "If one possesses present primary elements, does one also possess the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) of the present?"
Answer: It is so. If one is endowed with the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) created in the present, is one also endowed with the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the present? Answer: It is so.
This is because there are no present primary elements that lack a fruit. [End of treatise]. If sound were non-existent, yet the primary elements existed...
This means that the primary elements (mahābhūta) would have no fruit.

If these ripening (vipāka) primary elements were to exist or not exist according to the presence or absence of sound, then they would be subject to interruption like sound and thus could not be ripening. Some cite the *Nyāyānusāra*, Chapter Twenty.
To claim that one can possess derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) without possessing the primary elements (mahābhūta), or possess the primary elements without possessing derived matter—
and thus to assert that there is a class of beings in whom the four great primary elements of maturation (vipāka-mahābhūta) exist within the body but do not produce derived matter— is erroneous.
This translation establishes that there are no great elements (mahābhūta) which are the maturation of sound within the body,
and thus there is no sound that is derived from them.
That text cites the formulation regarding the great elements that produce unmanifest form (avijñaptirūpa).

Because such types of primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are not cited in the enumeration of categories. Question: If one accomplishes the primary elements that produce unmanifest karma (*avijñapti-karma*), yet does not accomplish the unmanifest matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), [how is this so]?
Is it not the case that there is no fruit for the great elements (*mahābhūta*) in the present?
Answer: This is stated with reference to derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) that is non-resistant (*apratigha*), not with reference to derived matter that is resistant (*sapratigha*).
If it were not so, it would contradict the fact that present primary elements (mahābhūta) necessarily have effects,
and derived matter (upādāyarūpa) necessarily has causes.
The four great elements (mahābhūta) must necessarily have results.

Regarding those belonging to the same world (*sabhāga-dhātu*), this is stated based on the discussion of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) with resistance (*sapratigha*). According to the reasoning established above, all sounds are produced by great elements that do not result from karmic maturation (*avipāka-mahābhūta*); they are derived matter produced by great elements of nourishment (*puṣṭi-mahābhūta*) and outflow (*niṣyanda*).
Because the precepts co-existent with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahabhū-śīla*) are produced by the great elements nurtured by concentration,

sounds produced by the nurtured great elements are nurtured sounds; because [they] are produced by the great elements of natural outflow (*niṣyanda*), sounds produced by the great elements of natural outflow are outflowing sounds.
There is no scriptural evidence that the two [elements] create one another;
all sounds produced by karma are outflows (*niṣyanda*),
because these outflowing great elements are not created by anything else.
Treatise:

From the eight unimpeded [factors] up to those that are not nurtured—this explains that the eight possess outflowing and retributive natures. This can be understood according to the text. That which recompenses prior causes is the nature of retribution (*vipāka*).
The others are results of outflow (*niṣyanda*). Since all unimpeded phenomena lack accumulation, they are not those that are nurtured (*aupacayika*).
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra* asks:
"Is it not the case that there is also nurturing within these?"
This means that the power of prior causes draws forth the arising of subsequent effects,
and it also causes their functional capacity to become increasingly intense.
Thus, the Sūtra also speaks of faith in formless phenomena.
"It increases and expands;
it should be nurtured. Although these words exist, it is not "nurtured";
rather, it is said that the outflow increases and expands.
If the power of a preceding cause draws forth the arising of a subsequent effect,
causing its functional capacity to become increasingly intense and flourishing,
this too is explained as being based on the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*).
Because they are produced by homogeneous and pervasive causes,
all obstructive phenomena are composed of atoms.
Simultaneous accumulation may be termed "nourishment" (*puṣṭi*),
because unobstructed phenomena (*apratigha-dharma*) are not composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*);
since they lack the sense of accumulation, they are not called nourishment.

The commentary states: "The remainder" refers to the other four elements—form, odor, taste, and tangibility—which possess the nature of being outflowing results (*niṣyanda*). This explains the four elements of form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
Regarding those sentient beings belonging to the category of form (*rūpa*), there are those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and those that are nurtured (*aupacayika*).
Those produced by karma of the three natures (*trividha-karma*) possess exclusively the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*).
Regarding the three—odors, tastes, and tangibles—that belong to sentient beings:
those that are resultant (*vipāka*) or nurtured (*aupacayika*) are indeterminate;
those associated with neutral karma are of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*).
All five external objects are exclusively outflows (*niṣyanda*). Regarding the treatise’s statement that "in reality,
only dharmas" exist, this refers to the fact that only [dharmas] are designated as having substantial existence (*dravya-sat*).
This can be understood according to the text. The treatise states:
"The mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness... up to what is called the dharma-dhātu."
This explanation refers only to the final three [moments]. This statement that they are ultimate and not outflowing (niṣyanda) means that,
among the remaining untainted states,
there is no homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) prior to the manifestation of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti).
When the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) is present, there is a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu), namely,
only that very patience regarding the dharma of suffering;
at all other times, it has no homogeneous cause.
Therefore, it is called "ultimate" and "not a result of outflow" (*niṣyanda*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"That is to say, the first untainted category of the Dharma-knowledge-patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) is called 'one moment' because it is not a result of outflow."
This explains that while these are currently active, they are also not outflows (*niṣyanda*);
for among all other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), there are none that are not outflows,
with the sole exception of the first moment of the five untainted aggregates (*anāsravaskandha*).
It arises without a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*);
other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) do not possess such a quality,
because the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is predominant.
Although the preceding causes were lacking, this [attainment] arises;
for the power of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is strong,
as it is of the same category as the initial factors of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
Because it is nurtured by immeasurable wholesome dharmas,
and because its nature is equal to that of the initial noble path;
for this reason.

Because of the extensive cultivation of various preparatory applications (*prayoga*). Question: Regarding that which arises from a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and is termed "outflow" (*niṣyanda*):
how can a person of sharp faculties who is an *ārya* [possess] dull untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*)?
Ultimately, there is no similar cause (sabhāga-hetu).
Among the five categories [of causes], to which category does it belong?
If one were to claim that for outflowing results (niṣyanda-phala) there is no similar cause:

If it is argued that the first moment of untainted [wisdom] is not included, would this not mean that the five categories of encompassed phenomena are not exhaustive? Answer: The five categories of encompassed phenomena are indeed exhaustive. How is this known?
Therefore, this treatise states:
"The category of the first untainted *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* is termed 'momentary' (*kṣaṇika*) because it is not a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*)."
This statement that "the ultimate [unconditioned] is not a result of outflow" implies that there are no other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) that are not results of outflow;
thus it should be understood.
With the exception of the first untainted [dharma], all other conditioned phenomena are comprised within outflows (niṣyanda).
Since the sharp-facultied noble one’s dull untainted path is also comprised within other conditioned phenomena, [it is likewise an outflow].
It is clearly understood that these are results of similar cause (*niṣyanda*). What is meant by "moment" (*kṣaṇa*)?
The answer is: only a single momentary phenomenon as it arises in the present is called a "moment."
All others are not [of this nature] because they are indeterminate.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"This explains that even those currently manifesting are not outflowing (*naiṣyandika*)."

There are no other conditioned phenomena that are not *niṣyanda* (outflow). Question: For a person of sharp faculties, even when practicing the dull untainted path (*anāsravamārga*), this is also ultimately without a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
How, then, can it be said to be of the nature of an outflow?

Answer: Because it is possible for them all to arise before the faculties have been refined, and because there exists the cause [for such arising], they are not momentary phenomena (*kṣaṇika-dharma*). Question: Within the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), is it not the case that some possess only the nature of sharp faculties?
Answer: It is the natural law that all sentient beings possess six types of dispositions within their bodies;
encountering different conditions, these develop into either sharp or dull natures.
Before encountering conditions, whether one is sharp or dull is indeterminate;
it is not due to the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
What principle contradicts this?
Treatise:
Having thus explained the [minds] born of maturation and so forth,
the second half of the verse follows.
Fifteenth: Clarifying the Door of Accomplishment (*siddhi*). Now, we shall briefly describe the distinction between the two names "attainment" (*prāpti*) and "accomplishment.
According to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 162: [text follows]
Acquisition occurs only at the beginning;
possession applies to both the beginning and the end. According to the intent of this treatise, one does not previously possess it.
Furthermore, when one has already abandoned [a dharma] and subsequently acquires it again, the acquisition of this dharma at its initial moment is termed "attainment" (prāpti) in two senses:
it is called both "acquisition" and "possession" (samanvāgama).
The subsequent thought attains only the accomplishment of the name;
it is not called "attainment. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Treatise on the Treasury of Abhidharma), Chapter Twelve, states:
"Is it not the case that at the time of becoming a Buddha, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is likewise not called 'attainment'?"
How much more so for the meditative attainment of cessation;
for when Bodhisattvas abide in the vajra-like samādhi, they are said to have attained the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).

Because the attainment [of a dharma] is defined as the moment it arises; the general meaning of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*’s discussion on the acquisition (*prāpti*) and relinquishment (*tyāga*) of dharmas is likewise the same.
According to the intent of this treatise, [the dharma] was previously not possessed (*aprāpta*).
Furthermore, having already abandoned [them],
one subsequently attains this dharma;
it makes no distinction as to whether the dharma attained has arisen or not yet arisen.
However, the "attainment" (prāpti) that first occurs is designated as "attainment" when it reaches the stage of the characteristic of arising (utpādākṣaṇa);
if it reaches the present, it is then designated as "possession" (samanvāgama).
Therefore, it is known that the first moment of attainment possesses two names:
it is called "attainment" (prāpti) and also called "accomplishment" (samanvāgama).
The acquisition of the subsequent moment is designated as "attainment" (*pratilambha*) alone;
whereas the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* maintains that the acquisition of the first moment has two names,
while the acquisition of subsequent moments has only one.
Therefore, it is said that "attainment" (prāpti) exists only at the beginning; this establishes that it applies to both the initial and subsequent stages.
Since the *Nyāyānusāra* explains the timing of attainment, it states that attainment exists only until the moment of the birth-characteristic (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).
In this treatise, within the section explaining the gate of attainment (*prāpti*),
the statement "that which was previously unaccomplished is now attained" refers to attainment at the first moment (*prathama-kṣaṇa*).
At the moment when the characteristic of arising occurs, it is called "acquisition" (prāpti);
upon reaching the present, it is called "possession" (samanvāgama).
This is because the two meanings are combined in the explanation.
Regarding the statement "now it has been accomplished": the masters of old say that "accomplishment" (cheng) applies to both the new and the old [traditions],
whereas "attainment" (de) refers specifically to the new treatise.
It does not establish a distinction between the new and the old. Regarding the abandonment [of the attainment], according to the *Abhidharmasamayapradīpikā*,
this is the same as the *Mahāvibhāṣā* in that the attainment exists only at the beginning.

Regarding the attainment and non-attainment of the initial and subsequent [moments]: if one says that the moment of relinquishing is called "non-attainment" and the moment of acquiring is called "attainment," it would be sufficient to change a single character;
there is no loss in the remaining meaning.
It should be said that when the substance is relinquished, it is termed "non-attainment," whereas when the substance is acquired, it is termed "attainment";
for although the times differ, their substance is one and the same.
If one speaks in terms of application,
the time of attainment is not the time of accomplishment;
the time of accomplishment is not the time of attainment.
Because the time of arising and the time of being present are different. Some say:
What is the distinction between "attainment" (*prāpti*) and "possession" (*samanvāgama*)?
What is the distinction between "abandonment" (*tyāga*) and "non-possession" (*asamanvāgama*)?
The commentary explains:
If a dharma first reaches the phase of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) by its very nature, it is then called "attained" (*prāpta*);
if it flows on until it reaches the present, it is then called "accomplished" (*siddha*).
At the time of acquisition, it is not called "attainment" (samanvāgama);
at the time of attainment, it is not called "acquisition.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 12, states:
Is it not the case that even up to this point,
the arising of the entity itself is called "attainment" (prāpti)?
Therefore, since the *Nyāyānusāra* states that the arising of the entity itself is termed "attainment," [this must be so].

Therefore, it is known that when a dharma reaches the moment of arising, it is called "attainment" (*prāpti*); it is only when it flows into the present that it is termed "possession" (*samanvāgama*). If one follows this interpretation, it does not capture the intent of the treatise.
For the treatise itself states: "The essence of attainment is designated as 'attainment' at the very moment of its arising."
For what reason do you falsely claim that a dharma reaches the moment of arising?

If you maintain that a dharma is only called "attained" when it reaches the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), then [you must explain] how conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is attained at the conclusion of the three types of subsequent knowledge (*trividha-anvaya-jñāna*).
How could this dharma be the characteristic of arising?
At the time of abiding in the World-First Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*),
one does not abandon but rather acquires the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
It does not arise from cessation.
At that time, are all the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) obtained said to be capable of arising?
Are all things that do not arise not called "attained"?
Why is it that only when a dharma reaches the moment of its arising is it termed "attained"? Furthermore, regarding the time of attainment:
Although in reality one does not obtain what is called "attainment," by taking the conventional designation, it may also be called "attainment.
This treatise, within the context of the gate of attainment, [explains this].
It is said that there are cases where the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is first not accomplished and is now accomplished,
while the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is not. This refers, for example, to one born in the desire realm who gradually acquires the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*).
Therefore, it is known that at the very moment of acquisition, taking up its corresponding designation may also be called "accomplishing the eye.
The cases of relinquishment and non-accomplishment are to be explained by analogy with the above.
All that has been analyzed above pertains to specific meanings. As for the general designation, there are two categories.
If explained according to their essential nature, all acquisitions (prāpti) may also be termed "attainment" (samanvāgama).
All accomplishments are also termed "attainment.
If discussed in terms of time,
the moment of accomplishment is likewise termed "attainment."
At the time of acquisition, it is not termed "attainment" (siddhi),
because that which was previously flowing continues into the present.
If the acquisition occurs precisely at the moment of the characteristic of arising (jāti-lakṣaṇa).
It is merely called "attainment" and not "accomplishment," because one cannot accomplish the noble dharmas while abiding in the stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Furthermore, if that were the case:
This would entail the error that at one and the same time there could be both the noble (ārya) and the ordinary (pṛthagjana).

You should consider this further. Question: According to the subsequent text, the two types of supernormal power (abhijñā) involving transformation (nirmāṇa) can be acquired across the three periods of time.
For what reason, in this context,
when one is born into the three higher dhyānas,
visual consciousness does not manifest and is thus not possessed?
The answer is that Master Tai, citing the commentary of the Tripiṭaka Master, states:
"The two types of supernormal powers (abhijñā) are bound to the first dhyāna;
relying on the stage of the first dhyāna, one brings forth supernormal powers belonging to that same stage."
The three time periods are accomplished.
For example, when one is well-practiced in the postures (*īryāpatha*) and crafts (*śilpa*) of one's own stage, there is attainment across the three time periods.
As the text below states, two [types of supernormal powers] are attained across the three time periods.
According to the explanation based on the first dhyāna,
because one born in a higher stage gives rise to two supernormal powers (abhijñā) belonging to a lower stage by means of the body,
there is only simultaneous acquisition (dharmasahaja-prāpti).

As explained in the *Pariśuddha-vijñāna-śāstra* (汎借識說): Question: When one born in the three higher dhyānas gives rise to the two supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the eye and ear belonging to a lower level, what kind of neutral (*avyākṛta*) state is this? Answer:
It is stated that this was composed by Dharmatrāta, the master of the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear are neutral (*avyākṛta*) in terms of deportment (*airyāpathika*).
Artisanal skills (*śailpasthānika*) belong exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and do not extend to the higher realms.
Retribution does not arise in a different stage;
transformation is produced solely by the mental consciousness, as it is certainly not produced by the other three.
It is clearly known that both [the *ābhāsvara* and *śubhakṛtsna* heavens] are certainly states of deportment (*īryāpatha*). Someone refutes this, saying:
"This interpretation is incorrect, for it contradicts both reason and scripture."
As the treatise states:
"The deportment mind of the form realm arises from five minds among the twenty minds."
To say that it refers to the five [minds] of one's own realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*), does not constitute proof;
for among the twenty minds, it is stated that the deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and supernormal fruition minds are exclusively mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) also pertain to both the four consciousnesses and the five consciousnesses.
However, the arising of manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) does not pertain to the preparatory stage of non-manifest form (*avijñapti*),
because that [non-manifest form] is not the direct object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the minds of deportment and craftsmanship.
As it is said that the seven paths of action have matter (*rūpa*) as their essential nature,
these seven preparatory stages (*prayoga*) also pertain to the non-material (*arūpa*).
This clarifies the seven paths of action without distinguishing them from the non-material.
This case is also like that.
Although these four consciousnesses are preparatory applications (*prayoga*),
when discerning the arising of characteristics, one does not take the preparatory application as the basis.
However, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā* states that the four consciousnesses and the five consciousnesses possess "postures" (*īryāpatha*) and "crafts" (*śailpasthānika*).
This is because they are designated as "postures" and "crafts" with respect to the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of postures and crafts.

Just as the preparatory effort for killing is also termed "killing," so too the mind of the immediate result (*tad-anantarya-citta*) is exclusively mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and does not extend to the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).
As this treatise extensively explains regarding the mind:
The unobscured-neutral states of the desire realm are divided into four types of consciousness;
these include, up to, the three unobscured-neutral states such as the deportment-mind (*airyāpathika*),
which take visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects as their objective referents (*ālambana*).
The arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*) and so forth also take sound as their object.
These three types of mind are exclusively mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Since it is stated that they are exclusively mental consciousness:
Thus, we know that [the *manovijñāna*] definitely excludes the five sensory consciousnesses.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* is likewise; one should examine it.
Since it states that the consciousness of the arts (*śailpasthānika*) also takes sound as its object.
Therefore, one should know that deportment does not take sound as its object.
This refers to the application of the paths of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the paths of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).
It also extends to the four consciousnesses and the five consciousnesses;
thus, one should know that the four consciousnesses constitute the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for deportment (*airyāpathika*).
The five consciousnesses are exclusively the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of craftsmanship;
the four [mental] consciousnesses and the five consciousnesses do not pertain to the fundamental state (*maula*). Other masters say:

There is the mental consciousness induced by the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), which takes all twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) as its objects;
according to this teacher, this [consciousness] is also exclusively mental consciousness.

Therefore, it is known that when it is said that the mental factors (caitta) of the mind of deportment (īryāpathika-citta) arise extensively, this refers to the mental factors of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) belonging to the mind of deportment.
According to the masters of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, both [types of mind] are considered minds of deportment (*airyāpathika*);
because they belong to the category of preparatory application (*prayoga*), they are also termed "deportment."
Since the mental consciousness arises with the characteristics of formal deportment,
how could it possibly be related to the preparatory stages of the five sensory consciousnesses,
which are of a different class?
However, within the broad category of the mind, the minds of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), deportment (*airyāpathika*),

and preparatory application (*prāyogika*) pertain to both the four consciousnesses and the five consciousnesses; whereas the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala*) is necessarily restricted to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) alone.
There is no other alternative.
For what reason do you cite this to refute the position of the *Miśrakābhidharmahṛdaya* master?
If you truly intend to refute it, you ought to seek out a different principle.
Regarding the statement that this contradicts the principle:
since the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* takes the four consciousnesses as the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for deportment (*īryāpatha*),
it may indeed be said that they constitute deportment.
Auditory consciousness is not a preparatory effort for deportment;
how then can the supernormal power of the divine ear be considered deportment?
For it is not a preparatory effort for deportment.
Furthermore, since even the mental consciousness associated with deportment (*airyāpathika*) does not take sound as its object,
how could the auditory consciousness be a preparatory application (*prayoga*)?
If it is argued that the mind resembling the mind of deportment can universally take the objects of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) as its domain, this is also not the case.
Since the treatise states that [this] occurs only on the level of the mental consciousness (*manobhūmi*), based on these principles,
the position established in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* is not correct.
One should say that the four types of indeterminate minds do not fully encompass all states of mind;
categories such as borrowed consciousnesses are not included within these four.
Furthermore, auditory consciousness is not part of the deportment.

In the higher stages there are no arts and crafts, because transformations involve only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Regarding the second line of the verse, "obtained alone" refers to the first two partial phrases;
