for it is not tenable that they occupy the same location while remaining without interstices.
Since you have already admitted that there is no interval [between atoms], why do they not touch one another?
Therefore, the term *nirantara* (without interval) certainly indicates the sense of "immediate proximity.
In this context, the syllable *ni-* may also indicate the sense of "definitive" (*niyata*).
Because there is certainly an interval, it is called "certainly having an interval" (*niyata-antara*).
This is like saying "certainly hot" because there is certainly heat;
this refers to the fact that there is certainly an interval.
The meaning is established by reasoning,
or it reveals the absence of meaning;
that is to say, there is not even a particle as small as an atom of the color of tangibility within this [space].
Because they are separated [by space], they are called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*).
When such uninterrupted great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise in close proximity as atoms (*paramāṇu*), this is metaphorically designated as "contact."
If one provides this explanation,
then what the Venerable One said— that all atoms do not actually touch one another,
but the term "contact" is merely applied metaphorically because they are contiguous— is established.
This has profound significance:
it is precisely because of the power of obstructive resistance (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*) that something is admitted to be "resistant" (*sapratigha*) when it can obstruct the movement of others;
it is not because one admits that they occupy the same location while mutually accommodating one another.
And it may be described as having "obstructive resistance" (āvaraṇa-pratighāta).
How could one, fearing that the same location would prevent immediate abiding,
allow for the existence of intervals while denying the movement [of atoms] toward them?
It is not that there is something to be feared; such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Those things that possess resistance (*sapratigha*) must necessarily occupy different locations.
Otherwise, they would occupy the same location and thus become composite parts; therefore, the principle of their abiding without interval is certainly untenable.
Although there may be slight gaps within it,
the power of resistance obstructs its movement.
What are these gaps?
Other masters say that this is a form (rūpa) that is intangible;
yet others say that there is nothing at all, neither form nor tangibility.
This is the matter of the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu*).
According to the treatise, furthermore, from the point of being separated from atoms (*paramāṇu*), this case should also be understood in the same way.
The refutation of the second teacher is consistent with the *Nyāya*.
Treatise.
Furthermore, there is no such fault even if one grants that atoms possess extension;
this refutes the first teacher.
The *Nyāya* [proponent] offers this defense:
The Master of the Sūtras further states: "Moreover, it is admitted that if atoms possessed spatial dimensions, they would necessarily have parts, whether they were in contact or not.
If, however, they lack spatial dimensions, there would be no fault even if one were to admit that they touch."
This argument is irrational.
"Partless" (niravayava) and "without spatial parts" (digbhāga-rahita) differ in name but are identical in meaning;
by establishing the term "partless," spatial parts have already been excluded.
How can one further give rise to doubt regarding this?
That is to say, if it is admitted that atoms possess spatial dimensions,
then since they lack such dimensions, how could they be subject to contact?
Furthermore, there is the fault in both cases: whether the entire bodies touch each other, or only a portion touches.
This has already been discussed in detail above.
How can you then say that even if spatial parts did not exist, there would be no such fault even if contact were admitted?
Therefore, as for what was said:
Because there is not even an infinitesimal amount of space or matter intervening,
it is called "uninterrupted" (*nirantara*).
Such uninterrupted great elements (*mahābhūta*) are [thus] atoms (*paramāṇu*).
The conventional designation "contact" is applied when [atoms] arise in proximity;
thus its meaning is established. If a master of the *Abhidharmakośa* were to offer this defense, one should counter-interrogate him by saying:
"You assert that atoms have no spatial parts (*digbhāga*)."
Why do atoms not touch one another? If you say that to claim they do touch results in a logical fallacy,
then to say they do not touch likewise does not avoid the fallacy,
because they face six directions with different orientations.
If it is said that atoms each possess a functional power such that they mutually obstruct one another and do not touch,
does this functional power exist apart from their substance?
If it were separate from the substance, it would be identical to the category of "action" (*karma-pada-artha*) in the Vaiśeṣika system.
If it were not separate from the substance,
since there is no function external to the substance, why do they not touch one another?
Therefore, this also results in a logical fallacy.
Furthermore, do the sense organs, such as the eye, reach objects that are of unequal size?
From here below, the third half-verse clarifies whether the six sense faculties possess equal or unequal access to their respective objects.
The treatise states: "Because they reach the nose-consciousness and so forth. Within this passage, there are three parts:
first, it clarifies whether the various faculties apprehend their objects equally or not.
Second, it clarifies that the atoms of the various sense faculties (*indriya-paramāṇu*) are arranged differently.
Third, it clarifies the "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and "non-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) states.

This passage specifically clarifies how the faculties grasp their objects; this section first clarifies that three faculties grasp objects of equal magnitude. Regarding the term "equal magnitude": [it refers to the following].
Just as the sense organ is subtle in measure, so too is its object;
when they meet in mutual correspondence, the olfactory and other consciousnesses arise.
As for the word "etc. (ādi) in this context:
The object and the sense faculty are said to be "equal" when their dimensions neither decrease nor increase;
it does not mean they must be equal in size to a fingernail.
Whether one takes them to be small or large, they are all termed "equal."
This is because these three consciousnesses are based upon and conditioned by [their respective objects]. The treatise states:
"The eye and ear are not restricted [to a specific size], reaching from small to large quantities. This distinguishes how the eye and ear apprehend objects that are neither fixed as large nor small.
This also explains that the sense organ which serves as the basis and its object are not equal in size;
it is not necessary for them to be exactly like a grape.

For example, when the eye perceives an object the size of a grape while being only half the size of a grape itself, this is still called "perceiving the large. As for the phrase "the sound of a swarm of mosquitoes," etc.:
This is a judgment according to their essential natures. Regarding the treatise:
it explains that the mental object (*ālambana*) is free from material obstruction (*sapratigha*), thereby clarifying the distinctions in the dimensions and forms of the mental sphere.
Although the objects apprehended may be large or small,
the apprehending consciousness has no such distinction of size.
Treatise.
What are the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the sense organs such as the eye?
Below, the treatise clarifies the distinctions in the arrangement of these atoms of the sense organs.
"How is it that the eyes and so forth have remained undispersed until now?
This explains the subtle arrangement of the eyes.
There are two interpretations in the treatise.
This is the first explanation. The treatise states:
"Some say they are stacked one upon another until they do not obstruct each other"—this is the second explanation.
Treatise:
The atoms of the auditory faculty extend as far as a pair of fingernails.
This explains the specific arrangement of the two faculties of the ear and nose.
Treatise:
These first three faculties reach as far as a crown or a floral garland;
this explains the locations and dimensions of these three faculties.
Treatise:
The atoms of the tongue-faculty extend as far as the atoms [of the object] they pervade.
This clarifies the measurement of the atoms of the tongue-faculty. Commentary: It is said that...
Regarding the two explanations of the nose and tongue faculties, the latter is superior.
If they were to spread out slightly and be clear and transparent, it would prevent them from being dispersed;
by this principle, the nose and tongue should also be understood in this way.
If one follows this master’s interpretation,
the three faculties would necessarily not perceive external odors, tastes, and so forth,
because they are obstructed by the clear and pure [medium].
If external odors and so forth were not apprehended by the sense faculties,
and if the non-appropriated odors and so forth were always of the same class as those [appropriated ones],
then it would be impossible to say that they are cognized by two types of consciousness.
Furthermore, there would be no sense of the five consciousnesses being bound by afflictions, which contradicts numerous principles and scriptures;
thus, the latter explanation should be accepted as superior. It is traditionally said that within the tongue, an area the size of a hair-tip is not pervaded by the atoms of the gustatory faculty.
This matter is difficult to know;
it should be understood as being vertical, with a measure like the tip of a hair, and not horizontal.
Because the Master of the Treatise did not fully believe this, he says it is "traditionally reported."
Treatise:
The atoms of the body faculty reach a shape like that of a finger-joint;
this may be understood according to the text.
Treatise:
Because the atoms of the eye-faculty are ultimately imperceptible, this [passage] distinguishes between the "functioning" (sabhāga) and the "non-functioning" (tatsabhāga). Thus it is said.
Because the atoms of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) are so subtle as to be invisible;
this explains that not all [atoms] of the body-faculty can be of the same class (*sabhāga*).
Because they are dispersed;
just as the eye of a wheel-turning monarch can see what is minute but cannot see the ultimate atom (paramāṇu),
whereas others cannot do so.
From the size of a copper atom upward, they appear according to their respective capacities;
as it is with the eye faculty,
so it is with the body faculty.
Since the body-faculty (kāyendriya) pervades the entire body,
if it were to pervade its respective homogeneous class (sabhāga),
then the contact with objects upon which it is accumulated would also have to pervade the entire body.
If that were so, the body would disintegrate;

yet by the power of karma, it does not fail to pervade the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*). The Sautrāntika school asserts that this is not the case, which is why the Master [Vasubandhu] characterizes it as "according to tradition" (*kila*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"Furthermore, according to the tenets of the Venerable Elder’s school (*Sthavira*), it is accepted that when the entire body is submerged in cold or warm water, the atoms of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya-paramāṇu*) throughout [the body] are capable of producing consciousness. ... [and so on] ... until it says: 'The Abhidharmikas state...'"

It stands to reason that the atoms of the body-faculty (kāyendriya-paramāṇu) must necessarily lack all homogeneity (sabhāgatā); as it says: "That is to say, by the power of karma, the atoms of the body-faculty within that body do not universally produce consciousness."
One should not assume that the entire body of consciousness perishes and disintegrates all at once, as occurs in the Reviving (Saṃjīva) and other hells;
rather, the parts of the body perish only where consciousness arises,
and do not perish in their entirety.

If it were entirely destroyed, one would have to undergo death and rebirth repeatedly. Question: Why is it that, despite the pervasive arising of consciousness, life is not severed by the power of karma?
Answer: It is like the case of recollecting Avalokiteśvara; by the power of the Sage, the blade does not penetrate the body or the head.
It is not possible that, by the power of a noble one (*ārya*), one should not meet their end despite being separated from body and head;
for there is no dharma that does not meet its end when body and head are separated.
This case is likewise.
Because the Dharma has no body and does not perish through dispersion.
Treatise:
As previously stated, up to "if it were not so, how would it be?"
From here below, the fourth half-verse clarifies whether the six consciousnesses have simultaneous or non-simultaneous supports. Within the prose commentary, there are two parts:
first, the analysis of whether the support is simultaneous or non-simultaneous.
Second, the classification by number of phrases.
The treatise states: "Up to the nature of the basis for penetration.
This clarifies whether the bases are simultaneous or not simultaneous.
Mental consciousness relies solely upon the immediately preceding ceased mind.
The five sensory consciousnesses rely both upon their simultaneous sense organs and upon the immediately preceding ceased mind.
This immediately preceding ceased mind is the past support.
Simultaneously, the material sense faculties (rūpīndriya) are the concurrent bases (sahabhū-āśraya), while the mind that has just ceased in succession is the universal basis (sarvatraga-āśraya).

The simultaneous dependence on the faculties constitutes the specific basis (pratiniyata-āśraya). The Sautrāntika masters maintain that the five consciousnesses also take past objects as their conditions.
As it is stated in the eighth chapter of the *Nyāyānusāra*,
this is said because it pertains to the classification of the number of categories up to the mental factor elements (*caitasika-dhātu*).
The nature of the supports for the five consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, is twofold.
At the same time, it relies upon the sense faculty;
it is of the nature of a faculty,
not of the nature of an equal-and-immediate condition.
The sequential cessation of the mind constitutes the nature of immediate succession (*samanantara-tā*) and also the nature of a faculty (*indriya-tā*).
The sequential cessation of mental factors constitutes the nature of immediate succession (*samanantarata*),
not the nature of a faculty (*indriyata*).
The nature of the sense faculties (*indriya*) is broad, extending to matter (*rūpa*),
yet it is narrow, not reaching mental factors (*caitta*).
The nature of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is broad, extending to both mind and mental factors.
The narrow [space] does not allow for color.
Because the width on the left and right differs, four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) are formed.
All four propositions below should be explained according to this principle.
The nature of being the support for mental consciousness belongs exclusively to the mind-king (citta-rāja),
whereas the nature of being the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya) extends to its mental factors (caitta).
If one were first to inquire about the nature of the equal-and-immediate condition based on the nature of the support for mental consciousness...
This is an answer that proceeds from the narrow to the broad, following the order of the preceding phrase.
If one were instead to ask about the nature of the basis by means of the nature of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
this would be an answer that proceeds from the broad to the narrow, following the order of the subsequent phrase.
The remaining text is easily understood.

From this point onward, all partial phrases should be interpreted according to this principle. Question: Is not the final mind of an Arhat the support for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), yet not its equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?

Why, then, is it said that this is the nature of the support for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and is certainly the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the mental consciousness? Answer:
Here, the discussion is framed by taking its status as the active support (*āśrayatva*) as the basis for the question and answer.

Therefore, it is not by citing the characteristic of the support (*āśraya-lakṣaṇa*) that [the mental faculty] is established. The final mind of an Arhat possesses only the characteristic of being a support and is thus termed the "mental element" (*manodhātu*); there is no subsequent consciousness that does not act as its support.
This belongs to the category of the "neither-nor" statement. Furthermore, another interpretation is that this is a question regarding the support by citing the result.
Therefore, the final consciousness of an Arhat is not mentioned. The treatise asks:
for what reason does consciousness arise as residing in the sense faculties rather than in the objects?
The second half of the verse explains that it resides in the faculties and not in the objects.
The *Śāstra* says: "Up to 'the eye and so forth,' and not others," which can be understood according to the text.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"If that is so, then the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) would also follow the body in its movement."
That is to say, when the body is afflicted by disorders such as wind-disease (*vāta*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) becomes disturbed;
when the body is clear and at ease, the mental consciousness is tranquil.
For what reason, then, does that mental consciousness not take the body as its support?
There is no such fault because [the consciousness] follows its own basis;
that is to say, when the body is afflicted by disorders such as wind-disorder (vāta),
a body-consciousness associated with painful sensation arises.
Thus, this body-consciousness is called the distracted mental element (*mano-dhātu*).
When it passes away together with a painful sensation,
it can serve as the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) to give rise to a distracted mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).
In contrast to this, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is tranquil;
therefore, the mental consciousness follows its own basis (*āśraya*).
Is it not the case that there are such differences as the arising of an uncontaminated consciousness (*anāsravavijñāna*) immediately after a contaminated mental element (*manodhātu*)?
How is it that the mental consciousness follows its own basis?
It does not mean "following its own basis" in the sense of being categorized as either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*);
rather, it refers to the distinctions of increase or decrease, and clarity or dullness.
Just as from an unobscured-neutral eye-faculty there arise wholesome, unwholesome, or obscured eye-consciousnesses,
yet the eye-consciousness is named after its own support.
This case should also be understood in the same way.
Therefore, that which depends [upon another] does not necessarily follow the nature of all things upon which it depends.
If it were otherwise, [the following would occur].
It should not be the case that the supported [consciousness] follows its support.
Treatise:
For what reason do [the consciousnesses] range from the consciousness of form up to the consciousness of phenomena?
From here below, half a verse explains the sixth point: that the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, receive their names according to their respective faculties.
The treatise says: "That" refers to what was previously stated regarding the names of the eye and so forth being based [on the faculties].
This explains the word "that" (*tat*) in the verse.
This refers to that statement.
That previous verse explained how the eye and so forth receive their names.
[End of] Treatise.
Because the sense faculties are the basis, consciousness is designated according to the faculty;
that is to say, the faculties are the basis,
whereas visible forms and so forth are not.
The meaning is as previously explained: because the eye and other faculties serve as the bases,
consciousnesses are designated according to those faculties— such as "eye-consciousness" and so forth—
and are not called "form-consciousness" and so forth.
The treatise,
from "and those that are unique" up to "and malt," explains the meaning of being unique.
This can be understood according to the text.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Is it not the case that the object of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is unique, and therefore it should be called 'dharma-consciousness'?"
This objection is irrational,
because the names "universal" (*sāmānya*) and "particular" (*viśeṣa*) apply to both common and non-pervasive phenomena,
and because the object does not possess the two aforementioned causes.
That is to say, the general designation "dharma" does not refer exclusively to what is unique [to the Buddha];

furthermore, the specific designation "dharmadhātu" does not universally encompass all consciousnesses. Moreover, although the specific dharmadhātu is not shared with others, [it is still not the case that it alone constitutes the totality].

It is not, however, the nature of the faculty that serves as the support for mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Therefore, when a phenomenon is both the support of a consciousness and its unique cause, consciousness is designated according to that phenomenon.
[The Commentary states: This is said with reference to the general designation of phenomena.
Thus, the five objects such as form are also dharmas. Consequently,
the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) functions together with the visual and other sensory consciousnesses,
as well as with those of oneself and others.
It is not merely uncommon;
if one were to designate it as "dharma-consciousness" based on its distinct dharmas,
it would fail to encompass the entirety of the manas.
Because this [mental consciousness] does not include those [objects] that serve as conditions for the universal mental consciousness,
it is designated by the name "mental consciousness" solely based on its faculty;
thus, it is both pervasive and unique.
Furthermore, the unique dharma-realm (asādhāraṇa-dharmadhātu) possesses only the single meaning of being "unique";
because it lacks the meaning of having a basis, it does not correspond to the sense organs. This is as in the case of the names "drum sound" and "barley sprout," and so forth.
The sound of a drum depends on the drum;
the sound of a bell depends on the bell;
and the sounds of the bell and drum also depend on the hands and other such factors.
The bell and the drum are the specific bases,
while the hands and so forth are the common bases;
therefore, it is called the "sound of the bell and drum."
Furthermore, although sounds such as those from a drum are produced by the hand,
the sound relies upon the drum and not the hand.
A barley sprout relies both upon the barley and upon water and soil.
Because the sprout depends specifically on barley,
it is called a "barley sprout," and is not called a "water" or "soil sprout.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
Furthermore, this verse has another meaning.
That is to say, because they are followed by the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth,
and because they are "unshared" (asādhāraṇa).
Furthermore, because the eye and so forth are not shared [by multiple beings],
it is said that while one birth may produce eye-consciousness for four births,
there is no case where a single eye-organ produces consciousness for two births.
How much more so for that which can give rise to the consciousnesses of the four types of birth?
Thus, because the elements (*dhātu*), destinies (*gati*), classes (*jāti*), bodies, and eyes each individually give rise to their own consciousness,
it is called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*).
To speak at length, it is even so with the body.

Is it not the case that, during the states of death and rebirth, the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) of another being also gives rise to the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) of another being? It is not entirely non-arising.
However, they do not arise simultaneously.
It is impossible for two mental consciousnesses belonging to a single sentient being to arise at once, as is the case with [material] forms and so forth.
Therefore, this statement was made.
There is not even two, much less four.
This is because [the sense bases] such as the eye are followed by consciousness,
and because distinct consciousnesses arise according to differences in birth, realms, and destinies.
For these two reasons, [the sūtra] follows the sense faculty rather than the object.
Question: Since visual consciousness arises only when a multitude of conditions converge, for what reason does the sūtra mention only the eye and visible form?
Answer: Because they possess the nature of being the support (*āśraya*) and the object (*ālambana*) of visual consciousness.
Although other dharmas are conditions for the arising of visual consciousness, they do not possess the nature of being its support or its object.
Furthermore, because it is an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for visual consciousness.
Question: Are not space, light, and the act of mental attention (*manasikāra*) also immediately preceding conditions for visual consciousness?
Answer: When visual consciousness arises, it necessarily relies on the power of its support (āśraya) and its object (ālambana);
other dharmas are not fixed in this regard.
For instance, the consciousness of nocturnal creatures arises without depending on light.
The consciousness of aquatic beings arises without depending on space;
the same applies to humans when perceiving objects obstructed by lapis lazuli, rock crystal, and the like.
Furthermore, the divine eye gives rise to consciousness without requiring space or light.
Mental attention (manasikāra) functions as a co-arising condition for all six consciousnesses,
whereas the eye and visible forms do not share this commonality.
Therefore, the sutra mentions only the eye and visible forms.
Alternatively, one may teach according to what is appropriate for those to be converted;
for in various sūtras such as the *Hastipadopama-sūtra*, the conditions such as attention (*manasikāra*) are fully explained. Thus concludes the treatise.
Treatise:
Following the dwelling of the body, this concludes the analysis up to this point.
Below, the seventh section clarifies the similarities and differences regarding the basis of the body, the faculties, consciousness, and objects, in relation to their respective stages (*bhūmi*).
Among these, first the method is indicated to clarify it;
second, the specific characteristics of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are separately revealed. [Treatise]
Regarding whether the places where these [four] reside are identical to the earth itself:
the treatise asks and answers that one should say these four are either different or identical.
General Response: Now, in detail:
if these three factors coexist with the body, they are termed "identical" (samāna-nāman);
if they do not coexist with the body, they are termed "different" (visama-nāman).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"That which is called 'similar' refers to one born in the desire realm who sees forms of their own level with an eye of their own level."
In all four cases, they belong to the same level (*bhūmi*).
When one is born in the first dhyāna, one sees forms of that same level with an eye of that same level;
these too are all of the same level. As for what is said to be different, and so forth—the remaining phrases should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the four dharmas of the second stage,
they are termed "identical" because they share the same name;
all the remaining phrases are "different."
Regarding birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is one phrase that is the same;
all other phrases differ.
Regarding birth in the first dhyāna (*prathamadhyāna*), there is one phrase that is the same.
The remaining phrases are all different.
In the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, there are only dissimilar phrases;
there are no identical phrases.
Because the five consciousnesses do not exist in the higher realms,
the same applies to the ear.
For the nose and tongue, there is only the same phrase [as for the body].
There are no distinct categories [for these],
because both objects and both consciousnesses belong solely to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
in the higher stages, there are sense organs (*indriya*) but no consciousness to serve as their support.
Because one whose body is in a lower stage lacks superior faculties.
If the body-faculty arises in the desire realm or the first dhyāna,
there is only the "identical phrase" (sāmānya-pada).
In the case of birth in the three higher realms, there are only distinct phrases (*bhinna-pada*).

Regarding the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), whether it arises with a body consisting of four aggregates (*catuḥ-skandhaka-kāya*) in whichever realm, there are both identical phrases (*samāna-pada*) and distinct phrases.
If one first considers the physical body (*rūpa-kāya*), it exists only in the five realms.
One should discern their similarities and differences as they ought to be reflected upon according to reason.
The statement that this applies "upward to the other realms" should also be analyzed in this same manner;
this refers to the dharmas in order to clarify the point.
Treatise:
Now, I shall briefly explain how it reaches its purpose with little effort and yields great results;
this explains the characteristic of certainty.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the verse is presented as a brief statement,
and then the prose commentary provides a detailed explanation.
The Commentary says: "The body, the eye, and visible forms—these three exist only in the Desire Realm and the First Dhyāna.

This explains the commonality and specific limitations regarding the locations of these four. Regarding the statement that "the eye faculty herein ultimately does not reside below [its level]," this explains the verse’s point that "the eye is not below the body."
The commentary states:
The lower [body] can accommodate the cultivation of the higher eye, and the higher eye relies upon the lower body;
however, because the higher does not cultivate the lower eye, the [higher eye] does not exist below the body. Thus it is said.
Regarding the statement that "visual consciousness, in relation to the eye and so forth, is not higher than lower," this refers to the second line of the verse.
It means that the lower eye cannot see forms of a higher level, and a higher consciousness does not rely upon an eye of a lower level.

This explains the meaning of the verse. It states: "Form, in relation to consciousness, is sometimes equal, sometimes superior, and sometimes inferior. Regarding the explanation within the verse that "form is either one with or entirely distinct from consciousness," it says: [The commentary continues: Form is sometimes identical to consciousness, sometimes entirely different from consciousness, and sometimes both identical and different. Why is this? Because form is sometimes the same as consciousness, sometimes different from consciousness, and sometimes both the same and different. What is meant by "the same"? It refers to the case where the five sense-faculties (the five *indriyas*) are considered to be the same as the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). What is meant by "different"? It refers to the case where the five objects (the five *viṣayas*) are considered to be different from the five consciousnesses. What is meant by "both the same and different"? It refers to the case where the five faculties and the five objects are considered to be both the same as and different from the five consciousnesses. Furthermore, there are cases where form is not the same as consciousness, not different from consciousness, and neither the same nor different from consciousness. What is meant by "not the same"? Supreme mastery is the meaning of the syllable *i*;

As for the statement, "Speech is not accomplished until the vocal apparatus has reached its function":
Just as the ability to see forms does not depend on training for its accomplishment,
if the tongue had a predominant efficacy regarding speech,
it should be able to speak spontaneously without depending on training for its accomplishment.
The *Nyāya* states: Furthermore,
the vocal organs and so forth are also not called faculties (*indriya*),
because this would entail the fallacies of being indeterminate, confused, and over-extensive.
Regarding the fallacy of indeterminacy:
what kind of vocal organ is established as the verbal root?
That which is capable of producing speech sounds is named the vocal organ.
This is simply the tongue.
If that were the case, then mental investigation (*vitarka*), analysis (*vicāra*), and other such factors, as well as the winds that give rise to vocal action,
would also have to be established as faculties (*indriya*).
Because it is capable of producing speech; furthermore, because vitarka and vicāra are the predominant causes for the production of vocal sounds.
If it is argued that since the cognition of form also occurs by means of speech, the eye should not be established as a separate faculty, [the response is as follows].
This is logically impossible;
for although those born blind hear descriptions of form,
they do not discern the distinct characteristics of blue and so forth.
Treatise:
The hands and feet should not be established as faculties (*indriya*), for they would contradict [the definition of] the faculties; they occupy different locations.
This refers to the movement of distinct characteristics, namely extension and contraction; the rest of the text is intelligible. The above constitutes the fault of indetermination and confusion.
Treatise.
Because this pleasure arises from the act of defecation,
the former objection suffers from the fault of confusion,
while the latter objection lacks a distinct predominance.
Commentary:
Furthermore, it would follow that the throat, teeth, and so forth should not be established as faculties;
this is the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"As for the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), the sense-faculties (*indriya*) established by that [opponent] would be without limit, and so forth. Question: Among the seventy-five dharmas, why is it that only five among the form-aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*) are designated as sense-faculties?
Within the universal [mental factors], only four are taken: sensation, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Within the wholesome [factors], only two dharmas are taken: faith and diligence.
Among the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*), only the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is taken up, and no other dharmas. Answer:

According to other masters, these thirteen dharmas are established as faculties because they possess a predominant function (*adhipatya*) in both the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*) and the process of cessation (*nivṛtti*).
Other functions are not established as faculties because they are not preeminent.
According to the Dharmaguptaka school,
these thirteen factors are the supports of the mind.
This is differentiation;
this is abiding;
this is affliction.
Because these serve as provisions and because they are pure, they are established as faculties;
other dharmas are not so, and thus are not established as faculties.
The *Nyāya* asks: Since each of the various phenomena possesses its own distinct predominant function (*adhipati-pratyaya*) in relation to others,
they should all be designated as "faculties" (*indriya*).
The answer states: "This is established as a distinct meaning of 'supreme predominance' (*adhipati*).

It is like the lion king or the village headman. As previously cited, this text asks: "In this context, since the predominant efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is being correlated with the predominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), should it not be established as a faculty (*indriya*)? How is it that, while [the other causes] can directly relate to their fruits through conditions, this one is instead not established as a faculty?"
Treatise:
Herein, the faculties beginning with the eye should also be extensively analyzed.
The twenty-two faculties have been established by the six preceding verses.
The final two verses provide the second explanation of the essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the faculties (*indriya*).
This section contains two parts:
first, the indication of the remaining faculties.
Next, the five feelings and the three untainted [feelings] will be explained;
this is the first [section].
Treatise:
Regarding the establishment of the three faculties based on the nine [factors], from the five feelings such as pleasure (*sukha*) up to their supports:
this subsequently explains the five feelings and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
There are three kinds of feeling (*vedanā*).
First, benefiting;
second, harming;
third, neither harming nor benefiting. Furthermore, there are two kinds.
First, bodily sensation,
which refers to that associated with the five consciousnesses.
Second, mental sensation.
That which is associated with mental consciousness and consists of bodily sensation that provides benefit is called the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*).

Bodily sensation that causes harm is called the feeling of pain (*duḥkha-vedanā*). Mental sensation that provides benefit from the second dhyāna downward is called the feeling of joy (*prīti-vedanā*).

Affliction and harm are called the sensation of sorrow (*daurmanasya-vedanā*); it pertains to both body and mind. That which is neither harmful nor beneficial is called the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
The treatise states: "Up to this point, it is termed the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
This explains the sensation of suffering.
Treatise:
As for what is called "delight" (*prīti*), it refers to the joy of the utmost sincerity; this is explained as the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*).
Treatise.
This very mental joy, when it reaches its full intensity, is called the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
This explains the feeling of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*). [End of] Treatise.
In the third dhyāna, it reaches the point where it is designated merely as the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya).
This explains why the third dhyāna is called "bliss" (sukha),
while those in the lower stages are called "joy."
Treatise:
From "associated with the mental consciousness" up to "is called the faculty of grief" explains the feeling of grief (*daurmanasya*).
Treatise:
“The middle” refers to that which is neither pleasant nor painful; it should be stated as “pervading both,” which explains the neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Treatise.
For what reason are these two established collectively as a single faculty?
This is the question.
For what reason are there both pleasure and displeasure?
In the body and in the mind,
the names of sensations are distinct:
that which is neither pleasant nor unpleasant.
It resides in the mind and in the body;
together they constitute the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Treatise.
This sensation extends from the body and mind to the unification of body and mind.
This explains and resolves potential objections. Treatise.
Furthermore, the faculties are established collectively because the sensations of suffering and pleasure arrive;
this is a further, more detailed explanation. Treatise:

The faculties of mind (*manas*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), joy (*sukha*), and renunciation (*tyāga*) culminate in the establishment of the faculty of one who possesses full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*). This explains the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*). Within this, there are two [sections];
first, by means of nine faculties.
The three roots are established based on these three paths;
this is the first part of the subsequent explanation regarding the reasons for their respective names.
Treatise:
For what reason are these three names established?
From this point forward, the names of the three faculties (*indriya*) are explained.

First the question, then the answer. The question asks: "For what reason are they called the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and so forth? The treatise states:
This refers to being on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), up to the point where one is designated as "I shall come to know the unknown."
This explains the name of the first untainted faculty (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Wisdom is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*),
whereas patience (*kṣānti*) is not knowledge.
In the path of seeing, at the stage of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*),
there is the functioning of the "unknown-to-be-known" regarding the eight truths.
Upon reaching the stage of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), there is the "unknown-to-be-known" regarding seven [truths].
Up until the stage of *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*, there is the path-truth yet to be known as "I shall come to know" regarding both the form and formless realms;
therefore, these fifteen moments of mind are all termed the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Treatise:
If one is on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), it is termed "already known" (ājñāta).
This explains the name of the second untainted faculty (anāsrava-indriya).
The subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) of the ultimate path has already fully and completely known the truths;
it does not arise from the desire to know noble truths that have never been known before,
but solely for the purpose of abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga).
Furthermore, one repeatedly realizes the objects of the Four Truths;
therefore, it is said that they are called "already known.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 143, states:
At the moment of the sixteenth mind, it should be like the seven knowledges;
why, then, is it specifically called the faculty of "already-known" (ājñātendriya)?
Because it is not a case of knowing what has not yet been known.
The answer is that this is also stated from the perspective of the majority.
That is to say, although it resembles seven knowledges in its initial moment,
all subsequent moments differ from them.
From the perspective of the majority, all are termed the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātendriya*), because they share the same nature.
According to this treatise, the first seven knowledges (*jñāna*) last for only a single moment;

however, the knowledge of the path of types (*mārgānvayajñāna*) necessarily consists of multiple moments for both vehicles. Alternatively, for Śrāvakas, there must be multiple moments when they emerge from meditative absorption.
According to this principle, it is known that [the path] is already known. Some say that thereafter there is no longer any "not-yet-known" path to be overwhelmed or covered;
it does not allow the lower to suppress the upper so as to deprive it of its sovereignty.
It must be so; therefore, when one knows,
one says "I know," just as that which is in the process of going is called "already gone."
That is also like this; according to this treatise,
those who have not yet realized the Path are classified as inferior,
while those who have realized the Path are classified as superior.
Patience is its lower part;
wisdom is its upper part;
the former is its lower part.
It is the latter that constitutes the "upper" [stage].
Although the first seven [knowledges] are already designated as "known" within the knowledge itself,
they may also be termed "already known."
The subsequent patience regarding the path (mārga-anvaya-kṣānti) is called "not yet known" (ajñāta);
thus, it is said that one "attaches to what is above by means of what is below.
Although all eight knowledges (jñāna) may be termed "already known" (ājñāta), [the specific designation applies here].
Because the seven knowledges have what is superior above them and what is inferior below them, they are not called "already known" (*ājñāta*);
because the eighth has nothing superior above it and nothing inferior below it, it is called "already known.
Although the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) cannot know itself, [it is still so designated].
It is only upon reaching the second moment that it is known by wisdom,
like a single mote of dust from Mount Sumeru or a single drop from the great ocean.

Furthermore, this is established in terms of the truths (*satya*) and not in terms of moments (*kṣaṇa*). Question: Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one contemplates the truths both for the purpose of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*) and for the purpose of refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) and attaining the bliss of the Dharma;

why then do you speak only of abandoning the afflictions? Answer: Following the path of the first fruit (*prathamaphalamārga*), the path of the superior fruit (*viśiṣṭaphalamārga*) necessarily arises.
That path of superior fruit is precisely the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for abandoning the afflictions.
Furthermore, because one fears the regression of afflictions through such practices as the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*),
and because it is also a path of further progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) for the sake of happiness in the present life, it serves to abandon the afflictions.
However, the meaning of "severing delusions" (prahāṇa) already subsumes the others;
for this reason, the Master of the Treatise speaks only of severing delusions.
[Treatise]
This explains the name of the faculty of "having fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) as it is taught at length from the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) up to its full exposition:
"one who knows that he has already known."
It speaks only of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), which refers to those of dull faculties;
that is, having attained the knowledge of exhaustion, they know: "I have already known suffering," "I have known its origin," and so forth.

Alternatively, one may attain the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), whereby one knows: "I have already known suffering; I have abandoned its origin," and so forth. Or, one may cultivate this knowledge until it becomes an inherent nature;
that is to say, one attains the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
This refers to those of sharp faculties who attain two knowledges:

"I have already known suffering"—this is the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna); "it is not to be known again"—this is the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna). This is explained at length, and so forth.
That is to say: "I have already abandoned the origin [of suffering] and shall not abandon it again," and so forth.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"The third faculty, the faculty of one who has perfect knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*), is called 'knowledge' because its essence consists in knowing that [the truths] have already been known."
Because it has been practiced until it becomes one's nature, or because one is able to protect that knowledge. The *Chao-shi* (Excerpts and Explanations) states:
"That which refers to the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) saying 'I have already known suffering,' etc., is called 'knowing that one has already known.'"
This is called knowing that the cultivation [of the path] has already become established;
it is the first attainment, termed the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna),
or the knowledge capable of guarding [the attainment].
The subsequent stage is precisely the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Because it is accomplished and capable of providing protection, it is termed "endowed" (*samanvāgata*).
The *Abhidharmakośa* also states that the first [moment] constitutes "having knowledge."
Later, through repeated practice, this becomes one's nature.
That which is capable of [this] and capable of practicing it is called "one who possesses full knowledge" (ājñātāvin).

The faculty of one who possesses full knowledge is termed the faculty of one who possesses full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*). According to the intent of these two treatises, there is a distinction between them.
If this treatise designates the wisdom of the three paths as "the unknown-to-be-known" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti*) and so forth,
then that very [wisdom] is the faculty;
this is explained by way of their common basis.
This is precisely the meaning of "root" (*mūla*); it is simply wisdom (*prajñā*). If one follows the intention of the *Abhidharmakośa*, those three names refer to that which accomplishes practice;
they are explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound.
The faculties possessed by that [state] are called "its faculties.
This fully comprises nine factors. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Nine faculties are associated to constitute this phenomenon;
therefore, the eight [factors] beginning with volition also receive this name. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* examines the establishment and exclusion of seventy-five factors.
Fearing prolixity, I shall not elaborate further.
However, it does not exceed the previously established categories:
that which lacks the aforementioned meaning is not established as a faculty (*indriya*).
Treatise:
"Whatever faculties they possess, up to the faculty of one who is destined for enlightenment" (ājñātāvīndriya) summarizes the names of the three preceding faculties.
Treatise:

Having thus explained up to how many [factors] are untainted (*anāsrava*), the third section below consists of fourteen verses that provide a detailed analysis through various categories. This section contains two parts.
The first six verses are analyzed according to six categories.
The subsequent eight verses are analyzed by way of various specific meanings.
Within these, the first verse analyzes the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). This section contains three parts.
First, exclusively untainted (anāsrava);
second, exclusively tainted (sāsrava);
third, both tainted and untainted.
The treatise states: "The names differ but the substance is the same.
This clarifies that it is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*). Thus says the treatise.
The seven material sense-faculties are included within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
This explanation regarding the inclusion of contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena is not exhaustive;
for uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is also included within the aggregate of form, as it is uncontaminated.
Treatise:
Intention (*manas*), aspiration (*chanda*), joy (*prīti*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) range from being with outflows (*sāsrava*) to being without outflows (*anāsrava*).
The third [category] consists of both the with-outflow and the without-outflow.
The treatise states:
"Other masters say it extends to the category of external ordinary persons (*bāhya-pṛthagjana*).
This recounts the tenet of the Mahīśāsaka school.
This refers to the Vibhajyavādins (also known as the Vibhaṣā-vibhaṣa-prativādins),
here translated as the "Distinguishers" (Fēnbié lùnshī).
They cite sūtras as proof that the five faculties, such as faith and so forth, are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because the sūtras state that these belong exclusively to the noble ones (*ārya*).
That is to say, it is taught that from the arhat down to the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*), there exist these five faculties, such as faith;
therefore, one knows they are untainted (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"If one entirely lacks these five faculties, such as faith, I say that person abides in the category of external worldlings (bāhyapṛthagjanapakṣa).
Furthermore, in the subsequent passage, it states that those who entirely lack the five faculties abide in the category of external worldlings.
Thus, one knows it is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Although the text repeats itself, its meaning is one and the same:
it exists in the noble ones (*ārya*) but not in ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Treatise:
This does not establish proof for the category of external worldlings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).
Below this, the Master’s refutation is twofold.
First, a citation from the Mahīśāsaka school is adduced to prove that [the path] is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Second, a scriptural passage is cited by oneself to prove that it is tainted (*sāsrava*).
This is the first [point]. This does not constitute a valid proof.
This is not a general negation, for these words are spoken in reference to the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Thus, the reason why the five faculties— faith and the others— are said to pertain to both types,
namely the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), is established.
They state that this exists for noble ones (*ārya*) but not for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
This is said with reference to the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), and not with reference to the five tainted faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth. How is this known to be so?
The Mahīśāsaka school raises this inquiry.
How is it known that this statement is spoken in reliance upon the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*)?
It is because the preceding statement was made in reliance upon the untainted [attainment] (*anāsrava-samāpatti*). Thus it is explained.
The Master of the Treatise explains the reason for relying on the five faculties, such as untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*), and so forth.
Now, the establishment of a noble one (*ārya*) pertains solely to conditioned untainted phenomena, not to unconditioned tainted phenomena.
Since that sutra establishes the noble ones (ārya) by means of the five faculties beginning with faith,
it is known that this is spoken solely in reliance upon the untainted (anāsrava) faculties.
It was stated previously that the noble ones possess [faculties] based on the untainted faculties.
Since it was stated that if these five faculties, such as faith, were entirely absent, one knows that [the text] refers exclusively to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Alternatively, the Master provides a second interpretation: that this refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have reached the category of external ordinary beings.
This can be understood according to the text.
Furthermore, the treatise states that the sūtra’s mention of "reaching" (*prāpti*) also applies to the contaminated (*sāsrava*).
The Master of the Treatise cites a sūtra to prove that the five faculties, such as faith and the rest, are common to both the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Before the Buddha had turned the Wheel of Dharma, there were yet no noble ones (*ārya*);
even at that time, he already spoke of the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of sentient beings.
Therefore, it is known that the discourse refers to the five faculties, such as faith and the rest, which are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Furthermore, the World-Honored One spoke [of them] up to the point of their classification and observation.
The Master of the Treatise cites the second sutra to prove that [the faculties] include those with outflows (*sāsrava*).
If the five faculties, such as faith and so forth, were exclusively without outflows (*anāsrava*),
how could one truly know [them] as accumulation (*samudaya*), disappearance (*vyaya*), gratification (*āsvāda*), and danger (*ādīnava*)?
These four modes of contemplation observe the tainted (*sāsrava*);
they constitute the accumulation that invites suffering and lead to the state of submergence.
Craving for flavors is the basis;
their peril is suffering;
renunciation is cessation.
The remaining text is understandable.
Therefore, the treatise concludes that the five faculties, beginning with faith, pertain to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
This concludes the summary of the proof.
The treatise states: Thus has it been explained, up to the point that [the result] is established as being non-heterogeneous ripening (*avipāka*).
The next verse clarifies, in its second part, the distinction between what is maturation (*vipāka*) and what is not maturation.
The treatise states: "Only the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is necessarily maturation.
This is the established tenet.

Among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), only the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is invariably a result of maturation (*vipāka*). This [text] merely excludes it from being other than that; it does not definitively exclude its connection with other [categories], nor does it definitively exclude its connection with what is not a result of maturation.
Thus says the *Śāstra*.
If it is as you say, to whose maturation does this belong?
This is an external objection;
the objection states:
If meditative concentration were itself a maturation (vipāka),
then when one prolongs the life-force (jīvitasaṃskāra) by means of the fourth dhyāna and so forth,
of what would this very life-force be the maturation?
Treatise:
As stated in the root treatise up to the point regarding the life-span as a maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*),
there are two intended meanings here.
First, citing the root treatise to prove the existence of the volitional act of prolonging life (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra-sthāpana*);
second, citing the root treatise to answer the preceding question. It says:
"Whose maturation (*vipāka*) is the volitional act of prolonging life?"
Citing the proof from the root treatise:
it refers to the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma previously accumulated that results in wealth and so forth. How does a bhikṣu retain his long life?
This asks about the retention of the dharma; that is to say, an arhat.
This excludes those still in training who have accomplished supernatural powers;
it excludes those liberated by wisdom who have attained mastery over the mind;
and it excludes those liberated by time—whether among the monastic community or as individuals.
Discerning other fields: one distributes gifts according to the circumstances of those who come seeking life’s necessities.
Discerning other objects: having given, one makes a vow.
Discerning the absence of vows: one immediately enters the fourth dhyāna and so forth.

Eliminating other concentrations: Regarding the statement that once one has arisen from concentration, whatever [karma] arrives will all transform and bring about the maturation result of longevity, this is because the power of giving and concentration can effect such transformation.
Through giving and concentration, previously indeterminate karma for wealth is transformed.

It causes the ripening fruit of longevity to be summoned at this present time; or, by means of this gift, one’s fixed vow causes indefinite karma to be extended. Question: How is it known that the fruit of longevity is not summoned in the present by means of this current gift?
Answer: There are many scriptural proofs.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 126, states:
Question: It is logically impossible for there to be a distinct ripening fruit of wealth that could constitute a ripening fruit of lifespan.
Why, then, is it said that a karma with the maturation of wealth can be redirected to bring about the maturation of longevity?
Answer: There is no redirection of the substance of the fruit, but there is redirection of the power of the karma.

That is to say, by means of giving and the power of the ultimate meditative concentration (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*), one redirects karma that would have matured as wealth to bring about the maturation of longevity.
Although both [types of karma] can be transformed, at this present time, one disregards the fruit of wealth and prays for the fruit of longevity;
according to this text, giving is described as that which can transform, rather than that which directly induces [the result]. Other masters say:
There is karma that has previously brought about the maturation fruit of longevity,
yet it is obstructed by calamities.
Through the power of present generosity and the meditative concentration of the "limit" (prāntakoṭika), those obstructions are extinguished and the maturation of longevity arises.
Although both [types of fruit] can be transformed, at this present time, one disregards the fruit of wealth and prays for the fruit of longevity;
according to this treatise, giving is what brings about [the result]. Some say as follows:
There is karma that previously brought about the ripening fruit of longevity,
yet it was not fixed; by means of the present act of giving and the power of the meditative concentration of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭi-dhyāna*).
This causes the karma of longevity to be determined and to necessarily yield its fruit.

According to this treatise, giving is that which brings about such determination. Furthermore, there are those who maintain that through the certainty of giving, one draws forth the maturation of residual lifespan from previous lives.

This refers to the remaining life-span of an Arhat’s residual maturation (*vipāka*), which is brought to manifestation through the power of a present gift and the power of the limit of meditative concentration (*prāntakoṭi-samādhi*).
The inconceivable power of meditative concentration causes that which has been long severed to resume. This is according to this scriptural treatise.
It is also drawn forth by generosity and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Following the four interpretations above, the first interpretation states:
through the power of the limit of generosity and meditative concentration, karma that ripens as wealth transforms to ripen as the fruit of longevity.
According to this treatise,
giving to the Sangha and other such assemblies serves as the cause for transforming karma;
it does not lead to one's own death.

However, this first interpretation is consistent with the root treatise, as it states that one turns away from karma that produces wealth in order to attract the fruit of longevity. The second master says:
"There is karma that first attracts the ripening fruit of longevity."
However, because there are obstructions, etc., this too may be an indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karma*). The third master says:
"There is karma that first brings about the maturation result (*vipāka-phala*) of life-span."
However, this is not certain. The fourth master says:

"By means of giving and meditative concentration, one draws forth the maturation of the remaining lifespan from a previous life. The explanations of the [first] three masters all contradict the root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*), which states: [as follows].

At that time, those karmas capable of producing the maturation of wealth all shift to produce the maturation of longevity as their fruit. None of these three masters state that the karma for wealth shifts;
they merely state that the karma for longevity is obstructed.
It is indeterminate;
it is a residual fruit.
Therefore, one should know that this does not support the original treatise.
The treatise states:
Furthermore, there are those who wish to maintain that [the object] reaches [the sense organ] so as to be drawn in and experienced;

Question: By what is the life-force (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) that is retained projected?
Is it by means of giving?

If it were by the power of giving,
one would not enter into meditative absorption.
If it were by means of meditative concentration,
one should not practice giving;

Some say it is due to meditative concentration;
those who speak thus maintain that it is due to both. Although one may practice extensive giving, [the result depends on these factors].
If one does not enter meditative absorption,
one can ultimately never produce the fruit of longevity;
this remains true even if one enters absorption repeatedly.
If one does not practice giving,
one will ultimately be unable to bring about the fruit of longevity;
however, the power of giving can indeed bring it about.
This establishes the certainty.
For this reason, it is said that both [types of karma] act together.
According to the aforementioned treatise, through the provision of life-sustaining conditions, one is able to draw forth the fruit of longevity from past karma that was intended to produce wealth.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* provides six masters’ explanations regarding the relinquishing of the life-force (*jīvitasaṃskāra*).
Question: Logically, there can be no distinct ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) for the life-force that constitutes a ripened fruit of wealth.

Only the lifespan and wealth differ;

There is karma that previously brought about a coarse, rather than excellent, ripening result of wealth;

That is to say, although they previously drew forth coarse fruits over a long period of time,

For example, it is like the prognosis given by a skilled physician, which none can exceed.

For one who has practiced the cultivation of longevity (*āyur-dhāraṇa*), both wealth and lifespan are indeterminate; thus, there can be the prolonging or relinquishing [of them].
However, if they were determinate, they could only serve as a fixed limit and could not be increased or decreased. Furthermore, according to this passage:
The practice for increasing longevity is not something that can be induced by present giving;

For the life-faculty that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala*) is not a maturation (*vipāka*).

"May all [karmas] instead transform to produce the ripened fruit of longevity.

According to the first of the four explanations in the *Vibhāṣā* and the final establishment, it is because giving can induce meditative concentration and bring about certainty;
that is, the volition of present giving induces the arising of past karma.
This is called the fruit of the volition of giving.
If one provides this explanation,

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* further presents the explanations of three masters,
all of which contradict the root treatise and thus cannot be relied upon.
If it were not so, it would contradict the explanation in the *Vibhāṣā*,
as well as the passage in this treatise concerning the relinquishing of the life-span.
The second explanation in the *Nyāyānusāra* is the same as the third explanation in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

Master Yu himself said:

"However, its profound significance is not yet fully understood; it should be further contemplated. Now, upon careful examination, it is clear that according to the Sarvāstivāda, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is certainly not a present result.
It is not permitted that a single projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) projects the fruits of multiple lifetimes,
nor is it permitted that multiple projecting karmas collectively induce a single lifetime; such is the case here with this prolongation of life (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra-sthāpana*).
If one were to provide a general explanation:
if, according to the fixed vow of prolonging life, one transforms the previous fruit of wealth to continue the present life,
then there would be the fault that multiple karmas would induce a single lifetime.

If one were to say that it causes the indefinite karma for [rebirth in] a lifespan to be extended, there would be the fault of its being inconsistent with the granting of the vow; therefore, these two points shall now serve as two interpretations. First interpretation:
By the power of concentration (*samādhi*), aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), and the volition of giving (*dānacetanā*), one can prolong indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karman*) and maintain a long life.
Question: If that is so, would this not be inconsistent with [the nature of] an aspiration?
Answer: Because it is through the abundance of karma induced by aspiration that the fruit of longevity is brought about.
This vow alone is able to prolong indeterminate karma,
just as giving and other meritorious acts based on the conditions of one's life-span can prolong it; this is the second explanation,
which means that it transforms the karma for wealth so that it instead brings about the fruit of longevity.
Question: If that is so, would it not follow that multiple karmas of a single lifetime could project [rebirth], and that karma which is not grasped could still yield its fruit?
Answer: We do not admit that two projecting karmas can produce the experience of a single lifetime together.
Because the power of giving and meditative concentration sustains the inconceivable,

Just as form is obstructive, through the inconceivable power of supernormal faculties, it can be rendered non-obstructive.

both are capable of manifesting [their results] in the present due to the power of karma. The homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) is the general,
while the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the particular;

As for the distinction between them:
although they differ in being general or specific, [they are nonetheless included].
Because they are equally capable of being manifested by the karma that induces them,

and when short they are equally short.

if it is shortened, they are all shortened together. The fourth explanation states:

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) may be experienced in the present;

Regarding the distinctions:

This contradicts the four explanations in the *Vibhāṣā* regarding the meanings of that which transforms and that which is transformed;

Based on this, we know that prolongation and contraction refer to life-force (*āyus*),
and not to the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*). Thus says the Treatise (*śāstra*).

it is not possible for nourishment (puṣṭi) alone to exist once the continuity of maturation has been severed;
for this would entail the fault of over-extension.
Nor should one maintain that these are of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*),

that which occurs in between is called "abiding and change" (sthity-anyathātva).

The term "formations" (*saṃskāra*) is used to indicate that the formations of vitality (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) and the formations of life-span (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*) are numerous and momentary, their substance being distinct in each instant rather than being a single entity that persists for a long duration. This is the third position, as stated by the Sautrāntika masters.
The use of the plural term "formations" (saṃskāra) is intended to show that there is no single, real entity of life or vitality;
rather, these two names, "life" and "vitality," are merely designated metaphorically upon the manifold formations of the five aggregates. Therefore, it is said that they are "many formations."
If one were to say this is not so,
one should not speak of "abandoning life" (āyus);
rather, one should only speak of "retaining much vitality" (jīvita) while "discarding much longevity" (āyus).
Because these formations are conditioned, they are collectively termed [the maras], not merely life and longevity.
