Treatise: [The following verse: "Faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are the five faculties; they are so called because they possess the power to overcome their respective opposites. (1.21) Commentary: Faith (*śraddhā*) is the conviction in the truths, the qualities of the Three Jewels, and the capacity for action (*karman*). Vigor (*vīrya*) is the exertion of the mind toward wholesome states. Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the non-forgetfulness of the object of focus. Concentration (*samādhi*) is the one-pointedness of the mind. Wisdom (*prajñā*) is the discernment of phenomena. These are called "faculties" (*indriya*) because they possess the power to overcome their respective opposites—namely, lack of faith, laziness, forgetfulness, distraction, and ignorance. They are enumerated as five because they serve as the primary causes for the attainment of the two fruits: the fruit of the worldly person (*pṛthagjana*) and the fruit of the noble one (*ārya*). Among these, the first four are the causes for the fruit of the worldly person, while the last one is the cause for the fruit of the noble one. Furthermore, the first three are the causes for the arising of vigor, and the latter two are the causes for the arising of concentration and wisdom. Thus, these five are established as the faculties. As it is said: "Because they are the causes for the arising of vigor, concentration, and wisdom, these five are established as the faculties. (1.22) The meaning is that faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are established as the five faculties because they are the causes for the arising of vigor, concentration, and wisdom respectively. That is to say, through the power of faith, one exerts vigor; through the power of vigor, one attains concentration; and through the power of concentration, one gives rise to wisdom. Therefore, these five are established as the faculties. Furthermore, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their cultivation. Specifically, first one cultivates faith in the truths; having cultivated faith, one then exerts vigor; having exerted vigor, one then maintains mindfulness; having maintained mindfulness, one then attains concentration; and having attained concentration, one then gives rise to wisdom. Thus, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their cultivation. Furthermore, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their functions. Specifically, faith is the faculty that leads one toward the object; vigor is the faculty that causes one to proceed toward the object; mindfulness is the faculty that prevents one from losing the object; concentration is the faculty that stabilizes the mind upon the object; and wisdom is the faculty that discerns the object. Thus, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their functions. Furthermore, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their refinement. Specifically, faith is the faculty that refines the mind; vigor is the faculty that refines the body; mindfulness is the faculty that refines the objects; concentration is the faculty that refines the mind; and wisdom is the faculty that refines all phenomena. Thus, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their refinement. Furthermore, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their support and supported. Specifically, faith is the support; vigor is the supported; mindfulness is the support; concentration is the supported; and wisdom is the support. Thus, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their support and supported. Furthermore, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their coarse and subtle nature. Specifically, faith is the coarsest; vigor is subtler than faith; mindfulness is subtler than vigor; concentration is subtler than mindfulness; and wisdom is the subtlest of all. Thus, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their coarse and subtle nature. Furthermore, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the path of seeing. Specifically, faith is the faculty that enters the path; vigor is the faculty that proceeds along the path; mindfulness is the faculty that guards the path; concentration is the faculty that stabilizes the path; and wisdom is the faculty that realizes the path. Thus, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the path of seeing. Furthermore, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the path of meditation. Specifically, faith is the faculty that enters the path of meditation; vigor is the faculty that proceeds along the path of meditation; mindfulness is the faculty that guards the path of meditation; concentration is the faculty that stabilizes the path of meditation; and wisdom is the faculty that realizes the path of meditation. Thus, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the path of meditation. Furthermore, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the path of no-more-learning. Specifically, faith is the faculty that enters the path of no-more-learning; vigor is the faculty that proceeds along the path of no-more-learning; mindfulness is the faculty that guards the path of no-more-learning; concentration is the faculty that stabilizes the path of no-more-learning; and wisdom is the faculty that realizes the path of no-more-learning. Thus, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the path of no-more-learning. Furthermore, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the attainment of the fruit. Specifically, faith is the faculty that leads to the attainment of the fruit; vigor is the faculty that causes the attainment of the fruit; mindfulness is the faculty that guards the attainment of the fruit; concentration is the faculty that stabilizes the attainment of the fruit; and wisdom is the faculty that realizes the attainment of the fruit. Thus, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the attainment of the fruit. Furthermore, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the purification of the mind. Specifically, faith is the faculty that purifies the mind; vigor is the faculty that purifies the body; mindfulness is the faculty that purifies the objects; concentration is the faculty that purifies the mind; and wisdom is the faculty that purifies all phenomena. Thus, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the purification of the mind. Furthermore, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the removal of obstacles. Specifically, faith is the faculty that removes the obstacle of doubt; vigor is the faculty that removes the obstacle of laziness; mindfulness is the faculty that removes the obstacle of forgetfulness; concentration is the faculty that removes the obstacle of distraction; and wisdom is the faculty that removes the obstacle of ignorance. Thus, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the removal of obstacles. Furthermore, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the attainment of the supreme fruit. Specifically, faith is the faculty that leads to the attainment of the supreme fruit; vigor is the faculty that causes the attainment of the supreme fruit; mindfulness is the faculty that guards the attainment of the supreme fruit; concentration is the faculty that stabilizes the attainment of the supreme fruit; and wisdom is the faculty that realizes the attainment of the supreme fruit. Thus, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the attainment of the supreme fruit. Furthermore, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the cultivation of the roots of merit. Specifically, faith is the faculty that cultivates the root of merit of faith; vigor is the faculty that cultivates the root of merit of vigor; mindfulness is the faculty that cultivates the root of merit of mindfulness; concentration is the faculty that cultivates the root of merit of concentration; and wisdom is the faculty that cultivates the root of merit of wisdom. Thus, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the cultivation of the roots of merit. Furthermore, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the attainment of the three knowledges. Specifically, faith is the faculty that leads to the attainment of the knowledge of the past; vigor is the faculty that causes the attainment of the knowledge of the future; mindfulness is the faculty that guards the knowledge of the present; concentration is the faculty that stabilizes the knowledge of the present; and wisdom is the faculty that realizes the knowledge of the present. Thus, the order of these five faculties is established according to the sequence of their function in the attainment of the three knowledges. Why is this? Because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are different.
Those two views function with a mode of activity characterized by joy,
whereas the faculty of grief functions with a mode of activity characterized by sorrow;

The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is also not non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), because it is not comprised within the deportment (*airyāpathika*), the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*), or that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Question: Why is the faculty of grief not comprised within the deportment?
Answer: The faculty of sorrow functions with discrimination;
the modes of deportment function without discrimination.
If the modes of deportment were possessed of the faculty of sorrow, [they would not be without discrimination].
If one were to form the discrimination, "I should now adopt such a deportment as that of the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
or like that of Aśvajit," then at the very moment of such discrimination, one would already be abiding in that deportment.
However, the modes of deportment (airyāpathika) do not possess this discrimination;
therefore, the modes of deportment lack the faculty of sorrow (daurmanasyendriya).
Question: For what reason is the faculty of sorrow not included among the bases of craftsmanship (śailpasthānika)?
Answer: The faculty of grief functions with conceptual discrimination (*savikalpa*), whereas the sphere of arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*) functions without conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*).
If the sphere of arts and crafts were to possess the faculty of grief, [it would likewise function with discrimination].
If one were to form the conceptualization, "I should now perform such a craft, like that of the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
or like that of the Devaputra Viśvakarman," then at the very moment of such conceptualization, one would have already accomplished that craft.
However, such discrimination does not exist in the spheres of craftsmanship;
therefore, the faculty of sorrow is absent in the spheres of craftsmanship.
Question: For what reason is the faculty of sorrow not born of maturation?
Answer: The faculty of sorrow functions through conceptual discrimination;
that which is born of maturation functions without conceptual discrimination.
If that which is born of maturation were to possess the faculty of sorrow, [it would contradict this].
If one were to form the discrimination, "I should now experience such a maturation of karma, just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, did,
or like a Wheel-Turning Sage King," then at the very moment of that discrimination, one would immediately have to experience such a maturation.
However, that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) lacks such discrimination;

therefore, that which is born of maturation does not possess the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*). This is explained at length in that [text]. Question: Why is feeling (*vedanā*) common to the three natures (*trividha*)?

Answer: Because the twenty-two faculties are established within the entirety of feeling (*vedanā*), it is said that the four feelings pervade the three natures.

as explained in the "Establishment of the Twenty-two Faculties. Therefore, they do not extend to the three natures.

What has been explained above refers exclusively to the faculties that are results of maturation (*vipāka*).
If those associated with defilement are included, the mental faculty (*manas*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā*) are added as well. Thus says the treatise.
The treatise explains [the process] from within the desire realm up to the form and formless realms,
providing the introduction and the citation.
The desire realm’s desire is superior and extends beyond the form and formless realms.
This commentary merely mentions "desire" and "form," but does not mention "realms. However, upon careful examination, this explanation seems overly prolix.
Treatise:
This explains the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), specifically the teaching that its initial attainment extends to the formless (*ārūpya*).
This is the exposition on the realm of form.
Treatise:
The section from "Above, only life-force" to "only life-force and nothing else" explains the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
In the verse, the term "superior" (ūrdhva) refers to superiority of birth resulting from the superiority of meditative concentration;
it does not mean being above the Desire and Form Realms, for there is no separate location [above them].
The remainder of the text may be understood. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"From this it is proven that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) exists as a real entity."
If this were not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), by what faculty would it be designated as "birth" (*upapatti*) in the formless realm?
It cannot be designated as the birth of the fruit of karma (*karmaphala*) if it is neither wholesome nor defiled,
because that birth has not yet been experienced and could still manifest.
Furthermore, a resultant consciousness (vipākacitta) lacks the capacity for rebirth-continuity,
as it is only admitted that defiled consciousnesses can effect such continuity.
This is the view of those who maintain that the past and future do not exist.
At that time, the maturation (vipāka) of the three periods of time would all be non-existent.
Since maturation is non-existent,
upon what could birth be said to depend?
One must certainly admit that there is a real dharma which serves as the basis for birth; thus, in the Mahāyāna, the existence of the ālayavijñāna is without fault.
However, the Sautrāntikas are at fault, as stated in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol. 147): [text follows].

Question: At that time, other formless faculties are also acquired—namely, the mental faculty (*manas*), the five feelings (*vedanā*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*). Why are these not mentioned here?
Answer: Some say:
At that time, "attainment by all" refers specifically to those mentioned herein;
although other formless faculties may also be attained,
they do not constitute attainment by all.
Therefore, it is not mentioned;
that is to say, when one dies in a higher stage and is reborn in a lower stage,
although one acquires those faculties, [they are not so designated].
If one dies from a particular stage and is reborn again in that same stage, none of those [acquisitions] are obtained;
therefore, they are not mentioned. The commentary states:
This explains that what was previously unaccomplished and is now acquired is termed "acquisition" (prāpti).
If one dies in a particular realm and is reborn in that same realm,
it is not called "attainment" because [the factors] were already established previously.
However, when one dies in a lower realm and is born in a higher realm, [it is so called].
At that time, the wholesome and defiled [roots] are also first accomplished.
Only the ripening roots (*vipāka-indriya*) cannot be acquired prior to the dharma;

they are designated as "acquisition" (*prāpti*) when first obtained in their respective places of birth. Question: If it is said that although they are equally within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they differ because their retributions (*vipāka*) are distinct.
Regarding this statement that "this root of the indeterminate is called 'firstly obtained,'" why is it said that one obtains consciousness but not the eye?
It is as when one dies from the second, third, or fourth dhyāna and is born into the first dhyāna or the desire realm.
One may attain its consciousness but not its eye, because the eye was already attained in a previous life. Answer: The preceding text composed its treatise based on the eighteen *dhātus*.

Regarding the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), it speaks of it in general terms without distinguishing between different realms (*dhātu*), different stages (*bhūmi*), or the distinctions of karma and its fruit.
In this context, the distinction is explained in terms of the karmic fruit regarding the faculties of maturation (*vipākendriya*).
Although one may have previously established the eye faculty within the same level (*bhūmi*),
it is designated as "attainment" (*prāpti*) because the karmic fruits are not identical.
Furthermore, it is said:
here, the question concerns only those [faculties] produced by karma acquired at the very beginning;
as for the other formless faculties, they exist at the stage of initial rebirth.
Although there are those who attain it, it is not mentioned here because it is not produced by karma;
although what is attained in the subsequent stage is produced by karma, it is not mentioned here because it is not the initial attainment.
The intent of this treatise is the same as that of the subsequent passage.
The treatise asks:
"Up to how many faculties does the maturation faculty (vipāka-indriya) persist before it ceases?"
The next verse, the second [of this section], clarifies the number of faculties that cease at the final moment.
The commentary states: "Abiding in the formless realm until the final cessation" explains the formless realm.
In the previous [passage], formless realms were mentioned first and the desire realm last;
in this text, the desire realm is mentioned first and the formless realms last, following the thematic convenience of the preceding discussion.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
Furthermore, the term "formless" (ārūpya) excludes the possibility that they possess form,
because other masters assert that they do possess form. This would be the case if one did not state that the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) exists as a substantial entity (dravya).
In what way is the cessation of maturation termed "death in the formless realm"?
If you say it is called death because the four aggregates of maturation cease,
then one should also be said to die at the moment when a wholesome or defiled mind manifests.
If it is said that the maturation experienced in that stage is not yet exhausted,
how could there be a point of exhaustion without further experience?
This occurs at the moment when wholesome or defiled minds manifest.
One should say that it is the maturation of karma that is experienced there; for that which is not manifest cannot be called "experience.
If it is argued that it is called "experience" because the latencies of that maturation constantly persist therein, [that is not so].
This reasoning is also incorrect,
because the habit-energies (vāsanā) you maintain are not universally established,
and because it entails the fallacy of over-extension.
Although the maturation (vipāka) may be exhausted, because the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) persist,
it would be as if there were no time of death for the habitual tendencies of karma.
If the maturation were exhausted and the habitual tendencies were absent, [death would occur].
Karma, moreover, should not possess residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
If it is argued that habitual tendencies, in relation to the present maturation (*vipāka*), are like my acquisition [of a body],
then just as my acquisition gives rise to maturation but does not produce habitual tendencies, those [tendencies] would likewise be non-existent.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the evolving ripening habitual tendencies are called "feeling" (vedanā),
because ripening is not of their nature.
Moreover, the habitual tendencies you postulate are logically non-existent.
This shall be explained in detail later. The *Chao-shi* (Excerpts and Explanations) states:
"In our school, acquisition (*prāpti*) exists upon the dharma that is the maturation (*vipāka*).
If the maturation ceases, the acquisition likewise ceases."
It is obtained through different karmas.
According to the treatise, this is because if one is in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one undergoes birth and death there.
This explains the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
It may be understood according to the text. [End of] Treatise.
If one is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are only the first eight [stages].
This explains the desire realm;
it can be understood according to the text.
Treatise:
What has been explained thus far concerns death by sudden termination;
this concludes the preceding discussion on cessation based on sudden termination.
Treatise:
Regarding the meaning of gradual death, which extends up to the point where [the faculties] cease first and last,
the explanation of the gradual cessation of the faculties— whether many or few— is as can be understood from the text.
Treatise:
Regarding what has been stated above concerning those who pass away upon reaching [the destination],
this summarizes the two types of death— sudden and gradual.
As for those who pass away while in a defiled or neutral state of mind,
the number of faculties that cease is identical for both defiled and neutral minds;
therefore, they are explained together.
Treatise:
If one is within the three realms, it should be understood accordingly as far as the state of suchness.
Next, the death-moment of a wholesome mind is explained.
According to what is appropriate, one adds the five faculties beginning with faith to the previously described stage of the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
[Question:
In the analysis of the faculties, at which fruit of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) does this occur?
The third verse below clarifies the number of faculties required for the attainment of the fruit.
Here, "attainment" refers to both the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Prior to the attainment of the fruit, it acts as the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*); subsequently, it functions as the sustaining cause (*niśraya-hetu*).
By virtue of this, the two preceding and succeeding fruits are necessarily attained by means of the two untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*). Herein, the term "attainment" (*prāpti*) is used.
The term "attainment" (*prāpti*) refers to the initial realization;
it does not refer to subsequent stages or the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).

If one were to speak of the refinement of the faculties, then the first and last fruits would each have to be attained by eight faculties. Furthermore, what is meant here by "attainment" is as follows:
This is called "attainment" (*prāpti*) because it serves as the proximate cause for the path that brings about the fruit.

The treatise states: "Because it reaches [the fruit] while remaining in the intermediate state," this provides a general explanation of the term "fruit" (*phala*) in relation to both the extremes and the middle.
Treatise:
From the initial stage of the fruit of stream-entry up to its nature as the causal basis,
this explains the first fruit.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Although the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is not a cause of similar type (*sabhāga-hetu*) with respect to the fruit of śrāmaṇya,
it is nonetheless called the 'attainment' of that fruit because it functions as a concomitant cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) and a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*)."
Nor is there any fault,
because the nature of śramaṇas arises through mutual dependence;
they are reciprocally related as the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Who, moreover, could obstruct it?
If it is argued that the preparatory, uninterrupted, and superior stages should likewise be so,
we grant this and see no fault.
Alternatively, the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātendriya*) may also serve as a homogeneous cause for attaining the fruit of stream-entry;
that is to say, when one transforms the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), it is possible— just as in the case of an Arhat—
to speak in this way without any fault.
Treatise:
Because the fruit of arhatship serves as the causal basis for reliance,
this explains the subsequent fruit.
The two paths support one another as explained in the commentary on the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).
Although the three faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) may be present,
at the precise moment of attaining the fruit, only one faculty is experienced.
It does not exceed nine faculties.
Although the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) do not occur simultaneously,
their results— the outflow result (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the virile result (*puruṣakāra-phala*)— are simultaneous.
There is also no fault in this. According to the treatise,
the two intermediate fruits are attained by means of nine faculties.
From this point onward, the two fruits within the [section on] "Exposition" are explained.
First, the total number of faculties is explained in general;
subsequently, each one is explained individually.
This is the first [point]. The treatise asks:
Why is it that [attainment] is achieved by means of nine faculties? It continues until: "achieved by means of nine faculties."
The explanation of the second fruit consists of three parts:
first, attainment by means of the mundane path through seven faculties;
second, attainment by means of the supramundane path through eight faculties.
Third, regarding attainment through transcendence, it is achieved by means of nine faculties. According to the treatise:
if one proceeds from the fruit of non-returner to the attainment of the fruit of once-returner...
From here below, the third fruit is explained; herein there are four sections.
Three are as explained for the fruit of the once-returner.
Treatise:
Although it is stated in general that there is no difference,
the following section provides a detailed explanation of the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
Although the number of faculties (*indriya*) for this fruit is the same as those of the preceding fruits, [there are distinctions].

However, there is a distinction regarding the faculty of feeling (*vedanendriya*); that is to say, the aforementioned leap-over (*vyutkrāntaka*) employs only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*),
because it relies upon the *anāgamya* stage.
This fruit transcends pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*prīti*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*),
because it is possible to realize the three fruits by relying on six stages.
Relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), and the fourth dhyāna, it consists of the feeling of equanimity.
In the first two dhyānas there is joy (prīti);
in the third dhyāna there is the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
Even for one who proceeds through the stages in succession, it differs from what preceded.
Regarding the ninth liberation, one either enters the fundamental stage or remains in the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*).
If one enters the fundamental stage, the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is added.
If one does not enter [the path], it is the same as the result mentioned previously.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 148, states:
"Question: Regarding the ninth path of liberation that abandons the defilements of the desire realm..."
Who enters meditative absorption and who does not?
The answer is: some say that those with a predominance of joy enter.
Those who are weary of much do not enter.
Some say that those who seek dhyāna and thereby become free from defilement enter.
Those who have become detached from defilements for the sake of seeking liberation do not enter.
Some say that those of sharp faculties do enter.
Those of dull faculties do not enter [the fundamental stage].
This is from the treatise (*śāstra*). Furthermore, all three explanations are equally valid;
therefore, there is no formal evaluation (*anirṇaya*). Question: For what reason does one successively realize the entry into the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*)?
For one who has attained transcendence through realization, such a principle does not exist. Answer: The afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation are of many different types.
Some are abandoned by taking delight in the higher realms and feeling aversion toward the lower ones.
If one possesses sharp faculties and an abundance of joyful aspiration, one may enter the fundamental state.
Alternatively, some may sever delusion for the sake of seeking liberation, while others do so for the sake of seeking meditative concentration (dhyāna).
If one possesses sharp faculties, they may enter the fundamental [dhyāna] for the sake of attaining meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
Although the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) belongs to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
it is possible for those with sharp faculties to remain engaged for many moments.
However, for the sake of realizing the principles of the truths (*satya*),
if one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) based on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*),
one does not do so out of a longing for higher stages.

It is not for the sake of seeking dhyāna that one enters the path of seeing; therefore, one does not enter the fundamental [dhyānas]. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that one first attains the fundamental dhyānas.
If the intention (*āśaya*) is based on a fundamental stage (*maula*), it relies upon that fundamental stage;
if the intention has not yet reached a fundamental stage, it relies upon the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*).
Consequently, the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*) and the liberation concentration (*vimukti-samādhi*) must necessarily belong to the same stage.
Because the delusions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception have been severed, there is no higher stage left to be sought with aspiration;
thus, one attains the fourth fruit based on the *anāgamya* (uninterrupted) concentration,
and does not enter the fundamental dhyāna during the path of liberation.
Treatise:
Is it not the case that the fundamental [attainment] is obtained by means of nine faculties?
Question:
Treatise:
Is it truly attained that one reaches the fourth dhyāna by means of nine faculties?
Answer: Yes.
Treatise:
Why is it not stated in this way regarding the fruit of non-returning?
This is a further objection.
Commentary:
Because the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) is utterly firm and stable,
it is pervasive.
This may be understood according to the text. As stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, fascicle 15:
"How many faculties (*indriya*) are permanently severed, extinguished, and arise when one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*)?"
Answer: When the rootless [defilements] are eternally severed,
seven roots cease and arise,
while one ceases and does not arise.
Together they attain the fruit of stream-entry without retrogression. The commentary states:
"Permanent abandonment" refers to the meaning of attaining dissociation through the permanent severance of fetters regarding the faculties.
Regarding "arising and ceasing," it means that the path of uninterrupted transition ceases and the path of liberation arises.
Regarding "ceasing without arising," it means:
The path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) ceases, while the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) does not arise.
As for the statement that it "arises but does not cease":
because the path of uninterrupted transition no longer exists, it does not cease.
It is said that [the faculties] "arise" because the path of liberation arises anew.
At the time of attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*),
there is not a single faculty that attains permanent liberation from bondage.
Therefore, it is said that the roots are eternally severed.
As for the statement that "seven roots arise and cease," this refers to the five faculties beginning with faith, as well as the mental faculty and the faculty of equanimity.
The path of uninterrupted transition ceases and the path of liberation arises.
That which ceases but does not arise is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya).
After the fifteenth moment of mind has ceased, it does not arise again;
that which arises and does not cease is called the faculty of knowledge (ājñendriya).
The sixteenth mind does not cease because the fifteenth mind is absent. How many faculties (indriya) are permanently severed, ceased, or arise?
One attains the fruit of the Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).
Answer: If one who has already partially abandoned the defilements of desire enters into the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), [the following occurs].
As it was explained regarding the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*):
if one realizes the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*) from the fruit of stream-entry by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*),
there is no permanent abandonment of faculties (*indriya*).
"By the cessation and arising of seven faculties, one attains the fruit of Once-returner.
Commentary: Regarding the permanent abandonment of faculties, it is explained in the same manner as for the Stream-enterer.
Regarding the arising and ceasing of the seven faculties:

this is also the same as for the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). If one realizes the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) from the fruit of stream-entry by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), no faculties are permanently severed.
Eight faculties arise and cease to attain the fruit of once-returner. Commentary states:
Regarding the arising and ceasing of the eight faculties:
by adding the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) to the seven faculties,
they are all extinguished through the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*).
Because the path of liberation arises, how many faculties are permanently severed, extinguished, or produced?
One attains the fruit of non-returning.
Answer: If one who has already become detached from the defilements of desire enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), no faculty is permanently severed.
Seven faculties cease and arise;
one ceases but does not arise;
one arises but does not cease.
Regarding the attainment of the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), the commentary states:
"As for the permanent abandonment of the faculties (*indriya*):
this is because the faculties are not extinguished during the fifteenth and sixteenth moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)."
Regarding the cessation and arising of seven faculties:
if one relies on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), or the fourth dhyāna,
these consist of the five faculties beginning with faith, as well as the mental faculty and the equanimity faculty.
If based on the first or second dhyāna, there are the five faculties beginning with faith, as well as the mental faculty and the faculty of joy.

If based on the third dhyāna, joy is excluded and the faculty of pleasure is added. If one realizes the fruit of non-returner from the fruit of once-returner by means of the mundane path, one does not enter meditative absorption.
The four faculties are eternally severed;
the seven faculties cease and arise as one attains the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*). Commentary:
Regarding "the four faculties are eternally severed":
That is to say, sorrow, suffering, femininity, and masculinity cease because of the abandonment of desire; thus,
seven faculties arise and cease.
As stated regarding the stream-enterer:
if one enters meditative absorption, four faculties are permanently severed and six faculties cease and arise.
"One ceases and does not arise;
one arises and does not cease.
Thus one attains the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). Commentary states:
The six faculties arise and cease;
that is to say, the five beginning with faith, as well as the faculty of joy and the mental faculty.
One [faculty] ceases and does not arise.
This refers to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), which arises and does not cease;

and the faculty of joy (*prītīndriya*). This occurs when one realizes the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) from the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*) by means of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).
If one does not enter meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), four faculties are permanently severed;
eight faculties cease and arise upon attaining the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*). The commentary states:

"The cessation and arising of eight faculties" refers to the addition of the faculty of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) to the seven faculties. If one enters meditative absorption, four faculties are permanently severed.
Seven faculties cease and arise;
one faculty ceases and does not arise;
one faculty arises and does not cease—one who attains this is a non-returner (*anāgāmin*). Commentary states:
Regarding the seven that cease upon arising:
these refer to the five faculties beginning with faith, as well as the faculty of mental cognition.
The one that ceases without arising is the faculty of equanimity.
Regarding the simultaneous non-extinction: what faculties are eternally severed and extinguished when one attains the fruit of arhatship?
Answer: If one realizes the fruit of arhatship based on the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) stage, [the following faculties are extinguished].
One faculty is eternally severed;
seven faculties are eternally severed, extinguished, and do not arise;
one faculty is extinguished and does not arise.
Together they attain the fruit of arhatship without retrogression.

As it is with reliance on the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage], so it is with reliance on the intermediate dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the three formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*). (Commentary:)

The single faculty that is eternally severed is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). The seven faculties that are eternally severed, cease, and arise are as follows: [the six faculties of sensation and the mind-faculty].
The five faculties beginning with faith, as well as the mental faculty and equanimity—when one is in the state of neither-arising-nor-ceasing, it is called the faculty of "knowing";
when one is in the state of arising-not-ceasing, it is called the faculty of "one who has fully known. If, based on the first dhyāna, one realizes the fruit of arhatship.
The two faculties are permanently severed;
the six faculties are permanently severed and cease to arise;
one faculty ceases and arises.

When one ceases, the other does not arise; when one arises, the other does not cease, and thus one attains the fruit of arhatship. This is the same whether relying on the first dhyāna, or the second or third dhyānas. [Commentary: The commentary states: When the practitioner relies on the first dhyāna, the mind that has entered the path of seeing (darśanamārga) ceases, and the mind that has entered the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) arises. Because these two minds do not coexist, the practitioner abandons the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing through the power of the path of seeing, and abandons the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation through the power of the path of cultivation. By means of this, one attains the fruit of arhatship. This is the same when relying on the second or third dhyānas. It should be understood that the same applies to the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti). Furthermore, it should be understood that this principle applies to all nine successive attainments (anupūrvavihārasamāpatti), from the first dhyāna up to the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñāvedayitanirodha). Why is this? Because the path of seeing and the path of cultivation cannot exist simultaneously within a single continuum of consciousness. Therefore, the practitioner must rely on the nine successive attainments to abandon the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing and the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation, thereby attaining the fruit of arhatship. Thus, it is said that "one ceases, the other does not arise; one arises, the other does not cease. This is because the two paths cannot coexist. If they could coexist, then the afflictions would not be abandoned. Since they are not abandoned, one would not attain the fruit of arhatship. Therefore, it is established that one attains the fruit of arhatship by means of the non-coexistence of these two paths. This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "one attains the fruit of arhatship," this refers to the attainment of the fruit of arhatship through the power of the path of cultivation. It does not mean that the fruit of arhatship is attained solely through the power of the path of seeing. Why is this? Because the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation are extremely subtle and difficult to eliminate. Therefore, one must rely on the power of the path of cultivation to abandon them. Consequently, it is said that one attains the fruit of arhatship through the power of the path of cultivation. This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "this is the same for the second and third dhyānas," this means that the principle of abandoning afflictions through the non-coexistence of the two paths applies equally to the second and third dhyānas. It should be understood that the same applies to the fourth dhyāna and the four formless attainments. Why is this? Because the nature of the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing and the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation is the same across all nine successive attainments. Therefore, the principle of their non-coexistence is identical. This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "it should be understood that this applies to all nine successive attainments," this means that the principle of attaining the fruit of arhatship through the non-coexistence of the two paths applies to all nine successive attainments. It is not limited to the four dhyānas alone. Why is this? Because the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments are all included within the nine successive attainments. Therefore, the principle of attaining the fruit of arhatship through the non-coexistence of the two paths applies universally to all nine. This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation are extremely subtle and difficult to eliminate," this means that the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation are more subtle than those to be abandoned by seeing. Because they are subtle, they are difficult to eliminate. Therefore, one must rely on the power of the path of cultivation to abandon them. This is the meaning. That is to say, equanimity is virtuous by nature and is induced by a mind that acts in accordance with reality;

That this treatise lacks alertness means that it is without restlessness (*auddhatya*).

The commentary below explains this. Regarding the treatise:

The treatise states: "Non-harming" means the absence of injury or affliction. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* says:

Regarding diligence (*vīrya*), its nature is defined as that which causes the mind to be courageous and resolute. As the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
Regarding all virtues already arisen, one guards them; regarding faults already arisen, one abandons them.
Regarding virtues not yet arisen, one causes them to arise; regarding faults not yet arisen, one prevents them from arising.
The absence of mental laxity is called diligence (*vīrya*).
Because of its presence, the mind applies itself with firm perseverance and without ceasing toward tasks that are performed in accordance with reason. This is based on the *Nyāyabindu*.
Within the category of wholesome states (*kuśala-dharma*), joy (*abhinandana*) and aversion (*vidūṣaṇā*) are further established;
however, these do not pervade all wholesome minds.
Therefore, that treatise says:
The mention of "the two" and the word "and" also includes both delight (*abhinandanā*) and aversion (*vidūṣaṇā*).
Aversion refers to the nature of a wholesome mind that carefully contemplates the quality of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as having immeasurable faults;
it is the state of turning away from [objects] through a mind of non-attachment (*alobha*) arising by the power of this contemplation.
That which corresponds to this is called the mental attention of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-manasikāra*).
"Aspiration" (*abhirati*) refers to the seeking of wholesome states regarding faults, renunciation, and remedies.
It is the nature of the mind’s longing for realization and cultivation, which arises through the predominant power of that [seeking].
Since this [mental factor] also manifests in states such as the *anāgamya* (preliminary stage) where joy has been abandoned, it is not the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*).
That which is associated with this is called "joyful attention" (*abhipramodana-manasikāra*).
These two modes of activity (*ākāra*) are mutually contradictory.
Therefore, it is impossible for [these factors] to arise simultaneously within a single moment of mind.
For this reason, they are not explicitly taught here,

Malice (*pradāśa*) is the outflow of views (*dṛṣṭi*); thus, it is subsumed under right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) by reversing the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Right view is precisely the wisdom within the universal mental ground (*mahābhūmika*).
Therefore, it cannot be established as a separate factor among the wholesome states.
Concealment (*mrakṣa*) is either a derivative of greed (*lobha*) or, conversely, is included within non-greed (*alobha*).
Alternatively, those that are outflows of delusion (*moha*) revert into non-delusion (*amoha*).
Since non-delusion is wisdom (*prajñā*), it is not established as a separate factor among the wholesome states.
Stinginess (*mātsarya*), deceit (*śāṭhya*), arrogance (*mada*), and sensual greed (*kāmarāga*) revert into non-greed (*alobha*).
Deceit (*śāṭhya*) is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the various views;
it is reversed by right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Since right view is itself a factor of wisdom (*prajñā*), it is not established as a wholesome [root] here. According to the gate of outflows, there are only nine that are reversed.
Because pride and doubt are root afflictions and not outflows,
these two types cannot be reversed.
Although *vihiṃsā* (harmfulness) is a specific, heavy derivative of *dveṣa* (hatred),
it has already been explained as such previously. As for what is called a "counter-correspondence based on similarity of aspect," examples include *krodha* (anger),
*upanāha* (enmity), *īrṣyā* (envy), and *pradāśa* (malice).
That which resembles the aspect of hatred is subsumed under non-hatred;
that which is an outflow of greed and resembles the aspect of greed is subsumed under non-greed;
and that which is an outflow of delusion and resembles the aspect of delusion is subsumed under non-delusion.
These are subsumed under wisdom.
The two types, stinginess and deceit, resemble the aspect of greed; conversely, they are included within non-greed.
Flattery (*śāṭhya*) refers to crookedness;
the opposite of crookedness is straightforwardness (*rjju*).
Straightforwardness is equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, chapter three, states:

Reverence (*gaurava*) is the opposite of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*); when it is reversed, it enters into shamelessness.

Although harm (*vihiṃsā*) resembles anger (*krodha*), its faults are more severe; it has been separately translated as such, as already explained previously.

Vitarka and vicāra should not be considered to arise simultaneously within a single moment of mind.

This statement is unreasonable.
I did not definitively state that vinegar is used as an analogy for vitarka and vicāra while water is used as an analogy;
rather, I merely meant that whichever factor increases in its function [is the one compared].
It is said that they are like vinegar; thus, within a mental state (*citta-pakṣa*), whichever of the two factors— vitarka or vicāra—

Therefore, although vitarka and vicāra are both substantially present within the mind,

Just as greed and delusion may both manifest simultaneously, yet one can say that the mind "acts with greed," so too,

It causes the mind to become arrogant and heedless, lacking all regard for its own nature;
regarding such qualities as personal prowess, wealth, status, morality, wisdom, and lineage,
it first gives rise to a mind of defiled attachment and thereby becomes arrogant and heedless.
Because one looks back upon the roots of all virtues with no regard, it is called *mada* (arrogance).
To have no regard for the roots of all virtues means that,

This is called the distinction between the characteristics of conceit (*māna*) and pride (*mada*).
According to other masters, [the explanation] continues up to the point of these distinctive characteristics.

Because they are equally conjoined,

It is called "having an aspect" (*sākāra*).

This is just as, among all phenomena that arise simultaneously with the outflows (*āsrava*),

Therefore, there is no fault.

The acquisition of conditioned phenomena varies according to the specific nature and category of the phenomenon acquired.
Because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) possess functional activity (*kāritra*) that can induce their own acquisition (*prāpti*),
the acquisition of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) varies according to the specific nature and category of the path that realizes it;
for analytical cessations themselves lack any functional activity.
However, because it is through the power of the path that one seeks realization at that time, and thereby brings about the attainment of that [cessation],
the attainment of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) follows the specific distinctions of the nature of its own basis;
for non-analytical cessation itself lacks causal activity and is not what is sought by the path.

That acquisition (prāpti) manifests solely in dependence upon the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) and the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga); therefore, these phenomena of the three natures are acquired by their own intrinsic nature.
Although one acquires analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha), it is not [acquired] by means of that which is acquired.
The attainment of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) depends upon the homogeneous class of beings (nikāya-sabhāga) and so forth.
The Path (mārga) shares the same nature as analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha),
while the homogeneous class of beings shares the same nature as non-analytical cessation.
Because of these two types, although they do not arise from what is attained,
they are necessarily of the same nature as that which is attained; thus,
these three natures are necessarily of the same nature as their attainment.
Treatise:
Furthermore, there are four kinds of acquisition (*prāpti*) regarding bound phenomena (*baddha-dharma*).
This is the section on the gates of the bound and the unbound.
The dharmas thus attained are of four kinds: namely,
those bound to the three realms constitute three,
and those unbound constitute the fourth.
The attainment that is capable of attaining also has four kinds, as explained above. Furthermore, there are two kinds of dharmas that are attained:
first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
That is to say, the phenomena of the three realms and the noble truth of the path;
the second consists of the unconditioned,
namely the two kinds of cessation.
The attainment that is able to attain is exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Furthermore, the dharmas that are attained are of two kinds:
first, those with outflows (*sāsrava*), namely, the dharmas bound to the three realms.
Two are untainted (*anāsrava*):
namely, the Noble Truth of the Path and the two types of cessation (*nirodha*). The acquisitions (*prāpti*) that can obtain them are also of two kinds:
first, those that are tainted (*sāsrava*).
That is to say, those bound to the three realms and the two untainted [factors],
namely the Noble Truth of the Path.
Because the dharmas bound to the three realms are conditioned,
the acquisition that attains them—
derived from those acquired dharmas— is itself exclusively bound to the three realms.
Because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are universally applicable,

the acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is bound by the body upon which it depends; the acquisition of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), however, follows from the path that effects its abandonment.
The Path is said to be "universal" because it penetrates both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
If it is a tainted path, it is bound to the realms of form and formlessness;
if it is an untainted path, it is unbound by virtue of being the Path itself.
Because the acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) follows the person (*pudgala*),
it pertains to all three realms (*dhātu*). Thus, while the acquisition of bound phenomena (*saṃyukta-dharma*) consists of only three types,
the acquisition of unbound phenomena (*asaṃyukta-dharma*) pertains to all four types.
The Treatise states:
Furthermore, the attainment (*prāpti*) of the dharmas of one in training (*śaikṣa*) is itself that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
This clarifies the gateway of the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*).
Because the dharmas of training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
the acquisition (*prāpti*) that attains them is itself an acquisition of the dharmas of training and those beyond training.
Because that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa) includes the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), there are three types of acquisition (prāpti):
the acquisition of conditioned (saṃskṛta) and outflowing (sāsrava) phenomena, as well as the acquisition of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha),
is the acquisition of that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Regarding the three types of acquisition (prāpti) of cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha):
if it is acquired by the path of training (śaikṣa-mārga), that acquisition is of the state of training;
if it is acquired by the path beyond training (aśaikṣa-mārga), that acquisition is of the state beyond training.
If it is a contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*), it induces that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, regarding the dharmas abandoned by seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*), they all reach the state of being non-abandonable (*aprahātavya*).
This clarifies the gate of the three types of abandonment.
Since dharmas abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
their acquisition (*prāpti*) may pertain to both types of abandonment according to the dharma acquired.
Dharmas not to be abandoned (aheya) comprise all three types:
namely, conditioned untainted (anāsrava-saṃskṛta) dharmas, cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), and cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
The acquisition (prāpti) of conditioned untainted dharmas is exclusively not to be abandoned, following from the dharmas they acquire.
The acquisition of cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is both contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava), because it arises from the Path.
That which is contaminated is abandoned by the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga); that which is uncontaminated is not abandoned.

The acquisition of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) arises from the homogeneous class of beings (nikāya-sabhāga) and the life-faculty (jīvitendriya); therefore, it is abandoned solely by the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga).
The remainder of the text is easily understood and thus is not cited for explanation.

excluding the supernormal powers of the eye and ear, as well as their co-arising acquisitions (*prāpti*).

there is acquisition [of them] across the three time periods. Treatise:
If it is also admitted that the same applies to the acquisition of the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*),
this clarifies that for those [actions] of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship that are extremely well-practiced,
it is also admitted that there is acquisition both prior to and simultaneously with the action.
This explains the mind, not matter.
Even for obscured-unspecified matter, there would be no prior or subsequent acquisition;
how much more so for unobscured-unspecified matter?
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 126, states:

this refers to that which can arise, having the two spheres of mind (*manas*) and mental objects (*dharma*) as its essence. Regarding the two types of neutral minds (*avyākṛta-citta*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are no acquisitions (*prāpti*) prior to or subsequent to them.
The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (or *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra*) states:

"One who possesses a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*) or an unwholesome mind (*akuśala-citta*) of the desire realm necessarily possesses the non-obscured neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) of the desire realm. Based on this text, it is certain that the non-obscured neutral mind has acquisitions belonging to the three time periods.
The treatise states:
"Only the acquisitions (*prāpti*) that are non-obscured (*anivṛta*) exist prior to and subsequent to the dharma.
This clarifies the case of obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter (*rūpa*).
This can be understood according to the text.
This refers to the bodily and vocal intimation (*kāya-vāk-vijñapti*) arising from a defiled mind within the first dhyāna or the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*);
therefore, this karma does not exist in any other stages.

[Abhidharma] Treatise.
Just as with indeterminate dharmas, there is acquisition at the time of arrival and subsequent arising.
This clarifies that for wholesome and unwholesome matter (*rūpa*) in the desire realm, there is no prior acquisition of the dharma;
it exists only simultaneously with the dharma itself.
Because the power of a dharma that follows cannot draw forth its preceding acquisition,
if this matter is in the future, its future acquisition is also [in the future].
If it pertains to the present or the future, it is acquired in the present;
if it pertains to the past, it is acquired throughout the three periods of time.
This applies to the first untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) and to wholesome states of application (*prayoga-kuśala*) that arise for the first time.
If it is in the future, it is acquired in the future;
if it reaches the present, it is acquired in both the future and the present;
if it reaches the past, it is acquired across all three periods of time.
Other dharmas differ from these; one may understand this by reflecting upon them.
[Question:
Regarding non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), it is as acquisition (*prāpti*) is; is it not so? If not, how is it?
From here below, one and a half verses clarify the distinctions of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).

Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 158, states:
Question: To which category of nature does non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) correspond?

Because they are contradictory,
and furthermore, they do not follow the Path;

According to the distinctions among the natures of their respective bases.

Question: If all non-attainments (*aprāpti*) and the attainment of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-prāpti*) alike follow the distinctions among the natures of their respective bases, [then...]
The basis is either the maturation (*vipāka*) or exclusively the outflow (*niṣyanda*);
whichever of these two types it may be, such is its specific nature.
Answer: It follows the nature of the outflow (*niṣyanda*) because its meaning is universal;

Question: If non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) were to follow the specific categories of the nature of the dharmas not yet acquired, what fault would there be?
Answer: One who has severed the roots of goodness should possess the wholesome;
one who is already free from the defilement of desire should possess the unwholesome;
and all those beyond training (aśaikṣa) should possess the defiled.
Ordinary beings would consequently possess the untainted dharmas of the three vehicles;
those who have fallen from a fruit would become those who have attained a fruit; and those who have abandoned the path of approach would become those who have attained that path.
The non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the two cessations (*nirodha*) would consequently have to be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because of such faults, it cannot be maintained that non-acquisition corresponds to whatever has not been acquired. Thus concludes the treatise.
Regarding the distinction of time, it extends to non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) across the three periods of time.
This is the second section on the three periods of time.
For both the past and the future, there are three periods each, which are the same as those previously established for acquisition (*prāpti*).
At present, there are only two types of non-entities (*avastu*) that lack both possession (*prāpti*) and non-possession (*aprāpti*),
because sentient beings necessarily possess those dharmas while they abide in the present.
If a present dharma has previously existed as a past dharma, [it is likewise possessed].
A phenomenon that follows is future.
If a phenomenon is past, that which precedes it is exclusively past,
while that which follows it may belong to any of the three time periods.
If a future dharma exists only as a future state in its subsequent phase,
whereas that same dharma may pertain to all three time periods in its prior phase, the *Vibhāṣā* (158) explains non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) accordingly:
There are three types of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) in total:
first, that which precedes the dharma;
second, that which follows the dharma.
Regarding the three types of non-attainment (*aprāpti*)— those prior to, subsequent to, and simultaneous with that dharma—
the dharmas that are not attained are likewise of three kinds.
First, there is only non-attainment prior to the dharma.
This refers to phenomena such as future sentient beings that are subject to ultimate non-arising,
as well as the final moment of consciousness at the time of entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
These two types of existent phenomena (*bhāva*) possess non-possession (*aprāpti*) both prior to and subsequent to the phenomenon itself.
This refers to other phenomena included among sentient beings as appropriate.
Regarding the three types of existence, there are non-attainments (aprāpti) that exist without being prior, posterior, or simultaneous with those [phenomena];
these are namely cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
It is certain that non-acquisition (aprāpti) cannot coexist with a dharma;
for when a dharma manifests, there must necessarily be an acquisition (prāpti) of that acquired dharma.
Because there is no non-acquisition (aprāpti) for a dharma that has not been acquired.

Furthermore, it is not the case that there is only the subsequent non-acquisition of that dharma, for such [non-acquisition] does not exist from beginningless time; rather, one must always possess it, and as long as it has not been relinquished, the entire class of that [dharma] necessarily arises.
However, because the nature of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is weak and inferior, it exists only in the present;
having been acquired in each successive moment, it is immediately relinquished.
This applies both to the state when that dharma has not yet been acquired and to the state when it has already been relinquished.
It should be understood that this non-possession (*aprāpti*) exists eternally. Now, let us examine the Sarvāstivādins: they maintain that there are those who absolutely lack the nature for *nirvāṇa*.
It is called "absolute" (*atyanta*) because of the extreme remoteness of time.
If this were not the case, then there would necessarily be a category of dharmas that possess only possession (*prāpti*) and no non-possession.
This refers to the afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (asaṃjñisattva) belonging to those who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa.
There is a class of dharmas that possess only non-acquisition (aprāpti) and no acquisition (prāpti);
namely, the paths of the noble ones of the three vehicles belonging to those who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa.

This would contradict the established principle that the possession of something must necessarily be counterposed by its non-possession. If it were claimed that those lacking the nature for *nirvāṇa* likewise lack the non-possession of the noble paths of the three vehicles, then such a person would not be an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*).
Because there is no nature of being a non-noble being (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, in the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, Vasubandhu Bodhisattva explains that the Sarvāstivādins establish the absence of the dharma of nirvāṇa based on the distinction of stages (*avasthā*).
It is not the case that it is fixed by the nature of things (*dharmatā*) to say that icchantikas who have violated the heavy prohibitions lack the dharma of nirvāṇa;
therefore, when the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi* speaks of "the nature of things," it is a provisional statement based on the fundamental [truth].

As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (She dasheng lun shi) explains the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it states that the perfuming of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) serves as the cause for the untainted (*anāsrava*), being described as "provisional" (*āgantuka*) while referring to the "original" (*mūla*). Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* distinguishes this from the "non-acquisition prior to the dharmas" (*aprāpti-pūrva-dharma*).
This refers to those phenomena belonging to the category of sentient beings that will never arise in the future,
as well as the final moment of consciousness at the time of entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. The term "future" serves to distinguish these from the past and the present.
To speak of "numerous" is to simplify that which is beyond conceptualization;
to speak of "ultimate non-arising" is likewise a simplification.
This refers to phenomena that do not arise even for a brief moment.

Although there is nothing lacking, this is identical in meaning to the past views-afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). The types of afflictions associated with views regarding the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) are numerous;

and although there is only the subsequent non-acquisition (aprāpti) of those dharmas.

If one explains it in this way,

Treatise:
Why is this so? From this point onward, the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva*) is elucidated.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 45, states:

"The Vātsīputrīya school maintains that the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva*) consists of the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 52, states: [as above].
Furthermore, what is the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)?

It is defined as the measure of the seeds of the dharmas of the three realms to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) that have not yet been permanently destroyed; this is called the nature of being an ordinary person. Now, let us examine this in detail.
The phrase "only not yet permanently destroyed" refers to the stage prior to the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*),
and not to the period following the Path of Uninterrupted Succession (*ānantaryamārga*);
this is because it refers to the destruction of the afflictions to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).
Since it has already been stated that "only" refers to the measure of not yet having permanently destroyed [the afflictions],
this means that the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) is not defined by the measure of destroying only a portion [of them];
for the word "only" serves to exclude such a possibility.
People of the present day explain it thus: "The nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is established upon the seeds of the two obstructions.

A Śrāvaka who has severed the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is called 'not an ordinary person,' yet because they still possess the obstruction to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), they are still termed 'ordinary persons.'"
If that were the case, since both obstacles pertain to both the paths of seeing and cultivation,
and only a Buddha can exhaust the seeds of both obstacles,
it would follow that only a single person— the Buddha— could be designated as a "noble one" (*ārya*).
All others are both ordinary beings and noble ones,
depending on whether the seeds of their obstructions have been severed or not.

Answer: Dhyāna first arises due to three conditions:
first, the power of causes;

Third is the power of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Formless states first arise due to two conditions:

Second is the power of karma.
The meditative attainment of cessation arises for the first time due to a single condition,

nor does it arise through the power of karma, as this meditative absorption is not of the nature of karma.
It is not by the power of the natural order (*dharmatā*), because there is no destruction of the world within the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*). The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The initial arising of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) occurs only among human beings."
There are those who explain and those who comment;

"This cessation-attainment (nirodha-samāpatti) reaches such a state;

Because one becomes weary of and averse to those two, this concentration arises.
That is to say, perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) serve as the basis for the defilements of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*);
therefore, one first becomes weary of and averse to these two factors, which possess many faults and afflictions.

one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) through a state of particular aversion and repulsion. Thus says the treatise.

This asks about the cause for the mind’s repeated arising.
Treatise:
Regarding the *samanantarapratyaya* (equal-and-immediate condition), the Vaibhāṣika masters cite the explanation from the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*:

However, life must necessarily depend on either form or mind.
The scriptural citation stating that consciousness does not depart from the body is not contradicted even in the case of meditative absorption without mind (*acittaka*),
because it is said that consciousness does not depart since it will necessarily arise again within this very same supporting body.
This means that within a single continuum of a homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*),
the stream of consciousness flows on without being ultimately severed, just as,
for example, when a demonic affliction (*bhūta-graha*) temporarily does not manifest.

Because it has not been permanently eliminated, it is still termed "not separated from"; furthermore, as for the fact that the subsequent mind of meditative absorption can arise again, this is because it was induced by the preceding mind of absorption acting as its equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, because it is induced by the force of a formal undertaking during the stage of preparation (*prayoga*),
the treatise states that other masters say it does not arise from the mind.
This describes the tenets of the Sautrāntika school.

It should be understood that the [attainment of] non-perception up to the others is as previously explained.

Furthermore, those who maintain that the essence of the attainment of cessation is merely conventional do not know what dharma serves as the basis for that conventionality.
"A conventional phenomenon cannot exist apart from its conventional basis. Commentary:
For example, in the case of a conventional entity such as a jar, its basis consists of the four objective spheres, namely form and so forth.
If the four objects do not exist, then neither do the vase and so forth; furthermore, they simply do not function.
Since their essence is non-existent, how can it be said that they are subsumed under conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*)?
They lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in their prior and subsequent stages, as well as in the present.
Because it cannot be apprehended at any time,
yet it is said to exist; thus, it is subsumed under the category of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
These are merely empty words and possess no meaning whatsoever.

and that it is designated as "concentration" because it is induced by a concentrated mind to arise in such a manner, [that too is untenable].
In that case, this meditative absorption (samādhi) should be categorized as indeterminate (avyākṛta).
It cannot be said that an indeterminate dharma is wholesome. [The commentary] states:
If the body serves as the basis, it is itself indeterminate.
The following establishes our own thesis: Therefore, it must be that [the mind] arises solely in dependence upon the mind;
the power of a preceding determinate mind cannot obstruct other minds.
From this, it is known.
Apart from the preceding mind, there must certainly exist a distinct dharma capable of obstructing the mind;
it is because of this dharma that, although the causes for the mind exist during the state of non-consciousness, the mind does not arise.
This distinct dharma is called the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
Its essence is conditioned (saṃskṛta);
it is real and not merely nominal.
Because the practitioner of meditation has been impelled by the power of the vow and aspiration made by the mind prior to meditative concentration,
the force of the attainment of cessation gradually diminishes.
Upon reaching the stage of total exhaustion, its function is unimpeded;
with the mind and dharmas as conditions, mental consciousness arises once again.
Based on this, one should interpret the preceding [sections] concerning the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñika*). Commentary:
These are likewise substantially existent.
The treatise asks:

"That which is called 'life' refers to the lifespan (*āyus*) of the three realms.

Therefore, the World-Honored One said that [the mind] is like wood, devoid of thought and awareness;

Treatise:
Therefore, there exists a distinct dharma which, when it reaches its full expression, is designated as "life-span" (*āyus*).
This concludes the discussion of its essential nature and function.
Treatise:
If that is so, what dharma is able to sustain this life-span?
This is the question.
The treatise states: "That is to say, heat and consciousness are further able to sustain life-force.
This is the answer.
Treatise:
If that were so, it would follow that [the self] is eternal and never ceases;
this is the objection.
Since it has been stated that these three factors mutually support one another,
there can certainly be no prior cessation;

If that is so, must one then wait until [the time] has arrived to require life?

In the Sautrāntika school, life-force (*jīvita*) is defined as the momentum (*sakti*) during the duration of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); it is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*) based upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) in the Mahāyāna, whereas in the Sarvāstivāda school,
it exists as a distinct, substantial entity (*dravya*).
Therefore, the Sautrāntikas say:
"For what reason do you not allow that karma alone can sustain heat and consciousness, rather than requiring life-force (*jīvita*)? [The Abhidharmika] replies:
"The treatise..."
This is logically untenable because it would lead to the consequence that [the body] would remain in a state of constant maturation (*vipāka*). The Vaibhāṣikas offer this rebuttal:
if all consciousness were exclusively maturation, one could say that karma alone is capable of sustaining [the body].
Sentient beings may give rise to wholesome or defiled minds,
as well as various consciousnesses of different stages or those that are untainted (anāsrava).
How, then, can it be said that consciousness is sustained solely by karma?
[The] Treatise:
Since this is so, why is this life-span necessary?

Thus, because consciousness reaches that state where there is no warmth,

[The author] asks:

The Sarvāstivāda establishes its own school's position. The treatise states:
