The Sarvāstivādins inquire about the essence of life-span (*āyus*). The treatise states:
"That which is produced by karma in the three realms and persists is designated as life-span."
The Sautrāntika replies:
It is like the momentum (śakti) present in things such as grain seeds during the period they remain stationary.
This is stated by way of illustration to clarify the point. The *Nyāyabindu* (Treatise on Right Reasoning) says:
"In this regard, one should simply inquire into the intention of the Sūtra's author:
'In what case would there be no internal fivefold form-sphere that is the maturation induced by karma?'"
In those states, there may at times be no sixth mental base (manāyatana) projected by karma; that is,
during the period when a defiled consciousness arises over a long duration,
or during the continuous state of wholesome contaminated or uncontaminated consciousness.
Since there is no force of maturation (vipāka-śakti) projected by karma,
what is said to be life?
It is that wherein there is the maturation of karma.
From the moment of birth until the stage of death, it functions continuously and without interruption;
that which can be described as the momentum of duration projected by karma within a particular locus,
whose continuity is determined, is called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Since this [state] lacks the force of momentum for the duration of the maturation (vipāka) induced by karma that would continuously and uninterruptedly revolve,
how can it be said that this possesses the life-faculty (jīvitendriya)?
Such is the reasoning.
What dharma is it that is called the "propelling force" (*ākṣepa-śakti*) of the duration [of existence] induced by karma?
Since there is no such propelling force for the duration of existence,
to what would the determination of the continuity belong?
Since there is no such certainty of continuity,
on what basis is it said that the duration for which [a being] abides according to its circumstances constitutes the essence of life?
Therefore, the Sūtra-master has merely constructed many words regarding this matter without expressing anything at all.
Furthermore, the analogies cited lack the power to prove [your point].
For example, the continuity projected by a seed proceeds without interruption until the time of maturation, constantly persisting;
likewise, the continuity projected by a discharged arrow proceeds without interruption.
Because it continues to function throughout the period of abiding, these two possess the force (*śakti*) of abiding for as long as they remain until the time of maturation.

It cannot be said that the maturation of karma continues in an uninterrupted succession at all times; rather, once the karma has ceased, one can only speak of a determined continuity of the force of abiding that was projected by it.
Since it remains for as long as it ought to remain,
the analogy cited is incapable of proving [the point]. This is based on the aforementioned treatise.
The *Nyāyabindu* refutes the Sautrāntika tenets;

"There exists a distinct substantial entity which is designated as 'wholesome' (kuśala). Although some individuals provide an explanation following the *Abhidharmakośa* master, it does not accord with the correct principle.

Their reckoning that all phenomena move from here to there with rapid revolution and so forth is entirely due to the power of conditioning forces (*saṃskāra*).
From the moment the arrow is shot until it falls,
its trajectory is like that of a bird carrying its fruit in its beak.

it remains until the time of its falling.

Furthermore, since there would be no distinct obstacle to proceeding toward other directions, the difference in temporal stages—wherein the initial movement is rapid and the subsequent is slow—could not exist;
moreover, there would never be a time of falling away.
Because the initial arousal [of the mind] and its subsequent practice are essentially one. The treatise states:
If it is argued that there is no distinction because they both reach [their destination] by means of wind.

if the wind could obstruct the first [moment], it should cause it to fall;

Death occurs because the life-span is exhausted, yet there are further causes for it.
From this point onward, the following is an excursus;
first the question, then the answer.
This is the question. According to the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*,
it is because one reaches the point of relinquishing the formations of vitality (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*).

This is the response using the four phrases of the introductory treatise. Regarding the first phrase, "because the power of the karma that produces the maturation of lifespan has been exhausted," this encompasses two meanings.
First, because the karma's own force has naturally exhausted itself, it is unable to summon its fruit.
Second, because the power of their karma is impaired by the meditative attainment of the limit (*koṭi-samādhi*) and other such states, it cannot bring about its fruit.
Furthermore, there are two meanings regarding the relinquishing of the life-force (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*):
first, that one may likewise attain [the ability] for external conditions to impair the life-force.
The second [type of death] also shares with the former the quality of occurring at the exhaustion of one's lifespan;
thus, it does not fully coincide in meaning with the impairment caused by external conditions.
While external conditions may impair the lifespan, they do not prevent the power of karma from bringing about its maturation (*vipāka*).
However, because conditions are stronger than karma, the life-span follows those conditions and is diminished.
The meaning of relinquishing the formations of life (*āyur-saṃskāra*) is to transform the power of that karma so as to bring about the fruit of wealth;
this is not entirely the same as the exhaustion of the karma for life.
The exhaustion of the power of the life-span (*āyus-karma*) is not due to external conditions;
rather, it is the abandonment of the power of the life-force (*jīvita-saṃskāra*) that acts as a distinct condition to bring about its exhaustion.
Each of these has a partial similarity.

The *Nyāyānusāra* maintains that it is through the exhaustion of karma of a similar kind; this treatise [the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*] maintains that it is through a common external condition (*bāhya-pratyaya*).
Each of the two masters relies upon one of these paths.
Mutually non-existent, they are neither entirely so nor entirely not so;
the correct principle first refutes [the opponent's view] and thereby incurs its own fault.
This first phrase refers to death due to the exhaustion of one's lifespan.
The second phrase refers to death due to the exhaustion of merit;
the third phrase refers to death due to the exhaustion of both;
the fourth phrase refers to death when neither is exhausted.

Regarding the statement, "But one dies due to external adversities, and it should also be said that it is because of the relinquishing of the life-faculties (*āyus-saṃskāra*)," this is introduced here because it shares a partial similarity with the fourth case.

"One should not further say 'because of relinquishing the life-force,' for its meaning is already subsumed within the first phrase. This is because it shares a partial similarity with the meaning of the first phrase.
This is explained in detail as previously stated.

Death occurs when one reaches the point where both [the life-faculty and the aggregates] are exhausted within the state of the exhaustion of the life-span.
This explains the resolution of the objection.
Death occurs when both types of karma capable of producing rebirth have been exhausted;

"Is it that the end of one's life is caused by the exhaustion of merit? The explanation says: Although the exhaustion of merit has no causal power over death, at the time of death both [merit and lifespan] reach their end simultaneously.

Furthermore, how could these characteristics— such as arising and so forth— be established as having a conventional existence through the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), whether direct perception, inference, or authoritative scripture, in the manner that a jar or similar object is?

The third proposal is untenable because it is necessarily non-existent.

The following is the explanation from the Sautrāntika school. Within this, there are five [points].

Fourth, the exposition of what is established by the Sautrāntika school;

This is the beginning of that [fifth section].

It is not merely that the various practices are revealed, but they can also be fully understood.
Second, it clarifies that what is taught in the sūtras is not momentary (*kṣaṇika*).

The Buddha’s younger brother Nanda was by nature heavily addicted to sensual desire.
The root of sensual defilement is craving for feeling.
The Buddha instructed Nanda to contemplate the arising, abiding, change, and cessation of feeling;
through this, Nanda attained the Way.
Among the assembly, the Buddha spoke to Nanda, saying:

And regarding the thorough knowledge of the decline, alteration, and destruction of feelings: according to this scriptural passage,

By the time the characteristic of destruction occurs, the phenomenon has already passed away. The succession of each subsequent moment following each preceding one is termed "abiding" (*sthiti*);

The *Cheng weishi lun* (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi) states: "Abiding" (*sthiti*) refers to this dharma having temporary utility;

it is called "abiding" in the sense that it continues from preceding moments without interruption. Because there is a distinction between its prior and subsequent states, it is called "abiding-and-change" (*sthity-anyathātva*).
When preceding and succeeding moments arise in a state of similarity,
there is nonetheless a distinction when they are compared to one another;

The *Cheng weishi lun* (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra) states:
"The term 'different' indicates that this dharma is not immutable. Thus says the treatise.

The treatise states: "It is seen as being similar [to the reflection] while in the vajra-samāpatti.

Just as with extremely hard objects such as vajras,

Although the primary elements (mahābhūta) remain similar from one moment to the next,

Since there is neither duration nor change,

The Sautrāntika replies: "This does not state that 'abiding' (sthiti) is a characteristic of the conditioned (saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa).
As for my third statement, it concerns the characteristic of 'alteration while abiding' (sthity-anyathātva)."

What is the meaning of this?
This is the Vaibhāṣika’s inquiry. The treatise states:
This means that because there is a change in duration (*sthiti*), there is no fault of [the mark of impermanence] not being all-pervasive;

That is to say, the final sound, light, and so forth, are called "abiding" because they arise as a continuation of what preceded them.
This very [final moment] is called "change-in-abiding" (sthity-anyathātva) because this final sound or light differs from its preceding moments.
It is called "change of duration" (sthity-anyathātva) because it abides while being different;
it is not that it is only called "different" upon waiting for a subsequent moment,
nor is it that it is only called "abiding" upon waiting for a subsequent moment.

That is to say, for a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*), that which was previously non-existent and now exists is called "arising."

If the essence of the characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) also does not exist, how can it be said that the characteristic of arising has utility while the other three characteristics are without utility? [The *Śāstra* says: The characteristic of arising has utility because it causes conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) to arise from their non-existence. The characteristic of duration (*sthiti*) has utility because it causes those already arisen conditioned phenomena to persist. The characteristic of decay (*jarā*) has utility because it causes those persisting conditioned phenomena to change. The characteristic of cessation (*anityatā*) has utility because it causes those changed conditioned phenomena to perish. Therefore, these four characteristics have utility. However, the characteristic of arising does not cause the essence of the conditioned phenomenon itself to arise; rather, it causes the conditioned phenomenon to arise from its prior non-existence. Since the essence of the conditioned phenomenon exists even before the characteristic of arising occurs, the characteristic of arising cannot be said to have utility with respect to that essence. Furthermore, since the characteristic of arising and the essence of the conditioned phenomenon do not exist simultaneously, how could they be related as cause and effect? Thus, the characteristic of arising is without utility. The same applies to the other three characteristics. Consequently, all conditioned phenomena are devoid of characteristics. This is why it is said that all conditioned phenomena are empty of self-nature (*svabhāva*). This is the meaning of the statement: "All conditioned phenomena are empty of self-nature. This concludes the section on the refutation of the characteristics of conditioned phenomena. Furthermore, the characteristic of arising is not established because it is not perceived. Just as the characteristic of arising is not perceived, the characteristics of duration, decay, and cessation are likewise not perceived. Since they are not perceived, they are not established. This is why it is said that all conditioned phenomena are empty of self-nature. This concludes the section on the refutation of the characteristics of conditioned phenomena based on non-perception. Furthermore, the characteristic of arising is not established because it is contradictory. If the characteristic of arising were to cause the essence of the conditioned phenomenon to arise, it would contradict the principle that the essence of the conditioned phenomenon already exists. If it were to cause the conditioned phenomenon to arise from its prior non-existence, it would contradict the fact that the characteristic of arising and the essence of the conditioned phenomenon do not exist simultaneously. Since both positions are contradictory, the characteristic of arising is not established. The same applies to the other three characteristics. Since they are not established, they are empty. This is why it is said that all conditioned phenomena are empty of self-nature. This concludes the section on the refutation of the characteristics of conditioned phenomena based on contradiction. Furthermore, the characteristic of arising is not established because it lacks a basis. Just as the characteristic of arising lacks a basis, the characteristics of duration, decay, and cessation likewise lack a basis. Since they lack a basis, they are not established. This is why it is said that all conditioned phenomena are empty of self-nature. This concludes the section on the refutation of the characteristics of conditioned phenomena based on the lack of a basis. Furthermore, the characteristic of arising is not established because it is infinite. If one characteristic of arising were to give rise to another characteristic of arising, there would be no end to them. Since there is no end, the characteristic of arising is not established. The same applies to the other three characteristics. Since they are not established, they are empty. This is why it is said that all conditioned phenomena are empty of self-nature. This concludes the section on the refutation of the characteristics of conditioned phenomena based on infinity. Even if it were granted that the characteristic of the present exists,
the Sautrāntika school would still face the difficulty regarding the future:
at the time when the characteristic of arising (jāti-lakṣaṇa) is functional, it cannot be considered future.
Once the characteristic of arising has already performed its function,
it cannot be designated as "present," because the Vaibhāṣika school defines the three time periods based on their functional activity (*kāritra*).
As the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
That is to say, when conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) can act as causes to draw forth and grasp their own effects, this is termed "activity" (*kāritra*);
when they can act as conditions to assist other categories [of phenomena], this is termed "efficacy" (*śakti*), as has already been explained above.
All present [dharmas] are capable of acting as causes to project and draw forth their own effects;
however, not all present [dharmas] are capable of acting as conditions to encompass and clarify those of a different category.
For instance, the visual faculty in darkness may have its functional capacity impaired.
Consequently, it cannot serve as a condition to assist the visual consciousness in its arising;
however, its function is not impaired by darkness,
for it is certainly able to act as the cause that draws forth the future eye.
Due to this activity, there is a distinction in their functional capacities.
However, regarding the production of results within a homogeneous continuum, there are both determinate and indeterminate cases.
The power that encompasses and draws forth [the result] is termed "activity" (*kāritra*) and is also termed "functional capacity" (*sāmarthya*).
If it gives rise to a fruit within a continuum of a different category, it can only act as a condition by providing assistance for its arising;
this is not an "activity" (kāritra), but rather a "capacity" (śakti). Commentary states:

According to the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, it is asked whether the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) constitute the five causes— such as the cause of production (*janana-hetu*) and so forth— or whether they constitute conditions (*pratyaya*).
One school asserts that they are indeed causes.

One interpretation states that "condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). According to the intent of this treatise, "cause" (*hetu*) refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), while "condition" refers to the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Among these, the causal condition necessarily involves the grasping of a fruit (*phala-parigraha*).
The activity of grasping a fruit is necessarily located in the present;
its dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya) assists heterogeneous factors,
among which there are those that grasp a fruit.
There are those that do not grasp a result.
Those that do grasp a result are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) abiding in the present;
they possess the functional capacity to grasp a dominant result (*adhipatiphala*).

Although the functional capacity (*śakti*) of future phenomena and of phenomena characterized by arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) does indeed provide assistance, it does not constitute "appropriation" (*upādāna*);
this is established according to the preceding and following context of the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*.
All that takes up a fruit is necessarily present.
Here, the statement that it takes up a fruit of its own kind is made according to explicit teaching.
The essence of all phenomena abides in the present time.
Since a cause is certain to grasp its fruit, there can be no obstruction to it.
However, if a cause, a fruit, or a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) assists other phenomena, then obstruction may indeed occur.
For example, as darkness obstructs the visual consciousness so that it does not rely upon its sense organ.
Furthermore, all other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) while abiding in the present are able to grasp their own effects; this is termed "activity" (*kāritra*),
because they lack the power to prevent the grasping of those effects.
When all conditioned phenomena abide in the present,
they assist heterogeneous classes [of dharmas] in an indeterminate manner;
for the power of certain dharmas is able to obstruct the functional capacity of others so that they cannot arise.
As in the case of visual consciousness and so forth,
this explanation of "results of its own kind" means that all which are apprehended by causal conditions belong to its own kind.
The treatise further states that the three characteristics, beginning with "abiding," are designated as "destruction.
The Sautrāntika school objects to the simultaneous functioning of these three characteristics.
Treatise:
This is the critique by the Sautrāntikas regarding the various explanations of the meaning of the momentary destruction of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
If [the stages] are distinguished by priority and posteriority,
then after all phenomena have arisen and already endured, there is a different time for their abiding and a different time for their cessation;
thus, the three times are distinct.
Since the minimum duration of three *kṣaṇas* is defined as a single *kṣaṇa*,
this contradicts the scriptural teaching on the meaning of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhanga*).
[End of] Treatise.
If it is argued that "arriving" is neither different [from the entity] nor its cessation,
the Sautrāntika objects that this entails the fault of [the entity] abiding in its prior state.

The characteristics of duration, change, and cessation arise simultaneously. For what reason does the characteristic of duration exercise its function prior to the other two? [Answer: Treatise: It is because the characteristic of duration is the basis for the other two. Just as a foundation must exist before a house can be built, so too, without the support of duration, the characteristics of change and cessation would have no basis to function. Furthermore, it is like a lamp: when the flame is lit, the wick is first established; only then do the subsequent stages of burning and exhaustion occur. Thus, the characteristic of duration necessarily precedes the other two.
Furthermore, it is difficult to explain: if the power of stability (*sthiti*) were strong,
why would it be subject to change (*anyathātva*) and cessation (*vināśa*),
such that both it and its primary dharma (*mūladharma*) would simultaneously undergo decay and destruction?
Treatise:
If it is said that the characteristic of duration (sthiti-lakṣaṇa) renders [the dharma] such that it cannot be used again,
this further refutes the objection.
If it is argued that the characteristic of abiding, like the characteristic of arising, does not function again, this reasoning is likewise inconsistent;
for a dharma cannot be produced again once it has arisen, and the characteristic of arising does not undergo a second production.

The dharma-abiding can be made to abide further; how then could the characteristic of abiding not be made to abide again? [Treatise: The term "dharma-abiding" (dharmasthiti) refers to the fact that conditioned phenomena abide for a duration consistent with their own nature. Since this abiding is established by its very nature, it cannot be made to persist beyond that limit. Regarding the characteristic of abiding (sthiti-lakṣaṇa): if this characteristic were to cause the phenomenon to abide repeatedly, it would follow that the phenomenon would never cease, because the cause of its persistence would remain constant. Furthermore, since the characteristic of abiding itself must abide, there would have to be another characteristic of abiding to sustain it, leading to an infinite regress. whether one advances or retreats in this analysis, there is no logical basis for its production.
How can it be said that [the unmanifest] is produced by speech?
The treatise asks:
How does it depend upon reaching [the point of completion] to produce the unmanifest?
The Sarvāstivādins raise an objection against the Sautrāntikas to establish their own position:
because the many moments of informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) arise gradually and enter the past,
it is only at the final moment of informative matter that non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) arises.
The production of sound from names and meanings is also to be understood accordingly.
Treatise:
If that were so, one would be able to cognize the meaning [directly].
This is the Sautrāntika objection:
If it is only the final sound that can produce a name,
then one should be able to comprehend the meaning upon hearing only the final sound.
Why must one wait for the sound of a preceding thought?
This argument is because such a position leads to the impossibility of accumulation.
This refutes the position that [the phonemes] are distinct.
If it is argued that speech produces the phonemes and the phonemes in turn produce the name, this faces the same difficulty as before:
because the phonemes of preceding and succeeding moments cannot be accumulated.
Treatise:
The statement that speech manifests names should be refuted by analogy with [the refutation of] production;
the previous objection concerned the production of names by speech.
Furthermore, this is based on the distinction between "producing" (*janaka*) and "manifesting" (*vyañjaka*).
"Producing" means that a name is produced by sound.
"Manifesting" means that a name already possesses its own substantial entity (*dravya*), which is merely manifested by speech.
The above refutes the existence of names apart from words according to the Sarvāstivādins;
hereafter, it refutes the existence of phrases apart from words.
Treatise:
Furthermore, when distinct from words and phonemes, their characteristics cannot be discerned;
those of clear wisdom know through direct perception that they do not exist.
Treatise.
Furthermore, the claims that "the letter arises from the sound" or "reaches [the object]" are both unreasonable.

Whether regarding its arising or its manifestation, both positions are refuted by applying the same logical fallacies used against the theory of the name (nāman) arising from or being manifested by the sound. As the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
This objection contradicts the tenet one has inherited;
for that [tenet] asserts that both the past and the future lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
and that successive moments of sound cannot arise simultaneously.
How do words, names, and phrases come into being?
If it is the case that preceding moments of consciousness successively assist one another so that the final moment constitutes the word, name, and phrase,
then one should only understand the meaning upon hearing the final [moment].
Furthermore, since there is no mutual dependence [between moments], there can be no going or coming.
Since it is eternally a single thought-moment, how could they mutually depend?

Since there is no mutual dependence, the subsequent moments would be identical to the preceding ones; thus, the later moments, being like the initial moment, should be incapable of denoting [their objects].
Since hearing [the sound] later would be no different from hearing it initially,
the principle that sound— as asserted by them— is a signifier through the mutual support of its preceding and succeeding moments is not established.
In our own school, [sound] exists in all three time periods and is not non-existent.
Therefore, although the final moment of the name and so forth arises only by depending on the preceding moments that are capable of producing it,
one cannot comprehend the meaning merely by hearing that [final] moment.
Because one does not possess [the capacity for] hearing;
for instance, it is through the previously established convention of names and so forth that sound can produce cognition.
Nevertheless, even upon hearing a single sound, there is comprehension due to habitual practice.
Based on this, one may infer the rest.
Therefore, the Sūtra-master says that [the opponent's position] is refuted, but this is not the case.
[End of] Treatise.
Furthermore, if one maintains that [the name] reaches [the object], this should not be accepted;
this refutes the divergent view.
If the name and the signified meaning were to arise simultaneously, [it would follow that they are co-existent].
Regarding the claim that the characteristic of arising arises simultaneously with its object,
there are three faults. First,
the name would exist in the present while the object exists in the past or the future.
The names of the two sons were born together with them;
their parents did not establish names according to their own wishes.
Furthermore, the three unconditioned phenomena are without birth and should likewise have no names.
Treatise:
However, when the Blessed One spoke of the distinctions in arrangement up to the point of "peaceful," this serves as a general response to the objection raised by the Sarvāstivādins.
An objection is raised:
If it is claimed that there is no name distinct from sound,
why does the Sūtra state that verse relies upon names?
The answer says:
"It is the arrangement of sounds that is conventionally designated as 'name' (nāma).
[Treatise]
From the adherence to the existence of real entities up to the succession of moments of mind,
the Sarvāstivādins do not collectively establish these as real entities; rather,
they are established individually, just as "motion" exists apart from the tree that moves.
The sequence of the mind has no substance apart from the mind;
names are likewise,
having no substance apart from sound.
[The] Treatise states:
"Alternatively, one should maintain that [the term 'reaching'] is simply useless;
for the Sautrāntika, by citing the scripture, refutes the existence of [an entity called] 'possession' (*prāpti*)."
The treatise [states]: "Because the Vaibhāṣikas have reached the point of being able to understand it.
This refers to the delusion regarding the Sarvāstivāda school.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The *Vibhāṣā* explains that names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) each have three types.
Regarding the three types of names, they are: the name (*nāman*), the collection of names (*nāmakāya*), and the large collection of names (*mahānāmakāya*)."
The same applies to phrases and syllables.
A name has many states, namely: that which arises from a single syllable, or that which arises from two syllables.
Alternatively, they may arise from multiple syllables.
Regarding those arising from a single syllable: when a single syllable is uttered, it can only be called a "name" (*nāman*);
when two syllables are uttered, it is called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*).
Some say that when three syllables are uttered, it is called a "multisyllabic body" (*nāmakāya*);
others say that only when four syllables are uttered is it called a "multisyllabic body."
Regarding those produced from two syllables: when two syllables are uttered, there is merely a name;
when four syllables are uttered, it is called a "name-body" (nāmakāya).
Or, it is stated as follows:
When six syllables are uttered, it is called a "multisyllabic word-group" (*nāmakāya*);
or it is said that only when eight syllables are uttered is it called a "multisyllabic word-group."
Among those produced from multiple syllables, that which is produced from three syllables is merely a "name" when the three syllables are uttered; however,
when six syllables are uttered, it is called a "name-group" (*nāmakāya*).
Some say that when the nine syllables are uttered, they are called a "multitude of names" (*nāmakāya*). Others say: [the same].
When twelve syllables are spoken, they are then called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) consisting of many [syllables].
Because this serves as the gateway, other name-bodies consisting of many syllables arise; these should be explained according to reason.
Sentences (*pada*) likewise have many states.
This refers to the intermediate phrase, the initial phrase, the final phrase, the short phrase,
and the long phrase. If eight syllables arise, it is called an intermediate phrase,
because it is neither long nor short.
That is to say, thirty-two syllables situated in the middle give rise to four lines;
these four lines constitute a *śloka*.
The prose and verses of the Sūtras and Śāstras mostly rely upon this numerical measure.
If six syllables or more are produced, it is called an initial phrase (*pūrvapada*);
if fewer than twenty-six syllables are produced, it is called a subsequent phrase (*uttarapada*).
If fewer than six syllables are produced, it is called a short phrase (*laghupada*).
Verses exceeding twenty-six syllables are called long verses (*gāthā*).
For now, based on the intermediate number of syllables per line, three types are distinguished.
When six or eight syllables are spoken, it can only constitute a single line (*pāda*).
When sixteen syllables are spoken, it is called a "phrase-body" (padakāya).
Alternatively, it is said that when twenty-four syllables are spoken, it is called a "multiple phrase-body" (bahupadakāya).
Some maintain this view:
it is only when thirty-two syllables are spoken that they are called a "multitude of phrases" (*padakāya*);
since a phoneme (*vyañjana*) is identical to a syllable (*akṣara*), there is only a single position.
When one syllable is spoken, there is merely a phoneme (*vyañjana*).
When two syllables are spoken, it is called a "body of phonemes" (*vyañjanakāya*).
Or, as some say, when three syllables are spoken, it is called a "multitude of bodies of phonemes."
Or it may be said: it is only when four syllables are uttered that one speaks of a "multisyllabic phoneme" (*vyañjanakāya*).
For this reason, one should state as follows.
When a single syllable is spoken,
there is a name, but no collection of names (nāmakāya).
There are no multiple name-bodies;
there are no phrases and no multiple phrase-bodies;
there are phonemes.
There is no phoneme-body (*vyañjana-kāya*) and no multiple-phoneme-body.
When two syllables are uttered, there is a name and a name-body (*nāma-kāya*).
There are no multiple name-bodies (nāmakāya),
nor the three beginning with phrase-bodies (padakāya).
There are phonemes (vyañjana) and phoneme-bodies (vyañjanakāya).
There are no multiple phoneme-sets (*vyañjana-kāya*).
When four syllables are spoken, there are the three [categories] beginning with "name" (*nāman*).
The three beginning with "no-phrase" (amūka) and the three beginning with "with-text" (savākya).
When these eight characters are spoken:
There are three types of names and so forth: those consisting of phrases, those consisting of non-phrases, and those consisting of multiple phrases.
There are likewise three types of phonemes and so forth.
When sixteen characters are spoken, [these distinctions apply].
There are three types of names and so forth: individual words (*pada*), groups of words (*padakāya*), and [the absence of] multiple groups of words.
There are also three types of phonemes (*vyañjana*) and so forth.
When the thirty-two syllables are spoken, each of the three—name (*nāman*), phrase (*pada*), and phoneme (*vyañjana*)—possesses three types.
Taking this as the gateway, the rest should be explained according to reason. Based on the aforementioned treatise, a single phoneme (*vyañjana*) arises from many moments of sound.
Regarding the statement that "the preceding moment of sound lacks syllables (vyañjana), while one syllable gives rise to one name (nāman) and one word-phrase (pada)":
this means that within a single moment of sound, three phenomena arise simultaneously—
namely, the syllable, the name, and the word-phrase.
If two syllables constitute a name, that name already exists in the preceding moment of thought;
however, as for phrases, they do not yet exist until the subsequent syllable reaches the position of completing the phrase, at which point the phrase finally comes into being.
Regarding the statement that many phonemes (*vyañjana*) give rise to one name (*nāman*), and many names constitute one phrase (*pada*):
it is not the case that every sound in every single moment possesses a phoneme, nor that every single phoneme possesses a name,
nor that every single name possesses a phrase.
However, there may be a name consisting of a single syllable;
there may be one syllable, one name, or one phrase,
or there may be no syllables or phrases at all.
A phrase must consist of at least two syllables.

Regarding those names that arise from two or more syllables, it is only upon the second syllable and subsequent ones that the name consisting of two syllables arises. However, if a name arises from two syllables or even more, comprehension is already attained upon the preceding syllable.
This arises because the listener has become habituated to the previously understood meaning;
it does not mean that within the preceding state there exist two syllables or a name that have already arisen,
such as the name "all conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*).
Among these, there are two types:
first, names consisting of one or two syllables;
second, names consisting of one or two characters.
Other examples should be understood accordingly.
Thus, when the two words "tathā" (thus) and "vācaṃ" (speech) are uttered,
one person hears them all.
Because each person hears and practices [the teaching] and gives rise to their own individual understanding,
if one hears of one [aspect] while simultaneously encompassing two, this constitutes familiarization through repeated practice.
If one explains it in this way,
it accords well with the fact that the minimum number of syllables in a name is one;
it is also like the statement, "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent," and so forth.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) constitute the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); impermanence constitutes the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa*).
Names (*nāman*) express the intrinsic nature.
The phrase expresses differentiation.
As for the two characters "impermanent" (anitya), they may arise from a name or not arise from a name;
thus, their referent is not yet fixed.
As it is said, impermanence is to be loathed;
impermanence itself is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
while being loathsome is its specific distinction (viśeṣa).
These two characters, "impermanent," ought logically to possess a name.
If they were to arise as a distinction, they would have no name.
To speak according to reality, if they were to constitute an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), [they would likewise lack a name].
If they were to be differentiated,
all would possess names,
just as when one speaks the phrase "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
Some people hear only the word "non-existent," some hear only the word "permanent," and some hear both words, "non-existent" and "permanent."
Alternatively, one may hear four characters.
If one hears only the character "non-existence" (wu), it means that only non-existence is taught.
If one hears the character "permanence" (chang), it means that only permanence is taught.
If it were appropriate for them to hear [the teaching], it would mean that "impermanence" was being explained;
however, this impermanence does not yet belong to any specific phenomenon.
Therefore, one knows that all that has been heard above consists of indeterminate phrases.
If one hears it said that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent,
this is a definitive phrase;
for by knowing the distinctions among these impermanent conditioned phenomena, one attains understanding.
Based on this, one should understand that for each of the four characters of the phrase "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" (sarvasaṃskārā anityāḥ),
there is a specific name consisting of a single character.
Within this, if one reaches the second character, there is also the name consisting of two characters.
Upon reaching the third character, there is the name consisting of one character as well as the phrase consisting of three characters.
For example, if one merely hears "all conditioned phenomena are [impermanent]," it consists of three characters.
This refers to the expression that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are non-existent.
Conditioned phenomena constitute the self-nature (*svabhāva*), while the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) constitutes their differentiation.
Upon reaching the fourth syllable, there are names consisting of one syllable,
names consisting of two syllables,
and names consisting of three syllables.
These consist of three- and four-syllable phrases.
Within these, one should reflect appropriately on how they may be increased or decreased. Furthermore, to explain why there are names of four syllables, there are also names of a single syllable.
Because the mind of the remote preparatory stage (*dūre-prayoga*) that initiates speech mostly takes this as its object;
it is like when one says the two syllables "saṃskāra," one must first take each individual name that expresses "all" and "formations" as its respective object.

Only then can they be combined to form the name of two syllables. According to the *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā*, names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) each have three types:
first, the individual name;
second, the collection of names (*nāmakāya*).
There are three types of name-bodies (*nāmakāya*); the same applies to phrase-bodies (*padakāya*) and phoneme-bodies (*vyañjanakāya*).
Regarding names, there are various states: some arise from a single syllable, some arise from two syllables, and some arise from many syllables.
The *Vibhāṣā* is said to have six stages:
one word, two words, four words, eight words, sixteen words, and thirty-two words.
According to this treatise, these stages are established based on doubling the preceding count up to the maximum length of a single verse.
Thus it is said.
However, in reality, the treatise does not lack names produced by three syllables, five syllables, seven syllables, nine syllables, and so forth.
As cited above from the treatise: "Names produced by one syllable, names produced by two syllables, and names produced by many syllables."
Regarding names formed from multiple syllables:
any name produced from three or more syllables is a "multi-syllabic name" according to the linguistic conventions of the West (India).
The term "body" (*kāya*) is applied to two [syllables] because it carries the sense of a collection;
from three upwards, they are all termed "many.
Alternatively, four syllables or more are termed "arising from many syllables" (*bahv-akṣara-jāta*).
Because it doubles the two syllables.
Regarding the name produced by a single syllable:
when a single syllable is uttered, it is simply called a "name."
When two syllables are spoken, there is what is called a "name-body" (nāmakāya).
Regarding the multiple name-bodies, there are two interpretations. Some state as follows:
When three syllables are spoken, they are called a "multitude of names" (*nāmakāya*);
or it is said that when four syllables are spoken, they are called a "multitude of names. Some say:
Question: Regarding the "group of many names" (*nāmakāya*), one view holds that it is called a group of many names when three syllables are uttered;
another view holds that it is called a group of many names when four syllables are uttered.
What is the meaning of this?
The explanation states: "The three syllables produce a name; the name consists of many [syllables] and forms a 'name-body' (nāmakāya).
This means that the first and second syllables constitute one body.
The first and third syllables together constitute one body;
the second and third syllables together also constitute one body.
According to the rules of grammatical phonology (*śabdavidyā*), it is only when three or more are mentioned that they are designated as "many."
If a name consisting of four syllables is called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) or a "multi-name-body" (*bahunāmakāya*),
then those combined in immediate succession constitute three bodies, which are termed a "multi-name-body.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it is simply called a "multi-name-body" because it consists of many names.
It does not refer to multiple bodies.

Furthermore, another interpretation is that when one body is added to another body, it is called a "multiple-body" (*kāyabāhulya*). According to the three preceding explanations, their respective characteristics are mutually exclusive;
they merely provide a comprehensive description and cannot be judged as either right or wrong.
According to what is clarified in the treatise,
it is taught that each of the three— names (nāman), phrases (pada), and phonemes (vyañjana)—
has three categories: namely, singular, dual, and plural.
First, because it is named as one, it does not constitute a "body" (kāya).
Second, because it is named as two, it constitutes a "body.
Third, it should likewise be combined: because they are named as many, they are called a "multitude-body" (nāmakāya).
For what reason is it said that the positions of one and two are themselves called the "name-sets" (nāma-kāya) of one and two?
And for what reason are the third and subsequent positions, according to their number, called "bodies" (kāya)?
If, within this context, they are called "name-bodies" because there are many names, [then the same logic applies].
This refers to the third explanation regarding the number of bodies (*kāya*).
Within this context, both "body" (*kāya*) and "body-body" (*kāyakāya*) are treated together.

According to the second interpretation, the four syllables arise as a sequence of many proximate correspondences, which is termed "body-body. Furthermore, one cites the *Vyākaraṇa* (Grammar) itself, stating that only after three [syllables] have been spoken can they be designated as "many" (*bahu*).
For what reason, then, is it said that adding a body upon a body is called "many bodies"?
If that were so, then when three syllables arise and combine in succession, there would likewise be two bodies:
namely, a body upon which another body is added.
It should also be called a "name-group" (*nāmakāya*).
Although it consists of a single interpretation, it is designated as a "name-group" based on the multiplicity of names;
since the reason for this cannot be established, [the objection remains].
This is as when it is said that "insects eat wood.
What is explained here—whether one, two, or many—is all spoken in terms of names;

There is further explicit clarification in the *Vibhāṣā*;
one should examine and record it. Furthermore, the text states:
"Three syllables produce a name; a plurality of names constitutes a 'name-body' (*nāmakāya*)."
This is erroneous.
Regarding those whose names consist of three syllables, there is only one instance of a name with exactly three syllables.
Within this context, there are two differing interpretations.
First, when one becomes many, it is called "multiple bodies," meaning three or more. Second,
according to their positions, they are doubled in number.
This means that from the fourth name upward, each is double the size of the preceding one.
Furthermore, both interpretations are consistent with the meaning;
therefore, the treatise cites them both.
However, there are instances where there are only the essences of syllables (*vyañjana*), names (*nāman*), and phrases (*pada*), but no essence of verses (*gāthā*).
Regarding these syllables, names, and phrases,
there are differences among those in the five destinies and among the ignorant and the wise in various regions.
All that can be spoken consists of sounds that give rise to syllables;
based on syllables there are names,
and based on names there are phrases.
Because they are all able to explain both the intrinsic nature and the specific distinctions [of phenomena],
they cause all beings to understand both the intrinsic nature and the specific distinctions.
Therefore, its verses can only be composed by those who are skilled in literary expression;
they consist merely of the arrangement of words, up to and including names and phrases, and contain nothing else.
Question: As it is said, there is a single name and a single word.
Regarding the names for the various directions, different interpretations arise:
do they have many names,
or do they have a single name consisting of a single syllable?
Question: Are there multiple characters? Answer: Characters are indeed only one; they are used universally across all regions without any distinction.
It is only the names that differ.
If a word belongs to the language of this region, it has only the name of this region and lacks the names of other regions.
This is how we know it is so. If it were otherwise,
then one should say that a single phoneme produces only one name, yet there would be many names [produced by it].
Since the treatise does not speak of multiple names, we know that there is only one name.

Furthermore, when one utters speech, the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) that precedes it takes as its object only a single name. Question: If this is so, why does it give rise to the cognition of many names? Answer: This is like the sound of stringed or wind instruments; it gives rise to a cognition of various names, which is merely apparent and not real.
Treatise:
These categories, beginning with the "body of names" (nāmakāya), should all be analyzed here.
From this point on, the second section of the verse analyzes them according to their different aspects.
The treatise says: "Up to 'however, it cannot be said.
This concerns the first gate, that of realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*).
Within this, there are two parts.
One view holds that it exists only in the desire and form realms;
another view holds that it extends throughout the formless realm as well.
However, this cannot be definitively stated.
Between these two explanations, the former is correct.
Within the former explanation, there are two further views.
One states that it is bound solely by the language [in which it was spoken].
This refers to only two stages:
namely, the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
Second, it is said to be bound to the body.
This refers to five stages:
namely, the desire realm and the four dhyānas.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* contains four explanations regarding this, including two layers of critical commentary.
Regarding the first two [positions], one says it follows speech,
while another says it follows the body;
the critique adopts the position that it follows speech.
Regarding the latter two views: the first states that [the fetters] pertain to the desire and form realms;
the second states that they also pertain to the formless realm.
The critique adopts the former view.
Master Shen said:
"Since a single treatise cannot have two critiques,
that which follows the words is the subsequent critique."
This merely states that it is not permitted for the formless realm to have a name;
it is not intended to allow for [names] to be bound to the body.

This interpretation by the Dharma Master possesses profound logical merit. According to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* and other texts, the "bodies" (kāya) of names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) are explained as follows:
All names depend upon sound;
names depend upon phonemes.
Furthermore, this treatise states: "The term 'sentient being' refers to sound, namely the informative action of speech."
Therefore, one should know that other sounds possess no names.
Since the vocal karma upon which they depend exists only in two stages,
how can the names dependent upon them extend across all five stages?
If it is argued that both [the form and formless realms] might be [the basis for the cessation of consciousness] because treatises such as the *Nyāyānusāra* mention both,
this too is unreasonable;
for this very treatise likewise mentions the name "formless realm" without either affirming or negating [its status as such a basis].

How could it be that both [the meaning and the expression] are taken together? Therefore, we know that while the name follows the linguistic bond, the meaning is determined. Question: If this is so, why is it that only the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) penetrates those five stages?

Regarding the statement that [the analytical knowledges] belong to only two stages: the answer is that, according to what the treatise states, within the discussion on the stages to which they are bound (*pratisaṃyukta-bhūmi*), two views are presented;
however, within the discussion on the stage to which the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) is bound, it is stated that it belongs exclusively to five stages.
Thus, it should be known that the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) is explained in terms of its cognitive object;
for whether it follows the words or the body,
it is possible for minds of all five stages to take them as objects.
For this reason, there is no textual passage that records these two views.
The analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) is the wisdom that comprehends phenomena.
How, then, could it be made to reside in the same stage as the names (*nāman*) that are its objects of comprehension?
The analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) is the wisdom that functions as the means for all regional dialects;
by virtue of this, it is restricted only to the level of verbal expression and does not extend to other levels. Regarding this, some raise a question and answer themselves as follows:

Question: Since the *nirmāṇa-citta* (fruition-of-emanation mind) that initiates speech does not take the three realms as its object, how can names (*nāman*) and so forth be able to express the three realms?
Answer: Although the *nirmāṇa-citta* that initiates speech does not take the three realms as its object, [the names and so forth it produces do].

However, because the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) can remotely give rise to the mind that takes the three realms as its object, that which is produced is called "that which designates (*vācaka*) the three realms.
A detailed examination of this dialogue reveals that it has not yet reached the point of understanding that all speech is produced by the mind.
All proximate causes— the minds that initiate action through their origination—
take form and sound as their objects.
For what reason do you specifically ask about the mind of supernormal power?
In the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), there is that which takes its name as the object;
it does not necessarily take the expressed meaning (*abhidheya-artha*) as its object.
This is like many people who do not recognize such things as mani jewels.
How could it not be that this jewel and its name exist? The treatise states:
furthermore, the "name-body" (nāmakāya) and so forth do not manifest the actual meaning.
The second [section] is the distinction between sentient and non-sentient beings.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 50, states:
Question: Who accomplishes [the acquisition of] names and so forth?

the mind also takes them as its co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu)? Furthermore,

Birth and the other [characteristics] are not non-coexistent causes (sahabhū-hetu) for the primary elements;
this case should also be understood accordingly, based on the intent of the aforementioned treatise.
Thus it is with the primary elements and birth and the others.
The great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) do not share a single fruit, yet they can function as simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Why, then, do you not allow that the mind and its secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*), though not sharing a single fruit, should likewise be simultaneous causes? Such an analogy is logically inconsistent.
Successive fruits and single fruits are not its fruits because they are many;
nor are they derived matter (bhautika-rūpa).
Since these primary elements (mahābhūtas) are subsumed within a single fruit among their mutually resultant fruits,
how could it be that derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is not a result of the arising and so forth of those primary elements?
Therefore, this is cited as an error.
Furthermore, it is as previously stated.
What was stated previously?
Because the mind does not arise by the power of those [great elements],
but rather through the mutual power of the great elements and the characteristics such as arising.
Because they arise [simultaneously], this fault does not occur. Furthermore, it is said:
"Moreover, within this co-arising assemblage of conjunctions, there is that which is the primary mover (pravartaka) rather than the follower (anuvartaka)."
That is to say, there are those that follow and turn along with the mind-king alone:
namely, matter and the formations dissociated from mind.
There are those that are both the primary mover and the concomitant mover;
namely, the mental factors (caitta),
because they turn in accordance with the mind.
Because they can transform both matter and the formations dissociated from mind, there are two that are neither;
that is to say, excluding the aforementioned characteristics. According to the above treatise, these are the factors that follow the movement of the mind (cittānuvartin) as clarified herein.
This differs from the meaning of "concomitant" (*anuvartin*) and "cooperative" (*anuparivartin*) explained in other contexts.
For instance, in the Abhidharma it is said that wisdom (*prajñā*) is the essence [of the path] and the five aggregates are its concomitants;
this refers to the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*) being subsumed under the category of the cooperative.
In this context, it is stated that the mind (*citta*) acts only as the primary mover (*pravartaka*) and not as a secondary mover (*anuvartaka*);
this means that the mind-king (*cittarāja*) itself is not a secondary mover.
However, the statement made here is based on the principle of king and minister, wherein the mind functions solely as the primary mover.
In the Abhidharma it is stated that wisdom functions according to the principles of the Abhidharma;
although the explanations differ, there is no contradiction in their meaning.

This comprehensively subsumes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) as appropriate,

All conditioned phenomena possess the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

logically, this principle should encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

within this [relationship], the fundamental dharmas themselves do not serve as mutual effects for one another.
This dharma acts as a co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) for that;
thus, it is not the case that they are mutual effects while serving as causes for one another. By this principle, [the same applies to other cases].

That is to say, if one simply asserts that being mutual effects constitutes the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), there are cases of co-existent causes that do not involve mutual causality; thus, establishing "being mutual effects" as the reason for the cause would fail to pervade the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).
This, therefore, results in the reason being narrower than the thesis.

this characteristic of being a cause must be further analyzed;

Conditioned phenomena that have a single fruit may serve as simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*). This is identical to the meaning of the *Vibhāṣā*.
The *Vibhāṣā*, in its sixteenth section, states that the meaning of "having a single fruit" constitutes a simultaneous cause. Now, let us examine this in detail.
If these causes were simultaneous,

since their own essence is not the effect of itself, how could they exist together and obtain a single effect?

This [reason] is thus a cause of a single effect that does not pervade the subject of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*).
Because the thesis is too narrow,
it is no different from the previous [position]. If you claim that they occur at different times, [the same fault follows].
Since these secondary characteristics (anuvyañjana-lakṣaṇa) are of the same outflow (niṣyanda) and the same maturation (vipāka) as their primary dharmas,
why do they not serve as causes for those primary dharmas?
This means that the cause of a single effect extends to heterogeneous instances (*vipakṣa*).
Its fault is even more severe when it occurs within heterogeneous instances.
According to the *Nyāya*, the reason (*hetu*) established is no different from the previous reason.
Why do you refute the *Abhidharmakośa* and establish [your own system] instead?
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmāvatāra* states:
"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are mutually effects of one another."
Alternatively, those that share the same fruit are called co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*). Based on this, these two types of causes are likewise without distinction of superiority or inferiority.
Now, upon careful examination, the causes established in both treatises are entirely free from fault.
Just as it is said that "that which undergoes transformation and resistance is called matter" (*rūpa*),
yet this definition does not apply universally to unmanifest form (*avijñapti*);
or as it is said that one who eats voraciously and walks swiftly is called a horse.
There are those who are not horses yet eat quickly and walk quickly;
there are also those who are horses yet eat slowly and walk slowly.
Nevertheless, these designations do not contradict worldly convention, as they function as mutual causes and effects, or as a single cause and effect.
The example is likewise.
Because the author of the *Nyāyānusāra* contradicts the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, he follows [the view of] a single fruit;
whereas when entering the *Abhidharma*, he will not contradict reason by citing both causes universally.
Because this treatise is concise, it cites only one instance. Someone asked and answered as follows:
"Question: According to both the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Volume 16) and the [Treatise] in One Hundred and Fifty [Verses], it is stated:"
The single fruit is the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* further states:
"The single fruit refers to the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and the fruit of disjunction."
Is this not contradictory?
The explanation is that when the *Vibhāṣā* speaks exclusively of the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*),
it does so by referring only to those cases within this category of fruit that are definitive and free from ambiguity.
Its result of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala) is termed "broad" and "indeterminate";
it may be co-nascent, or it may occur immediately thereafter, and so forth.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* should also mention the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*),
yet it does not do so because it fears confusion with the mutually produced fruits of human effort;
for a given entity, when viewed in relation to itself, cannot be its own fruit.
The reason the *Nyāyānusāra* speaks of "virile activity" (*puruṣakāra*) is to encompass the entirety of the virile fruit (*puruṣakāraphala*) within a single result; therefore,
it is mentioned separately.
Each [explanation] relies on a specific meaning and they do not contradict one another. Now, to examine this in detail:

when the *Nyāyānusāra* speaks of the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāraphala*), it does so because the fruit of disjunction (*visamyogaphala*) does not encompass all instances of the fruit of human effort that consist in non-arising.
This is not intended to include the immediate, delayed, or remote *puruṣakāra-phala* (human effort results) of other conditioned phenomena.
The equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) consists of the immediate *puruṣakāra-phala*,
as well as the simultaneous, immediate, and delayed *puruṣakāra-phala* of the four great elements and their derived matter.
None of these constitute a single fruit in this context;
they do not possess the meaning of being simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) that share a single fruit.
This refers to those minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
Furthermore, although the four great elements and [the derived matter such as] birth and so forth are all causes, they do not share a single fruit;
nor is it the case that the preceding aggregate of matter induces these [subsequent ones].
The seeds that produce fruit in spring and the fruits that ripen in autumn are both termed "fruits";
yet, although they are the same kind of fruit,
they are not simultaneous causes for one another.
In the *Pañcavastuka-vibhāṣā*, within the explanation of the name "associated" (*saṃprayukta*) regarding the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*),
there is one interpretation which states:
"Furthermore, at the same moment."
Having the same basis,
the same mode of activity,
and the same object of cognition.
They have the same result, the same outflow,
and the same maturation.

This is the meaning of "associated. According to this treatise, those which take the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) are all associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
These are the associated [factors].

All [causes] equally take the *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort) as their equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), but they do not all equally take it as their co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Nevertheless, there is a correspondence in the attainment of the *puruṣakāra-phala* of the equal-and-immediate condition, whether it exists or not.
Just as with the final mind of an Arhat; now, upon detailed examination,
the single fruit elucidated in this treatise is the same as that in the *Vibhāṣā*.
This does not accord with correct reasoning,
for this verse was composed based upon the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
If there were any divergent views, one should have pointed out the reasons for them.
The claim by some that this is also consistent with correct reasoning is erroneous. [This is] from the *Treatise* (*Śāstra*).
Regarding the relationship between a primary dharma and its secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇas*), up to the point where the secondary characteristics do not apply to the primary dharma.

they are mentioned separately because the cause does not pervade this dharma.
Treatise.
In this context, it should be clarified what is meant by these [terms].
The final three phrases clarify the phenomena that follow the mind (*cittānuvartaka-dharma*).
As stated previously, the mind and the phenomena that follow the mind also act as mutual causes for one another.
It is not yet known which phenomena are those that follow the mind (cittānuvartaka).
The treatise says: "Up to the phenomena that follow the mind.
This sets forth the essential nature of the phenomena that follow the mind. As for what are called "phenomena associated with the mind" (cittasaṃprayukta):
This refers to all mental factors (caitta-dharma) and the two types of restraint;
these are the matter that evolves in accordance with the mind.
As for the phrase "those dharmas":

Regarding those three categories of phenomena—the characteristics of speech and the arising of the mind, and so forth—these refer to the aforementioned three categories of phenomena and the primary characteristics of the mind; all such things are called "phenomena that follow and turn with the mind" (cittānuvartaka-dharma).
To summarize the above, the *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā* (Treatise on Right Reasoning) asks:
"For what reason are their secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) not mentioned?"
The reasons for this will not be stated here, as they shall be explained later. Now, the treatise asks:
in what sense are these factors called "concomitants of the mind" (*cittānuvartin*)?
The next line asks why the term "concomitant" (*anuvartin*) is established.
The treatise states: "It is called 'concomitant with the mind' (*cittānuvartin*).
This is answered briefly by means of three meanings.
Later, ten points are raised as answers.
Briefly stated, they are called "concomitants of the mind" based on three meanings: time and so forth, fruit and so forth, and nature.
Treatise.
Furthermore, regarding the temporal [aspects], from "by way of time" up to "falling into a single world-period," the time is divided into four:
namely, one arising and one abiding.
One ceases and falls into one world-period. Question: Why, among the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), are only three mentioned and not the characteristic of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*)?
Answer: This is because they are said to share the same time; it is shown that they coexist in the future and are about to enter the present.
Cessation reveals that the activity [of the dharma] exists in the present and enters the past;
abiding reveals that this dharma takes up its fruit in the present.
This demonstrates that the three periods of time—future, present, and past—are identical in their temporal nature.
Because the single characteristic of difference lacks the capacity for manifestation at that time,
it is not mentioned here. The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Does one not simply know that arising, abiding, and ceasing belong within a single lifetime by merely stating so?
Although one thus knows they fall within a single lifetime,
one has still not yet realized that these phenomena and the mind are likewise inseparable throughout the past and the future.
Alternatively, it is to demonstrate that all dharmas are non-arising. The commentary states:
Although it is said that arising, abiding, and ceasing belong to the same single moment, one does not yet know what exists prior to the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).
After the characteristic of future cessation has passed,
this dharma remains inseparable from the mind even in the past; or,
those factors that do not arise do not share the same arising, abiding, and cessation as the mind.

Fearing that one might doubt whether those dharmas are not simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), it is therefore said that they "belong to the same time period" (*eka-adhvapatita*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"If that is so, one should simply say that they belong to the same time period."
If it were not so, one would not be made to know that they are definitely destined for a single lifetime. The commentary states:
If one were to simply say "destined for a single lifetime," then one would not be made to know that they are definitely destined for a single lifetime.
Because they are identical in the future, at a later time, if they were to arise, they would not belong to the same world-period (*adhvan*).
Although they initially belonged to the same world-period, they subsequently do not belong to the same world-period.
This is so unless one says that their arising, ceasing, and so forth, are identical.
This does not mean that one should know for certain that [the person] will definitely fall into one lifetime;
rather, it speaks further of "one life," "extinction," and so forth.
One should know that within a single lifetime, there is certainly no sequence of before and after.
Commentary:
From "by way of fruit, etc. up to "and so forth, which are outflows" (*niṣyanda*), this opens up the category of fruit into three types.

It is indeed so.

Is it not the case that because this statement is general, it also includes outflowing (*niṣyanda*) and ripening (*vipāka*) results?

they are not what is being clarified here.
However, there are generally four types of virile fruits (puruṣakāra-phala):
co-arising, immediate, separated, and non-arising.
This indicates that it is not a fruit that exists simultaneously with its cause.

for while the members of this composite aggregate serve as fruits for one another,
the [composite] itself is not the human effort fruit of its own self.
This demonstrates that there is not a single fruit-meaning among the co-arising, conjoined, or virile fruits;
therefore, the outflowing and ripening fruits are mentioned separately. This is according to this treatise.
This excludes simultaneous effects;
it does not mean that those [causes] do not take immediate, intervening, or remote results of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).

this is the beginning of that section. The mental sovereign (*cittarāja*) can be at its maximum [of associated factors], namely, the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) present in the mind of the first dhyāna.

The mind has already served as the cause for one hundred and fifty-eight dharmas. At the very minimum—referring to the non-obscured-neutral mind in the two higher meditative attainments (dhyāna)—there are only eleven dharmas present.

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Chapter Nine, states:
"Because the primary characteristics and the dharma possess equal power, they function as simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for that same fundamental dharma;
this is because each possesses efficacy with respect to the other."
They are exclusively co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu) for their respective characteristics.
The *Nyāyānusāra* asks:
"For what reason are the secondary characteristics of the mind not co-existent causes of the mind?"
Because the mind does not arise by virtue of that power;
because the mind and that [matter] do not serve as mutual effects;
and because the majority of the aggregate is not its effect.

Precisely because of these many reasons thus explained, [these factors] are not called "concomitant mental factors" (*cittānuvartaka-dharma*) according to their characteristics; the preceding passage refers to this very point. Why is this so? Because questioning is not the means [to realization].

This citation points out the contradiction with the scriptural text.
If this were not explained extensively, its summarized meaning would be difficult to understand,

Regarding the question concerning the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in relation to the Four Truths, it asks:
