Two [of these] do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause.
They do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause.
Regarding the two [types of] cessation and the two [types of] path mentioned previously, they should be analyzed; the latter two are suffering.
Regarding the aggregate of suffering, the Noble Truth of Suffering: some have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause but are not themselves causes of the view of a self-identity;
some have the view of a self-identity as their cause and are also causes of the view of a self-identity;
and some neither have the view of a self-identity as their cause nor are they causes of the view of a self-identity.
In this context, there are only three propositions;
there are no four, because the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is a universal cause (sarvatragahetu).
Among all defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*), there is nothing capable of producing the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); it does not arise from the view of a self-identity.
Furthermore, among non-defiled phenomena (*akliṣṭa-dharma*), there is likewise nothing capable of producing the view of a self-identity.
In this context, because the treatise is composed based on causes and conditions,
the phrase "that which has the view of a self as its cause but is not a cause of the view of a self" cites the first partial statement.
Because these dharmas are numerous, the narrow [classification] is set aside to adopt a broader one.
There are four sections of text,
excluding the "conjunction" (ubhayānta) category.

This refers to the exclusion of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the past and present, as well as their associated (*samprayukta*) and co-existent (*sahabhū*) factors; the word "etc.
(*ādi*) refers to their acquisitions (*prāpti*).
This arises from the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) through its homogeneous and pervasive causes (*sabhāga-hetu* and *sarvatraga-hetu*).
It acts as a homogeneous cause to produce the view of a self.
Furthermore, the factors associated with and co-existent with the view of a self function as its associated and co-existent causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu* and *sahabhū-hetu*).
Furthermore, excluding the past and present universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*),
as well as their associated and co-existent truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*);
this is the second section.
This is excluded because it arises from the pervasive cause of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
and because it acts as a pervasive cause for the arising of this view of a self; furthermore,
since it does not obtain a non-pervasive cause, the term "and so forth" (ādi) is not used.
Furthermore, with the exception of the future *satkāyadṛṣṭi* associated with the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*),
this third section excludes [them].
Here, by mentioning *satkāyadṛṣṭi*, it excludes the factors associated with it, but does not exclude *satkāyadṛṣṭi* itself.
This excludes [the factors] because they produce the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) through being associated and co-existent causes;
furthermore, it excludes future *satkāyadṛṣṭi* and its associated factors.
Birth, aging, subsistence, and impermanence;
as well as all other defiled truths of suffering,
with the exception of the fourth section.
This refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and its associated phenomena,
which grasp at arising, aging, duration, and impermanence;
it is excluded because the view of a self-identity arises through the cause of coexistence (*sahabhūhetu*).
All other afflicted truths of suffering arise from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
yet they do not serve as the cause for that view of a self-identity.
That which has the view of a self as its cause and also has the view of a self as its cause refers to the factors previously excluded.
That which neither has the view of a self as its cause nor has the view of a self as its cause refers to [the remaining factors].
That is to say, it refers to the undefiled *duḥkhasatya* (truth of suffering).
The same applies to the *samudayasatya* (truth of origination); this is as stated in the treatise.
The reason why the number of categories for suffering and origination is the same is as follows:
The Truths of Suffering and Origination both take all that is contaminated (*sāsrava*) as their essence.
It is called "origination" in the sense of being a cause; it is called "suffering" in the sense of being a fruit.
Just as consciousness and the mental faculty (manas) are neither broader nor narrower in essence,
yet there are distinctions among the afflictions that delude them regarding the two truths;
that is to say, if one possesses all ten.
The aggregates consist of only seven.

The alternative explanations provided by certain masters do not accord with the intent of our own school. As that treatise states: "There may be a truth of suffering that has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, yet is not the cause of the view of a self-identity."
This cites the first phrase of the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
"Excluding future *satkāyadṛṣṭi* and its associated factors—namely, their arising, aging, abiding, and impermanence—as well as all other defiled *duḥkhasatya*."
This transcends the first three sections and cites the text of the fourth section.
Since the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and its associated factors possess the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*),
they are excluded because they belong to the category of "coexistent" (*sahabhū*).
Therefore, it is known that the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) associated with the mind can also produce the mind;
this is because of the four characteristics associated with the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the future world.
Because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises solely from the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) and has no other causes, it is said:
"There are some [factors] belonging to the Truth of Suffering that are to be abandoned by seeing. This refers to those factors that are excluded from the aforementioned categories.
This cites the second phrase from the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
It establishes that the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the factors associated with the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) constitute the "simultaneous" category (*sahabhū-pada*).
By this, it is proven that the fourteen [factors] are not [associated].
Treatise:
There are other masters who do not recite "and its associated dharmas," describing this as a variation from the recitation of other masters.
If one excludes the five characters "and those associated dharmas," this means excluding only the four secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa) of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
The four secondary characteristics of the associated dharmas are not excluded because they cannot produce the view of a self-identity.

The mind base (*manas*) and the mental-object base (*dharma*) consist of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), acquisition (*prāpti*), and the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*). As for the "mental-object base of contact" (*sparśa-dharmāyatana*):
It is attained; it consists of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Commentary:
If one experiences the body and its location, it should be understood that the same applies [to the other aggregates].
The three bases of clear perception: as for the three bases of the body, they are the body, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharma*). Tangibles are the four great elements;
mental objects are the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and so forth.
It should be understood that the same applies to the three—visible form, odor, and taste. The treatise states:
"If it is so for the sense base of the eye, it should be understood that the same applies [to the others] up to [the sense base of the mind]."
It is clear that there are four bases of feeling:
namely, the eye, the body, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharma*).

Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (19), there is a type of karma that results in the maturation of only a single basis, namely, the karma that brings about the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*).
That karma ripens only as the result in the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
There is karma that ripens only as the result in two spheres; namely, karma that results in the acquisition of the sphere of the mind (*manāyatana*).
That karma results in maturation only in the sense-sphere of mind and the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Karma that results in contact (*sparśa*) results in maturation in three sense-spheres:
namely, the sense-sphere of body, the sense-sphere of tangibles, and the sense-sphere of mental objects.
The same applies to karma that acquires the spheres of visible form, odor, and taste;
each receives its own sphere as maturation, while the sphere of tangibles and the sphere of mental objects receive their maturation.
Karma that acquires the eye-sphere receives the maturation of four spheres.
That is to say: the eye base, the body base, the tangible-object base, and the mental-object base.
The same applies to the kamma that results in the ear, nose, and tongue bases;
that is to say, each receives its own respective base as the maturation of the body base, the tangible-object base, and the mental-object base.
Other masters say that all great elements produce both visible form and sound,
and that no visible forms in the desire realm are devoid of odor and taste.
He asserts this: the karma that brings about the acquisition of the eye-base results in the maturation of seven bases,
namely, the eye-base and the body-base.
And there is the maturation of the spheres of visible form, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena.
The same applies to the karma that results in the acquisition of the spheres of the ear, nose, and tongue;
that is to say, each receives its own respective sphere and the body sphere.
And the maturation of the sense bases of form, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects.
One obtains the maturation of the six sense bases from the karma of the body base;
that is to say, the body base.
And there is the maturation of the spheres of visible form, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.
One who performs an action that results in the sphere of visible form experiences the maturation of five spheres, namely:
the maturation of the spheres of visible form, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.
The same applies to the karma that results in the acquisition of the bases of odor, taste, and tangibility;
that is, each respectively experiences its own base as the maturation of the bases of visible form, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects.
What has been stated thus refers to those [karmas] whose results are definitely obtained;
as for those whose results are not definitely obtained, their number is indefinite.
Nevertheless, there is karma capable of undergoing maturation in eight locations.
There is karma that can experience the maturation in nine bases;
there is karma that can experience the maturation in ten bases;
and there is karma that can experience the maturation in eleven bases.
In all cases, the sphere of sound is excluded. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"There is karma that produces the maturation of only one sphere; namely, that which produces the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)."
That is to say, the life-faculty and so forth.
If one experiences the sense-base of mind, one necessarily experiences two bases,
namely, mind and mental objects.
It should be understood that the same applies to the sense-base of tangibles—
that is, to tangibles and mental objects.
If one experiences the sense-base of visible forms, one necessarily experiences three sense-bases.
These are visible form, tangible objects, and mental phenomena.
One should know that those which experience odors and tastes are likewise threefold,
each constituting one [of these categories].

Including the sense-base of touch and the sense-base of mental objects (*dharma-āyatana*). If one is born with a fixed destiny for the body sense-base, one is necessarily destined for four sense-bases:
namely, the body sense-base, the form sense-base, the touch sense-base, and the mental-object sense-base.
If one experiences the sense base of the eye, one necessarily experiences five bases:
namely, the eye, body, visible forms, tangibles, and the mental-object base (*dharmāyatana*).
One should know that for the ear, nose, and tongue, there are likewise five.
That is to say, each is considered a single [base]:
body, visible form, tangible object, and mental objects.
Now, regarding the various treatises that present differing explanations, the distinctions lie in their respective underlying intentions.
All phenomena exist in mutual dependence, being either proximate or remote causes; these include the four characteristics,
the primary dharma itself, and its associated dharmas,
all of which serve as causes for one another within their respective spheres.
This is the most intimate [relationship]. Second, there are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*);
these are also intimately related. Although they do not stand in a relationship of mutual causality, the five causes produce derived matter.
They are also necessarily mutually dependent;
for those of the category of maturation (*vipāka*), these two have never been separated from one another. Third, there are four faculties that depend on the body faculty (*kāyendriya*):
although the eye and other faculties lack the five causes [for their arising], if the four faculties exist, the body faculty necessarily exists.

While one naturally possesses the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), it is not necessarily the case that there are four faculties; rather, there are five faculties based upon the support and the objects of the faculties.
That is to say, wherever the five faculties exist, if one is in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there are visible form and tangible objects.
If one abides in the desire realm, there are four objects; in the five [subtle] elements, there are eight atoms in the sense that they are inseparable.
This treatise and the first master of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explain this based on the first three meanings.
The *Nyāyānusāra* explains it based on the first four meanings;
however, because the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is determinate,
the later masters of the *Mahāvibhāṣā* explain it by means of all five meanings.
However, it is stated that this refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and not the higher realms.
Furthermore, the initial explanation regarding the "feeling of contact" (*spraṣṭavya-vedanā*) recorded in the *Vibhāṣā* differs from this treatise;
this should be further examined in detail.
Treatise:
There are fruits capable of inducing rebirth in either five, six, seven, or up to eleven bases (*āyatana*).
This clarifies that there may be karma that is certain to induce rebirth in five, six, seven, or up to eleven bases.
Treatise:
Karma may have few results, such as those reaching the size of a *nyagrodha* tree and so forth;
this clarifies that the cause is small while the result is great. Within this context, "few results" refers to [the following].
This does not mean that many causes produce a single effect; rather,
it intends to demonstrate that a small or residual cause can produce many effects,
as is the case with grains such as rice and wheat.
When a single seed as the cause yields hundreds or thousands of fruits, it is called "small fruit from a seed," such as in the cases of the lotus or the pomegranate; that is,
a single seed as the cause produces fruit after one year.
It has already yielded fruits for hundreds of thousands of years, beyond measure. According to the treatise,
there are karmas of a single lifetime whose fruition exceeds the cause.
This clarifies the three periods of time.
Just as karma created in one period may be experienced across three periods,
there is no instance where karma created across three periods is experienced in a single period.
This is according to the cited explanation.
One should not exert effort when the fruit is small compared to the cause.
Treatise.
There is one thought-moment of karma that reaches [the result] as described above; this should be understood accordingly.
This explanation of the minor three periods of time is stated according to their full extent.
As for why it should be understood as above in this context: Question: If that is so, the Bodhisattva cultivates the causes for the karmic retribution of the marks over a hundred eons.

Why is it that [karma] is experienced in only one birth? Answer: Because the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) cultivated supports a single karma; however, that which truly brings about the result has many fruits relative to its cause.
This is because the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) is drawn forth by the power of the causal force.
This clarifies that the fruit of maturation necessarily requires a long period of time for it to transform before it can reach maturity.
Treatise.
Furthermore, because the retributive cause must reach its full capacity before it can produce its effect,
this clarifies that the production of a dissimilar result necessarily requires a long period of time.
Commentary:
Since these six causes have been introduced, they should now be further distinguished.
Below this, the differences between the causes and the time periods are again clarified.
The treatise states: The ultimate principle is as previously explained.
It is explained that the universal (*sarvatraga*) and similar-type (*sabhāga*) [causes] exist only in two time periods;
they do not exist in the future period.
As previously stated:
because there is no priority or posteriority. Treatise.
The associated, coexistent, and pervasive [causes] are all universally present;
this clarifies the three causes,
as two of them exist simultaneously.
Because their nature as maturation (*vipāka*) differs.
As for the treatise,
since the verse does not state that they reach the three time periods or the non-temporal (*aparyāpanna*).

The *kāraṇahetu* (efficient cause) is explained as being able to function because its essence is broad; it thus extends across the three periods of time as well as the non-temporal (*adhvavinirmukta*).
Treatise:
Having already explained the six causes up to their establishment in relation to one another.
From here on begins the second major section, which clarifies the six causes in relation to the five fruits.
The treatise states: "Up to and including analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."
This citation from the root treatise establishes the nature of the fruit.
Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), every one is a fruit;
among unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), only analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is taken as such.
It is argued that cessation through meditative concentration (*samāpatti-pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is not a fruit. [The opponent replies:
If that were so, then up to this point it would follow that [cessation] is a fruit.
This objection implies that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) must possess a cause.
Generally, the designation "effect" is established in relation to a "cause.
The unconditioned is an effect.
It should logically possess causes. The treatise states:
furthermore, because this unconditioned [phenomenon] serves as a cause for this [conditioned phenomenon].
This objection implies that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) must possess a fruit.
Generally, the name "cause" is established in relation to its fruit;
since the unconditioned is a cause, it ought to be called "possessing a fruit."
Treatise:
Only conditioned phenomena [apply], not the unconditioned.
This is the general answer.
Conditioned phenomena are causes and they are effects;
they both possess causes and possess effects.
Unconditioned phenomena are causes and they are effects.
It is not that there is a cause without a fruit.
Why is this so? The treatise investigates why the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) differs from the conditioned (saṃskṛta) in having both cause and fruit.
Treatise:
Because there are no six causes and because there are no five fruits.
This is the answer.
Regarding the six causes and five fruits, it is taught outside [of this system] that the realization of causes and so forth is not without cause;
nor is there the giving of fruits by those who do not take them up—
thus, it is not without fruit.
It is called "causeless" because it lacks the six causes as its causes;
it is called "fruitless" because it lacks the five fruits as its fruits.
Treatise.
On what grounds is it not admitted that "arrival" (*prāpti*) acts as an efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*)?
This is an objection:
since the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) is obtained through the power of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
For what reason is it not admitted that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) can function as a productive cause (*kāraṇahetu*)?
[The *Śāstra* replies: Regarding their non-obstruction in the arising [of dharmas], what contribution does the path (*mārga*) make?
Answer: Among the six causes, the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) is so named because it does not obstruct arising.
Since unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) do not arise, they lack an efficient cause.
Treatise:
If that is so, what is the fruit, and what is the meaning of "fruit"?
Herein lie two questions.
First, since the cause does not exist, of what could this be the fruit? What is it that is called "fruit"?
Second, the term "fruit" has meaning only in relation to a "cause";
since the cause does not exist, [the fruit cannot exist].
What is the meaning of "fruit" (*phala*)?
The treatise states:
It refers to that which is obtained through the power of the Path, being the fruit of the Path.
Answer: The treatise states:
"If that were so, it would not apply to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."
This is difficult.
That which arises by means of the Path may indeed be considered the fruit of the Path.
If cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) exists prior [to its realization], how could it be a fruit?
The treatise does not hold this to be so, because there is a distinction up until its actual existence.
Answer: It is because the path is distinguished by its attainment of cessation and its function regarding analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Treatise:
How is it that there is efficacy regarding the attainment of the Path?
This is the question.
"Śāstra" means "that which can produce";
this is the answer. Śāstra.
What is the efficacy regarding the path of cessation?
This is the question. [The] Treatise [responds]:
"Because it is capable of realization.
This is the answer.
[From] the Treatise.
For this reason, up to the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is considered a fruit of the path;
this concludes the explanation.
Because the path cannot cause the extinction of that which has already arisen, it lacks the six causes as its cause.
Because it is realized through the path that extinguishes the causes,
this is the fruit of the path among the five fruits.
Treatise.
Since all unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) can function as efficient causes (kāraṇahetu),
a question is raised:
Now, the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala) is established in relation to the efficient cause.
Since it is granted that unconditioned phenomena have no dominant fruit,
how can they be considered efficient causes? [The Treatise says:]
This is the answer: because all unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) possess the function of yielding a fruit.
They are called the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) because they do not act as an obstacle at the moment another phenomenon arises.
That which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not obstruct the arising of others is called the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
It is said to "possess a fruit" based on the sense of grasping (*grahaṇa*) and bestowing (*dāna*).
A dharma is designated as "grasping the fruit" only when it reaches the present moment.

Because the unconditioned is free from the world and without appropriation, it is not designated as having a fruit of utilization; therefore, unconditioned phenomena have no sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Thus far has the Vaibhāṣika school been described.
Treatise:
The Sautrāntika masters assert that [the unconditioned] exists only as a designation for conditioned phenomena.
The Master of the Treatise here restates the Sautrāntika position.
The Sautrāntika school does not admit that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are causes,
because it is so stated in the sūtras. [Abhidharmakośa] Bhāṣya.
"In which sutra is this stated?
This is a question from the Sarvāstivādins. [The] Treatise [responds]:
As it is said in the Sūtra regarding [the range] up to consciousness, so it is here as well;
this is the citation from the Sūtra provided by the Sautrāntikas.
If that is the case, then [consciousness] acts as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
This is the objection of the Sarvāstivādins.
The Sūtra states that all forms produced by causes and conditions are impermanent;
you, however, claim that their cause is exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Since the Sūtra states that consciousness arises from impermanent causes and conditions,
it follows that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) should also not be objective conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*). [Abhidharmakośa-]bhāṣya.
The objection is not established because it is stated [in the sūtra] that only that which can produce and reach [the effect] is [meant].
The answer is:
the sūtra states that impermanence can produce matter (*rūpa*).
Even those things that can produce consciousness are all impermanent;
it is not said that only those which serve as conditions for consciousness are impermanent.
Therefore, your objection is invalid.
Treatise:
Is it not also stated that "reaching" (*prāpti*) serves as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*)?
The Vaibhāṣika school provides this explanation.
The Sūtra states that "that which can produce" is impermanent, yet this does not negate the existence of permanent dharmas.
For what reason does the Sūtra state that impermanence is "that which can produce"?
Does it thereby negate that non-obstruction is "the productive cause" (kāraṇa-hetu)?
Treatise:
There is a sūtra that extends [the discussion] up to the nature of being a non-obstructing cause;
this is the refutation by the Sautrāntikas.
I offer this interpretation because there are sūtras stating that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) serve as object-conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*); however,
since there is no scriptural statement regarding non-obstructing causes (*anāvaraṇahetu*), I do not posit them here.
For what reason do you establish this and falsely cite it as an example of my "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya)?
[The opponent asks:
Although there is no sutra that says so, does this mean there is no sutra that says so at all?
The Vaibhāṣika offers this defense:
The treatise asks,
"If that is so, what dharma is designated as 'disjunction' (visamyoga)?"
This is the question of the Sautrāntika school:
According to the tenets of the Sautrāntikas, cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) lacks substantial reality and is not established as a cause;
yet now you, of the Sarvāstivāda school, have established it as a cause.
What distinct dharma is called "disjunction" (visamyoga)?
The treatise states: it is precisely the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) as described in this very treatise.
The Sarvāstivāda school cites a treatise to answer this. The treatise asks:
"Is it not the case that [the question] was previously raised up until the revelation of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?"
This is the critique from the Sautrāntika school.
In the preceding *Dhātu-pāda*, it was asked: "What is cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?
It is disjunction (*visamyoga*)."
Now, regarding the question here as to what disjunction (*visamyoga*) is and how it is cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) remains entirely unmanifested.
Treatise:
This dharma’s intrinsic nature is also called "disjunction" (*visamyoga*).
This is the explanation of the Sarvāstivāda school.
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), as an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomenon, is said to be inexpressible;
it can only be described through expedient means as being "wholesome" (*kuśala*).
To distinguish it from space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is further described as being "eternal" (*nitya*).

The treatise states: To distinguish it from other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and to reveal its intrinsic nature, it is called "analytical cessation" (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and also "disjunction" (*visamyoga*).
The Sautrāntika masters say that these [unconditioned phenomena] do not exist here; thus,
the Master [Vasubandhu], representing the Sautrāntika school,
states that all three types of unconditioned phenomena are devoid of substantial reality.
Since things have no established existence,
[the text] asks:
"If that is so, for what reason are they called 'space' and so forth?"
This is a question from the Sarvāstivādins:
"Since phenomena have no intrinsic substance,
upon what basis is their name established?"
Since they are designated as "space" and "cessation through deliberation," it is known that they possess substantial reality.
Treatise.
"Only that which is without contact up to this point is space.
Answer: "Space has no substantial entity; it is a designation established by convention."
Treatise:
From the arising of latent dispositions up to what is called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
this explains the conventional designation of cessation through discernment.
The treatise states:

"The remaining aggregates of one who dies prematurely due to the absence of the power of analytical discernment" explains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as a conventional designation.
Treatise: The masters of other schools (nikāyāntarīya) state that "attainment" (prāpti) is called non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
This is the author of the treatise’s presentation of the tenets of the Sthavira school. They maintain that [cessation] is due to the functional power of discernment by means of wisdom (prajñā).

The non-arising of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) is termed analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). The non-arising [of dharmas] due to the deficiency of conditions for the latent dispositions,
as well as the non-arising of the fruit of suffering, is termed non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The treatise states:
"That which is attained through the power of analytical discernment is subsumed under cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This is the Master of the Treatise’s refutation.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and the non-arising of suffering both result from the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*).
This non-arising is also subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). [Abhidharmakośabhāṣya].
Some say that the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of all phenomena consists in their reaching the state of being designated by a name.
This describes the tenet of the Mahāsāṃghika school:
they maintain that once conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) have arisen, their subsequent natural absence is called non-analytical cessation.
Treatise:
Since that which is thus grasped does not exist until its cessation, the Master of the Treatise refutes it.
As it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), how could it be that it was previously non-existent and later came into existence?
[The opponent] argues:
"Does it not follow that cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) must also be impermanent?
Thus, the Mahāsāṃghikas raise this counter-objection against the proponent.
The Sautrāntika school maintains that because analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is also produced by analysis, future existence does not arise.
The treatise states: "That which is preceded by non-analysis (*apratisaṃkhyā*) is likewise impermanent."
The author of the treatise replies:
Cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is inherently existent; it does not come into being only after non-deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā) has preceded it.
How can cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) also be impermanent?
The treatise asks: Why is this so?
This is the argument of the Mahāsāṃghikas:
since the seeds for the arising of latent dispositions (anuśaya) have already been produced,
the state of their cessation is termed "cessation through deliberation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Therefore, one knows that non-existence does not exist as long as [the defilements] have not been extinguished.
This is why it can be said that analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) exists only after non-analytical cessation has preceded it. Thus says the treatise.
"It is not that [the non-arising] exists only after analytical cessation has occurred.
This is the Master’s response.

The non-arising of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) is not due to their being preceded by analytical cessation; rather, they do not arise because they have existed inherently from the beginning and are not something newly produced.
Treatise:
What is it that is unarisen yet exists from the beginning?
This is the objection raised by the Mahāsāṃghikas and others.
What is it that is unarisen and has existed from the beginning? The treatise states:
If there were no discernment, one would reach the state of non-creation and non-arising.
The Master of the Treatise explains this according to the Sautrāntika school:
the meaning of the non-arising of the seeds of latent dispositions (anuśaya) exists inherently;
it is simply that when the conditions for their arising are obstructed, the meaning of non-arising becomes manifest.
It is not that it is unproduced because it is not created;
rather, the Path merely serves as an obstacle to production—
it is not that it is unproduced because it is not created.
Treatise:
If [it is argued that] "only non-arising" [is the case], does this not contradict [the sūtra]?
This is the Vaibhāṣika challenging the Sautrāntika.
If nirvāṇa were merely the non-arising of phenomena without being a distinct real entity,
it would simply be the future existence of dharmas that do not arise.
How, then, could the sūtra state that it can bring about the eternal cessation of all suffering— past, future, and present?
This essence of permanent abandonment is itself nirvāṇa.

Therefore, it is known that the realization of the attainment of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) through the abandonment of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and so forth throughout the three periods of time is nirvāṇa.
[Treatise]
Although this text exists up to the phrase "the severance of all sufferings," the Sautrāntika school interprets it thus:
the intention of this sutra is as follows.
Because the afflictions conditioned by the past and so forth are severed,
it is called the "severance of all suffering.
This does not mean that the severance of afflictions of the past and present is what is termed the "severance of all suffering."
Treatise:
As the Blessed One has taught regarding the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), it should be understood in the same way.
This is an explanation by means of citing an example.
Just as afflictions are designated as "form" and so forth because they take form and so forth as their objects, yet are not themselves form;
and just as afflictions are designated as "past" and so forth because they take the past and so forth as their objects, yet are not themselves past.
Treatise:
Even if there are other sūtras that reach this same meaning, there is no contradiction.
One should apply this principle to interpret other sūtras as well.
Treatise:
The passage from "In this sutra" up to "should also be understood as such" provides a further separate explanation.
This means that because one has severed the seeds perfumed by past and present [defilements], it is called "severing the past and present.
For example, the eighteen modes of craving (*tṛṣṇā-carita*) that arise in the past are spoken of in reference to past births.
It should be understood that the same applies to the future and the present.
Treatise:
Thus, these two time periods [are explained] up until what is called the exhaustion of karma.
This is an explanation by way of citing the Dharma.
Because afflictions arise in the past and present, they perfume and form seeds;
through the power of the Path, those seeds are severed.
When the seeds perfumed by past and present [afflictions] are severed,

It is like the distinction between the two mothers who give birth and those who nourish.
Furthermore, it is only through the power of supporting conditions that a cause can produce [an effect];
once produced, it is sustained and developed by the force of the conditions for its continuity.
Some say that the cause is singular while the conditions are manifold,
just as there are differences between the seed, the fertilizer, and the soil.
Furthermore, it is due to non-commonality.
That which is common is a condition,
such as the eye.
As with form (*rūpa*):
furthermore, that which performs its own function is called a cause (*hetu*), while that which performs the function of another is called a condition (*pratyaya*).
Just as with seeds, fertilizer, and so forth:
that which can bring about [an effect] is called the cause (*hetu*),
while that which can sustain it is called the condition (*pratyaya*).
Like a flower;
like its stalk.
Furthermore, "proximate" refers to the cause.
That which is distant is called the "condition" (pratyaya),
such as a jewel or the sun.
Furthermore, the cause is that which can produce,
while the condition is that which can differentiate;
it is like the production of butter from curd.
A person can discern this through the instrument of investigation.
Furthermore, that which possesses the actual meaning is called a "cause" (hetu),
while that which assists in its manifestation is called a "condition" (pratyaya).
Just as the phonemes (*akṣara*) and syllables (*vyañjana*) differ according to their meanings,
there are many such varieties of distinctions. Therefore,
distinct names and concepts are established for causes (*hetu*) and conditions (*pratyaya*).
This general meaning reveals that causes are proximate while conditions are remote.
Therefore, among the proximate causes, five are proximate and one is remote;
among the remote conditions, three are remote and one is proximate.

Having followed the principles and teachings, the various conditions have been briefly analyzed. Since the treatise states this, by what reasoning is it proven that the mutual inclusion [of these conditions] is correct? Answer: It is not that there is no difference between the general categories of causes (*hetu*) and conditions (*pratyaya*).
The "cause" (hetu) is a term for what is proximate, while the "condition" (pratyaya) is a name for what is remote.
Among the six causes, five are proximate; therefore, they share the designation of being "proximate."
Among the four conditions, three are remote; therefore, they are designated by the common term "remote.
However, within the causes, there is also that which is remote, namely the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Among conditions, there are proximate causal conditions (*nidāna-pratyaya*).
One cannot claim that because the meaning of "condition" is remote, the causal condition is remote and thus capable of acting [as such];
nor can one claim that because the meaning of "cause" is proximate, it alone is capable of acting as the proximate causal condition.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
"Although the substance (*tattva*) of the six causes and four conditions is not distinct, their meanings differ.
Furthermore, according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*:
I teach that activity constitutes cause and effect;
the substantial reality of all phenomena is eternally without transformation.
Since it is neither cause nor effect, one should know this by analogy.
The nature of causal conditions consists in their activity;
since activity is one, it is known that there is no difference [between them]. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
"Moreover, since the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) are not included among the causes..."
Thus, we know that the other two meanings also have distinctions.
Since their meanings as "conditions" (*pratyaya*) are equivalent, I shall now examine this statement and find it to be incomplete in meaning.
This is because one master’s explanation of "cause" (*hetu*) does not include the two conditions; namely, the *hetu-pratyaya* (causal condition) and the *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant condition).
The cause is also not included [in the conditions]. Why? Because the cause is included within the "predominant condition" (adhipati-pratyaya).
Furthermore, these two conditions are also combined and included within the cause. Moreover, regarding these two conditions:
The two masters of the *Vibhāṣā* both agree that it is included within the causes;
one master explains its inclusion as being through the two conditions.
One [teacher] says it is not included.

How can one use the partial meaning of a single teacher as a premise to refute the doctrines of two teachers? Furthermore, one teacher asserts that the cause does not include the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the object condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
There is a specific intention here.
The efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) has two meanings:
first, it merely does not obstruct.
The second [condition] possesses both [aspects].
If one takes only the aspect of non-obstruction, it subsumes only the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);
if one includes its active function, it subsumes all three conditions.

From these two masters, there is a distinction in their explanations. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Exposition of the Treasury) quotes an explanation from another source regarding the distinct meanings of causes (*hetu*) and conditions (*pratyaya*), stating:
"A cause is like a birth mother, a seed, and so forth."
Regarding the statement "conditions are like foster mothers, dung, soil, and so forth":
this explains that the immediate cause is termed the "cause" (hetu),
while the remote cause is termed the "condition" (pratyaya).
As in the *Vibhāṣā*, it is asked whether the four great elements producing derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) constitutes the sense of "cause" (*hetu*) or the sense of "condition" (*pratyaya*).
Here, it is held that they constitute the sense of "cause" by way of being causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The meaning of "predominance as a condition" (adhipati-pratyaya)—
is this not simply the meaning of "cause," such that the six causes constitute the meaning of cause and the four conditions constitute the meaning of condition?
Furthermore, among the efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*),
"direct" refers to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*),
as well as the bases (*āśraya*) of the sense faculties and consciousnesses.
"Distant" means merely not being an obstacle.
This applies to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the object condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
If it is argued that because they are distant, they are not included among the causes (*hetu*).

Is it not rather that [the object] is distant, yet does not constitute an obstruction? If you claim that it is not included among the causes because it is "proximate," how could it be proximate to the sense organ, consciousness, or their supports?
Therefore, one should know that the statement regarding its non-inclusion is an incomplete (or figurative) explanation.
All treatises state that, with the exception of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the remaining five causes constitute the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
"Nature" (*svabhāva*) here carries the meaning of essence (*tattva*) and the meaning of category (*jāti*).
This type of dharma is the essence of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is like a dharma that does not obstruct."
The enabling cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is also called "non-obstruction";
thus, one should know that they are the same.
How could it be that the cause is non-obstructive while the condition (*pratyaya*) is obstructive?
The second point concerns their difference.
Since one kind [of mind] does not obstruct, how could there be a distinction between the intimate and the remote? Some people fail to awaken to this at all;
they pose a question and answer it themselves as follows:
Regarding these two explanations, it must be clarified whether they describe mutual inclusion in terms of essence or in terms of function.
If explained according to their essential nature (*tattva*),
the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) should subsume those four conditions,
and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) should subsume those six causes.
Because their substance is all-pervasive.
If explained in terms of function,
the operations of the six causes and four conditions are each distinct.
How do they mutually subsume one another?
The explanation states:
Regarding the mutual subsumption of the six causes and four conditions, there are two meanings.
First, it is explained by way of its essence;
second, it is based on the similarity of its function.
The first master in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains it by way of its essence.
The causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) comprises five [conditions], while the efficient condition (kāraṇa-hetu) comprises three.
However, if one considers the broad scope of the essential nature of the efficient condition, it actually comprises all four conditions.
The nature of the predominant cause (*adhipati-hetu*) is broad and can encompass all six causes;
therefore, it is said that the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) alone encompasses three [of those six],
while the predominant cause encompasses one.
The intention of this master is to explain the inclusion [of phenomena] by correlating the six causes and the four conditions; furthermore,
he does so according to a single characteristic that exhausts the essential nature of what is included.
Therefore, it is said that the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) subsumes five [causes],
while the acting cause (*kāraka-hetu*) subsumes three;
for outside of the acting cause, there are the other five causes.
Apart from the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), there are three other conditions;
since their mutual inclusion has been clarified,
the capacity of the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) to include all four is not mentioned separately.
The six are subsumed by the predominant [condition].
Question: If one clarifies their mutual inclusion based on their essential natures, then the essential nature is eternally present.
This means that the six causes and the four conditions are not distinct;
how, then, do they subsume one another?
Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
I teach that functional activity constitutes cause and effect;
the substantial reality of all phenomena is eternally without transformation, for it is neither cause nor effect. The commentary states:
In terms of its essence, it is unchanging;
its causes and conditions are identical.
Thus, the essence follows from the function.
Therefore, the distinction is stated.
As for the second master of the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā* and this treatise,
they distinguish mutual inclusion based on the similarity of function.
If one discusses the six causes and four conditions, their functions are distinct and do not mutually subsume one another; nevertheless,
it is said that the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) subsumes five of these causes.
Regarding the predominance-condition as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*),
this clarifies their mutual inclusion based on the similarity of their functions.
This also applies to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
"Because it does not resemble a cause, the cause does not include it. A detailed examination of this explanation reveals that it has not grasped the intent of the treatise;
how is it that all these virtuous qualities are entirely devoid of discernment?
Since the treatise states that all five causes constitute the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), how can it be said that they are "similar" [to it]?
Furthermore, the meaning of "not obstructing" constitutes the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
This also carries the meaning of being a predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
It is the non-obstruction of the cause and the non-obstruction of the conditions.
What distinction is there such that they are said to be similar rather than identical?

Furthermore, it is stated that because they are similar, they are subsumed; and it is further said that, "for the time being, based on a single characteristic, the substance of what is subsumed is exhausted."
As for those who immediately cease [their practice],
upon what sutras and śāstras do they rely,
and what precedents exist for this?
Furthermore, the essence of the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) is identical to the essence of the four conditions (pratyaya).
Why is the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) considered remote, while the efficient cause consists of only three conditions?
Moreover, the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) is identical to the essence of the six causes.
Why are the five causes [of arising] considered remote? Because the dominant cause (*adhipati-pratyaya*) alone subsumes the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).

Based on this interpretation, it is not consistent with reason. Question: Regarding the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), what are the five causes such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth?
Is it because of these causes and conditions?

Is it because of these predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*)? Answer: According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 131, "How many conditions do the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) serve as for derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)?"
The answer is: by way of cause and predominance.
"Cause" refers to the productive cause, the supporting cause, the establishing cause, the maintaining cause, and the nourishing cause.
"Predominance" refers to non-obstruction.
"And only the absence of obstruction. Explanation:
This is an explanation of the text from the *Jñānaprasthāna*.
This treatise is composed in accordance with the four conditions (*pratyaya*).
The term "cause" (hetu) refers to the causal condition (pratyaya).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 127, states:
"Question: What is the meaning of 'karma' (action/creation)?"
Does this mean "cause" (hetu) or does it mean "condition" (pratyaya)? If so,
what fault would there be?
Both views encounter faults.
If it were in the sense of being a cause,
these four great elements would lack all five types of causes with respect to derived matter.
How can it be said that [the primary elements] are able to produce derived matter?
If this means "condition," then for all derived matter,
with the exception of its own self-nature, all other phenomena would [be its conditions].
There is nothing that is not this predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Why, then, is it said only that [the derived matter] is "produced by the primary elements" (*mahābhūta*)? One should answer thus:
"Produced" (*kṛta*) has the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*).
Question: Since these [derived forms] lack all five causes for derived matter, how can they possess the meaning of "cause"?
Answer: Although they lack the five causes, such as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and so forth, [they still function as causes].
Furthermore, there are five other types of causal meanings, namely:

the cause of production (*janana-hetu*), the cause of dependence (*niśraya-hetu*), the cause of establishment (*pratisthā-hetu*), the cause of support (*dhṛti-hetu*), and the cause of nourishment (*anugraha-hetu*). It is by means of these that [the primary elements] act as creators.
Other masters say that "derived" (bhautika) has the meaning of "conditioned by.
Question: Regarding all derived matter, with the exception of its own self-nature, are all other dharmas exclusively predominant conditions (adhipatipratyaya)?
How is it that they are said to be merely derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)?
Answer: Regarding the meaning of the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), there are both proximate and remote [relationships].
There is the near;
there is the far;
there is the union.
There are those that do not coincide;
some occur in this life,
while others occur in other lives.
Those that are proximate and so forth are called causes (*hetu*);
those that are remote and so forth are called conditions (*pratyaya*).
It is by virtue of this meaning [that they are so designated].
To state that the primary elements (mahābhūta) serve as both cause and dominant conditions (adhipati-pratyaya) for derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is not contrary to reason.
Furthermore, the *Pañcavastuka-śāstra* also records these two views side by side without offering a critical evaluation. Now, let us examine these two positions in detail.
The former master’s [position] is correct.
We know this to be so because the *Jñānaprasthāna* already frames its questions and answers in terms of the four conditions (*catur-pratyaya*).
How can that which is actually a predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) be answered as being a causal condition (*hetupratyaya*), given that there is no other such precedent?
If this is so, why does the treatise state that the five causes constitute the causal condition?
This is not included among the five causes, such as the similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) and so forth.

How then is it subsumed under the condition of cause (hetu-pratyaya)? Answer: Because its meaning differs from that of the five causes, such as the similar cause and so forth, it is not subsumed within those five causes.
The power and function of the produced fruit are shared with the five causes;
they are not like other dominant conditions (adhipatipratyaya).
Therefore, it is a causal condition (hetupratyaya).
For this reason, the root treatise states that ten causes constitute the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

One [of these] is the dominant condition (*adhipati*). Question: If that is so, why does it not speak of eleven causes, but speaks of only six? Answer: Because the five causes, such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth, have distinct meanings as causes.
If a phenomenon functions as both cause and effect, it pertains to all three realms and four or five aggregates;
this is what is discussed here.
The causes of derived matter consist of only two elements, while its effects comprise a portion of one aggregate.
For this reason, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon serves as a cause for a collective fruit consisting of multiple aggregates (*skandha*),
it is discussed herein.
The four great elements serve as causes for only a small portion of a single aggregate that shares a common result;
this is not mentioned here.
For this reason, apart from these five causes—such as the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) and so forth—[no other cause is required].
Since the five causes, such as arising (*jāti*), are not established separately,
they are subsumed within the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
It is by virtue of this that derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) possesses functional efficacy.
Because it excels the other three conditions,
it is subsumed within the condition of cause (*hetu-pratyaya*). If one were to expand [the categories],
there are five causes, such as the producing cause (*janaka-hetu*) and so forth.
There are ten causes that constitute the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Since various treatises all rely on the complete inclusion of the characteristics of the causes,
they state that five causes constitute the causal condition.
One should reflect further on this. The treatise states:
excluding the nature of the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya) from the stage of Arhat down to [the lower stages].
The second [section] explains the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

This passage sets forth the essential nature of the immediately preceding condition: it refers to all that has already arisen, namely, past and present minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
The only exception is the mind of an Arhat at the moment of entering parinirvāṇa;
although it has already arisen, it is not an equal-and-immediate condition because there is no subsequent mind.
Treatise:
This section on the dharma of dependent origination, up to the term "equal and immediate," explains the name of the equal and immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
The treatise establishes or rejects the nature of conditions based on the fact that these [mental states] arise either equally or unequally with respect to form and so forth.
That is to say, when the substance of the mind and mental factors is identical before and after, it is termed "equal."
That which has no interval between them is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*).
That which is equal and uninterrupted is called "equal and uninterrupted" (*samanantara*).
Matter (*rūpa*) and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are not like this.
Although they arise without interval, because their essential natures are not identical,
they arise in a disordered manner and thus do not constitute equal and immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* quotes the *Mahāvibhāṣā* as saying:
The mind and its mental factors possess resistance (sappatigha) with respect to their basis, object, and mode of activity;
it is for this reason that the immediately preceding condition (anantarapaccaya) is established.
Matter and non-associated formations do not have such characteristics.

Therefore, it is not established that those [factors] constitute the substance of this condition (*pratyaya*). Below, he himself explains: "That is to say, regarding a single basis (*āśraya*), object (*ālambana*), and mode of activity (*ākāra*), there is certainly no occurrence of two consciousnesses and so forth arising simultaneously."
Therefore, it must necessarily arise based on its preceding [condition] and its location.
If the preceding [condition] were an obstruction, the subsequent could not arise.
From this, it is proven.

"Only mind and mental factors can serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for those that follow. Furthermore, it says: "However, this nature of the condition is established based on [the preceding moment's] yielding of space and its drawing forth [the subsequent moment]."
Therefore, although atoms and the like may precede and avoid one another, they do not constitute this condition.
The arising of mental states and the like involves both determinacy and indeterminacy;
thus, we know that it also depends on the power to draw forth [the subsequent state].
It is directly observed that a single mind continues in a sequence from prior to subsequent moments;
although the principle is the same whether the former avoids the latter or not,
there is a distinction between arising and non-arising, as well as between being determinate and indeterminate.
Furthermore, regarding that which is produced in a fixed succession:

it means that immediately following the mind of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), the "receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises; and so on, as explained at length. Question: If the preceding and succeeding entities are one and the same, with no interval between them?
It is only in a preceding or subsequent state, or in a subsequent stage, that [a result] can arise; furthermore, it arises only when there is a definitive certainty.
This proof possesses the power to draw forth [the result].
The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) arises such that its preceding and succeeding entities are one and the same,
with no interval between them;
it persists from the prior moment to the subsequent moment.
Only afterwards can birth occur;
this is also necessarily born.
This life-force is precisely that which has the power to draw forth birth.
Why is the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) not established? The *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
This analogy does not hold, because both life-force (*jīvitendriya*) and birth (*jāti*) are produced by the power of a prior projecting force (*ākṣepaka-karman*).
That is to say, this life-faculty is not drawn forth by the power of a life-force that ceases without interval;
rather, it must be produced as drawn forth by the power of karma performed in a prior state.
If that were so, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) should arise all at once in a single moment,
because everything is equally induced by the power of karma and mental formations (*samskāra*) within a single moment.
[Furthermore,] it would follow that the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) are produced solely as what is induced by prior karma.
It should not depend upon the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Furthermore, there is no fault in the vital faculties (*jīvitendriya*) arising simultaneously,
precisely because their sequential arising is determined by the power of karma.
It is the nature of cause and effect that a single moment of karma induces the arising of multiple moments of maturation.
Furthermore, because it would serve no purpose, life does not arise instantaneously;
rather, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is induced to arise for the sake of sustaining the homogeneous group (*nikāyasabhāga*).
A single life-continuum (jīvitasaṃtati) is sufficient to sustain [the body];
many would be useless.
Although the mind and mental factors are projected by prior karma, [they require a basis].
Yet it is not that it does not depend on the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
for it arises by relying upon the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).
Since it arises by relying on the conjunction of the faculties and objects, [it is established].
Even if many were to arise simultaneously, they would not be useless;
however, because there is no second equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
two [identical] things of the same kind do not arise together.
Furthermore, mind and mental factors are not produced solely by the force of prior karma,
because they arise as both maturation (*vipāka*) and other types of disordered occurrences;
this would not be possible if they did not further depend upon the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
There should be multiple [factors] arising simultaneously in a single moment;
that is to say, the substance of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is exclusively a result of maturation (*vipāka*),
being produced solely by the power of prior karma.
It may be said that [dharmas] of the same category necessarily arise in succession;
however, such a thing does not apply to the mind and mental factors.
Once the retribution has ceased, there arises a flow-on (niṣyanda).
The outflowing and immediate [causes] arise momentarily;
alternatively, the arising of maturation is not necessarily of the same kind.
Therefore, although mind and mental factors do arise from maturation, [they are not restricted to being of the same category].
Furthermore, it cannot be said that [the mind] is identical to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth.
Therefore, only that which arises constantly and without interval is called "equal and immediate" (*samanantara*).
It is said that this serves as the condition for that, based on the aforementioned treatise.
The equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) has several general meanings by which it distinguishes itself from other phenomena:
first, it involves the vacating of space so that a subsequent state may arise;

if this vacating did not occur, the subsequent states would not arise. Second, it possesses the power to project what follows. Third, its substance is equal [to the preceding]. Fourth, it arises without interval and serves as a condition for what follows.
This excludes the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth;
it is on this basis that only mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) are established as having the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "The Dārṣṭāntika masters assert that all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), like mind and mental factors, possess the equal-and-immediate condition."
Just as one sees milk, fermenting seed, or a flower,
and subsequently [sees] curdled milk, vinegar, a sprout, or fruit,
so too do the mind and mental factors cease before and arise after.
Therefore, one should know that all material forms possess this nature of being conditions.
Furthermore, since no sūtra states that only mind and mental factors can serve as such conditions,
this condition is established [as applicable to matter as well].
The claim that what is not matter (arūpa) is a false attachment; this attachment is extensively refuted in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Here, in this treatise, the explanation that matter is not an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) likewise serves to refute the attachment of the Dārṣṭāntikas.
The treatise states:
"This refers to the desire realm, form, and so forth, as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

This is an explanation by way of specific instances. Alternatively, it refers to the two types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*)—those of the desire realm and those of the form realm—that arise subsequent to [a mind of] the desire realm.

This refers to one whose body is in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) entering the six contaminated (sāsrava) dhyānas; or it refers to the two types of uncontaminated (anāsrava) non-informative matter (avijñaptirūpa) in the desire realm, namely, the six uncontaminated dhyānas.
Because the two types of restraint— the path-restraint and the meditative-restraint— do not arise simultaneously,
there are no three kinds of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) that arise subsequently in the desire realm. [Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya] Treatise.
The Venerable Vasumitra, up to the point of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
recounts various dissenting views:
that within a single body, there is first a long-nourished material form (*aupacayika-rūpa*) whose continuity remains uninterrupted.
Because a second type of "nourished matter" (aupacayika-rūpa) subsequently arises without mutual contradiction or harm,
this master’s interpretation does not establish the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
Because they lack the sense of opening and yielding space,
and because they are disordered and unequal,
the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is not established.
The Treatise states: The Venerable One further says that it reaches as far as the area of greatest shade.
This is because the Venerable One’s [measurements] differ in terms of front and back, and in terms of being greater or lesser.
[Objection: "It is not an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
[Response: Is this not the same difficulty as [the objection] regarding mental factors reaching meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and so forth?
Since matter is not equal between its preceding and succeeding moments, it cannot be an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Mental factors (*caitta*) are likewise not equal between their preceding and succeeding moments;
how, then, can they be equal-and-immediate conditions?
Treatise:
This [explanation] avoids the fault of non-equality when applied to different categories;
this is the interpretation. To say they are "equal" is stated according to their own respective categories.
It is not that they do not belong to the same category.
The treatise asks:

Only the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) extends to all things without exception;

Because [the cause] exerts its activity both at the time the resultant dharma ceases and at the time it arises, it is said that there is no obstruction whatsoever.

The Commentary states: "Up to 'all other phenomena' explains that mind and mental factors arise from four conditions. Question: Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the others, their activity arises only when the fruit reaches the moment of cessation.

How is it said that [phenomena] arise from four conditions? Answer: The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 136, states that mind and mental factors arise from four conditions. Regarding this term "arise":
Because "arising" (utpāda) is the collective designation for that which has begun but is not yet extinguished, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Is it not the case that the functions of the conditions (*pratyaya*) and causes (*hetu*) do not exist at the very moment that the dharma arises?"
How is it that [dharmas] arise by way of the four conditions, such as the mind?
How is it that the causal condition possesses the nature of the five causes?
Although their function is established only at the moment of the dharma's cessation.
Yet when a phenomenon arises, it is not devoid of causal efficacy,
for in the absence of this [condition], that phenomenon would necessarily not arise;
this is because the mind and mental factors must invariably rely upon an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Furthermore, because it arises only by relying on two causes,
if a phenomenon serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) or the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for another phenomenon, there is no time when this is not the case.
Because this treatise states:

Yet it is not said that this [subsequent mind] is the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for those [mental factors], because they are produced by the power of the mind and its factors;
just as the mind and mental factors, once produced, are necessarily bound to the preceding mind that has already ceased.
It is not like material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), which can arise simultaneously with other minds;

However, because it is produced by the application of mental skillful means (*upāya*),

it may be said to be the "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*) of the mind; yet, because it is diametrically opposed to and destructive of that which arises simultaneously with the mind (*cittasahaja*), it is [so designated].
It is not a non-mind [dharma] and so forth acting as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). According to the treatise,
all other dissociated (*viprayukta*) dharmas arise from up to two conditions.
This explains other forms and non-associated phenomena.
Treatise:
All that exists in the world arises from a single cause.
This conclusion is correct and not erroneous.
All phenomena in the world arise from the six causes and four conditions as described above.

They do not arise from a single cause, such as the followers of the Ājīvika (ash-smearing) heretics who cling to Maheśvara as the creator and source of all phenomena; nor like the Vaiśeṣika heretics who cling to the self (*ātman*) as a real entity that acts as the creator and producer; nor like the Sāṃkhya who cling to *prakṛti*—also called *pradhāna*—as the cause of all phenomena. It is not produced by any such single cause.
Treatise:
What is the reason for this?
This is a question.

What is the reason for knowing that all phenomena arise from preceding causes and conditions, rather than being produced by a single cause such as Īśvara? The answer below provides two reasons why phenomena are not produced by a single cause.
Treatise:
If everything were established as arising from a single cause,
the Master of the Treatise replies.

Treatise:
Furthermore, all things in the world arise from a single cause;
this is the second cause.

Therefore, we know that all phenomena do not arise from a single cause. If it were granted that all phenomena arise from a single cause, then since the cause is one and there are no other causes, the results produced by it would necessarily arise simultaneously rather than in a sequence of before and after.
Regarding the phrase "sequence and so forth": it refers to the fact that phenomena arise in a temporal succession.
Furthermore, this is equal to the subsequent refutation.

This is the objection regarding the non-identity of causes.
According to the treatise, it is because there may be a transition from differentiated desire to non-differentiation.
This raises the objection that [the distinction] would arise all at once. The treatise states:

This is not a refutation based on a single cause contradicting the thesis. [The] treatise states:

This leads to an infinite regress.

It is not difficult for desire to arise out of sequence.

The treatise states: "Since it is thus with regard to joy, it extends even to the point where [the object] cannot be apprehended."
In other cases, it is difficult to establish [the existence of] Īśvara.

There is the objection that it is useless for one who has mastery over birth to undergo suffering.
Since he intentionally brings about birth in the various worlds and realms such as the hells,
how can he experience joy amidst the suffering of sentient beings?
Treatise:
According to that verse, he is called Rudra because he has arrived;
the following citation of a non-Buddhist verse serves as proof that this is a well-spoken statement.
Taking delight in the suffering of sentient beings, those who are fierce, sharp, and capable of burning—
those non-Buddhists (tīrthika) say that there are three asuras who possess three kingdoms and fly through the air.
Beyond the realm of the Lord of Heaven (Īśvara),
there is a heaven that cannot endure the shooting of fire-arrows;
it burns three lands, reducing them all to ashes at once.
The fire-rocket is perilous and sharp, capable of incinerating the three realms; it is fearsome and constantly threatens to cause harm.
It can pierce a person’s skull and bind it to the crown of the head, and furthermore, it binds the arms with a dragon.
They kill elephants to take their skins;
this is a constant, terrifying affliction. Those who delight in eating flesh, blood, and marrow—this is what they consume. Therefore, he is named Rudra.
This is one of the thousand names of Maheśvara.
This name means "Violent and Wicked.

if he must depend on other causes to produce all phenomena, then he is not sovereign.

it further refutes subsequent counter-arguments.

this concludes the proof.

concluding the preceding section and initiating the subsequent one.
