Below, the fourth single verse clarifies the number of primary elements (mahābhūta) and derived matter (upādāyarūpa) that act as causes for one another.
The Commentary states, up to the point concerning the meaning of "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*), explains the first phrase:

it clarifies that the four primary elements (*mahābhūta*) possess two types of causes with respect to elements of a different class, whereas among those of their own class, they possess only one type of cause.
This refers to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Water is not a coexistent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) with respect to water. Thus says the treatise.
The distinction regarding the causes of the great elements (mahābhūta) as they relate to derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
This clarifies that the great elements act as causes for derived matter;
specifically, there are five types of causes.
That is to say: producing, supporting, establishing, maintaining, and nourishing.
These are the five causes distinguished within the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*);
if stated collectively, they are simply the efficient cause.
If explained individually, there are five. The *Śāstra* states:
"Because it arises from that, it is called the cause of arising. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* says:
That which acts as a generative cause is so called because [the effect] arises from it,
just as a mother gives birth to a child.
The treatise states that once [the mind] has arisen, it follows [the body] until it is designated as its supporting cause (*āśraya-hetu*);
the intended meaning of the *Nyāya* is the same.
Treatise:
Because it is able to sustain [the thesis], it is designated as the "reason for establishing" (*sthāpanahetu*). The *Nyāyabindu* states:
"As for the term 'reason for establishing'..."
Because it is capable of supporting [them],
just as the earth supports objects.
Treatise.
It is called the cause of maintenance because it is the cause of non-interruption; as the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Regarding its being the cause of maintenance:
it is by virtue of that power's maintenance that [the continuum] is prevented from ceasing."
Just as food sustains life,
it is called the cause of nourishment because it is a cause of increase. As the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* says:
Regarding what is called the "nurturing cause" (*poṣaṇahetu*):

it is so called because it is able to cause that [result] to grow, just as the roots of a tree are moistened and nourished by water. If one wishes to understand the differing functions and powers of these five causes:
One should contemplate five similes:
the productive cause is like a mother giving birth to a child;
the supporting cause is like a disciple relying upon a teacher.
The establishing cause is like the earth supporting objects;
the sustaining cause is like food sustaining life;
the nourishing cause is like water moistening the roots of a tree.
Treatise:
This thus clarifies the nature of the cause for abiding in long-term duration;
this is the summary. The mother is able to give rise to the child.
The teacher can transform the disciple;
the earth sustains all things;
food enables life to endure.
Water causes trees to grow;
that is, the four great elements together act as five causes. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Alternatively, the productive cause (*janana-hetu*) is..."
All great elements (mahābhūta) give rise to derived matter (upādāyarūpa),
because derived matter does not arise apart from the various great elements.
Once derived matter has arisen, during the stage in which its homogeneous continuity remains uninterrupted—
Fire is the causal condition of dependence (*āśraya-hetu*), for it enables drying and prevents decay.
Water is the causal condition of establishment (*pratisthā-hetu*), for it provides moistening and prevents dispersal.
Earth is the causal condition of support (*dhṛti-hetu*), for it sustains those [elements] and prevents them from falling.
Wind serves as a supporting cause (*puṣṭi-hetu*) because it can induce [the derived matter] and cause it to increase;
thus, although the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) do not possess the five types of causal relations—such as coexistent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*)—with the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
However, because there are five distinct causes, such as arising and so forth,
there is no contradiction with the Sūtras or the Śāstras.
[End of] Treatise.
This explains the number of derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) that serve as causes for one another,
from those produced [by the primary elements] up to the results such as the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).

this treatise clarifies the number of primary elements that serve as causes for derived matter.

Treatise:
Other masters state that it reaches the objects of the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
This describes a divergent opinion. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* also contains two such views.
This is the same as in this treatise.
According to the passage concerning the mind that initiates karma based on deportment (*airyāpathika*) and so forth,
deportment takes only form (*rūpa*) as its object.
Skillful [action] involves both physical and vocal [manifestations],
such as the mental states that initiate wholesome or unwholesome karma. As for the previous teacher’s statement that [the mind] takes four or five objects as its conditions,
this does not refer to the mind that actually initiates karma.

Regarding the distinction between the former and the latter masters concerning the "proximate minds" (*āsannacitta*): the former holds that these consist only of those minds that take four or five objects, termed "minds of deportment" (*airyāpathika*) and so forth;

the latter master includes all twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*). As for the "paths of deportment" (*airyāpathika*) and "places of craftsmanship" (*śailpasthānika*): [the former refers to the minds associated with walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, while the latter refers to those associated with various arts and crafts].
They are named according to their basis:
postures primarily depend on roads,
while crafts primarily depend on locations.
Treatise:
Thus, from the twenty [minds] up to the two minds of one's own form realm—
this clarifies the mutual arising of the eight minds of the desire realm.
As analyzed previously,
the treatise next explains the two minds of the form realm that reach their own realm.
This clarifies the mutual arising of the six minds of the form realm.
The treatise next explains the formless realm, stating that [minds] arise from up to four minds of their own realm.
This explains the mutual arising of the four minds of the formless realm.
The treatise next discusses the untainted [minds], up to and including those of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
This explains how the two types of untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) give rise to various other states of mind.
The treatise asks:
Furthermore, for what reason does it reach the point of giving rise to the wholesome state produced through application (*prayoga-kuśala*)?
From this point onward, there is a detailed analysis through questions and answers.
This is the question. [The] Treatise [states]:
Because their power is inferior, they reach up to the wholesome mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*).
This answers [the objection] by clarifying that these three minds do not arise in the state of preparatory application. First, because their power is inferior.
These comprise the three types of mind: first, the resultant mind (*vipākacitta*), because it is not produced through the exertion of effort;
second, the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānikacitta*) and deportment (*airyāpathikacitta*), because they proceed by being induced through the desire to exert effort.
The latter two refer to the mind. The fourth is the summary.
The treatise explains that the mind does not arise from the ultimate [state], but can give rise to those [subsequent states].
First, by means of the cause, it explains how the three types of neutral minds arise from a mind of preparatory virtue (*prayoga-kuśala*).
The treatise says: If that were so, it would be difficult [to maintain] because the defiled states are incompatible with one another;
the three minds are not concordant with the preparatory wholesome state.
The preparatory effort does not arise from the three types of minds;
since the nature of defiled preparatory effort is contradictory [to those],
how could a defiled mind give rise to preparatory effort?
Although this is so according to the treatise, it is possible for weariness to arise until one initiates application (*prayoga*).
This is the answer:
because the wholesome mind of application is contrary to the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The wholesome state of applied effort (*prayoga-kuśala*) arises from extreme revulsion toward the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Since the three minds cannot produce extreme revulsion, they do not accord with it and cannot produce the wholesome state of applied effort.
The treatise discusses the birth-acquired minds of the desire realm that lead to and produce those [other] states of mind.
This explains the wholesome birth-acquired minds of the distracted stage (*vyagracitta-bhūmi*) of the desire realm,
because they are clear and sharp.
It arises from two types of untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) and from the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) of the form realm.
It does not arise from those [other minds], because the innate minds produced in the stages of the form realm concentration are not sharp.
Nor does it arise there. Furthermore, the treatise states that the desire-born [attainment] arises immediately upon reaching [the state].
This explains the desire-born attainment.
Because it is clear and sharp,

it can continue the subsequent birth associated with form-taint (*rūpa-rāga*) and protect that meditative absorption (*samādhi*). The wholesome absorption acquired through birth in the realm of form (*rūpāvacara-upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala-samādhi*) is superior to the distracted state, which is inferior.
Because it is not clear and sharp,
it does not arise from a defiled mind of the formless realm.
Treatise:
There are three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*), up to and including the mental attention associated with attainment.
Second, it clarifies the three types of mental attention:

the mental attention of the arising of the noble path, the mental attention of specific characteristics, the mental attention of general characteristics, and the mental attention of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
This can be understood according to the text: that which is wisdom associated with mental attention (*manasikāra*) is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).
Of these, the first two are named after the object of contemplation, while the third is named after the predominant resolve (*adhimokṣa*) associated with the contemplating subject.
This is what was formerly called "contemplation through mental construction.
Because the object transforms in accordance with the mind, and the mind is superior to the object,
the act of definitively sealing and maintaining it is termed "resolute conviction" (adhimokṣa).
Treatise:

Regarding these three types up to the three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*), it is clarified that all three forms of mental attention are capable of giving rise to the noble path (*āryamārga*). This statement applies to both the beginning and the end.
When first entering the noble path, the attention is necessarily and exclusively that of a universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa-manaskāra),
as in the case of the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgradharma) and so forth. Thus says the treatise.
If one says, "up to the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness," this reveals conformity with the teaching.
As for the word "together" (saha) used here:
These occur in immediate succession,
not simultaneously. The contemplation of impurity is a mental application consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*).
Since it proceeds both before and after the untainted factors of enlightenment (*anāsrava-bodhyaṅga*),
one should understand from this principle of continuity that the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*) is able to enter the Noble Path.
Entering is difficult and emerging is easy;
however, this treatise only discusses its difficulty.
Other masters say that up to the stage of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), three types [of attention] arise.
This describes a divergent opinion.
The intention of this master is that entry into the state of an Arya is difficult and occurs only through attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*).
Because the arising of the mind is easy, it pervades all three types of attention (*manasikāra*). According to the treatise,
one cultivates the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) up to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), such as mindfulness.
Other masters explain the sūtra as follows:
the word "together" (*saha*) refers to the arising of the factors of enlightenment based on traditional transmission.
The Commentary states: "Others further say [it extends] to the attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*).
This describes the intention of the third master.

This master [argues] that since one enters and emerges from the noble path by means of attention to general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*), one must again employ attention to general characteristics when returning [to the mundane state].
[The opponent asks: If that were so, what kind of attention would there be for one who relies on the attainment (*samāpatti*) and arises [therefrom]?
This is stated after raising an objection. Now, one emerges from the Path of the Sage by emerging from a mind that has already been attained, not from a mind that has never been attained.
Within the desire realm, there exists a previously attained attention to general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) from which one may emerge.

Within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is no distinct fourth wholesome [state] that separately exists as a previously acquired attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) emerging from the noble path.
It relies upon the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the first dhyāna, and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
Since the first dhyāna is not separated by distance, it can serve as the basis for arising [in the desire realm].
This applies likewise from the second up to the fourth dhyāna.
When entering the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), what kind of attention (*manasikāra*) arises immediately after the noble path?
Treatise:
It does not arise from the desire realm because it is extremely distant;
this refutes the first position.
If it is said that one also arouses the attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) of the desire realm,
this is because it is extremely remote; thus says the treatise.
This refutes the second position— that [the path] exists in those stages up to the level of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). Furthermore,
it cannot be said that [it exists] in the stages of the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and so forth.
Regarding the *nirvedhabhāgīya* [factors conducive to penetration], there is a previously cultivated and acquired attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*).
This is because it is not the case that all noble ones (*ārya*) have already reached the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*).
This refutes the third position.

Fearing that they might argue that [the path of preparation] arises from the noble path because it was previously attained as a factor conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), [the author] states:
"If this were so, it would mean that the prior preparatory application (*prayoga*) arises after one has already attained the fruit of the path."
This is not logical. The treatise states:
If one claims that there is a distinct [attainment], it contradicts correct reasoning.
Refuting the fourth position: Regarding the contradiction with correct reasoning, the *Nyāyabindu* states:
"This defense is irrational."
It is bound to the attention cultivated through preparatory application;
it cannot be induced to manifest after the fruit has been attained,
because it belongs to that same category.
The previous statement— that the three types of attention (manasikāra) can all manifest immediately following the noble path—
is logically sound. As the two preceding masters stated,
they all agree that these three types of attention emerge from the noble path.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), in its eleventh [section], raises this objection: "This master says that one gives rise to the attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) of the desire realm based on the *anāgamya* concentration;
he does not mention the first and middle stages. This treatise, however, states that there are three.

This is a general statement. Alternatively, one may raise an objection based on the third [section] of the *Vibhāṣā*, which states that the desire realm arises together with the *anāgamya* (uninterrupted) dhyāna;
this is also one view in the seventy-second [section] of the *Vibhāṣā*.
The second [master] says it reaches the preliminary stage (anāgamya) of the first dhyāna;
the third says it reaches the intermediate dhyāna;
the fourth says it reaches the second dhyāna.

The commentator approves of the second explanation. Alternatively, when this treatise raises difficulties regarding the three stages, it does so by speaking in accordance with that [second] position, asserting that only the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) emerges;
thus, it challenges only the third school.

In the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, volume eleven, the Master of the Final Assessment (the *pūrvapakṣa*) who adopts the position of the first teacher explains that this refers generally to all noble paths (*āryamārga*). If one takes it as referring to the initial entry [into the path],
it likewise pertains only to the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
In the *Nyāyānusāra*, the second [moment] is taken because it brings forth the mind of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Treatise.
If one relies on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration, it extends only to its own level and not to other levels;

this clarifies that the emergence from the mind of an Arhat occurs within the eleven levels, excluding the desire realm and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). Among these eleven levels, [the desire realm and the peak of existence are excluded].
There is no untainted abandonment of desire or of the delusions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Even if one has previously attained mastery over desire, it is still based on the *anāgamya* [preliminary] stage;
even if one has mastery over the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it is still based on the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
In all other stages, because there exists the untainted (*anāsrava*) within their own respective stages,
one who has attained mastery over a particular stage enters that stage by relying upon it,
rather than the higher or lower stages; this is because the mind emerging from those [other] states does not exert effort in seeking them.
Those that arise from the earth and those that change from the earth all emerge from the earth itself.
Those who attain mastery by relying on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) emerge from that very basis.
Although one attains arhatship by relying on the *anāgamya* [attainment],
while the body remains in the desire realm, one gains mastery over the mind of the desire realm and emerges from it in immediate succession;
furthermore, while the body remains in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one abandons the afflictions of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Because one must necessarily rely on a lower stage to give rise to the untainted (anāsrava) mind,
the emerging mind returns to emerge from the mind of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), as there is no lower-stage mind remaining.
While abiding in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one relies on the higher "unattained" (*anāgamya*) concentration to abandon the afflictions of the desire realm.
When emerging from that state, the mind may rely upon a mind of the desire realm to emerge;
although one has been born in a higher stage, one does not give rise to the lower meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
Regarding the Discourse on those who ascend to be born in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception,
they must necessarily give rise to the lower untainted concentration (anāsrava-samādhi).
Within the desire realm, up to that which is obtained in the second birth,
one can understand the eight types of attention taken collectively.
Treatise:

Among these, because five types are clear and sharp, they are explained as being able to enter and emerge from the Noble Path within the eight types; furthermore, the wholesome states acquired through desire (*kāmopapatti-labdha-kuśala*) also continue the Noble Path.
Because of its clarity and sharpness, the arising and ceasing of the Noble Path within the three realms can be known. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"If, having been born in the second dhyāna or above, one gives rise to the three lower sets of consciousness..."
For those who have not yet abandoned the defilements of their own level,
three types of consciousness manifest immediately following a wholesome, afflicted, or neutral mental attention (*manasikāra*) of that same level.
Immediately following these three types of consciousness, the three kinds of mental attention belonging to that same level arise again.
For those who have already abandoned the defilements of their own level,
when the three consciousnesses manifest immediately after an attention that is either wholesome or neutral— excluding the attention associated with the abandonment of defilements—

only these two types of attention arise immediately after the three consciousnesses. Based on this, it follows that the "borrowed consciousness" (pratilomya-vijñāna) does not include the result-of-ripening consciousness (vipākaja).
Treatise:
Regarding what has been stated previously, up to how many minds can be attained?
Herein begins the third section, which clarifies the number of minds attained within the twelve minds.

The Commentary states: "Up to this point, it has been established that one attains the six minds within a defiled mind. Regarding the term "attainment" (*prāpti*) here, it means that which was previously unestablished is now attained.
This is established.
It does not mean that the continuity [of the roots] exists beforehand; rather, it is distinguished as "attainment" across three stages.
First, the continuity of the wholesome mind is restored.
Second, the state of being born after falling away from a higher realm,
which is defiled by the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*). Third, falling away due to the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*).
These three are all defiled minds. According to the treatise,
because one reconnects the roots of goodness through doubt, it is called "attainment" at that time.
This clarifies the acquisition of wholesome minds in the desire realm.
At the time when one reconnects with the roots of goodness through doubt, or when one falls back from a higher realm, at that moment a defiled mind is present before one.
When the wholesome [roots] of the desire realm have already reached the state of "arising" (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), this is termed "acquisition."
In the desire realm, wholesome consciousness exists only in these two states. According to the treatise,
by arising from delusion and falling back, one reaches a single obscured state of mind.
This refers to the two minds of the desire realm and the mind of the form realm.
When one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm, there are the two minds of the desire realm and the acquisition of one mind of the form realm.
The same principle applies to the frequency of arising desire-afflictions when one falls away from detachment from the form realm.
If one descends from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or falls away from the detachment from desire,
one acquires only the two [types] of the desire realm. Thus says the treatise.
One acquires six [minds] by falling away through the arousal of afflictions;
these are the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and the defiled minds of the formless realm,
which are acquired solely through falling away due to afflictions.
Because there is no further realm above the formless realm,
one attains these six minds when a mind defiled by desire is currently manifest. Furthermore,
one attains the wholesome mind of the desire realm at the stage of restoring the roots of goodness through the cessation of doubt.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* presents two views:
one states that only those obtained by birth are acquired; the other states that those produced through application are also acquired.
If one is already habituated [to it], one also attains it;
there is no commentary on this point. Treatise.
The defiled mind of the form realm is also acquired through falling away (*parihāṇi*).
This second point clarifies that the defiled mind of the form realm can be obtained in six ways.
When one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the form realm, [the defiled mind of the form realm is acquired].
One who attains the mind capable of transformation acquires the unobscured-neutral, the wholesome, and the defiled minds of the form realm;
the defiled mind is also acquired through falling away.
Other minds are acquired solely through returning to a realm.
Treatise:
Because they are acquired through falling away due to the arising of afflictions, six [types of minds] are said to be "acquired by falling away.
This clarifies that defiled minds of the formless realm and the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) are acquired solely through falling away.
The various texts may be understood accordingly. The treatise states:
"Because the defiled mind of the formless realm reaches [this state], it is called 'attainment' (prāpti) in two ways."
This clarifies the defiled mind of the formless realm (*ārūpya*).
Because that [formless realm] lacks a higher realm, there is no falling back from a realm.
When one falls away due to the arising of afflictions, one arises in a higher state and does not obtain a lower one.
When one falls back [from a higher state], one must necessarily attain [a lower one].
For this reason, a defiled mind of the formless realm attains only two types of minds.
Thus says the Treatise.
Regarding the wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is called "form-wholesome" because it arises through spiritual advancement (*abhyudgama*).
Through this wholesome advancement, one attains the *anāgamya* concentration and thereby acquires the wholesome mind of the form realm.
One who attains the fundamental dhyāna acquires two transformative minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*);
therefore, it is said that one acquires three. Question: After which mind does one fall back? Answer: The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 61, states:
"After which kind of mind do afflictions (*kleśa*) arise immediately and manifest?"
If one who has completely detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception falls away because the fetters of that stage manifest before them,
then immediately after that wholesome mind of that stage, afflictions will manifest.
If one has not yet completely abandoned the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
because the fetters of that stage arise and manifest,
for one who thus regresses, it is immediately after that— whether from a wholesome mind or a defiled mind— that [the state of regression occurs].
The afflictions arise and become manifest;
it should be understood that this is likewise true up to the first dhyāna.
This is because one who has completely abandoned the defilements of the desire realm may still give rise to the fetters of the desire realm.
Regarding "falling back," it refers to the immediate arising of active afflictions following either a wholesome mind or an unobscured-neutral mind of the desire realm;
this occurs because one has not yet completely abandoned the defilements of the desire realm and thus gives rise to the fetters of the desire realm.
Regarding "receding," it refers to the immediate succession of a defiled affliction arising after either a wholesome mind, a defiled mind,
or an unobscured-neutral mind of the desire realm.
In this context, if one has not yet attained the fundamental wholesome dhyānas or formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti) and they are not currently manifest,
that person cannot fall away because the obsessions (paryavasthāna) of the form and formless realms do not become manifest.
However, one falls away only when the fetters of the desire realm arise and become manifest;
this does not occur when a fundamental wholesome dhyāna—
rather than an absorption of the formless realm— is manifest.
He cannot fall away because the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) of the formless realm manifest before him;
rather, he falls away only because the envelopments of the desire and form realms manifest before him.
This is provided that he has attained the fundamental wholesome dhyānas and formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) which are currently manifesting.
He falls because he is able to give rise to the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of the three realms so that they manifest before him; thus says the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Regarding the falling from the desire realm, it states that immediately after an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*), one can produce a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*).
One school asserts three indeterminate minds;
another school asserts two indeterminate minds.
There is no critical assessment [of these views].
Treatise:
If a mind of one in training (śaikṣa) reaches the state of being free from the defilements of the realm of form (rūpa-rāga),
this clarifies that the mind of one in training attains four types of minds.
Upon first entering the path of seeing, one attains the mind of a learner (*śaikṣa-citta*).
When one becomes free from the defilement of desire through the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*),
one attains two types of transformation minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*).
When one is detached from the defilements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one attains the wholesome states of the formless realm (*ārūpya*).
If one is detached from the defilements of both realms, it applies to their entirety.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
In this context, "separation from speech" is not ultimate separation,
because even when one has not yet completely abandoned attachment to form,
wholesome minds of the formless realm can already be attained.
Some say that when one is completely detached from the defilements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
one attains the wholesome states of the fundamental stages of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If that were so, one should also say that when one is detached from the defilements of desire, one likewise attains the wholesome states of the form realm and the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*).

This should be explained as follows: when one who is training in the mind attains the five [liberations], relying on the lower untainted [attainment] to abandon higher afflictions, they cultivate the tainted *anāgamya* [dhyāna];
in this regard, there are only two interpretations that differ.
As analyzed below, the treatise states:
"The remainder" refers to what was previously explained up to the point where it is said that "only [the object] itself can be apprehended."
This clarifies the remaining minds.
Among the twelve minds, the defiled minds of the three realms consist of four types;
namely, the unwholesome mind of the desire realm.
And as for the obscured mind:
each of the two upper realms has one obscured mind.
The wholesome mind of the form realm and the mind of training are obtained by a total of six minds.
As previously described: the non-obscured [neutral] states of the three realms,
and the wholesome states of the desire and formless realms.
And the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
These six minds can only be attained by oneself. Question: This treatise states that, according to the word "etcetera," the defiled mind of the desire realm attains only these six minds.
However, the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (or *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra*), chapter thirteen, says:
If one who possesses an unwholesome mind necessarily possesses a desire-realm non-obscured neutral mind,
then at the moment of rebirth when returning to a realm,
one would at that time possess an unwholesome mind.
At that very moment, one should also attain those deportments and crafts;
thus, seven minds are attained.
How can you say there are only six?
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* is also like this, for the intent of the treatise differs.
Instances of this kind are not limited to one; although some have provided various interpretations, all of them remain incomplete in their meaning.
One should further examine the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*.
The treatise states: Others have here provided a summary verse,
which consists of one stanza below that binds the preceding material into three general sections.
This refers to the number of defiled, wholesome, and neutral minds attained; the statement "there is more" is from the *Miśrakābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.
Regarding the statement that "attainment" (*prāpti*) refers to the state within a wholesome mind,
this is a verse from the *Miśrakābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*. As for the phrase "the attainment of seven," it is as previously explained,
with the addition of wholesome desire (*kuśala-chanda*).
Regarding "wholesome" (*kuśala*) herein, it includes both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).

The *Nyāyānusāra* also maintains that when right view reconnects with the wholesome, one obtains a wholesome mind of the desire realm. [The opponent] replies: "If that is so, why does it say one obtains six minds? As the Master of the Sūtras (*Sūtrāntika*) objects, one should rather say seven.
However, because both those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are alike untainted (anāsrava),
there is no error in speaking generally of one mind as being sixfold.
Treatise:
The characteristics of the remaining cases should be understood by analogy with the preceding explanation.
"By analogy with the preceding explanation" means that all defiled minds collectively attain nine minds.
First, the wholesome mind of the desire realm;
second, the unwholesome [mind] of the desire realm;
third, the obscured [mind] of the desire realm.
1. The obscured [mind] of the four form realms; 2.
the obscured [mind] of the five formless realms;
3. the mind of training (śaikṣa).
Seventh, the non-obscured mind of the desire realm;
eighth, the wholesome mind of the form realm;
ninth, the non-obscured mind of the form realm.
Because an indeterminate mind is realized only by oneself, it is called "indeterminate-only" (*avyākṛta-kevala*).
The treatise states this to encompass the preceding meaning, up to the point that it does not fail to exist prior [to realization].
There is one verse summarizing the meaning of the aforementioned attainment of the mind:
first, by means of rebirth;
second, by means of entering meditative absorption.
Third, by means of detachment from passion;
fourth, by means of the time of falling away;
fifth, by means of reconnecting with the roots of goodness, because it is not something previously accomplished.
A General Explanation of the Meaning of Attainment. By Fan Ya (范雅). May you live long! (Kajūshu)
Commentary on the Abhidharmakośa-śāstra, Scroll Eight, Composed by the Śramaṇa Fabao. Part Three:
Analysis of the World (Lokanirdeśa). Section One of the First Part of the Analysis of the World.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Analysis of the World" (*Lokaprajñapti*):
because the three realms (*tridhātu*) are characterized by outflows (*āsrava*) and are subject to destruction,
they are called the "world."
This chapter is called "Analysis" (*vibhaṅga*) because it explains in detail;

it is called the "Chapter on Dependent Origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) because it elucidates the meaning of dependent origination. The preceding two chapters explained, in general, the defiled (*sāsrava*) and undefiled (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
The final six chapters specifically clarify the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
Within these final six chapters, the first three clarify tainted dharmas,
while the latter three clarify untainted dharmas.

Because of the sequence of first generating revulsion and subsequently giving rise to joy, within the first three categories, the "World" category is explained first, followed by karma and afflictions;
this is because the effect is presented before its cause. Within the "World" category, sentient beings are explained first, followed by the inanimate vessel-world.
Because the external [arises] from the internal, the dependent is explained first and the basis second;
likewise, the internal fruit is explained first and the external fruit second. Regarding the explanation of sentient beings, there are nine distinct sections.
First, an explanation of the three realms;
second, an explanation of the five destinies;
third, an explanation of the seven stations of consciousness.
Fourth, it explains the nine abodes of sentient beings;
fifth, it explains the four stations of consciousness;
sixth, it explains the four modes of birth.
7. Explaining the intermediate state (antarābhava).
8. Explaining dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
9. Explaining the four states of existence (catur-bhava).
Treatise:
Having already established, according to the distinctions of the destinations within the three realms,
how many there are, the following three verses first clarify the three realms.
Prior to this verse, there are two questions:
first, a question regarding the substance of the three realms;
second, a question regarding their location therein.
The Commentary says: "This is called the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu*).
This generally sets forth the essence of the desire realm;
that is, within the desire realm, there are both sentient beings (*sattva*) and the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
These always belong to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Only the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) includes both the animate and the inanimate; this is discussed in the treatise.
The "six heavens of the desire realm" refers to the heavens up to the Heaven of Mastery over Transformations (*nirmāṇarati*).
This is a specific enumeration of the names of these six heavens;
they are so designated because the inhabitants of these six heavens predominantly experience the objects of exquisite sensual desires.
Regarding those called the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadeva*): first, as for the gods of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*),
the "Four Great Kings" are the lords,
and the "multitude" refers to those they govern.

This refers to the various classes of devas, such as those on the tiered levels, as well as those on the seven golden mountains, and those of the sun, moon, and stars. Because these types are not one, they are called "multitudes. As for the "Thirty-three Heavens" (Trāyastriṃśa):
At the summit of Mount Sumeru,
Śakra resides in the center;
with eight [gods] on each of the four sides, there are thirty-three in total.
They are also called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Third, the Yāma Heaven;
this is translated as "Time-Portion," because they experience the objects of the five desires while knowing the divisions of time. Fourth, the Tuṣita Heaven.
This is translated as "contentment" (saṃtuṣṭi);
the old translation was "knowing contentment.
It refers to the arising of contentment upon experiencing the objects of the five desires. As for the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (Nirmāṇarati):
That is to say, in those heavens, they enjoy the objects of desire that have been transformed by pleasure. As for the sixth, the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin):
this refers to those gods who dwell in the objects of desire emanated by others.
Because the enjoyment [of objects] is exercised with mastery.
Treatise:
How many distinct locations are there in this desire realm?
Question: The treatise states that because the hells and continents differ, there are twenty [realms].
Answer: There are four—namely, those in the hells, humans, hungry ghosts, and animals.
These are presented as a collective name rather than being enumerated individually.
The *Śāstra* states: "From the eight great hells up to the Avīci Hell.
This explains the distinctions among the hells. The *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
When various sufferings oppress their bodies, they faint repeatedly as if dead;
because they revive immediately as before, it is called "Equal Revival" (Saṃjīva).
This means that although those sentient beings encounter various forms of cutting, stabbing, grinding, and pounding, [they revive].
When they are briefly struck by a cool breeze, they immediately revive as before;
because they return to life just as previously, it is called the "Reviving" [Hell]. First, their limbs and bodies are measured out with black cords.
Because they are subsequently cut and sawn, it is named Black Rope (Kālasūtra).

Because numerous instruments of torture come together to oppress the body, and because those in the same faction slaughter one another, it is named Crushing (Saṃghāta). Oppressed by manifold sufferings, beings of different species wail in lamentation.
Because they give vent to cries of resentment, it is called the Hell of Screaming (*Raurava*);

because they are oppressed by intense suffering and utter great, harsh sounds, crying out piteously and invoking their grievances, it is called the Hell of Great Screaming (*Mahāraurava*). As fire swirls around their bodies, blazing intensely on all sides.
It is named "Intense Heat" because its burning suffering is unbearable; whether internal or external,
from one's own body or another's body,
fierce fires erupt and mutually incinerate and harm them.
Because the heat is extreme, it is called "Extreme Heat" (Pratāpana). As stated in the latter part of this treatise:
"It is called 'Uninterrupted' (Avīci) because there is no interval between the experience of suffering; it is called 'Uninterrupted' because there is no interval of pleasure amidst the suffering."
Treatise:
Regarding the phrase "differences among the continents," it extends up to the northern continent of Uttarakuru;
this clarifies the differences among the continents.

Jambudvīpa is named after the Jambu tree; it is called the Continent of Excellent Bodies because its inhabitants possess superior bodies; it is called the Continent of Cattle Barter because cattle are used as currency; and Kuru is translated here as "the Excellent Place."
Because this is the most excellent among the four continents, the treatise states:
"Thus, the twelve *gatis* (destinies) become twenty."
This clarifies that animals and hungry ghosts [are included]. The treatise states:
"If the realm of sentient beings extends to all, they are subsumed within the desire realm."
This summarizes the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). According to the treatise,
from this desire realm upward, it is collectively named the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The following explains the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). This section contains three parts:
first, a brief enumeration;
second, a detailed explanation.
The third is the school of definitive tenets; this is the first [of its kind].
Treatise:
The first dhyāna extends up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven;
this is the second [point]. The *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
"It is called Brahma because it is produced by extensive virtue."
This Brahmā is called "Great Brahmā" because he is great;
for he has attained the intermediate dhyāna and was the first to be born there.
Because they are the last to perish and because their majesty and power are superior, they are called "Great" (Mahā).

Because they are transformed by and subject to the governance of Mahābrahmā, they are called the "Assembly of Brahmā" (Brahmapāriṣadya). Because they stand in formation and serve before Mahābrahmā, they are called the "Retinue of Brahmā" (Brahmapurohita). Because their internal radiance is the least among the gods of their own stage, they are called "Limited Light" (Parīttābha). Because their radiance is increasingly superior and its measure is difficult to fathom, they are called "Immeasurable Light" (Apramāṇābha). Because pure light universally illuminates their own abode, they are called "Pervasive Pure Light" (Ābhāsvara). The experience of pleasure on the mental level is termed "pure"; this occurs within their own stage.

This purity is called "Limited Purity" because it is the most inferior; this purity is called "Immeasurable Purity" because its increasing measure is difficult to fathom; and this purity is called "Universal Purity" because it is all-pervasive.

This indicates that there is no other pleasure that can surpass this. Because the ground where the gods dwell in the space below is like clouds densely joined together, it is called "Cloud" (Abhāsvara).
Above these heavens, there are no further grounds consisting of clouds.
Because they are at the head of those without clouds, they are called "Cloudless" (Anabhraka).

Because there are further ordinary beings with superior merit who can be reborn in that location, it is named "Merit-Born" (Puṇyaprasava). They dwell in that location within the fruit of ordinary beings.

Because this is most excellent, it is called "Vast Fruit" (Bṛhatphala). Because the noble ones who have abandoned desire wash away the defilements of affliction with the water of the Noble Path, it is called "Pure" (Śuddha).
Because it is the dwelling place of those pure bodies, it is called "Pure Abode" (Śuddhāvāsa).
Alternatively, they dwell here at the limit of the exhaustion of birth and death;
because they have repaid their debt in full, they are called "Pure" (*śuddha*).
Because these are the abodes of those who are pure, they are called the "Pure Abodes" (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Alternatively, because there are no ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) mixed within these heavens,
and they are inhabited solely by noble ones (*ārya*), they are called "Pure Abodes" (*śuddhāvāsa*). "Prolixity" (*prapañca*) means either "confusion and mixture" or "vastness and expansion."
Because this is the first among those that are not manifold,
and because it is the most inferior among the manifold heavens, it is called "Non-Manifold" (Avṛha).

It is also called "Without Seeking," because one does not seek entry into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Because one has already thoroughly subdued and eliminated the obstacles of the superior and middling grades of the meditative cultivation of dhyāna,
and because one's mental disposition is pliant and free from all feverish afflictions, it is called "Without Heat" (*atapa*).
Alternatively, the arising of afflictions below is called "heat" (*uṣman*);
by initially distancing oneself from this, one attains the name "without heat.
Or again, "heat" has the meaning of being "blazing" or "intense."
This refers to the cultivation of dhyāna and its fruit at the highest degree;
because this has not yet been fully realized, it is called "Without Heat" (Atapa).

Having already attained the highest degree of mixed cultivation of dhyāna, the qualities of its fruit are easily manifested, hence it is called "Well-Appearing" (Sudṛśa). The remaining grades of obstacles to the mixed cultivation of concentration have become extremely subtle.
It is called Sudarśana (Good Vision) because it is seen with extreme clarity. It is called Akaniṣṭha (Ultimate Form) because there is no other place among those possessing form that can surpass it;
or, it is called Akaniṣṭha because this has reached the final limit of the body which is the basis for all suffering.
Treatise:
From Kaśmīra to being surrounded by the fourfold assembly—
this is the third [section].
The statement that there are sixteen locations in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is the position of the *Vibhāṣā*;
this master’s intention is as follows.
The Brahmā Kings and the Ministers of Brahmā are not divided into two separate locations;
the Non-percipient beings and the Vast Fruit gods are combined into a single location.
Thus, there are sixteen [abodes]. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
These seventeen locations of the receptacle world,
together with all sentient beings therein, are collectively termed the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
There are other specific explanations regarding the names of these seventeen locations.
In the first dhyāna, two locations are established in total;
in the fourth dhyāna, the "non-percipient" (asaṃjñin) is mentioned separately.
According to that master, there should be eighteen locations.
Since there are differences in lifespan, physical stature,
the absence of vitarka, and the experience of sensation when comparing that Great Brahmā to the Brahmapurohita heaven,
would it not also be the case for the Asaṃjñisattvas when compared to the Bṛhatphala heaven?
Only ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) and others have distinctions; therefore,
it should also be stated that there are eighteen bases (āyatana).
This objection is irrational,
because those born in the Heaven of Non-conception are bound by the karmic fruits of the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*).
If that is so, [then consider] the body produced by birth experienced by Mahābrahmā.
Furthermore, because it is bound by the same karmic results as the Brahmā-purohita heaven,
it should not be designated as a separate celestial realm;
rather, superior karma bound in the Brahmā-purohita heaven brings about the fruit of Mahābrahmā.
This karma differs slightly from that [of the other Brahmās];
therefore, the lifespan it brings about also differs slightly.
This is like the difference in lifespan between Mahābrahmā and those [gods] of the Brahmakāyika realm.
If they were combined into a single location,
then although the lifespans of the Parītta-ābhāsas and others differ, they would have to occupy one place,
which would result in a great logical fallacy.
This example does not apply,
because Mahābrahmā is a single individual.
It is necessary to rely on a common designation to establish the name of a celestial realm.
A single Brahmā king cannot be designated as a "homogeneous group" (sabhāgatā).
Although his lifespan and other attributes differ from others,
a single body does not constitute a homogeneous group.
Therefore, the [Heaven of] Brahmā’s Retinue is established as a single heaven together with [the Heaven of] Great Brahmā;
although their heights differ, there is no distinction in their ground.
This is not the case for the Heaven of Limited Radiance and the others.
Therefore, one should not cite that as an example. According to this treatise,
the *Nyāyānusāra* also maintains that sixteen [bases] are correct,
because both the Brahmā King and the beings of the Unconscious Realm (*asaṃjñisattva*) are each singular.
Because there is no distinction of levels,
the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* establishes eighteen heavens within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*). According to the treatise:
Because the ultimate principle within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is definitively settled,
the following section clarifies the third [topic], the formless realm; herein there are four parts.
First, there is no location and no form;
second, it pertains to the locus of birth;
third, its realization is without spatial direction.
The basis for the four questions and answers;
this is the beginning of the text. Because they are formless, there are no distinct locations within the formless realm.
Treatise.
However, there is a distinction between the superior and inferior grades of those born through maturation (*vipākaja*).
The second [classification] divides the locations based on these superior and inferior grades of birth;
yet in reality, they do not depart from the four locations within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Nor is there any distinction in their location.
The treatise asks:
Furthermore, how is it known that [the intermediate state] arises upon reaching [the place of rebirth]?
The third proof is that there is no spatial location [for them].
Since those who have attained the four types of meditative concentration are born in the same place,
we know that the four formless attainments arise without distinct locations.
Furthermore, there are differences in the four dhyānas, the nine abodes of the desire realm, and the sixteen abodes of the form realm.
If one is born in the formless realm, one is always reborn at the place where one passed away in either the desire or form realms.
Thus, one should know that there is no other distinct location apart from these two realms.
When one passes away from those four celestial abodes and is born into a lower realm,
the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) manifests at the very place of the previous birth and death, and the consciousness is transmitted.
Therefore, one knows that it does not come from another place.
Treatise:
For example, there is the continuity of the mind and so forth when reaching the form realm.
The following is the fourth question and answer regarding the basis [of the teaching].
This is the question. [From] the Treatise:
The masters of the Abhidharma attained [this realization] through continuity;
this is the response set forth from the perspective of the Abhidharma school. Treatise.
If that were so, it would be difficult [to explain] how material form reaches these two continuities. [This is the] treatise.
Because these two [types of birth] are inferior within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*),
this is the answer. Thus says the treatise.
Question: For what reason are these two [factors] in the formless realm so powerful?
Treatise: [The following is the explanation.]
In that realm, two [factors] reach the point of being able to subdue the characteristics of form;
this is the general principle. Treatise.
If that is so, what is the purpose of a separate basis for those [minds]?
This is the objection.
The continuity of the mind and its associates depends solely upon the superior meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
What is the use of relying on that [homogeneous character] (sabhāgatā) and the life-faculty (jīvitendriya)?
Furthermore, it must now be explained what serves as the basis for these.
Furthermore, it is argued:
the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*) have no basis in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Treatise:
These two function by depending upon one another;
this is the position of the Sarvāstivāda school.
Treatise:
Regarding the statement that there are those with form, why do these two not rely upon one another?
This is the objection. "Those with the realm of form" refers to...
That is to say, the desire and form realms.
Why do this life-force (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) not function in mutual dependence as they do in the formless realm?
As for the statement "based on form," the treatise says:
because these two are inferior when one is born in the realm of form.
Answer: Because these two—desire and form—are inferior, they proceed by depending on form;
because these two are strong in the formless realm, they depend upon one another.
Treatise:
Why are these two causes so powerful in the formless realm?
This inquiry seeks the reason for the predominance of the formless realm.
Treatise:
Regarding the statement that "in those realms, these two [factors] reach the point of being able to suppress the appearance of form," the answer is:
it is due to a powerful cause.
Because concentration is superior, these two are also superior. The treatise states:
"This is then equivalent to [the case where] they merely depend upon one another."
These are two explanations of the "two gates. Regarding the difficulty concerning the continuity of the same mind:
this refers to the same objection as before. Therefore, the previous objection stated:
"If that is so, then the continuity of those minds and so forth would depend solely upon superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*)."
What need is there for a separate basis?
The second section states:
"Formless mind and mental factors arise from superior meditative concentration."
In that case, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) should depend upon one another;
why then would they need to further depend on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*)?
This is the intended meaning of the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*.
Only the six sense faculties can serve as the basis;
the others are not the basis.
However, these six consciousnesses have only their co-nascent bases.
In the desire and form realms, the four aggregates serve as the co-nascent support (*sahaja-āśraya*).
In the formless realm, the mental consciousness has no further support in matter;

its co-nascent support consists only of the three [mental] aggregates. If this is so, why is it said that in the formless realm the mind and its concomitants depend only upon the homogeneous group (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and life-force (*jīvitendriya*)? This is stated because these two are the fixed and non-confused supports.
This means that although the mind and mental factors serve as mutual supports for one another,
they are not necessarily identical because they do not depend on themselves; nor are they without confusion,
because when one is born in a particular stage (*bhūmi*), confusion arises from both one's own and others' minds and mental factors.
The homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*), life-force (*jīvitendriya*), mind (*citta*), and so forth,
have a common basis (*samāśraya*). Furthermore, because one born in a particular stage belongs only to that stage,
even if a mind belonging to a different stage arises based upon it.
By this, the mind of its own level is caused to arise again;

it is based solely on these two that one is said to be "born" in this stage (*bhūmi*), because the karma of projection (*ākṣepaka-karman*) arises without interruption. This is proven according to this passage.
The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is precisely the fruit of projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*); for this reason, it is said to be the common, non-confused basis (*asādhāraṇa-avyabhicāra-āśraya*).
The mind and other [faculties] are not so;
therefore, they are omitted and not mentioned.
If these two were absent, then when the four aggregates of other stages were present,
sentient beings at that time would have to be designated as belonging to those other stages, and so forth.
Just as in the desire and form realms, the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and life-force (*jīvita*) serve as the support for the mind and its concomitants;
even though at times a mind belonging to a different level may arise,
it nonetheless relies upon the body and so forth.
In this life, at the end, it will certainly draw forth the arising of a mind belonging to its own level.
Thus, although the formless realm lacks a body,
the mind and its associates necessarily depend upon the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Therefore, the verse specifically mentions the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),
because these are the maturation (*vipāka*) of projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*). [Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya]
Therefore, the Sautrāntika masters maintain that [the mind] does not proceed in dependence upon matter.
The Master [Vasubandhu], in recounting the Sautrāntika tenet,
states that the intention of that school is as follows:
If one does not feel revulsion toward form within its cause,

If one feels revulsion toward form within the cause,
such as the mind and mental factors of the result,

This too is irrational.
If it were by the power of an adduced cause...

if this were so, then at the moment when wholesome or defiled minds manifest,

Furthermore, for example, sentient beings in the desire realm and the form realm have their mental continua induced by the power of projecting causes.
Just as [the mind] arises together with form and functions in dependence upon form,
so too do the mental states and so forth of sentient beings in the formless realm continue in succession through the power of the projecting cause.
It arises simultaneously with the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) and the homogeneous character (nikāyasabhāga).

What is meant by "the factors that destroy consciousness"?

According to this treatise:
How could it be that all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the three heavens of the fourth dhyāna stage would all yearn for the state of the maturation (*vipāka*) of non-conception (*asaṃjñi*)?
This cannot be the correct meaning.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Other masters say that sentient beings have three abodes.
This refers to being attached to various objects, to pleasure, and to perception.
Those who are attached to objects are humans and the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Attachment to pleasure" refers to the three lower dhyānas;
"attachment to perception" refers to [the fourth dhyāna].
The three lower formless realms are established as "stations of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*) solely on the basis of these [three] states;
since the others lack these three, they are not stations of consciousness. Furthermore, it says:
Regarding the explanation transmitted from master to disciple in ancient times:
if a location possesses consciousness that is abandoned by seeing, abandoned by cultivation, and that which is not abandoned, it is established as a "station of consciousness" (*vijñāna-sthiti*).

Otherwise, it would not be subsumed under the stations of consciousness. [Objection: Would this not imply that humans in the desire realm and the six classes of gods lack the untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*), and thus should not be stations of consciousness?
If it is argued that [the Peak of Existence] could be called a station of consciousness because it can serve as the basis for the outflow-free (anāsrava), this objection is irrational;
for there is no meditative concentration (samādhi) in the Desire Realm.
One might argue that the existence or non-existence of the untainted (*anāsrava*) could be predicated based on its support (*āśraya*).
However, since the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is comprised within the meditative stages (*dhyāna-bhūmi*),
one ought to speak of its presence or absence based on its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are not stations of consciousness; nor does a single basis belonging to a person at the Peak of Existence possess all three types of consciousness.
This refers to a person in a wholesome state within the desire realm.
Since a single basis can accommodate all three consciousnesses,
the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) should not be used as an analogy.
Although the Fourth Dhyāna possesses all three consciousnesses, [it differs from the case at hand].

Since five locations are complete and one location is partially lacking the three consciousnesses, the latter is not established as a station of consciousness because the deficient is subsumed under the predominant. Therefore, the number of stations of consciousness is only seven;
as for the mention of "three consciousnesses," it refers to those [consciousnesses] present in the aforementioned locations.
That is to say: consciousness abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*), consciousness abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousness.
In all noble ones (*ārya*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), there is no consciousness abandoned through seeing.
In all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there is no untainted consciousness.
Within the desire realm, there may be a person who has previously possessed both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation,
and who further possesses the untainted application of the first patience (*kṣānti*) in its entirety across five locations—
namely, the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*)— or in a single portion thereof.
They are the gods of the Bṛhatphala heaven.
Within the Heaven of Non-conception, there is no untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*),
because within the Bṛhatphala heaven, all three types of consciousness are present.
Only the two lower heavens possess all three consciousnesses;
since these three are not complete within the six higher heavens,
it is said that because the few follow the many, they are not designated as "abodes of consciousness."

The fourth section clarifies the nine abodes of sentient beings (*navasattvāvāsāḥ*).
Although the nine abodes of sentient beings are not explicitly taught in the sūtras,
they are explained here as a consequence of explaining the seven stations of consciousness (*saptavijñānasthitis*) mentioned within the sūtras.
The Commentary states: "Up to 'not dwelling with delight'":
this explains the abodes of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*).

That is to say, by adding the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and the Heaven of Non-Perception (*asaṃjñisattva*) to the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), they become nine.
Therefore, these nine are established as abodes of sentient beings because they are pleasant dwellings;
whereas among the previously mentioned stations of consciousness, there exist factors that cause the destruction of consciousness.
Because consciousness is dull and inferior, it is not a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).

Other places are neither pleasant nor abodes of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*). Question: Regarding the stations of sentient beings and the stations of consciousness, do the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) extend to the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*)? Answer: The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
This means that for all sentient beings, it is the actual entities such as form (*rūpa*) that serve as the basis for their own dwelling in happiness, and nothing else.
This is because sentient beings are conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*),
whereas these actual entities are what are inhabited by those conventional designations.
The abodes of sentient beings consist only of the phenomena pertaining to sentient beings;
for it is the attachment to their own supporting bodies that causes sentient beings to dwell with increased intensity, rather than their attachment to physical locations.
Furthermore, if one were to establish abodes of sentient beings based on physical locations, there would result an unavoidable confusion.
Since there is no external confusion there, but only the internal body,
the abodes of sentient beings consist solely of the phenomena belonging to sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is stated that once one has been born, it is called an "abode of sentient beings."
One should know that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not included among the abodes of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*).
Furthermore, because the various intermediate states are not places where one dwells for long,
sentient beings do not take pleasure in remaining there.
Furthermore, it must necessarily be so;
for the *Mūla-śāstra* states that "abodes of sentient beings" (*sattvāvāsa*) are established to indicate places of birth,
while "abodes of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*) are established within the cycle of birth and death to indicate how the various consciousnesses dwell through attachment due to craving.
It is shown that all sentient beings, out of attachment to their own physical bases, delight in and abide therein;
thus, these two gateways are established as distinct.

Treatise.

Why is consciousness not described as a station of consciousness? [Question: What is the reason that only four are called stations of consciousness? [Treatise: The Treatise states: Consciousness itself is not established as a station of consciousness because it lacks a support (*āśraya*). Just as a bird cannot remain in the air without a perch, so too consciousness cannot abide without a basis. Furthermore, the other four aggregates—form, feeling, perception, and formations—are the supports for consciousness; they are like the earth, water, fire, and wind, which serve as the foundation for all sentient beings. Because consciousness arises and persists by depending upon these four aggregates, they alone are designated as the stations of consciousness. Consciousness, however, does not depend on itself; therefore, it is not established as a station of consciousness. Moreover, if consciousness were itself a station of consciousness, there would be no distinction between the subject and the object of cognition, and the principle of mutual dependence would be undermined. Thus, for these reasons, consciousness is not said to be a station of consciousness.

Because it is free from that which can abide [therein] up to what may be called a "king's throne," this explains why consciousness is not an abode of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). Thus says the treatise.
Alternatively, if there is a dharma that reaches what has been thus explained—
this is the second interpretation. When it says "as stated by the Vaibhāṣikas," this refers to their tenet (*siddhānta*).
Treatise:

Treatise:
Although there is this statement, it does not exclusively state that [the object] is consciousness;
the answer addresses both difficulties.
Within the nutriment of consciousness, there is joy, defilement, and so forth,
as well as the seven stations of consciousness;
all of these are comprised within the five aggregates of the place of birth.
One does not generate joy by analytically distinguishing [the aggregates] individually; nor is it said that defilement belongs to consciousness alone.
However, the aggregates such as form (*rūpa*) can be explained in relation to others.
This explains the four stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*). According to their specific distinctions,
various forms of delight and defilement arise with respect to each individual aggregate (*skandha*).
Therefore, because consciousness is distinct from the other four aggregates, it is not established as a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Thus says the treatise. Furthermore, such is the intention of the Buddha’s teaching and the meaning of the authoritative scripture.
This is the second explanation. The treatise states:
Furthermore, because phenomena (dharma) and consciousness (vijñāna) [coexist], they are not abodes of consciousness (vijñānasthiti).
This clarifies that the four types of phenomena necessarily exist simultaneously.
Since consciousness cannot logically coexist with itself, it is not a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Consciousness and the stations of consciousness are like a seed and a field."
This principle may be so,
as it does not contradict the teachings.
However, regarding what was stated by him concerning phenomena and consciousness:
To establish the "abodes of consciousness" (*vijñāna-sthiti*) as being the fertile field for consciousness that arises simultaneously with it is not consistent with correct reasoning. Why is this so?
He previously stated himself that consciousness is called a "station of consciousness" (vijñāna-sthiti) because it is that upon which consciousness relies and adheres;
it is not the case that within the simultaneously arising aggregates such as feeling, there exists a locus for the reliance of consciousness.
Since those [aggregates] rely upon consciousness, this consciousness is their support, rather than being a place where consciousness itself relies.

If consciousness does not rely upon them, how can they be said to be the stations of consciousness? If "station of consciousness" is explained in the sense of a support, then consciousness does not rely upon those factors such as feeling.
How is it that feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [aggregates] constitute stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*)?
Furthermore, it is not because they share the same object of perception (*ālambana*);
nor is it because simultaneously arising feeling and the others are not themselves what is grasped. This is because the basis (*āśraya*) has two meanings.
First, regarding the meaning of "basis":
mental factors and so forth are not bases,
as has already been refuted previously.
Second, regarding the meaning of the object-condition (*ālambana*):
since phenomena such as feeling (*vedanā*) are themselves not objects [in this context],
it is refuted here as follows.
The three bases of association are refuted later. Furthermore,
one must not explain the meaning of the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) by relying on the basis of association.

All material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) and dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) are not abodes of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), because they lack the sense of association; for if "abode of consciousness" were explained as having the meaning of association,
then all material phenomena and dissociated factors would lack that sense of association.
It should not be a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).

Furthermore, because there is no distinction in the principle of association (*samprayoga*), it would follow that the untainted (*anāsrava*) would also be the substance of a station of consciousness; for there would be no difference in the association between tainted and untainted minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
For what reason are the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) states established as the substance of the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), while the untainted (*anāsrava*) are not?

How can it be said that the co-arisen form (*rūpa*) and so forth constitute a fertile field for consciousness and are thus established as stations of consciousness? The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "However, my own teacher’s school offers this explanation."
In order to eliminate the mind that perceives a self within consciousness,
the Sūtra does not speak of "abiding in consciousness" regarding consciousness itself.
As it says in the Sūtra:
We have understood the Dharma teachings expounded by the Blessed One:
that which flows through saṃsāra is consciousness alone and nothing else.
"Consciousness," the Blessed One has said, is another name for the self (ātman).
In order to eliminate the mind of self-view and other-view, it is revealed that the nature of consciousness is dependent;
its essence is not "I," nor is the nature upon which it depends the "mine. It is not what is supported [by the support].
Therefore, the gateway of the stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) speaks of only four;
it is not that there are only four actual stations of consciousness, but rather that these four are not [themselves] consciousness.
Now, as for what the Blessed One has taught regarding the stations of consciousness:
Regarding the four factors such as form (*rūpa*) that are not explicitly called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*):
it is because form and the others alone serve as auxiliaries for the continuity of consciousness throughout the three periods of time.
