Question: If there is a difference in results due to a difference in karma, then for instance, among humans, both the internal body and external objects are produced from karma.

Why is it that external objects produced by karma, such as saffron and sandalwood, are so exceedingly delightful, while internal physical forms and the like are impure, foul, and loathsome? [Commentary: This is because external objects are produced by the power of shared karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*), whereas internal bodies are produced by the power of individual karma (*asādhāraṇa-karman*). Furthermore, external objects are produced from the transformation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) through the power of merit (*puṇya*), and thus they are pleasant to behold; whereas internal bodies arise from the accumulation of various impurities and are therefore naturally foul and disagreeable. Moreover, external objects serve as the basis for the enjoyment of sentient beings, and thus their production is governed by the collective force of their shared karma; internal bodies, however, are the locus of suffering and the vessel for the experience of pleasure and pain, and thus their production is governed by the specific force of each individual's karma. For these reasons, there is a disparity between the two.
Because sentient beings reach a state where both matters are excellent.
Answer: The categories of karma differ; those born from mixed karma experience internal bodily forms that constantly flow with impurities.
The treatise states: "Perceiving external odors and the like that can counteract those [defilements], and being born in heaven through pure karma—
both of these matters are pure."
This refers to the karma by which [the result] arises, namely that produced by volition (*cetanā*);
this clarifies the two types of karma.
One of these is volition itself.
Second, karma after having willed. Karma after having willed refers to that which is produced by volition,
namely, bodily and vocal karma.
Treatise:
These two types of karma extend to the karma of body, speech, and mind;
these two are further divided into three.
Treatise:
How is it established that [the classification of] the three types of action is based on their motivation (*samutthāna*)?
This question concerns the reason for establishing the three types of action.
Treatise: Even if that were so, what contradiction would there be?
[This] is a counter-question regarding the contradiction.
Treatise:
If one considers the basis, since all [actions] are originated by the mind (*manas*),
this explains the reason for the contradiction.
The treatise states:
The Vaibhāṣika masters respond by means of the three aforementioned reasons:
bodily action [is defined] by way of its basis.
Vocal action is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), while mental action is its motivating cause (*samutthāna*). The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (or *Nyāyānusāra*) states:
"Action is called 'bodily action' because it depends upon the body."
Because the nature of karma is speech, it is called vocal karma (*vākkarman*).
This karma depends on the mind;
furthermore, when it arises together with the mind and initiates body and speech, it is called mental karma (*manaskarman*). According to this treatise, [these are the definitions].
Mental action (*manas-karman*) is precisely that which initiates [the action].
The treatise states: "However, because the mind intends and proceeds until it reaches the point of initiation."
It is clear that the two types of karma belong to the three types of karma.
Treatise:
What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the two karmas of body and speech?
The following half-verse clarifies the second point:
the nature of the five types of karma.
The Treatise says: "Up to the nature of informative and non-informative [action]."
It is explained that bodily and vocal actions both take informative and non-informative [matter] as their essential nature; thus, action is divided into five types.
Treatise:
Now, what are the characteristics of bodily and vocal informative [action]? Each of the preceding [categories] is further divided into two.

This [particle] "qiě" (provisionally) is used because it follows the explanation of the two types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*). The following two and a half verses constitute the third section, which explains the essential nature of bodily and vocal informative action (*vijñapti-karman*).
The treatise says, up to the point: "called bodily informative action."
Regarding the definition of the body, the *Nyāyapraveśa* states:
"The collection of hair, body hair, and so forth is collectively termed the 'body.
Within this body..."
The differentiation of shape and color, which is the fruit of the four great elements produced by the mind and is capable of representing the mind, is called bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
According to the treatise, other schools maintain that it exists for a duration of several moments.
The Saṃmitīya school maintains that bodily intimation consists of the movement of the body, because when the body moves,
it is moved by karma; [they hold] that the body has no momentariness.

When this body is moved by the movement of volitional action (*cetanā-karman*), that very movement of the body is called bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*). To refute this, it is stated that there is no movement; this is the thesis of non-movement established against the thesis of movement. This is because all phenomena (*dharma*) are momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
Establishing the reason:
All momentary phenomena are devoid of motion,
just like the flame of a lamp or the sound of a bell.
Treatise:
What is meant by "moment" (*kṣaṇa*)?
This is the question posed by the Saṃmitīyas.
Treatise:
It is called "possessing a staff" (*sāyudha*) because it reaches the state of immediate cessation after its substance has been acquired.
Answer: It is momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
The momentary nature (*kṣaṇa*) of all phenomena is defined as their immediate cessation upon attaining their own essence;
that which possesses this momentariness is said to "have moments," just as a person possessing a staff is called "one who has a staff. The *Nyāyānusāra* critiques this, stating:
That explanation by the Śākya is unreasonable,
because it cannot be said that the staff is distinct from the person, as in the case of a person being distinct from a staff.
This is an analogy for dissimilar dharmas.
It is not the case that there exists a separate dharma distinct from the essence of acquisition (*prāpti*), characterized by immediate cessation;
how then could one say that this [acquisition] possesses momentariness, as a person possesses a staff?
Treatise:
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) that reach movement are termed bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
[This] refutes [the opposing view].
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) are momentary;
they arise in one very same place and perish in that very same place.
How, then, can it be said that movement constitutes bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti)?
Treatise:
If conditioned phenomena can be established as having a referent, this is the correct proof;
such is the defense [of the opponent].
In our school’s doctrine, the flame of cognition and the sound of a bell may possess momentariness;
however, material entities such as the physical body do not undergo momentary destruction.
If all conditioned phenomena were indeed momentary, the logical possibility of movement could not be established.
In our school, it is not admitted that all things possess momentariness;
thus, this reason is unestablished. How can it be proven?
Treatise:
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) do not depend on a cause for their cessation.

The Master’s intention is that because they must necessarily perish in the end, their cessation does not depend on a cause; this proves that all conditioned phenomena possess momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
Treatise:
Why is this so? Because the Saṃmitīya school maintains that cessation does not depend on a cause.
Treatise:

"Dependent upon causes" means that because effects such as existence and so forth have reached [their state], the Master of the Treatise refutes [this]. A phenomenon that depends upon causes must necessarily be an effect.
Since cessation is non-existent, it is not a fruit and thus does not depend on a cause.
Since it does not depend on a cause, it ceases as soon as it arises.
If there were no cessation at the beginning, it would likewise have to be so at the end; for the later [moment] is identical in nature to the initial one.
If a phenomenon depends on causes, and those causes have not yet ceased to exist,
then since it does not depend on causes, why would it not cease at the earlier time and only cease at the later time?
[The Treatise says:]
Since the subsequent existence is known to have an end and the prior existence is known to have ceased,
this serves as the proof. The Sautrāntika school maintains that birth has adventitious causes and lacks a primary cause.
The Sarvāstivādins maintain that cessation occurs without both a subjective (internal) and objective (external) cause.
The Saṃmitīyas maintain that cessation occurs with a subjective cause but without an objective cause.
[The Sautrāntikas hold that] the cessation of dharmas such as form depends upon both subjective and objective causes.
The cessation of mind, mental factors, flames, sounds, and so forth, occurs through the primary cause without depending on a secondary cause.
Cessation itself is the primary cause, while other causes are secondary. Thus says the treatise.
If it were to change later, this would necessarily contradict ultimate principle;
thus, the destruction [of a thing] depends upon something else.
This cites the rebuttal of the Saṃmitīya school. The Saṃmitīyas say:
Once form and the other aggregates have arisen, they only undergo cessation after depending upon a subsequent characteristic of change;

it is not the case that they cease at the very moment they arise. It is logically impossible for this very same entity to be called "different" while remaining identical to itself. Therefore, the principle that this very thing is different is certainly untenable.
This is the master of the treatise refuting the notion of distinct characteristics.
If one were to allow that the essential natures (dharmatā) of preceding and succeeding moments are different, only then could they be characterized as distinct;
however, from beginning to end, they are one and the same.
How can it be said that there is a difference between their characteristics?
The treatise asks:
Is it not the case that in the world, everything down to the most mundane things does not depend on a cause?
The Saṃmitīyas offer this defense:
"Previously, you refuted the self by means of inference (anumāna);
however, this inference does not reach the level of direct perception (pratyakṣa)."
It is directly perceived that fuel and the like depend upon conjunction with fire as their cause;
it is not the case that all phenomena perish without depending on a cause.
Treatise:
How is it known that fuel and so forth are extinguished through conjunction with fire?
The Master of the Treatise asks in return:
The Sautrāntika school argues that because fire is no longer perceived once it has come into contact with fuel and so forth.
The Saṃmitīya school replies:
The treatise states:
"One should together carefully consider [the matter] up to the point where, due to non-existence, it is not perceived.
This is the master of the treatise urging the Saṃmitīya school to reflect with care.
The conjunction with fire serves to prevent future arising;
it does not cause that which has already arisen to cease.
Treatise.
Just as when wind and a hand meet, it should be understood through inference that the subsequent flame does not arise because the preceding one is extinguished;
thus the Master of the Treatise cites this as proof.
When the wind meets the lamp-flame, the subsequent flame is not produced, which does not mean it causes the preceding one to cease.
The same principle applies to the union of the hand and the bell.
Since there are two types of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and it has not yet been established as definitive, this point must be proven through inference (*anumāna*).
Treatise:
What is meant by inference (anumāna)?
The Saṃmitīya school asks.
Treatise:
As previously stated, [it] reaches [its object] and therefore does not depend on a cause.
This is the Master’s response.
Treatise:
Furthermore, if one waits for causes to arrive so that there is no lack of cause,
this explains the fifth line of the verse.
There should be no such thing as causelessness.

If the extinction of fuel and so forth depends upon causes, then flames and so forth should likewise depend upon causes for their extinction, just as they depend upon causes for their arising; there can be nothing that is without a cause.
Treatise:
However, it is observed in the world that even reaching [a destination] does not depend on a cause;
this citation serves as an example to support the argument.
Treatise:
There are those who maintain that cognition arises before and perishes after sound;
this is the tenet held by a dissenting teacher of the Vaiśeṣika school.
The preceding cognition perishes through the arising of the subsequent moment because the nature and characteristics of the subsequent contradict those of the preceding;
it is like the subsequent water displacing the preceding flow of water.
This is because that master does not posit the four characteristics [of conditioned phenomena].

The argument that it is solely by means of a subsequent arising that a preceding moment of thought is extinguished is also irrational; for if that is so, by what, then, is the subsequent moment itself extinguished?
The Master of the Treatise refutes this with three principles: first, because the two do not coexist;
for when the subsequent moment arises, the preceding moment has already ceased.
How can they both cause cessation simultaneously?
It is just as suffering and pleasure, or greed and hatred, do not coexist before and after one another;

how then could a subsequent moment of consciousness cause the preceding moment to cease? Second, regarding clarity: how can an unclear cognition or sound cause a clear one to cease? Third, in the case of the final cognition or sound, since there is no subsequent moment [to follow it], [it would have to cease by itself].
Furthermore, by what is it extinguished? The treatise states:
some maintain that the extinction of a lamp’s flame is caused by its non-existence.
This is the position of the Elder Master: he maintains that there is a characteristic of duration (sthiti-lakṣaṇa).
If this characteristic of duration were present in a phenomenon, its cessation would be impossible.
Because it is precisely through the absence of abiding that phenomena can be extinguished,
that flame is extinguished;
it takes the absence of abiding as its cause.
The treatise states that some maintain that when a flame is extinguished, it is due to the power of *dharma* (merit) and *adharma* (demerit).
This is the tenet of certain Vaiśeṣika dissenters.
*Dharma* and *adharma* are subsumed under the category of quality (*guṇa*).
That which is beneficial to people is called the Dharma;
that which is not beneficial to people is called non-Dharma.
By the power of these two, one can give rise to all phenomena and can extinguish all phenomena—just as there is a bright lamp within a dark room.
If one expects its utility,
the lamp is beneficial;
this is precisely the arising of the dharma.
The extinguishing of the lamp is of no benefit;
it is not through the lamp that the unrighteousness is extinguished. If one considers the thief, the lamp being present is of no benefit.
That which is non-dharmic arises;
when the lamp is extinguished, there is benefit,
which is itself the cessation of dharma.
Commentary:
Both [positions] are irrational because they are respectively consistent with and contrary to [the logical requirements].
This is the Master’s refutation.
Within this, there are two [points]:
first, the refutation of the cause for abiding in the unconditioned;
second, the refutation of the causes of dharma and non-dharma. Both of these are irrational.
"Neither both" refers to the two types of grasping. "There is no non-cause" means that the abiding in the causeless unconditioned is refuted;
one does not abide in the causeless unconditioned.

The reason given is that because these do not exist, they are like the horns of a rabbit; it is not the case that non-dharmas serve as the causes for arising and ceasing, since [these characteristics] are mutually contradictory moment by moment.
This refutes the Vaiśeṣika tenet that, regarding a lamp in a single moment,
it is "concordant" when it has utility and "discordant" when it lacks utility.
How can that which is favorable and that which is unfavorable arise simultaneously? The *Nyāyabindu* refutes this, stating:
"Neither dharma nor adharma is a cause for cessation.
This is because one observes flames flickering within an empty cave; the explanation is that since no person is utilizing the flames within the empty cave, there is neither benefit nor harm.
Since there is neither loss nor gain, neither dharma nor non-dharma,
it merely causes the flames to be extinguished.
Treatise.
Alternatively, because [the entity] exists at every moment until the point of death,
the Master of the Treatise again refutes the two schools' positions regarding abiding,
unconditioned causes, and the phenomena of dharma and non-dharma.
It is not only consciousness, flame, and sound that are dissociated from form;
all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) possess the characteristics of duration and cessation, as well as the factors of dharma and non-dharma.
Without depending on any other cause, they perish immediately upon arising.
Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) possess momentariness and are thus identical to my own position, our fundamental dispute should cease;
there is no need for further elaboration. Thus concludes the treatise.
Furthermore, if the fuel and so forth were to become the cause of their own destruction upon reaching the state of extinction,
the preceding argument would already refute such a heterodox view.
Now, we shall further refute the Saṃmitīya position that conjunction with fire is the cause [of the fuel's destruction].
This refers to the sixth line of the verse.
The cause for the cessation of what is below is precisely the cause for the arising of what is above;
the cause for the arising of what is above is precisely the cause for the cessation of what is below.
Treatise:
Why is this so? The Saṃmitīya school raises this inquiry.
The treatise states:
"This refers to the non-existence [of the object] due to contact with fire or something similar thereto.
This is the Master's response. Within this, there are two parts.
First, identity;
second, resemblance.
That is to say, through contact with fire, the fuel undergoes transformation into a state of ripeness; this is the cause of ripening within the process of production.
This is the cessation of the ripening cause for the lower [realm], or that which resembles the cessation of the ripening cause for the lower [realm]; it is the ripening cause for the higher [realm].
This is the cessation of the ripening cause for the middle [realm].
Or, it would be like a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) existing within that which is ceasing.
If that were so, then the essence of a productive cause (*janana-hetu*) should be a cause of cessation;
or else, the causes of cessation and production would be indistinguishable in their characteristics.
Refutation: It should not be the case that the very same thing which acts as the cause of arising is also the cause of destruction, or that they appear similar.
For it would follow that the very same fuel, through contact with fire, would be both the cause of its arising and the cause of its destruction, just as it undergoes transformation by being cooked.
How is this so?
This exists because that exists;
that does not exist because this does not exist.
This is not logical. The treatise states:
"Even if there were a difference between the causes of the arising and ceasing of a flame."
This is a refutation by concession directed at the Saṃmitīya school.
Because the flames are distinct in each preceding and succeeding moment, it may be possible for the cause that ceases to be distinct from the cause that arises; such is the tenet of the Saṃmitīyas.
It is asserted that ash, snow, vinegar, sunlight, water, and earth do not undergo momentary destruction;

rather, their essence remains identical before and after, yet they cause firewood and other things to undergo transformation through ripening. This refutes the [opposing] lower and middle positions regarding the cause of destruction.

Regarding the superior cause among those produced with birth, how can there be any difference? [The Treatise says: The term "produced with birth" (*sahaja*) refers to that which arises simultaneously with its own nature. Among these, the "superior cause" (*adhipati-hetu*) is defined as that which does not obstruct the arising of other phenomena. How, then, can there be any distinction between them? In response to this, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "There is no distinction in their essential nature; however, they are distinguished by way of their specific functions. Specifically, while all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) serve as superior causes for one another because they do not obstruct each other's arising, the "simultaneously arisen" category is established based on the fact that certain phenomena—such as the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) or the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*)—arise together in mutual dependence. Thus, the distinction lies in the specific mode of co-arising, even though both share the common characteristic of non-obstruction.
"If that is so, what function does direct contact (prāpti) perform?
This is the counter-question from the Saṃmitīya school.
"If the transformation of fuel (indhanapariṇāma) does not occur through contact with fire..."
It is observed directly.
What function does the conjunction with fire perform therein?
[The] treatise [says]:
Regarding the statement, "By means of the application of fire to the object, one acts within it," this is the Master’s response.
"The application of fire" refers to the visible mass of fire beneath a cauldron or pot. "The fire element" [is that which is present therein].
That is to say, the heat-tangible [element] within the mass of water is the manifest and shaped mass of water; it is the fire that arises within the water as its heat-tangible [element].
By means of this heat-tangible [element], it acts as the cause for the subsequent moments of the mass of water to arise gradually in a state of attenuation.
It is not that [the cause] acts as the cause of destruction for water already arisen. Therefore,
there is no cause that results in the absolute absence of motion.
The author of the treatise concludes by returning to his own school's position:
cessation does not depend on adventitious causes,
because it is the very nature of phenomena to perish.
Arising and ceasing simultaneously,
there is thus the moment (kṣaṇa).
Since it ceases in each moment, there is no movement.
Treatise: Now,
regarding the overweening pride (*abhimāna*) concerning the progression from the "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) stage to the "practice" (*prayoga*) stage,
the Master of the Treatise explains away these doubts.
The objection asks:
"If there is no movement, how can one see a phenomenon go from here to there? The Master explains:
"It is like when the flame of a burning blade of grass is seen at a distance."
One sees this flame move from here to there;
yet, in reality, the flame is extinguished at each point as it arises.
However, because one's vision is not clear, one says that there is movement.
The same applies to form and the other aggregates:
they truly perish moment by moment.
Those whose eye of wisdom is obscured perceive them as having motion.
To claim that what does not exist exists is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
According to this reasoning, the ultimate truth is thereby established.
Having refuted the divergent views, the conclusion is drawn back to our own school: that bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) is shape (*saṃsthāna*).
This principle is thus established.
However, it has not yet been analyzed whether this shape is conventional (*prajñaptisat*) or substantial (*dravyasat*).
Treatise: Now,
regarding the statement that "it should be understood according to what is appropriate" as spoken by the Sautrāntikas,
the Master [Vasubandhu] recounts the Sautrāntika position to refute the Sarvāstivāda.

The Sarvāstivādins maintain that shape exists as distinct atoms, different from color, and that these very atoms constitute length and so forth; the Sautrāntikas, however, assert that there are no separate atoms for shape.
The accumulation of visible colors (varṇa) constitutes length and so forth;
this is conventional (prajñapti) and not substantial (dravya). That is to say, when a collection of visible colors arises predominantly on one side, it is termed "long color.
This means that among the four sides, one side is particularly more abundant [than the others].
For example, like a flagpole and the like;
that which grows slightly on one side is called "short color" (*hrasva-varṇa*),
such as a gourd vine and the like.
The rest of the text is understandable. Regarding the treatise:
it is like seeing a flame reach the substance of a different class of color.
This citation of an analogy concludes the Sautrāntika tenet. The treatise states:
"If it is claimed that [an object] truly exists as something apprehended by two sense faculties."
It is difficult for the Vaibhāṣikas [to maintain this].
If form were a distinct category with a substantial entity,
it would be a sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*).
That is to say, both the eye and the body— these two faculties— grasp the past [object],
because length and so forth are apprehended by means of both the eye and the body.
(Treatise)
However, just as one perceives shape based on the tangible,
the Master [Vasubandhu] explains that there is no distinct shape;
yet, just as one perceives characteristics such as length based on the tangible.
As for [the claim that] length and so forth are merely deceptive, it is because there is no distinct tangible object of length apart from the accumulation of many [atoms] such as squares;

rather, shape is apprehended based on the manifest color. Therefore, one should know that there is only the accumulation of many manifest colors and no separate length or the like. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* says:
However, the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) states:
"Shape is not substantially existent;
rather, in this way, one apprehends shape by depending upon color."
This reasoning is incorrect,
because their characteristics are distinct.
If one aspect were to manifest only many births, [the other would not].
In that case, there should be no distinction in the apprehension of their characteristics;
yet, since there are differences in the apprehension of length and whiteness,
there must be a distinct shape-color (saṃsthāna-rūpa) existing apart from manifest color (varṇa).
It is observed that there are tangibles apprehended by the same sense organ which,
because their perceived characteristics differ, must have distinct natures.
Just as hardness and coldness, or warmth and hardness, so too,
although whiteness and length are apprehended by the same sense organ,
their essences must be distinct because the characteristics perceived of them differ.
Therefore, one should know that as aggregated matter is analyzed step by step,
until within it there can arise a cognition of shape,
there must necessarily arise at least some slight degree of the cognition of shape.
The reason why the atoms of shape and color still arise therein must necessarily be so;
for within a mass of matter, there are cases where only manifest color arises while shape does not.
Within this [perception], there is only the cognition of color (varṇa) and not of shape (saṃsthāna).

It is like seeing colors such as light and brightness in the sky. If one were to claim that color itself is what is called shape, then the cognition of shape should also arise with respect to color that lacks spatial dimensions.
Because they are inseparable,
just as heat is inseparable from the fire element; thus,
that metaphor of the firebrand is incapable of proving [the point].
Because in other cases, that which is universally established can be described as metaphorical;
that is to say, in other instances there exist real causes— such as length, circularity, and so forth—
which simultaneously and without interval appear across multiple locations.
The aggregation of matter (*rūpa-kalāpa*) established by the differentiation of spatial arrangement is well-known as being long and so forth.
For this reason, in the case of a flame or similar phenomena,
which transition uninterruptedly from one place to another at different times, [the perception of length and so on arises].
One conceptually constructs and establishes [terms such as] "long" or "circular" as conventional designations;

however, we have never seen anything that is not established for both the conventional and the ultimate that could be so conventionally established. Furthermore, the objection regarding the necessity of being apprehended by two sense faculties would likewise fail to be established.
Length and so forth are merely objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
because all that exists as a conceptual construct (*prajñaptisat*) is exclusively the objective domain of the mental consciousness,
as has already been established previously.
The arrangement of atoms, such as those that grow and so forth like seeds, is called shape (saṃsthāna);
it is apprehended by non-conceptual visual consciousness (avikalpaka-cakṣurvijñāna).
It is not the body that can apprehend [them].
Just as one perceives solidity, moisture, and so forth by relying on the body faculty,
one does not perceive length, shortness, and so forth in the same manner.
Because one does not perceive solidity, moisture, and so forth in the dark,
at that very moment or immediately thereafter,
one is able to cognize characteristics such as long and short.
One must first discern the contact through the gateway of the body faculty within the arising of multiple contacts on one side,
and only then can one infer [the object].
One knows that which is experienced by the mental consciousness, drawn forth by the visual consciousness acting in conjunction with contact;
such are the specific characteristics and distinctions of form and color,
just as one who sees the color of fire or smells the fragrance of a flower can recollect the fire’s touch and the flower’s color that accompanied them.
It is observed that visual consciousness, according to its specific conditions,
may at times cognize both shape and color simultaneously.
The mental consciousness (manovijñāna) makes distinctions [regarding color] such that there is no fixed order between what precedes and what follows.
This is because color and shape are both the objective referent (ālambana) of a single visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna),
yet they are differentiated by the mental consciousness when it performs its discernment.
Because their characteristics are distinct,
their essences are different; furthermore,
shape is not itself a tangible object.
How could the body-faculty (kāyendriya) possibly apprehend the meaning of shape?
Therefore, one should not raise the objection that it must be apprehended by two faculties.
Now, upon careful examination, the two treatises possess relative strengths and weaknesses; [this refers to] the author of the Abhidharmakośa-śāstra.
To say that a single shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) should be apprehended by two sense-faculties, and that length and so forth—
which are produced from the accumulation of manifest colors— are visible to the eye,
is a reasoning that is somewhat loose. Thus says the Master of the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Because the cognition of distinct characteristics arises from the perception of different forms,
and because it does not invariably produce the cognition of those forms,
it must be associated with visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
This must be associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
If it were associated with visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*),
it would be possible to establish that it possesses a distinct substantial entity.
By what reasoning can it be proven that the cognitions of "white" and "long" necessarily arise in the same moment as visual consciousness?
If they were associated with mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), how could one know that they do not function simultaneously with other cognitions, such as those of a wheel and so forth?
Outside of the ant-tree there is no separate movement or wheel;

how can this definitively prove that there exists a distinct shape? Furthermore, regarding shadows and the like, which give rise to cognitions of growth and so forth, why do you not admit that they possess shape? It is also like the color of written characters.
Since the patterns of the letters differ in their forward and backward curvatures, they give rise to perceptions of high and low;
why, then, would there not be forms of high and low within them?
If one were to say that there are such forms, it would contradict one's own tenet.
If one says they do not exist, by what cause does the cognition arise? Furthermore, it is said:
"Therefore, we know that when aggregated matter is analyzed and gradually diminished..."
Even to the point where a perception of shape can arise therein,
there must necessarily be some cause for the arising of that perception of shape;
the atoms of shape-color (saṃsthāna-rūpa) still arise within it.
This must necessarily be so;
for within a collection of matter (*rūpa-skandha*), there are cases where only visible color (*varṇa*) arises and shape (*saṃsthāna*) does not.
In such instances, there is only the cognition of color, and no cognition of shape.
Just as when one sees colors such as light and brightness in the sky,
if it were the case that shape is merely the manifest color (varṇa) and lacks spatial dimensions,
then the cognition of shape should also arise with respect to those manifest colors.
Because they are inseparable.
Just as the fire element is heat, this [visible form] also lacks the principle of having spatial dimensions.
This is because the light appearing in a room gives rise to the cognition of shape only when there is visible form.
Furthermore, smoke, clouds, and the like also give rise to the cognition of shape.
How then can you yourself claim that there are eight types of shape-color (saṃsthāna-rūpa) and twelve types of manifest color (varṇa-rūpa)?
Treatise:
Is it not the case that when the sense organ contacts the form, one is able to recollect the color of the flower?
This is the Vaibhāṣika defense.
This means that touch and shape proceed together as a single aggregate;
therefore, by apprehending that touch which accompanies the shape,
one is able to recollect the shape seen by the eye.
It is not that [the object] is a visible form (*rūpa*) nor is it grasped by the body faculty (*kāyendriya*);
rather, just as upon seeing the color of fire one immediately recalls its heat,
and upon smelling the fragrance of a flower one can recollect its color.
Question: When one ascends and sees warmth with the eyes, does the nose smell that color? Treatise: [Response follows].
Regarding these two dharmas reaching the point where one can definitively recollect the form,
the Master [Vasubandhu] refutes the defense:
"Seeing fire, one knows its heat."
By smelling a flower, one knows its color;
these two are certainly inseparable.
First, one perceives their mutual connection.
One knows it only by smelling;
if one does not know it beforehand,
one will not recognize the warmth of the fire or the color of the flower upon seeing or smelling them.
It is not the same with touch and shape.
Whether one knows them as being connected or does not know them beforehand,
if the body follows the touch, one immediately perceives length and so forth.
However, since length and smoothness do not necessarily coexist,
how could one recollect shape in the dark? Therefore, we know [that it is not by means of the tactile faculty].
If there were a distinct form, it would necessarily involve tactile contact with the body. [The] treatise states:
"If touch and form reach the point where one can recollect the form..."
This rebuttal establishes the thesis. According to the Master’s own fundamental position,
if form were substantially real, it would entail the error that it is apprehended by two sense organs.
The Vaibhāṣikas offer this defense:
"Because one perceives tangibility, one is able to recollect shape.
The Master [Vasubandhu] counters with this objection:
Tactile sensation and form are not necessarily inseparable;
yet, when one perceives tactile sensation, one is able to recollect the form.
This is like previously not knowing that this [object] possesses such a fragrance.
When one smells such a fragrance in the darkness, one perceives that the flower has such-and-such a color, yet this is not actually the case;
therefore, it should not be said that one can recollect shape by apprehending the tangible. The *Nyāya* [proponent] offers this defense:
This is also unreasonable,
for it is observed that among the various aggregates of tangibles in the world, there is a fixed shape.
This means that although shape has no fixed existence apart from tangible objects,
when many tangible objects arise on one side, there is necessarily a long color;
and when tangible objects arise pervasively across all locations, [there is necessarily a square color].
There must be a circular color.
One should understand such categories accordingly.
Therefore, there is a determinate relationship between the tangible and shape.
It is not the case that there is a fixed determination regarding the visible [color] such that it can be discerned like shape;
for when one touches, one can recollect the visible color,
because there is no tactile contact with such an arrangement [of color].
In this regard, regarding the determination of the manifestation according to its form,
the treatise [addresses] the difficulty that within a single location, such as a multicolored cloth (*citra*), there would be multiple entities that are not substantially real.
It is like a square brocade that has circular patterns;
within these very patterns, there are again various distinct figures and forms.
Since they occupy the same location, there would have to be many [entities] therein.
In reality, this is not so.
Since multiple manifestations cannot exist in the same location, how could multiple shapes exist in a single place? Now, let us examine this in detail.
This objection does not apply to the Sarvāstivāda school,
because the patterns and images on brocade are not shape-colors (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*). Thus says the treatise.
Furthermore, regarding all things that reach the point of being conventionally designated as "long" and so forth,
it is difficult to maintain that there are distinct shape-atoms (*saṃsthāna-paramāṇu*).
This is because, just as when blue and other colors with resistance are analyzed down to their ultimate atoms, those distinct ultimate atoms are still called "blue" and so on.
If shape were a real entity, then when it is reduced to its ultimate limit, that subtlest point should be designated as "long" and so forth.
If shape were something distinct [from color],
there should exist ultimate atoms (paramāṇu) that are themselves named "long" and so forth.
Therefore, it is known that length and so forth are merely conventional designations for the arrangement of visible color (*varṇa*).
The treatise states: "If one were to claim that [length] exists simply through the arrangement of the collection [of atoms],"
This refutes the previous defense.
If it is argued that the manifestation of an aggregate does not establish the existence of long and so forth in the atoms—
just as an aggregate of fragrance or taste is not called "long"— then [the following applies].
There is no distinct, separate atom (*paramāṇu*) whose specific arrangement constitutes length and so forth;
this is merely the sectarian tenet of the Vaibhāṣikas,
as it is not universally established.
Since the subtle form (*rūpa*) is not established as a consensus,
who would allow that its arrangement constitutes a long shape and so forth? Some explain this as being partisan.
The claim that the *Bandhu* school’s theory is superior to the masters’ tradition is incorrect.
The *Siddhikarmasāstra* refutes the Sarvāstivāda position that shape exists as a distinct entity.
Is it that a single entity pervading within form is called "long" and so forth?
Or is it that an accumulation of many atoms is called "long" and so forth?
If it is an accumulation of many atoms that is called "long" and so forth...
How does this differ from manifest color?
If you claim that a single entity pervades all colors,
you are identical to the Śāṇavāsa school.
Now it is said:
because one accumulates these minute increments over time,
we know [the truth].
This is not the meaning of factionalism or heterodox views.
Does the treatise not clearly demonstrate that those who have reached [the ultimate] differ in their manifested forms?
The Sarvāstivādins offer this defense:
Just as with worldly earthenware vessels,
although they may be alike in color— such as yellow or white— their respective characteristics, such as being a jar or a basin, are each distinct.
Therefore, we know that it is clearly established that there exists a subtle form distinct from the external.
The treatise has already clarified this; the ultimate principle should likewise be understood as such.
This is the commentary by the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*).
It may be understood according to the text. [End of] Treatise.
"Is it not the case that in the darkness, the arrangement of atoms constitutes the shape?
This is the Vaibhāṣika defense.
If one were to say that shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) is simply the accumulation of the differentiation in the arrangement of manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*), [then...]
Since one does not see shape when the manifest color is not seen,
and since one does not see manifest color when shape and color are seen,
we know that shape and color exist separately from manifest color.
The treatise states that when an object is obscured or distant, one perceives only the aggregate as a whole.
The Master of the Treatise explains this as follows.
This can be understood from the text itself. The *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning) states:
"How does the Venerable One allow for the existence of an established atom of manifest color (*varṇa*) that is not a subtle part of shape (*saṃsthāna*)?"
Just as with all manifest colors (*varṇa*), there is no principle for individual atoms (*paramāṇu*) to arise in isolation;
even if they were to arise in isolation,
because they are extremely subtle, they would not be apprehended by the eye, whereas they are apprehended by the eye when they are accumulated.
It is established that there must certainly exist atoms of visible color (*varṇa-paramāṇu*);
the same should apply to atoms of shape (*saṃsthāna-paramāṇu*).
Why, then, do you alone refuse to admit this?
The self-characteristic is universally established: in all locations where resistant forms are accumulated,
atoms are invariably obtainable.
Since, within the arising of the differentiation of aggregated matter,
the cognition of shape arises without depending on color,
just as the cognition of another color arises without depending on yet another color.

Therefore, it must necessarily exist as something distinct, just as a seed is capable of producing growth and so forth. [Objection: Regarding the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) of shape (*saṃsthāna*), we now examine that there is no logical basis for this.
One perceives the dimensions of what follows and thereby knows the dimensions of the preceding seed.
To claim that the "seed" is the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) of form is also irrational;
for there would subsequently be conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and the wheel [of existence].

How could one allow for a separate course of action outside of [the analogy of] a tree and ants? Furthermore, regarding the subtle divisions of the wheel, it is said: "Since all manifest atoms possess material obstruction, they must be accumulated and conventionally designated as 'long' and so forth."
This is also irrational;
for then the atoms of fragrance and so forth would likewise have to be accumulated to constitute length and so on.
Therefore, those atoms of fragrance and so forth must also possess physical resistance (*sapratigha*).
It is only on the basis of occupying space and being mutually exclusive that they are termed "resistant" (*sapratigha*).
If it is argued that the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of odors and so forth do not possess this fault because they are not visible (*anidarśana*), [we reply: no.
Furthermore, since the atoms of all manifest colors (varṇa) are likewise not shape (saṃsthāna),
how could they constitute length and so forth?
How is it known that the substance of the manifest-color atom is not shape?
As previously stated,
because their characteristics are distinct,
and because the cognition of shape arises without depending on the cognition of color.
Alternatively, there may be manifest aggregates that do not appear as shapes; therefore, their substance is not shape.
When many things are accumulated together, even if they are unobstructed and one possesses eyes, it may be that their shape is not seen.
For this reason, it should be understood.
Distinct from visible color (*varṇa-rūpa*), there are atoms of shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) included within the category of material form (*rūpāyatana*).
From the aggregation of these, conventional shapes such as "long" and so forth are established;
therefore, the subtle parts of shape are not unestablished. This is according to the aforementioned treatise.
The subtle form is real;
length and so forth are conventional designations.
These subtle [forms] such as length—
They may be the same or different,
as explained in the *Dhātunirdeśa-prakaraṇa*. However, the Sautrāntika school maintains that long and other such forms are constituted by the aggregation of manifest atoms (*varṇaparamāṇu*).
These are conventional and not real.
It would likely be unreasonable for them to be apprehended by visual consciousness;
[the chariot] and its wheels, etc., are merely conventional designations.
Because it is solely an object of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), although the masters of the *Nyāyānusāra* offer many defenses,
their proof that the arising of cognition establishes the existence of a distinct form is not a definitive proof.
Since there is no movement in the substance of the wheel, yet there is the cognition of a moving wheel,
it must be that when color manifests as long and so forth,
this very color is what is designated as "long" and so on.
The eye sees the physical form, not a provisional form.
This follows the tenets of our school and skillfully supports the ultimate truth.
Treatise.
Having thus refuted [the existence of shape], the Saṃmitīyas and the Vaibhāṣikas inquire: "What then constitutes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)?
The treatise establishes that shape is bodily intimation, but it is merely conventional (*prajñaptisat*) and not substantial (*dravyasat*).
The Sautrāntika replies:
"If you maintain that bodily action consists solely of the reaching [of the hand], then..."
The Vaibhāṣikas ask:
According to this, for the Sautrāntikas, bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) is not bodily action (kāyakarman).
One should know that the same applies to whatever action depends upon the body.
The Sautrāntika school replies:
The Sautrāntikas maintain that the three types of action all have volition (*cetanā*) as their essence,
which is the same as in the Mahāyāna.
This very volition (cetanā),
when based on body and speech, is called bodily and vocal action;
when it proceeds solely based on the mind, it is termed mental action.
Treatise:
If that is so, why is it brought to this? What is the difference between these two?
The Sarvāstivādins raise this objection.
The Sūtra speaks of "karma of volition," which clearly indicates that it is volition itself.
The Sūtra also speaks of "karma after having willed."

If it is clearly known that [volition] is not [the same as] intention (*cetanā*), how can the three types of action have volition as their essence? [The *Śāstra* says: The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "How is it that the three types of karma have volition as their essence? This refers to the objection that if volition were distinct from intention, then the three karmas—bodily, vocal, and mental—could not be established as having volition as their intrinsic nature. How, then, could they be so defined? The treatise provides the following response: [text continues].
This refers to the preceding preparatory stage up to the point where it is designated as "the karma of volition.
The Sautrāntika replies:
"Volition is of two kinds."
First is the volition of reflection;
second is the volition of execution.
The former is called the karma of volition (*cetanā-karma*).
The subsequent [type] is called "action after having been thought.
The treatise says:
If that were so, it would entail a great fault regarding manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*).
The Vaibhāṣika objection:
That which can manifest the mind is called informative action (*vijñapti-karman*);
based upon that informative action, non-informative action (*avijñapti-karman*) is produced.
The two types of karma consist solely of mental volition (*cetanā*);
since volition is not manifest action, there is no such thing as non-manifest karma (*avijñapti-karman*).
If there were no manifest action (vijñapti-karman), then there would also be no non-manifest action (avijñapti);
this would result in a great error. [Thus says] the Treatise.
"What fault does such a great error entail when it reaches this point?
This is the Sautrāntika explanation.
It is the intended meaning of the Sautrāntika school.
The physical body, speech, visible forms, sounds, and names are termed "informative" (*vijñapti*).
Their nature is neutral (*avyākṛta*),
which is the same as in the Mahāyāna.
The volitions of body and speech are termed bodily and vocal informative karma (*vijñapti-karman*);
these pertain to all three moral natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).
Through the power of volition, the perfuming of seeds is termed non-informative karma (*avijñapti-karman*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "In this context,
is this intended to encompass all karma without exception,
or does it encompass only a portion of its specific varieties?"
Some say that this [definition] encompasses all karma. Others say that it does not encompass the untainted (anāsrava) [karma].
These are the two interpretations of the Sautrāntika school regarding the sūtra on "the karma of volition" (cetanākarma) and "the karma after having willed" (cetayitvākarma).
This explanation does not accord with the meaning of the sūtra,
because mental action (*manas-karman*) should not be included herein;
for it refers to the volition (*cetanā*) that initiates the two types of action, namely body and speech.
Furthermore, there is the volition that initiates and sets in motion the two types of activity—
body and speech. Since these two both proceed by way of the gates of body and speech,
they should both be subsumed within bodily and vocal karma.
If that is so, what is here called "mental karma" (manas-karman)? The faults [of this position] have already been explained above in contrast to the previous two [explanations].

Furthermore, if one intends for all three types of karma to be fully subsumed [within it], since phenomena (dharma) necessarily proceed in dependence upon body and speech, [how could they be subsumed under mental karma alone?]
How is mental action (manas-karman) subsumed?
If volition (cetanā) that operates through the two doors of body and speech is also admitted to be,
in part, mental action, [then how is it so?]

This would entail the fault of confusion regarding karma; for even if one were to concede that this [mental action] proceeds by way of the doors of body and speech, it would follow that mental action itself is also bodily and vocal action.
This would result in the fault of confusion.
Even if one were to grant that volition (cetanā) which initiates bodily and vocal action for the sake of desire is of the nature of mental action (manas-karma),
it still does not comprehensively encompass all types of karma within this context.
Because there exists uncontaminated mental karma (*manas-karman*) that operates without depending on the gates of body or speech,
and its magnitude is boundless—
since all such instances are not subsumed within this sūtra— the fault previously raised regarding the non-establishment of mental karma does not apply.
Even if we were to grant that mental karma exists,
there would still be the fault of failing to encompass all instances of mental karma;
specifically, it would certainly not include those volitions (*cetanā*) arising in dependence upon the eye, touch, and so forth.

Because those various volitions (*cetanā*) are not subsumed under the two types of volition previously mentioned—namely, the volition of reflection (*manasikāra-cetanā*) and the volition of performance (*kṛtya-cetanā*).
By this principle, the volition associated with the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) is mental action (*manas-karman*).
This volition associated with the five consciousnesses is neither the volition that initiates reflection nor the volition that performs action,
and so forth.
He devised a deceptive stratagem, which is omitted here without further description. Furthermore, he says:
"Moreover, according to your Sautrāntika school, when the various rishis kill living beings out of mental indignation, under what category of karma is this subsumed?"
Is this bodily action or mental action? However,
herein there is no distinction between two types of volition— namely, the volition that arises earlier and the volition that performs the task later.
Because volition (*cetanā*) constitutes an action through the very act of intending,
one cannot avoid the fault of the confusion of karma. According to this treatise,
there are two kinds of volition regarding the sage’s mental indignation.
Since you have already established that the two types of volition (cetanā) constitute the distinct actions of body and speech, yet there is no difference in the nature of volition itself,
these two types of action should not exist.
Otherwise, mental action would be identical to bodily and vocal [action],
and thus there would be confusion. Furthermore,
it is also incorrect to claim that volition based on body and speech is what is called bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*).
This is because he himself stated that shape constitutes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) as a mere designation and not as something real;
however, volition (*cetanā*) ought not to be shape nor unreal.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states that "raising the joined palms in greeting, paying respect, and prostrating" constitute bodily informative action (*kāyavijñaptikarma*).
Other sūtras further state:
"The manifest [action] is itself karma.
From this, it is proven and known.
The distinct shapes of the hands and other limbs produced successively by the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of desire and so forth are called bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*);
this is precisely what constitutes bodily action (*kāyakarman*). Therefore, the Abhidharma school establishes both bodily and vocal actions.
The teachings of the *Fujiao* (Talismans) follow principle without confusion or error.
Now, we shall defend the Sūtra-nikāya regarding the statement in other sūtras that "manifest action (*vijñapti*) is itself karma."
The effect takes on the name of its cause,
yet it is not identical to that karma;
alternatively, it is named according to what it represents.
Because it is a volition that manifests through the forms of hands, feet, and so forth.
The treatise states: "This should be called 'concomitant with the mind of intent' (*cetanā-sahabhū*)."
The Vaibhāṣikas respond:
Since the specific capacity (śakti-viśeṣa) infused into the mind evolves simultaneously with the mind,
it should likewise be categorized as "coincident" (sahabhū), and the precept of communal restraint (saṃvara-samvara) should be termed "concomitant with the mind" (cittānuvartin).
Commentary:
"There is no such fault... because their nature is dull" is the explanation of the Sautrāntika school.
This non-informative [action] (avijñapti) of the desire realm, which is a differentiation of volition (cetanā),
differs in meaning and intent from that of the meditative state (samāpatti). This refers to the non-informative [action] of the desire realm.
The movement induced by the power of these two types of volition is called "informative action" (*vijñapti-karman*),
because it brings about the manifestation of bodily and vocal actions.
This [unmanifest action] perfumes the mind and forms its seeds; thus it is called "unmanifest" (avijñapti).
The unmanifest of meditative concentration (*samāhita-citta*) is not like this;
because it arises through the power of the mind that exists simultaneously with it, it is called "conforming to the mind" (*cittānuvartin*).
According to the Sarvāstivāda school,
the unmanifest (avijñapti) arises from manifest action (vijñapti-karman);
it is likewise induced by the volition (cetanā) that produces the manifest action.
It is not manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*),
because the nature of matter (*rūpa*) is dull.
Treatise.
The Vaibhāṣika masters [hold this] as previously explained.
The Master of the Treatise (the author) recounts the position of the Sarvāstivādins. The Treatise says:
The Sautrāntika school also maintains that [bodily manifestation] reaches as far as the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
The Master [Vasubandhu] here recounts the Sautrāntika position.
Previously, it was stated that bodily manifestation (*kāya-vijñapti*) lacks any substantial reality (*dravya-sat*).
The unmanifest (avijñapti), like the manifest (vijñapti), likewise lacks substantial reality;
therefore it is said that this too is not substantially existent.
This is how it is known.
There are three reasons for this proof: first, because it is limited by a prior vow of non-performance.
Since the original vow did not intend for a distinct matter (rūpa) to arise, but merely vowed not to perform this action.
How can it be that [unmanifest form] arises separately from the vow? Because the primary elements (mahābhūta) that serve as its basis do not exist [in the present].
Since unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa) is designated based upon past primary elements.

Since the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the past are non-existent in essence, one knows that the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) likewise lacks an essential substance. Thirdly, if it possessed a real substance, it would necessarily possess the characteristic of material form (*rūpa*) with resistance (*sapratigha*).
Since these characteristics do not exist,
one knows that there is no substantial entity.
Treatise.
The *Vibhāṣā* states that this also exists substantially (*dravyasat*).
The Master [Vasubandhu] here recounts the position of the Sarvāstivādins.
The treatise says:
How is this known? This is the question of the Sautrāntika school:
how is it known that non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) also substantially exists?
The following half-verse constitutes the fourth proof for the existence of non-manifest form (*avijñapti*).
The treatise states: "Up to 'invisible and non-obstructive'—this is the first proof."
That which is visible and resistant is the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
That which is invisible and resistant consists of the other nine sense-spheres.
Since the Sūtra further mentions form that is both invisible and non-resistant...
Thus, it is known that this is indeed non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
The treatise further states: "Also, in the Sūtra, [it says] 'and untainted matter' (*anāsrava-rūpa*)," which is the second proof.
Since all resistant forms (*sapratigha-rūpa*) are with outflows (*sāsrava*),
and there exists separately a form that is without outflows (*anāsrava-rūpa*),
it is known that this is non-informative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
Thus, the second proof concludes by summarizing the two proofs.
If non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) did not exist,
among the ten types of resistant matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*), what dharma could be designated as "invisible and non-resistant" (*anidarśana-apratigha*) and "untainted matter" (*anāsrava-rūpa*)?
Treatise:
Furthermore, a sūtra states that meritorious karma increases.
This is the third proof.
Regarding the seven bases of meritorious action:
they are called "merit" because they are wholesome,
and "action" because they are performed.
It is called a "basis" (*vastu*) because it is that which is intended by thought.
There are seven such bases for meritorious action involving a physical support (*sāśrayapuṇyakriyāvastu*).
That is to say, when there is an object of giving (*deyavastu*) that serves as a support, it is termed "involving a support."
First, giving to travelers;
second, giving to those on the road;
third, giving to those who are ill.
Fourth, giving to those who attend to the sick;
fifth, giving gardens and groves;
sixth, giving regular food.
Seventh is giving at the appropriate time.
Although these seven kinds of merit arise from different states of mind and the activity has already ceased,
they persist whether one is walking, awake, sleeping, or otherwise.
It increases at all times,
except when non-informative matter (*avijñaptirūpa*) arises from another state of mind,
or during states of mindlessness (*acittaka*).
Regarding the statement, "By relying on what dharma does meritorious action increase?
It is the same even when there is no basis," this means that there is no physical object of giving to serve as a basis;
rather, it occurs simply through encountering sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), recollecting the Buddhas, and mental reverence.
Furthermore, it is as explained in the treatise regarding the increase of merit based on reliance [on others]:
"Moreover, because this nature remains unchanged even when not performed by oneself."
This is the fourth proof.
If there were no non-informative action (avijñapti),
then one would merely be commissioning another to perform acts such as killing.
It would follow that the path of action is not established,
because at the very moment one dispatches another to kill,
one’s own action is not the act of killing.
Because one cannot kill by merely dispatching another through a manifest action (*vijñapti*),
when one subsequently carries out the killing, the karma of both the self-instruction and the instruction of another is no different from what was previously described. Thus says the treatise.
Furthermore, it would follow that the sūtra’s statement [regarding reaching a destination] would be rendered useless;

In this treatise, the term "transforming cause" (*vivartana-hetu*) is synonymous with "producing cause" (*nirmāṇa-hetu*).

Some say it is between the eyebrows; some say it is at the tip of the nose; some say it is at the heart; some say it is at the navel; some say it is at the toes. Others have made this statement:
The place where the mind was settled during the preceding preparatory stage appears before one there.
Other masters say that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the desire realm are coarse, while those of the form realm are subtle.
It enters coarse apertures like oil entering sand;
however, when the fundamental dhyānas manifest,

The great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm arise only at the periphery of the mind.
Some say that when the preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka*) manifest, the great elements of the form realm also arise throughout the entire body;

It is like two people who both go to a pond to bathe:

the other enters the pool and immerses his body to cleanse himself.
Although both individuals use water that completely covers their bodies, the one who enters the pool for the sake of nourishing the body is superior; subsequently, liberation is considered superior.

34. It says: Question:

One takes refuge in the cessation of all aggregates within one’s own and others’ continuums, as well as those categorized as insentient.

The answer is: although they do not possess the quality of providing protection for me, they do possess the quality of providing protection for others;
because their nature as protectors is equivalent, they too are taken as objects of refuge.
This is stated in terms of acquisition (*prāpti*).
If considered in terms of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), since it exists as many as there are contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*),
there is no difference between the cessation attained by oneself and that attained by others.
Because I have attained dissociation from all contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*),

Because they are not in conjunction,

according to their respective order.

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
Among these, the vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) constitutes its essence,

Because all verbal expressions of taking refuge arise from the mind and are not separate from the mind.
As the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 34, states:
Regarding those who are able to take refuge,
some say it consists of names and so forth;
others say it is vocal action (*vākkarman*).
Some say it is also bodily action (*kāyakarman*);
some say it is faith (*śraddhā*).
It should be stated that it consists of both bodily and vocal action (*kāyavākkarman*).
Furthermore, the wholesome five aggregates— including the mind and mental factors that arise,

The *Nyāya* (Right Principle) differs from the various masters of the *Vibhāṣā*;

One should state it thus; this is the correct principle.
For what reason do both treatises differ from the correct meaning of the *Vibhāṣā*?
Some say that the author of the treatise intentionally set forth an incorrect interpretation of the *Vibhāṣā* to test whether later students possessed understanding or not.
The Venerable Saṃghabhadra was unaware of this text and instead relied upon this very commentary.
If one follows the correct interpretation, which accords with the *Vibhāṣā* commentator (the *pūrvapakṣin*), this explanation is unreasonable;
for the Master of the Treatise possesses many points that differ from the *Vibhāṣā*.
Is it that everyone must undergo testing before they can learn?
Furthermore, if those who merely read the *Vibhāṣā* already perceive [the truth],
why is it that Saṃghabhadra does not perceive it?
Furthermore, Saṃghabhadra additionally possesses the capacity for "concomitant arising" (anuvartana), which differs from that of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
How, then, could these two be the same? Now, upon careful examination, the three treatises are distinct.
The reason for this is that there is a specific intention [behind the statement].
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains it generally as being capable of taking refuge.
Therefore, regarding the taking of the body, speech,
and so forth, the *Abhidharmakośa* states that "this one who is capable of taking refuge" refers precisely to the essential substance of taking refuge within this very restraint (*saṃvara*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* states that among these,
"those who take refuge" refers to those who take refuge within the vows;
each [term] carries a distinct meaning.
This is because, following the exposition of the vehicles in the treatise, the three refuges are explained after the reception of the vows.
Herein, the three refuges that constitute the act of taking refuge in the reception of the vows have vocal intimation as their essence,
because the instructor first utters them and the recipient repeats them accordingly.

If one were to perform prostrations with the body, it would likewise not constitute the method of taking refuge as taught by the Dharma; for these two treatises take only vocal informative action (*vāgvijñapti*) as their basis, while the *Abhidharmakośa*—relying on what is manifest—omits mention of the mind and so forth for brevity.
The *Nyāyānusāra* explains this in detail, clarifying the nature of the mind and its associates as well.

If one were to claim that there is a distinction between the mental faculty (*manas*) and its association, there would be right and wrong; since such a distinction does not exist, [the objection] is invalid.
The general meaning is the same;

Commentary.
Therefore, taking refuge is the ultimate gateway and the concluding summary.
For the eight classes of followers to receive the vows of discipline, they must necessarily take the three refuges as their gateway.

[It refers to] the noble dharmas within the bodies of others, as well as wholesome unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)."
How can one bring about one's own salvation?
It is by taking refuge in that which can extinguish the great terror of the boundless wheel of birth and death;
it is not like a cowherd merely guarding his cattle.
Devadatta and those who protect him merely ensure that others do not disperse;
they are not a source of refuge.
Because they cannot cause the cessation of the fear of birth and death,
although they likewise take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Saṅgha, they do not receive immediate relief.
Because he has transgressed the principles of the Buddha’s teaching;
it is just as when someone relies upon a king but violates the king’s decree, and the king does not provide protection—this case should be understood in the same way. Other masters say:
Because that [refuge] also serves as the seed for the roots of goodness belonging to the final limit,
taking refuge merely acts as the seed for correct practice; it does not,
by itself, bring about the cessation of the wheel of suffering.
Therefore, there are those who have taken refuge but have not yet received salvation. Other masters say:
although they have taken refuge, they have not yet been able to practice that for which refuge is intended.
What is the essential nature of that which constitutes taking refuge?
It is the vision of the Four Noble Truths.
Thus, a verse in the *Gāthā* says:
The *gāthā* refers to the final three lines of the five-line verse from the *Abhidharmakośa*: "All those who take refuge in the Buddha... It further states:
"Moreover, the Buddha is like a guide who can show the way."
The Dharma is like a secure destination;
the Saṃgha is like companions traveling together upon the correct path.
Furthermore, it is said that there are distinctions among the three objects of refuge.
The Buddha is exclusively one who has completed training (aśaikṣa).

The Dharma is neither of the two; "neither of the two" means it is neither that of training (śaikṣa) nor that of no-more-training (aśaikṣa). Furthermore, the essence of the Buddha consists of a portion of the ten faculties, namely the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā).
The faculties of joy, pleasure, equanimity, mind, and full comprehension;
the Sangha includes all twelve, plus the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" and the faculty of "having known."
The essence of the Dharma is not a faculty (*indriya*),
because analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and nirvāṇa are not subsumed under the faculties. Furthermore,
taking refuge in the Buddha means taking refuge solely in one conditioned fruit of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), for the Buddha is also called an Arhat.
Taking refuge in the Dharma means taking refuge in all four unconditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya;
taking refuge in the Saṃgha means taking refuge in all four conditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya.
And regarding the four fruits that lead toward [liberation],
the treatise asks:

Furthermore, that all noble ones (ārya) have reached the point of being certain not to [commit such acts] is the third reason.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Because even noble ones (*ārya*) who have undergone rebirth do not engage in it;
this is not the case regarding the abstention from unchaste conduct."
If it were otherwise, then a *śaikṣa* who has been reborn would be unable to maintain the precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), non-celibacy would be a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*),
and he would be unable to maintain [the avoidance of] natural transgressions.
In reality, one is also able to maintain the prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), namely, not drinking alcohol;
how much more so, then, the natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*)! Furthermore, another explanation states:

Because these are natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*), they are called natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*); it is not the case that all five types of abstentions are natural transgressions. Regarding sexual misconduct, all noble ones (*ārya*) certainly attain the state of non-doing, which is termed restraint (*saṃvara*); this restraint of non-doing has no separate substantial entity.
The previous precepts have already been relinquished,
and since one has not yet received them in this life,
they merely represent the five precepts previously received in a former body.
Even if one undergoes further rebirths and does not receive the precepts again,
one will certainly refrain from sexual misconduct and the like;
however, this is not the case for non-celibacy.
Even though one who is still in training (śaikṣa) may have previously received full ordination,
if they lose their precepts through rebirth and have not yet received them again,
they immediately commit the offense of unchaste conduct (abrahmacarya). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

If one who has previously engaged in sexual misconduct later makes a formal commitment before a teacher to receive [the precepts] again, does he obtain this previously unobtained restraint by abstaining from non-celibate conduct? Other masters say: [he does].
Regarding the attainment of this restraint, some say that one does not obtain what was previously unobtained;
nevertheless, by acquiring the most excellent qualities of *dhuta* (ascetic purification), one is said to have acquired the most excellent dharma of seclusion (*viveka*).
This means that because one is able to distance oneself from the phenomena of sexual desire,
the latter explanation is superior.
One who has not obtained the formal restraint (saṃvara) should still obtain the distinct non-informative matter (avijñapti) of distancing oneself [from such acts].
Why is this? Because apart from the restraint of celibacy (abrahmacarya-virati), there is no such thing as receiving [the precepts] individually;
they must necessarily be received and attained collectively in groups of five, ten, two hundred and fifty, or five hundred, and so forth.
Because these [individuals] lack the necessary factors, they do not generate the restraint (*saṃvara*).
The treatise asks:
"Are there any who, having previously received it, still possess the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the restraint?"
Question:
According to the actual principle, one should indeed obtain the prātimokṣa restraint through the acquisition (prāpti).
Answer: [The] treatise says:
If that is so, why is it that later one does not become one who has violated the precepts?
Difficult.
The answer is given from the second half of the verse.
The treatise says: up to "it does not constitute a transgression of the preceding precept."
The commentary on the verse can be understood according to the text.
Treatise:
For what reason is it that the restraint is prescribed only up to the level of the lay practitioner (*upāsaka*)?
The second half-verse clarifies the reason for abstaining from false speech.
Treatise:
It is also because, as previously stated, one attains non-action. Answer:
Treatise:
Furthermore, there is another reason.
This is a repeated question.
The commentary states: "Up to 'it is able to prevent future transgressions' explains the verse.
This may be understood according to the text. The *Vibhāṣā* (123) says:
Some say that it is easy to maintain abstinence from false speech,
but not so for the other three.
This refers to one living as a householder who governs servants and the like;
it is difficult for such a person to distance themselves from the three [unwholesome actions], including divisive speech.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
The path of action consisting of false speech is the most serious, while the other three are slightly lighter;
for this reason, they are not established [as the gravest]. Other masters say:
Only false speech is established as a training rule because it can cause the destruction of the Saṃgha;
the other three are not so. Furthermore, others say that if noble ones (āryas) do not commit an offense even after passing through a birth, they are established as upāsakas.
A noble one (ārya) will certainly be free from the karma of false speech throughout their successive births, whereas this is not the case for other types of verbal karma. Why is this?
Because there are three other types of verbal karma.
This means they arise from greed, hatred, and delusion.

Although noble ones who have been reborn do not commit offenses arising from delusion— because such offenses are subsumed under the category of views regarding delusion— [they may still act] through the influence of those [other two].
The Noble One has already severed [the underlying tendencies], yet he commits offenses arising from greed and hatred;
therefore, this is not established as a further [defilement]. Thus the treatise explains it.
Treatise:

That is to say, abstaining from drinking alcohol.

Treatise:

When one drinks alcohol for a limited time as a treatment for illness,

Treatise:

Furthermore, since the Buddha prohibited alcohol even for those who were ill,
we know that drinking alcohol is subsumed under the category of natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

Treatise:

Treatise:
Furthermore, for all noble ones (ārya), even regarding such acts as taking life—

Since the Noble Ones also do not drink alcohol, this too is a natural offense.
Treatise.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states that this is an evil physical action; this is the fourth proof.

[it is argued that] this is because the patient would thereby commit a transgression of a fundamental nature (prakṛti-sāvadya).

and so forth...

"For what reason are these all natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*)? and so forth.
