how could this be considered a transgression?
Therefore, not all instances of drinking alcohol are subsumed under unwholesome conduct (*duścarita*).
If one drinks for the sake of arrogance and indulgence, or for the sake of pleasure and amusement,
or out of craving despite knowing it will lead to intoxication and confusion.
All of these arise based on a defiled mind;
regarding this, it is taught in the sutra as "bodily misconduct.
One should know that these are subsumed under natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). According to this treatise, such is the case.
If one drinks alcohol with a defiled mind, it is a transgression by nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
Furthermore, according to this principle,
cutting grass and so forth with a defiled mind is also a transgression by nature.
Only an undefiled mind constitutes a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibited offense).
Regarding the statement in the treatise that habitual practice leads to rebirth in the evil destinies:
This is a citation of the specific text. The treatise states:
"It reveals that drinking alcohol repeatedly increases until it becomes excessively intense."
The general and specific texts contain three causes,
which can be understood from the text itself.
Treatise:
As stated in the Sūtra, from "To what extent" up to "In what sense is it said?"—
this is the question.
In the Sūtras, based on what meaning are *surā* liquor and *maireya* liquor designated as such?
Furthermore, why are they both said to be *madya* (intoxicants) and the "basis for negligence"? [The Abhidharma] Treatise says:
Because fermented food becomes wine upon reaching its locus of dependence;
the following is the explanation. "That which is fermented from other substances" refers to grapes and the like.

Therefore, the Sūtra speaks of three names: *surā* and *maireya* refer to intoxicants that are the basis for negligence; these do not prohibit the drinking of betel nut and similar substances which can also cause intoxication.

As for *madya*: *(Note: This passage clarifies the distinction between specific types of intoxicants prohibited by the Buddha and other substances that may also cause intoxication but are not subject to the same prohibition.)*
When fermented food is made into liquor, or when other substances undergo fermentation and spoilage, those that cannot intoxicate people are not subject to this rule.
Regarding the drinking of fermented food, other substances, or the dregs of liquor (*madya*): [the following applies].
Regardless of the quantity,
this is a basis for negligence; therefore,
it is prohibited so that one shall not drink it.

all of these are merely present provisional aggregations.

From "from the constant time" up to "obtaining the aggregates, bases, and elements.

The various masters of the Sautrāntika school, up to the point where they state "except for the eight precepts," set forth the tenets of the Sautrāntikas.
According to their school, the virtuous and non-virtuous ethical discipline (śīla) does not consist of all seven branches, nor is it universal with respect to its objects.

with the sole exception of the eight precepts;

Commentary:
This is because, according to the extent of those [precepts], they lead to mutual exclusion.

Because one acquires non-restraint (asaṃvara) such as killing solely by contravening [the precept] of non-killing and so forth according to that specific measure,
it is not possible to simultaneously exclude [non-restraint] regarding false speech and the rest;

By this, both the virtuous and non-virtuous precepts become deficient in their constituent parts;

The Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) explains:

they are called 'śramaṇas' only because they possess the remaining signs of a śramaṇa."
Like charred timber, a parrot’s beak,
or a dried-up pond.
Rotten seeds,
a fire-wheel,

These are merely words; the various analogies cited are all ineffective, for even when pieces of wood have been slightly scorched by fire, they are called "scorched wood" in the world.
That which has not been entirely turned to charcoal is not called "burnt wood.
If you claim that it is called "burnt wood" regardless of whether the whole or a part has been burnt— accepting both cases as such—
then both the example and the property to be proven (dharma) will be subject to uncertainty.
The analogy lacks the capacity to prove what it is meant to illustrate; it is like a dried-up pond that may still contain a small amount of water.
However, because it lacks the function of a pond, it is designated as "dried up.
Even if there were no water at all, it would still be called "dried up."
The same applies to the doubt regarding the inability to realize [the goal]; by this, the dead person and the rotten seed are already excluded.
That is to say, although they may still possess a slight degree of causal capacity, people in the world nevertheless refer to them as "rotten seeds."
Or, although not destroyed, its functional capacity is impaired such that it no longer produces sprouts;
this too is called a "destroyed seed. There are those who, sharing the same nature as the dead, are also called "dead people."
Therefore, the sūtras state that those who are heedless are as if constantly dying,
using the two analogies of the parrot’s beak and the whirling firebrand;
these both contradict what is taught in the sūtras, which state that there are four types of śramaṇas and no fifth.
If one were to receive the name "śramaṇa" based solely on outward appearance,
then there are people in the world who, desiring the marks of a śramaṇa, employ deceptive means to assume the form of a śramaṇa;
they should be called śramaṇas and designated as the fifth [type].
It is not that which is a false cakra or a whirling firebrand that can be designated by the names "cakra" or "wheel" with respect to other characteristics;
for these are preceded by what is not a real cakra or wheel.
In this way, there would have to be a fifth who was previously not a śramaṇa but assumes the form of a śramaṇa;
however, the Buddha spoke of four and said there is no fifth in order to stop such attachment to the characteristics of a śramaṇa.
Therefore, all the cited analogies lack the capacity to provide proof.

The Commentary says: Up to the point of establishing the name "indeterminate," the three types of karma are collectively divided into two: namely, determinate and indeterminate. Thus says the Commentary.

This describes an alternative explanation.
This master divides indeterminate karma into two types:
that which is determinate and that which is indeterminate with respect to its maturation (*vipāka*).
These constitute five types of karma.
Regarding those that are determinate or indeterminate in their maturation (*vipāka*):
first, although this karma is determinate in its three periods [of action],...
It is called "indeterminate karma" because its timing of fruition is not fixed;
however, at a certain time, it will inevitably experience its maturation.
Furthermore, this karma is not indeterminate with respect to only three periods of time.
The ripening of the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) is likewise not fixed.
The treatise states:
"Karma to be experienced in the present life may ripen in subsequent successive stages."
This explains the fixed karma of the three periods.
Although the karma to be experienced sequentially over many lifetimes may span numerous births,
it is collectively subsumed as one.
Treatise:
Other masters say that [the number of moments] until the ripening fruit is small;
this describes a divergent view of the Sautrāntika school.
The intention of this master is to say that because the power of karma is strong, it is experienced in the present life.
Since the present karma is already strong, how can it produce only a result of a shortened lifespan in the present life?
The treatise states:

The treatise states: The Dārṣṭāntikas also say that arrival (*prāpti*) is of two kinds.
This master says:

thus, they form four categories,
which together constitute eight types of karma.
Within the category of the five types of karma, only those that are indefinite are divided into two kinds:
first, those with determinate maturation;
second, those with indeterminate maturation.
The characteristics of karma are difficult to discern;
we shall now extensively cite the text of the *Vibhāṣā*.
The *Vibhāṣā* states:
Question: Are all karmas that are to be experienced in the present life necessarily experienced in the present life?
The same question applies to those to be experienced in the next life and those to be experienced in subsequent lives.
The Dārṣṭāntikas say:
This is not certain,
because all karma can be transformed; even the karma of the immediate offenses (ānantarya-karma) can be made to turn away.
Question: If that is so, why are they called "karma to be experienced in the present life" (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman) and so forth?
Answer: They explain it thus:
karma to be experienced in the present life is not necessarily experienced as its ripened fruit (vipāka-phala) within the present life itself.
If the ripening is necessarily experienced in the present life and not in another, it is called "karma to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*).

The same applies to what is said regarding [karma] to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*) and in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*). According to this master, [the definition is as follows].
Karma whose timing of fruition is indefinite is called "indefinite karma. The masters of the Abhidharma treatises state that all karma to be experienced in the present life is determinate,
because it is certain to be experienced within the present life itself.
This is called "karma to be experienced in the present life.
The same applies to what is said regarding [karma] to be experienced in the next life and in subsequent lives.
Therefore, if one asks:
Why are they called "karma to be experienced in the present life" (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman) up to "karma to be experienced in subsequent lives" (aparaparyāyavedanīya-karman)?
This should be answered accordingly.
Furthermore, other masters state that there are five kinds of karma.
That is to say, there is only one type each for the [karma] to be experienced in the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives.
Within the category of karma to be experienced at indefinite times, there are further two types:
first, that which is determined as to its maturation (vipāka-niyata).
Second, the ripening [of karma] is not fixed.
Among the four types of karma, karma whose ripening is fixed cannot be altered;
however, this is not the case for karma that is to be experienced at an indefinite time.
Regarding karma whose maturation is not fixed, this karma can be transformed. Furthermore, other masters speak of eight types of karma;
that is, there are two types of karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
First, those with determinate maturation;
second, those with indeterminate maturation;
and karma to be experienced in the next life, karma to be experienced in subsequent lives, and karma to be experienced at indefinite times.
Each of these also has two types:
first, those with determinate maturation;
second, those with indeterminate maturation.
These are called the eight types of karma.
Among them, those karmas whose maturation is fixed cannot be altered;
however, all karmas whose maturation is not fixed can be altered.
In order to transform this, one undertakes the observance of the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*) and so forth.
Therefore, four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be formulated herein.
[Treatise:]
Within these explained distinctions of karma, the following two verses clarify the second [topic]: the distinctions among the four types of karma.
The treatise says: "Up to the characteristics of the four types of karma."
The author of the treatise evaluates and accepts the four types of karma as correct;
herein, he merely clarifies their determinate and indeterminate timing in order to explain the characteristics of the four karmas taught in the Sūtras.

Therefore, it is known that "determined by time" refers precisely to the three types of karma—namely, that which ripens in the present life and so forth—while "undetermined" refers to the fourth type, indeterminate karma. The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"In this context, it is solely to reveal that karma conducive to pleasure and so forth is either determined or undetermined with respect to the present life and other times."
The Sūtras explain the distinctions among the four types of karma— such as that to be experienced in the present life and so forth;
therefore, determinate karma is divided into three kinds,
which, when combined with indeterminate karma, constitute four.
This is said to be correct.
Logically, there can be no such thing as a determinate karma whose maturation (*vipāka*) is indeterminate while its timing is determinate;
for a determinate timing is merely a specific stage within the determinacy of maturation itself.
The temporal nature does not exist as something distinct from the ripening [result].
How then could the determination of time not itself be a ripening result?

In this context, the categories such as "karma to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) are established solely on the basis of the specific stages at which karma with determinate ripening attains its fruit.
If it is claimed that there is karma fixed as to its time—
meaning that its ripening must necessarily occur at this specific time and not at another,
and that if this time is bypassed, it will never be experienced at all.
Therefore, it is determined with respect to time, not with respect to maturation (*vipāka*).
This [determination] should also be certain with respect to maturation,
because the meaning is analogous.
What is meant by "similarity"?
It refers to how, just as there may be irrationality regarding time,
yet it is termed "determination of the time-period" (*kāla-niyama*), so too there may be irrationality regarding ripening (*vipāka*).
It should be called "determined by maturation" (*vipāka-niyata*), or else one must admit that both are undetermined.
Therefore, if an action is determined with respect to its timing,
it must also be determined with respect to its maturation.
If it were the case that the maturation (*vipāka*) is indeterminate,
then its timing would also have to be indeterminate.
For this reason, there are certainly not eight types of karma.
Since there is an indeterminate meaning within various karmas,
one should establish a single category of "karma conducive to indeterminate experience" in general. Why is this so?
Because their meanings are similar;
that is to say, it is like the case of "fixed maturation" (niyata-vipāka) versus "unfixed timing karma" (aniyata-kāla-karma).
Since its timing is indefinite, it is already accepted by all as being "karma to be experienced at an indefinite time.
Likewise, why is karma that is definite in timing but indefinite in ripening not also accepted as being "karma to be experienced at an indefinite time," given that its ripening is indefinite?
Therefore, the Dārṣṭāntikas establish eight types of karma within this context, which is extremely confused;
according to the aforementioned treatise, even five types of karma are not the correct meaning. Furthermore, it says: "The Dārṣṭāntikas state..."
Karma to be experienced in the present life and so forth may also receive its maturation in other future lives; however,
they are designated by the names "to be experienced in the present life" and so on according to their initial stage of maturation.
It is not merely that a name brings about such-and-such a result;
rather, what is intended by that statement is this:
any karma performed that, arising from this very life, is able to act as a cause and yield a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) is called "to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
If it is capable of acting as a cause for maturation (*vipāka*) only after the immediately following birth, it is called "to be experienced in the next life" (*upapadyavedanīya*).
If it skips the next birth and only yields maturation from the third birth onward, it is called "to be experienced in subsequent lives" (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).
For what reason do they speak thus?
It is because they fear that the maturation (*vipāka*) of powerful karma would be too slight;

To say that the distinction between the six and the four is illogical is incorrect.
Because the meaning of the preceding sutra and the subsequent sutra is similar, the preceding sutra states: The Buddha addressed the Great Mother, "What do you think?
Regarding all forms that are not seen by your eye, and so forth."
Later, in this [sūtra], he again addressed the Great Mother:
"Among these four, you should understand that which is seen as 'merely what is seen,' and so forth."
The Sautrāntika commentary states:
"The former refers to the six objects;
the latter refers to the four objects, beginning with 'view' (dṛṣṭi)."
The *Nyāya* does not accept that this is due to a different intention of the sūtra.
As for the meaning of what is taught in this sūtra as I see it,
it refers to the *Mahāmātṛkā*.
Just as, regarding objects such as forms during the three times,
if one does not see them and so forth,
one does not seek them.
Desire and so forth do not arise.
Likewise, if one knows that objects such as what is seen are merely what is seen and so forth,
desire and so forth likewise do not arise.
Since desire and so forth arise solely through one's own conceptual construction,
I explain this scriptural passage in accordance with the meaning of the Sūtra.
This is not like the Master of the Sūtra (Sautrāntika), who, following his own conceptual constructions, interprets the Sūtra as implying two kinds of non-arising of desire and so forth.
First, not seeing form and so forth;
second, knowing that the forms and so forth which are seen possess only the characteristic of form, devoid of the characteristics of the pleasant or the unpleasant.
The preceding sutra clarifies that because there is no seeing, there is no desire and so forth.
Later, through the knowledge that what is seen and so forth possesses neither the characteristic of the agreeable nor the disagreeable,
desire does not arise. Thus, both sutras—
preceding and following— equally clarify the non-arising of desire and so forth.
It is not that the former sutra clarifies the six objects while the latter sutra clarifies the four objects such as "what is seen";
this is extensively proven by citing the verses from the *Mātṛkā* regarding the realization of understanding. Furthermore, it says:
Furthermore, with what intention do those two masters align themselves with explanations that contradict reason and scripture,
while simultaneously harboring such partiality and hostility toward the *Vibhāṣā* masters whose words accord with reason and scripture?
Moreover, the explanations provided by those two masters contradict the teachings.
In the sūtras, the Buddha has clearly and specifically distinguished the characteristics of "the seen" and so forth with respect to objects such as form (*rūpa*).

Yet, because [the opponent] abandons that distinction and establishes something else, they also contradict the correct reasoning of the teachings; for the sūtra clearly states that "form is called the seen."
That which is heard is called "sound";
that which is known is called "phenomena" (dharma).
According to the principles of the teaching, only odor, flavor, and tangibility are objects of direct sensory cognition.
The positions established by the two masters contradict the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*.
Since there is no other scriptural authority to prove them,
the [opposing] clarification is taken as correct.
It is said that among the five objects, each possesses all four [aspects],
whereas in the sixth object there are only three. However,
it is the *dharma* (phenomena) alone that can most appropriately be designated by the term "the seen."
It cannot be said that sounds and so forth are "seen," as in the expression, "the Buddha sees the past and future.
This is because these are all objects exclusive to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
There has never been a statement in the holy teachings that the ear sees sound,
the nose sees fragrance, and so forth.
How is it that all five objects are called "seen," while the sixth alone is not?
Furthermore, he himself stated:
"If that which is directly realized by the mind is called the 'knowable,' then since dharmas are knowable..."
It should be called "the seen," because it is presently realized,
just like visible form and so forth.

What is the reasoning here that only those things perceived by the five [senses] are designated as "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), while sound, odor, taste, and touch are not? It is not established by scripture that these are called "seen.
Furthermore, to designate *dharmas* as "seen" contradicts the scriptural teaching that they are non-existent [in that sense]. Moreover, this is established through inference (*anumāna*).
That which is established by valid cognition is what is seen,
because it is presently realized,
just like form and so forth.
Regarding the inference according to other schools, the former master says:
"The objects directly perceived by the five sense faculties are called 'the seen' (*dṛṣṭa*);
since it is also admitted that phenomena (*dharma*) are directly perceived, [they too must be the seen]."
How is it that [visual] seeing is not "internal experience"? Furthermore, the later master explains:
that which is internally experienced by oneself and personally realized by oneself is called "the known" (*jñeya*).
If this is so, for what reason is visual seeing not considered internal experience?
In that case, what is seen should be identical to what is known;
furthermore, there should be no distinction between what is perceived and what is known,
because both are self-attested by the mental consciousness itself.
Furthermore, it is universally accepted by those who understand correct reasoning that all forms of inference (anumāna) are preceded by direct perception (pratyakṣa).
If the object of inference were to be designated as "the cognized" (vijñeya) only then [after such perception], [it would follow that nothing could ever be cognized].
The object of cognition cannot exist prior to the act of cognizing it;
therefore, the positions of those two masters lack any logical foundation. Thus concludes the treatise.

Let us now set aside these incidental remarks. When it comes to the time for the *prasāthika* (the invitation), the threefold question and answer may be understood according to the text. Thus says the treatise.
If one does not move the body, effort must be exerted [to produce it].
The Master of the Treatise objects:
"In the desire realm, there is no non-informative [action] that arises apart from informative [action]."
If one neither moves the body nor utters speech,
there is no manifest action (vijñapti-karman).
From what can non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) be obtained?
One should apply diligent effort to resolve all such objections. The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (*Sūtrāntika*) raises the following objection."
If one neither moves the body nor utters speech,
it is impossible for non-informative [action] (avijñapti) to arise independently of informative [action] (vijñapti).
How can these two be established as courses of action (*karmapatha*)?
One should apply diligent effort to this objection.
For how could it be permissible not to establish these two as courses of action when, in reality, there are no manifest (*vijñapti*) or unmanifest (*avijñapti*) actions?
He should also distinguish the two causes for the offense of touching;
it is not merely the arousal of an evil thought that constitutes a grave transgression.
If one intends to act through the two doors of body and speech, one must arouse the thought and the desire to kill or deceive.
It would then follow that they have committed a heinous offense (*ānantarya*). If that were not established, then seers (*ṛṣi*) and others would be the same [in this regard].
Yet, they do not move their bodies.
Furthermore, since no speech is uttered,
how can there be a path of action (*karmapatha*),
and how can it be based upon the doors of body and speech?
One should exert effort to resolve such an objection.
However, for now, I shall explain it in the context of the *poṣadha*:
just as verbal action (*vāg-karman*) arises through bodily movement that can express the meaning of speech.
If the body does not move, yet the karma-path of verbal expression arises through its ability to signify meaning,
then at the time of reciting the precepts, one who has committed an offense may remain silent to signify purity, thereby causing the assembly to perceive them as being in accordance with the rule.
How is it that the karmic path of false speech does not arise?
It is when a rishi, out of indignation, instructs others in matters such as the meaning [of a teaching],
and they, having no regard for sentient beings in their hearts, [act accordingly].
Non-humans respect him and know that he harbors an evil intent;
they move their bodies to kill him, thereby completing the karmic path of action (*karmapatha*).
By what sign does the seer manifest his intention so that the ghosts may understand his mind?
Because of mental anger, his body and speech necessarily undergo change;
or, due to the act of cursing, his body and speech are inevitably moved.
Other masters say:
It is not the case that all unmanifest [karma] in the desire realm arises based on manifest [karma],
as when the five bhikṣus and others obtained the prātimokṣa precepts at the moment of attaining the fruit.
The same should also apply to unwholesome [karma].
However, since it was previously established that there is definitely manifest action (*vijñapti*),
the same should also hold for the others.
The "seer" (ṛṣi) is as previously described.
Regarding the instance where one incurs the offense of lying during the *praśāstṛ* ceremony:
it refers to one who, being impure, falsely enters the midst of the Saṃgha and assumes an air of dignified deportment.
Some have explained this as referring to the prior manifest [action];
the rest should be considered accordingly.
Treatise.
Having already analyzed false speech, the remaining three types of speech shall now be analyzed.
Below follows one and a half verses clarifying the characteristics of how these three types of speech accomplish the path.
The treatise says: Reaching this point in the flow [of the argument], we explain the characteristics of speech intended to destroy others.
First, there is the defiled mind that desires to destroy others.
Second, the meaning is understood;
third, it is not erroneous.
Whether the other person is defeated or not defeated, both constitute speech that defeats the other.
If another person does not destroy [the virtue] nor cause it to be destroyed,
there would be no destruction of the noble ones;
yet at the time of correct comprehension, whether there is destruction or non-destruction constitutes the path of action (karmapatha).
Treatise:
If it is held that [the act] is completed only when one reaches the path of action with a defiled mind,
this explains harsh speech.
First, with a defiled mind;
second, uttering unpleasant speech to disparage another;
third, the other person understands the meaning.
Fourth, there must be no error.
When the one being reviled understands [the words], the path of action is established.
Treatise:
All defiled minds extend up to this point; herein, the explanation of frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*) is given.
Within this, there are two interpretations.
All speech uttered from a defiled mind is called frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).
Since everything uttered from a defiled mind is frivolous speech,
the preceding word "speech" (*vāk*) flows over into this context as well.
"Understanding the meaning" differs from the previous [category] in that it is not erroneous;
for in the former case, even an error constitutes [the category].
Thus, these first three terms each possess two names.
Excluding the previous three types of speech, that which is merely named "frivolous talk" (*sambhinna-pralāpa*) is discussed.
In the treatise, other masters state that it includes [speech] such as "to" (*yāvat*) and "indeed" (*yathā*).
This is the second explanation.
The first three terms are designated according to their specific characteristics.
That which is produced by a defiled mind apart from those first three terms is called frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).
Commentary:
"Flattery" refers to sycophantic speech directed toward those one holds in high regard;
this is a further explanation.
This can be understood according to the text. Regarding the treatise:
"and so forth" refers to defiled minds up to those included under frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).
The commentary on the words "explanation" (*śloka*), etc.,
may be understood according to the text. [End of] Treatise.
From the time of the appearance of a Wheel-Turning King until the inclusion of frivolous speech—
this is the question. Now,
the treatise:
The answer is that because those words proceed from a state beyond [the defilements] rather than from a defiled mind;
there are two [types].
First, because it is not defiled;
second, because it is light.
This refers to the first.
The *Śāstra* states: Other masters say that [the second alternative] is not established as a course of action (*karmapatha*).
This is the second interpretation. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* says:
Because they are of the nature of attenuated defilements (*tanu-rajas*), they do not induce non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
It is not the case that there could be no non-informative action subsumed under the paths of action (*karmapatha*). [Abhidharmakośabhāṣya] Treatise.
Having already distinguished the three [paths of action] of speech, one should now distinguish the three of the mind.
This clarifies that the three karmic paths of the mind are established through the conjunction of the basis, the agent, and the object.
The treatise says: "Up to the point where it is called the path of action of greed."
This explains the characteristics of the first path of action.
Coveting the wealth of others is termed the path of action of greed;
other instances of a greedy mind do not constitute a path of action.
The treatise states: Some masters say that this extends to the general description of sensual craving (*kāmarāga*).
Other masters cite the *Pañcanīvaraṇa-sūtra* as proof that all forms of greed constitute this karmic path of greed.
Treatise:
Some say that sensual desire constitutes the karmic path of greed.
This master holds that only the coarse variety [of such desire] constitutes a karmic path.
It does not distinguish between greed for wealth and greed for other matters.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Although all such worldly greed is termed 'greed,' not all of it constitutes a course of action (*karmapatha*)."
Since it was previously stated that among the various unwholesome actions, the coarse categories are selected to constitute the paths of action (*karmapatha*),
only the arising of malicious desire and greed toward the property of others is designated as the path of action of covetousness (*abhidhyā*).
If it were otherwise, the path would become attached to one’s own property;
the same difficulty applies to the Universal Monarch (cakravartin) and the inhabitants of Uttarakuru.
According to the text of the *Nyāyānusāra*, the first and third [positions] are correct.
Treatise:
Regarding sentient beings, reaching the point where it is designated as the path of action of hatred (*dveṣa-karmapatha*) explains and establishes the characteristics of the second path of action.
Only when one intends to inflict harm upon sentient beings does such malice constitute a path of action (*karmapatha*);
all other instances of anger do not constitute a path of action.
The treatise explains the characteristics of the third course of action (*karmapatha*) by way of [discussing] wholesome and unwholesome meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and wrong views.
Treatise:
As stated in the Sūtra up to the point regarding the Arhat,
the following citation from the Sūtra provides a detailed explanation of the word "and so forth" (ādi) contained within the verse.
In total, there are eleven differences:
first, the absence of giving;
second, the absence of affection.
Regarding the three [types of] non-sacrifices (*atīrthika*), the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 98, explains these three as follows:
first, some explain that they are without distinction because they equally manifest a single meaning;
second, another explanation states: "The proponents of external treatises say..."
"Without giving" means there is no giving of the three types of merit.
"Without affection" means...
This means there is no distinct merit in giving to brahmins, nor is there merit in performing sacrifices;
that is to say, there is no merit in giving to a multitude of brahmins. There are further many such assertions in the non-Buddhist treatises.
As explained at length therein,
the proponents of the Inner Treatises (Abhidharmikas) say: "There is no giver."
This means there is no past merit;
it means there is no one who delights [in virtue];
it means there is no future merit.
"One who performs no sacrifices" means one who possesses no present merit.
Furthermore, "one who gives no gifts" [is meant].
That is to say, there is no merit of bodily action;
there is no one who delights [in it].
That is to say, there is no merit of verbal action.
"Those who do not perform sacrifices" refers to those who lack the merit of mental action (*manas-karman*), and so forth; there are many such interpretations.

"Neither performing sublime conduct nor performing evil conduct" is a wholesale repudiation of both sublime and evil conduct. The four points above constitute the false view that denies causes (*hetu-apavāda*).

The five [types of wrong view] abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) are the maturation (*vipāka*) resulting from unwholesome courses of action (*akuśala-karmapatha*). This denial of fruition is a wrong view abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). The six [types of wrong view] are: (6) "There is no this world" and (7) "There is no other world. These pertain to the denial of both cause and fruit, and are abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of the origin. The *Vibhāṣā* explains as follows:
Question: It may be appropriate to deny the existence of the next world, as it is not perceived;
but why deny this world, which is directly perceived?
Answer: Those non-Buddhists are blinded by ignorance and thus even repudiate things that are directly perceived.
One should not blame the ignorant and blind for falling into a pit.
Furthermore, there are those who say that while those non-Buddhists merely slander cause and effect, they do not slander the essential nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
"There is no this world" means that there is no this world as a cause for another world,
or that there is no this world as an effect of another world.
"There is no other world" means that there is no other world as the cause of this world, or no other world as the fruit of this world.
(8) "There is no mother" and (9) "there is no father"—these two are views that deny causes (*hetu-apavāda-dṛṣṭi*). The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains: [text omitted].
Question: Since parents in the world are all directly perceived, how can one see them and yet slanderously claim they do not exist?
Answer: One interpretation is the same as before.
First interpretation:
Some say that those various non-Buddhists...
To slander one's father or mother is an action that brings about the retribution of having no children;
it does not, however, refer to slandering their physical bodies. Some teachers have said this.
Those various non-Buddhists slander the meaning of "father" and "mother," but they do not slander their actual substance.
If one slanders them while investigating the cause of suffering, that [view] is abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
Now, to slander the cause by failing to seek the cause of suffering and thereby slandering it is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*),
just like the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Regarding the ten [types of beings] who are not born by transformation (*aupapāduka*),
the *Mahāvibhāṣā* explains as follows:
There are certain non-Buddhists who maintain this view:
that the cause for the birth of sentient beings consists of present factors such as semen and blood;
there is nothing that arises suddenly without conditions.
For example, the growth of a sprout necessarily depends upon seeds, water, fire, and the seasons;
there is nothing that can arise without conditions.
Therefore, it is certain that there are no spontaneously born sentient beings.
Some say that among beings born by transformation— namely those in the intermediate state (antarābhava)—
there is neither this world nor another world.

To deny that there are beings born by transformation is to slander [the existence of] non-arising and being; to deny that there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is likewise to slander [it], and so forth— there are many such interpretations.
This may also be understood as a denial of cause and effect. (11) There are no śramaṇas in the world,
nor brahmins, nor arhats.
This is the false view of slandering the noble ones;
it is abandoned through the path of seeing.
Treatise.
That sūtra fully reveals that the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes what follows;
this can be understood from the concluding summary.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and other texts further state that it refers to the false view of slandering cessation (*nirodha*).
The details are as explained therein.

On the twenty-second day of the eighth month in the third year of the Hōen era, after noon, at the former residence of Zenkō on the East Corridor, the blind and impoverished monk Kakujū completed the collation of one copy of the Huangyuan edition. Gishō completed the collation.
*Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Scroll Seventeen.

Chapter Four, Section Five, composed by the Śramaṇa Fa-bao.
Thus, having already established that the term "attainment" (*prāpti*) refers to a course of action (*karmapatha*),
the second major section begins with the following half-verse.
Explaining the names of the paths of action (*karmapatha*), the treatise states: "Because they are performed upon reaching [the object].
This explains the latter three paths of action: covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view.
The essence of greed and so forth is not karma itself; rather,
it is volition (cetanā) associated with greed and so forth that constitutes the nature of karma,
as it proceeds in dependence upon greed and the rest.
It proceeds by way of craving and so forth;
because it is produced through the power of craving,
it is like a person relying on a path.
Therefore, although the essence of greed and so forth is not itself karma,
they are paths of karma (*karmapatha*). [Abhidharmakośabhāṣya] Treatise.
The first seven are karma; they receive the designation "paths of karma" (karmapatha).
This explains the first seven paths of karma:
these first seven paths of karma are of the nature of karma.
Therefore, they are called "karma.
Because the karma of volition (cetanā) turns by relying upon them as its objects, they are called "paths of action" (karmapatha).
These seven are karma.
This is the path of karma;
thus, it is established with the name "karmic path.
[Treatise]
Therefore, because both [definitions] are established as equally valid in this context,
the designation "path of action" (*karmapatha*) applied here applies to both categories;
the first seven possess both characteristics.
That is to say, regarding karma and the paths of action,
the final three consist of only one each.
This means that although they belong to different categories,
the single designation "path of action" (karmapatha) applies to both locations.
The remaining two categories are collectively termed "paths of action" (*karmapatha*).
Regarding the phrase "like the worldly treatises," the *Nyāyānusāra* states that these are the *Lokaprajñapti-śāstra*. Within the *Lokaprajñapti-śāstra*, there are likewise dissimilar categories.
Furthermore, because a single [term] may be applied as a common name for others,
it is like how the categories of heaven and earth share the same names such as "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth.
(Treatise)
The seven [paths of action], beginning with abstaining from killing, should be explained by analogy in this manner.
This explains the wholesome paths of action by analogy with the unwholesome paths of action.
Treatise.
For what reason are these preliminary applications (*prayoga*) and subsequent actions (*pṛṣṭha*) not considered paths of action (*karmapatha*)? One might ask:
the preliminary application and the subsequent action should indeed be called paths of action, because volition (*cetanā*) also proceeds by taking them as its objects.
Treatise:
To this, the answer is that it depends on this, reaches this, and differs from this; otherwise, it would not be so.
There are three answers to this.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "In principle, it should also be explained."
As for that which is not explicitly stated,
it serves as the basis;
because it evolves from that basis, it is described as follows:
The preparatory application arises based on the fundamental [action]; because it depends upon the fundamental,
the subsequent action receives this name.
The end is not called the path. The second explanation states:
because the root is coarse and manifest, it is taught that the coarse category constitutes the karmic path. The third interpretation states:
because it causes internal and external things to undergo decrease or increase.
Just as killing, stealing, and so forth cause things to increase or decrease,
the two parts preceding and following them do not;
for this reason, these two parts are not termed courses of action (*karmapatha*).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 113, states:
"That which is inhabited is called 'external';
life-span and so forth are called 'internal. The *Vibhāṣā* further states:
Question: Why is it called a "path of action" (*karmapatha*)?
Answer: Volition (*cetanā*) is called "action" (*karman*).

Because it proceeds to its ultimate consummation through that which is traversed by the action, it becomes a "path of action. Question: If that were so, would all neutral (*avyākṛta*) states [be paths of action]?

One should question that master.

You should ask that teacher."

The Master of the Treatise provides this explanation for the sake of his teacher.

Regarding what has been explained thus far, what are the distinctions?
The following two verses clarify the third point:
the severing of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*).

"By which courses of action (*karmapatha*) are the roots of goodness severed? The answer states:

Treatise:

This is difficult.

Treatise:
From the unwholesome roots up to the village being plundered and burned by bandits—
this is the answer.

and this body is not a fit vessel for those higher wholesome states.
Treatise:
For what reason does one sever only the innate roots of goodness?
Question: Why are the acquired roots of goodness of the desire realm not severed?
Treatise:
Because the roots of goodness of the preparatory stage have already been lost. Answer:
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Because the roots of goodness of the preparatory stage (*prayoga-kuśalamūla*) are the first to be abandoned when one is about to sever the roots of goodness. Thus says the treatise.
For what reason can wrong view sever the roots of goodness?
This is the question. The treatise [proceeds as follows].
This refers to the definitive denial that there is a ripening result (vipāka-phala) reaching that [future] state.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
Regarding the causes and the stage for this severance of the roots of goodness:
it refers to a certain class of individuals who have previously established a violent and evil disposition and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
which are subsequently reinforced by the power of external conditions through association with evil friends.
Because they increase further and become more intense,
their roots of goodness diminish while their unwholesome roots grow;
subsequently, they give rise to the false view that denies causes and denies effects.
It causes all virtues to become entirely obscured;
by this, the continuum remains devoid of virtue.

Alternatively, relying on a virtuous friend,
one may suddenly again give rise to doubt regarding cause and effect,
wondering whether what is summoned for future lives exists or does not exist.

There are those who suddenly give rise to right view regarding cause and effect, realizing that their former attachment to the non-existence of future lives was erroneous. At that time, their roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) are accomplished; they regain what was previously unaccomplished and extinguish what was not yet extinguished—this is called "reconnecting the roots of goodness. Commentary: This refers to the process by which a person, through the sudden emergence of correct insight into the law of karma and its results, abandons the false view of nihilism and restores their spiritual continuity. By accomplishing the roots of goodness, they recover those faculties that had been dormant or lost, thereby severing the state of being devoid of virtue. This restoration is termed the reconnection of the roots of goodness.

one would be able to give rise to false views and be unable to reconnect with the roots of goodness;
if it did not exist previously and later came to exist—
Because it can generate right view, it can continue the continuity of the roots of goodness;
thus the *Nyāyānusāra* says:

the transgression is grave,

Regarding these two statements, what fault is there in principle? First, the initial statement contains a fault:
it implies that within a single lifetime, the fruit of prior karma ceases while the fruit of subsequent karma arises;
since the karma and its fruits would be distinct, there would necessarily be death and birth [within that same life].
Alternatively, one would have to admit that there is no death during multiple births, because the arising of karmic results occurs just as it does in a single birth. Both positions entail faults:

What were the circumstances of this?
As stated in the sūtra:
In the past there was a Buddha named Tiṣya,
or alternatively, Puṣya.
That Buddha had two bodhisattva disciples who diligently practiced the holy life:
the first was named Śākyamuni,
and the second was named Maitreya.
At that time, that Buddha observed which of his two disciples had first reached maturity of faculties;
he knew according to reality that Maitreya would mature first,
while Śāntamati would mature later.
Furthermore, he observes which among the sentient beings to be converted by these two sages has their faculties ripening first.
Moreover, he knows as it truly is that those to be converted by Śākyamuni should have their faculties ripen first;
having known this, he reflects:
"How may I now cause those with the karmic capacity and the response to meet?
It is easier to bring a single person to swift maturity than to bring many."
Having formed this thought, he then addressed Śākyamuni:
"I wish to travel through the mountains; you may follow me.
At that time, that Buddha took his sitting mat (niṣīdana) and proceeded ahead along the road.
Having arrived at the mountain, he entered the Vaiḍūrya cave,
spread out his *niṣīdana*, sat down cross-legged,
and entered the fire-element meditative absorption (*tejodhātu-samādhi*) for seven days and nights.
Experiencing sublime joy and radiating intense majesty,
Śākyamuni also went to the mountain in an instant,
searching for the Buddha everywhere like a calf seeking its mother.
As they traveled on, they arrived before that grotto chamber.
Suddenly, they beheld the Buddha’s majestic and solemn demeanor, his radiance shining brilliantly;
moved by sincere and earnest devotion, they were overcome with joy and wonder, unable to proceed.
For seven days and nights, he did not forget for a single moment to lower one foot to gaze upon the Honored One’s countenance, his eyes never turning away even for an instant.
With a single verse, he praised that Buddha, saying:
"O Heaven, O Earth, this world, and the Hall of Much Learning."
In the celestial palaces, the abodes of the gods, and throughout the ten directions—
nowhere is there a man who is a bull among men, a Great Śramaṇa, equal to him;
he has searched the earth, the mountains, and the forests, and found no peer.
Having praised him in this way, he transcended nine *kalpas* and attained unsurpassed enlightenment before Maitreya.
