This is because all afflictions conditioned by outflows are deluded regarding suffering;
it is not the case that all afflictions conditioned by outflows take the fruit of suffering as their object.

How could there be such an excessive error? Someone relates the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* commentary as saying: "The [view] of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) directed toward the lower realm of suffering takes the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) as its object;
it arises precisely with respect to the fruit."
Other contaminated afflictions also exist within the contaminated;
why then would they not arise in the locus of the fruit? Now, upon careful examination, this is merely a restatement of the previous objection.
This refutes the intent of the *Nyāyānusāra*. For instance,
regarding the false view at the bottom of the "Origin" [truth],
one seeks the cause of suffering and then slanders it.
Although these [wrong views] take contaminated phenomena as their objects, they are not delusions regarding the fruit of suffering;
how, then, can they be equated with those that take the "cow-vow" (*go-śīla*) and so forth as their objects? Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
"If [a wrong view] is more powerful than the Path of Seeing..."

Thus, it is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). This intention is to say that [practices such as] "ox-vows" (*go-vrata*) and the like are merely delusions regarding the fruit of suffering, which they mistakenly reckon as the path;
they do not seek any other meaning.
They are not like the false view deluded about the path, which reckons itself as correct reasoning (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
This refers to first grasping something else as the cause of purification,
and now regarding what is not the Path as correct realization;
although its object of focus is the Truth of Suffering, [it is nevertheless a misconception].
The misconception regarding the meaning of the Truth of the Path is strong and is not abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Since the *Nyāyānusāra* states that this [misconception] merely regards coarse results as being their causes, it has already excluded other types of abandonment;
furthermore, this includes an additional distinct point.
For what reason is it difficult to cause [beings] to abandon the delusions regarding other meanings,
while they all merely calculate coarse fruits as being delusions?
The treatise says:
Furthermore, what characteristic leads to the delusion regarding the Truth of Suffering?
This is the second objection concerning the lack of distinct characteristics:
in your own school, the prohibitions (śīla-vrata) pertain to both suffering and the Path of Abandonment.

Furthermore, what specific characteristic does the grasping at rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) possess that could allow one to say it is abandoned by the path of seeing (darśanamārgaprahātavya)?
For [grasping at rules and observances] arises taking as its object those phenomena which are themselves abandoned by the path of seeing.

That [view] should also be called "deluded regarding the truth of suffering" and should therefore be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). The *Nyāya* (Principles) defends this by saying:
"This objection is not valid."
Because viewing the Truth of Suffering as impermanent and so forth is not the antidote to that [view],
it is not the case that when one views the Truth of Suffering as impermanent and so forth,
one can simultaneously counteract the adherence to what is not the path as being the path; therefore, that adherence to the path is not abandoned by the vision of suffering.
By this, those [afflictions] abandoned through the vision of the origin are also excluded,
because the vision of the cause and so forth is not their antidote;
that is to say, it is not at the time of seeing the cause and so forth regarding the origin.
It is able to counteract the adherence that regards what is not the path as being the path;
this occurs when one perceives the path and so forth within the Truth of the Path.
Only then can one treat that adherence to what is not the path as being the path;
therefore, such deluded adherence should be understood as abandoned by the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Furthermore, it says:
"However, regarding the calculation of what is not the path as being the path..."
If it contradicts what is strong in the path of seeing,
it is abandoned by the path of seeing. Furthermore,
it is said that there are two types of misapprehending what is not the path as being the path.
First, those that take up precepts and observances as their object; second, those that take up what is personally mistaken regarding the path as their object.
Taking up precepts and observances as an object contradicts the faith that realizes the path.
The power [of these views] is not equal to that of those who are directly deluded regarding the Path;
for those whose objects of focus are such things as ritual precepts and observances,
their modes of activity are extremely coarse.
Because they do not follow [the path] for long and because their intention is not firm,
they abandon and extinguish it even with little exertion. This is the opposite in the case of those who are deluded by intimacy regarding the path.

From this it should be understood that there are two categories of the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) which regard what is not the path as the path: first, those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).

Regarding the two types of views abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*): Master Kuang’s commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that both kinds of "precept-and-vow adherence" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) take contaminated phenomena as their object and both falsely reckon what is not the path to be the path.
Why is it that one [type of cognition] arises with respect to the object itself as its fruit, while the other does not arise with respect to the object as its fruit,
even though their meanings are otherwise identical?
They should arise simultaneously as their fruit.
If they arise simultaneously as their fruit,
then their characteristics would have no distinction from one another.
To deviate from the Way and offer mere words— now,
upon close examination, this explanation merely reiterates the previous objection and fails to constitute a valid rebuttal.
The intention of the *Nyāya* rescuer is this:

[the view] that takes the same object as contaminated phenomena and what is not the path, yet conceives them as the path, takes up precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and so forth; its power of conviction is weak because it contradicts the [true] path.
Because their mode of activity is extremely coarse and does not follow [the truth] for long,
and because their intention is not firm,
those who are deluded regarding the path due to its proximity are first abandoned when the Truth of Suffering is seen.
The opposite of this is that [the view] can only be abandoned when one perceives the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). Alternatively,
this explanation is identical [to the previous one] in that both take the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) as their object, while erroneously regarding what is not the Path as being the Path.
One is abandoned by seeing suffering;
one is abandoned by seeing the path.
Therefore, they are now again brought together as having the same object, the Truth of Suffering.
However, it is difficult to regard what is not the Path as the Path;
how, then, can this be refuted? [The] Treatise [states]:
Furthermore, it is also not established that the path-truth (mārga-satya) serves as a condition for reaching the ultimate reality.
This is the third point: the difficulty regarding the adherence to views and doubt.
If wrong view and so forth negate or doubt the path, [how could they lead to its realization?]
How could one then grasp this very view, along with doubt and so forth, as the path?
If you claim that one grasps something else,
then it would not be taking false views and the like as its object.
The *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
"It is not that the essence of this grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is not established;
for it is admitted that there exists a false view that slanders the path (*mārgadṛṣṭi*), which is clung to as the means for attaining permanent purification."
Because they conceive of it as being a correct understanding;
that is to say, having first held another path of liberation in their minds, they subsequently grasp the false view that slanders the true path as being a realization in accordance with reality.
Regarding the term "in accordance with reality" (*yoniśas*):
they claim that the path of true liberation which negates doubt is non-erroneous;
because it is in accordance with reality, they grasp it as the cause of purification.
By this, the essential nature of the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is established.
That aggregate of mental factors (*cittasamprayukta-skandha*) is not abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), but rather by the remaining paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
This is because the object of focus (*ālambana*) for the clinging to rules and observances consists solely of phenomena belonging to its own category (*svanikāya*).
There are many categories of paths, which is not a logical error. Someone, recounting the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, stated:
"There are also precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) that are views regarding the cause of purification and are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*)."
This too is clung to as such;
why would it not be abandoned through the cessation of suffering? If one does not cling to that very thing, [how could it not be abandoned?]
To grasp other [factors] as causes of purification would mean that there should be nothing to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Now, examining this explanation, it does not capture the intended meaning: one must first understand that the remaining paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) reside within one's own mind.
This refers to the adherence to all false paths other than the Eightfold Path.
This is not the view or doubt that denies the Eightfold Path;
rather, it should be said to be abandoned through the realization of suffering (*duḥkha*).

The path-truth that dispels doubt is considered a realization in accordance with reality (*yoniśo-manasikāra*); it is abandoned through the path of seeing because it does not contradict the aspects of suffering and so forth,
but rather contradicts the aspects of the path and so forth.
Furthermore, since this object of focus has been abandoned,
why do you raise again the same objection that was already explained previously?
Why do you persist in this repeated challenge?
Treatise:
Furthermore, if there is an object-condition that reaches [the object], this must be further examined;
this is the fourth objection.
This refers to one who first retains within their mind another form of liberation,
and subsequently clings to the false view that slanders true liberation as being a correct realization;
because they consider it to be correct, they cling to it as the cause of purification.
As before, it would follow that one would fall into the clinging to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). The *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
"There is no such principle;
for [the opponent] generally admits that liberation is eternal and quiescent."
The reasoning that holds the mind of denigration to be a cause of purification is untenable.

This is because, just as you assert that the essence of nirvāṇa is both real and unreal, so too must one who seeks the means to liberation necessarily admit that liberation exists; for all those who assert liberation must certainly accept its existence.
One must necessarily admit that its essence is eternally quiescent;
if one does not admit this,
it should not be sought after.
Just as within the True Dharma, although there are those who claim that the essence of nirvāṇa is real and those who claim it is not real,
they nevertheless agree that it is eternal and quiescent.
Therefore, both [the denial of nirvāṇa and the denial of its permanence] are seen as faults.
Likewise, if one holds within their mind some other conception of liberation,
they must necessarily concede that nirvāṇa is eternally quiescent.
Because of this, one does not grasp at the view that slanders liberation as being a correct understanding;

therefore, among those things to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is certainly absent. Furthermore, although Devadatta generally reckons that there is a permanent and quiescent nirvāṇa...
If one were to abandon the eightfold path and instead calculate five separate factors as the path to liberation, the reasoning of the non-Buddhists would likewise be valid.
Therefore, there exist those who hold the wrong view of slandering the noble eightfold path.
This refers to awakening in accordance with reality.
It means not misapprehending cessation as being in accord with reason;

for since the intrinsic nature and modes of practice of ascetic observances and the like differ from the Noble Path, one does not misapprehend Nirvana as being eternally quiescent [through such means].
Regarding the distinction between their essential natures and characteristics,
for this reason, non-cessation (anirodha) shares the same meaning as the Path (mārga).
Commentary states:
This is because, by calculating that there are many ways to realize the path,
one slanders the true path and clings to other false paths as the cause of purification,
asserting that this wrong view is the path that accords with reality.
Both the internal and external paths alike reckon that nirvana is permanent and quiescent;
if one were to negate it as non-existent, one would not separately reckon the path for attaining cessation.
Consequently, one does not grasp the false view that denies cessation as being a realization in accordance with reality.
The same applies to the truth of origination and to all internal and external paths.
Desiring to sever the cause of suffering, one cultivates the path of abandonment;
if one slanders the cause as non-existent,
one will certainly not further reckon that there is any other path of abandonment.
Because of this, one does not cling to the false view that denies the origin [of suffering] as being the cause of purification.

Because of this, there is no clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) among those things abandoned through the path of seeing the origin and cessation. Someone recounts the explanation from the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, saying:
Just as if one were to deny the Path, there would be no one capable of realizing it;
yet, even while denying that [specific] Path,
one may still reckon that another path exists which is capable of realization.
What prevents [the opponent] from denying the existence of origination and cessation,
yet reckoning that there remains another origination and cessation which constitute their abandonment and realization? Now, upon close examination,
this defense is not the explanation of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Because it is illogical,
you deny that there are two paths:
first, you admit the existence of suffering and the cessation of suffering.
To reject the true path and instead cling to a false path as the cause of purification—
taking the view of rejecting the path (mārga-dṛṣṭi) to be correct cognition—
is what is called "clinging to a false path as the cause of purification," and this is subsumed under the clinging to rules and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
Second, they deny the existence of the path and the cessation of suffering.
This denial of the path implies that there is nothing capable of realizing [that cessation].
[The Noble Truths] are reckoned as the cause of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the cultivation and realization of the path.
If there were no origination, cessation, cultivation, or realization, what would be the use?
For there would be nothing to abandon and nothing to realize.
To falsely calculate that which is not cessation as true cessation and thereby repudiate nirvāṇa—
this is the adherence to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa). To take wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi) as correct reasoning (yoniśo-manasikāra) is likewise [an adherence to views].
How can this [view] that accords with the grasping at views be called a "path"?
If one were to designate what is not the origin as the origin,

this would be false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) and would not be subsumed under the grasping at precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), for it differs from the grasping at precepts which designates what is not a pure cause as such.
How can this be called "clinging to precepts"?
Thus, the defense is irrational. [End of] Treatise.
As previously stated, the notion of permanence arises from the inversion [of perception].
The following single line of verse constitutes the second major section, which addresses and explains these objections.
The text contains three sections:
first, an explanation of the four inversions;
second, the seven and nine types of pride.
Third, non-occurrence despite not being severed.
This passage is the first to clarify the four inversions.
The treatise says: "...up to regarding [the impermanent] as the inversion of self."
This is the interpretation of other masters.
The treatise states: Some say that the inversion of self (*ātma-viparyāsa*) encompasses the entirety of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
The Correct Meaning of the *Vibhāṣā*. The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"What has been explained thus far represents the tenet of a single master;
however, the definitive meaning of the *Vibhāṣā* is as follows."
In the analysis of the twelve views, only two and a half views constitute the essence of inversion: namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in its entirety,
and the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) in its entirety.
Within the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the portion that grasps at permanence and the two views of annihilationism and eternalism have mutually contradictory modes of activity;
therefore, it can be said that their two entities are distinct.
All proponents of the theory of a self (ātmavādin) maintain that the self possesses sovereign power over those [aggregates]; this is their view of "mine" (mamakāra).
This very view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi) operates through two doors; according to this treatise, the latter explanation is correct.
Treatise:
How does the view of "I" (ātma-dṛṣṭi) subsume the view of "mine" (ātmīya-dṛṣṭi)?
This is the question posed by the former master.
Since the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of what belongs to self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*) are two distinct views,
how can the inversion of self include the view of what belongs to self?
Treatise:
How is it that they are not included?
The latter master counters by questioning the reason why they are not included.
Treatise:
From "due to the inverted sūtra" up to "this is what I have seen," the explanation does not fully encompass the underlying reasons.
Since the explanations in the sūtras regarding the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the object seen differ,
how can the inversion of self (*ātma-viparyāsa*) be said to include the inversion of "mine" (*ātmīya-viparyāsa*)?
Commentary:
This explains that the view of self operates through two doors;
this is the exegesis.
The position that "form is the self" is termed the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*);
the position that "form belongs to the self" is the view of what belongs to the self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*).
Commentary.
The view that "this is I" and "belongs to me," up to the point of "seeing," should also be distinguished;
this is a counter-objection.
The term "this is I" is called the "view of self."
The first case ending belongs to the "I" and is termed the view of "mine";
the sixth case ending belongs to the "mine."
This means that the two views are not different modes of expressing one thing;
rather, they are distinct and separate views. The phrase "by me in this way" is a genitive (third case) construction, while "for me in this way" is a dative (fourth case) construction.
This should be understood as the view that "the self is one" and "the self is a single entity.
Treatise.
For what reason are other afflictions not established as having the nature of inversion?
Regarding the establishment and exclusion of the four inversions,
three causes are provisionally set forth among all the afflictions.
Among these, grasping at the superior as the essence of perversion possesses three causes,
as does the intermediate-superior [grasping].
Among all the afflictions, only two views and a half possess the three causes;
that is to say, they are exclusively inverted.
Because it is of a nature that involves conceptual estimation, because it falsely increases and nourishes [the afflictions],
and because its substance is superior and predominant.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "The grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is not exclusively inverted, because it takes as its object a small degree of purity.
This is intended to distinguish it from [the view of] self (*ātmavāda*), which is exclusively inverted.

This is because what they conceive may indeed possess the capacity to depart from the defilement of desire, and because one attains purity when there is little conceptual discrimination. The commentary explains: "The ascetic practices conceived by the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*)..."
Because they are able to abandon defilements and so forth, and because they attain a partial purification at a different time;
and because among those of our own tradition who reckon that maintaining ethical discipline alone constitutes the path,
they likewise attain purification partially and at a different time.
It is not the case that one regards false views regarding the Truth of the Path, doubt,
and so forth, as being the path;
this is called attaining purity at the stage of slight discernment.
Because that [view] is not a cause of purification through its correct realization; because it is of the nature of conjecture (*ūhana*);
and by excluding other non-view-afflictions, it distinguishes itself from the view of false attribution (*samāropa*) and the views of nihilism and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the term "superior" (*śreṣṭha*),
it distinguishes [this view] from the views of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) that are to be abandoned by the other three truths. The *Nyāyabindu* states:
The other schools [claim] that the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is not predominant; thus, the treatise asks:
"If that is so, why is it likewise [stated] up to 'not-self'? This constitutes an external objection.
If there are only four inversions, why does the Sūtra state that there are twelve?

This is because each of the four inversions—such as the inversion of permanence and so forth—consists of three types: inversion of perception (*saṃjñā*), inversion of mind (*citta*), and inversion of view (*dṛṣṭi*). Thus says the Treatise (*śāstra*).
In reality, one should know that this is because they are identical up to the point of their mode of activity (*ākāra*).
To address an external objection, it is said:
"In reality, only the view itself is the inversion."
The treatise states: "Perception and mind are also designated as 'perversions' according to their views.
If this is so, why are feeling and the other [aggregates] not so described?"
An external objection states:
"The conceptualization associated with views and the views themselves are also called 'perversions.
Furthermore, the feeling and other factors associated with views are called 'perversion of feeling' (vedanā-viparyāsa)."
Commentary:
Because that [attainment] reaches the worldly state, the Sūtra does not mention it.
This is the *Vibhāṣā*’s general response to an external objection.
The world’s conventional perception is a perversion of the mind;

it does not say that there is a perversion of feeling, but rather speaks of a perversion of perception and mind in accordance with worldly convention, without mentioning feeling. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
It is not so, because perception and mind do not involve inferential deliberation (*abhyūhana*). Nevertheless,
they are designated as "perversions" (*viparyāsa*) by virtue of the power of the perversion of view,
since their associated mental factors (*citta-samprayukta-saṃskāra*) share the same characteristics.
However, sensations (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates cannot be designated as "perversions" in the same way as perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*),
because there is a distinct reason:
namely, when one gives rise to views of permanence and so forth regarding what is impermanent and so forth.
One must necessarily apprehend characteristics such as permanence from within the object;
that which is able to apprehend these characteristics is perception (saṃjñā),
and nothing else.
Therefore, the name "perversion" is established [only] for perception and not for feeling and the other aggregates.
Furthermore, the wisdom that remedies perversion is also designated by the name "perception."
This means that among the modes of practice such as impermanence and so forth, they are designated as "perceptions" (saṃjñā) of impermanence and so forth.
Because wisdom (prajñā) and perception mutually support one another in close proximity, the name is established by following their association.
This is not the case for feeling (vedanā) and the other [mental factors].
Because there is erroneous inference and increase due to the power of the basis,
and because the apprehension of objective characteristics is established,
the mind is termed "erroneous."
As stated in the Sūtra:
"The mind leads the world, causing it to drift and drown everywhere in the torrential flow of delusions. The commentary explains:
Because one relies on the mind to engage in inverted seeking and false conceptualization, one becomes subject to perversion (*viparyāsa*).
The mind is the basis for perversion and is itself called "perversion.
The treatise states: "Because these various perversions are abandoned through the path of seeing."
The twelve inversions are explained as being abandoned solely by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).

Although perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) are not themselves views, because they are associated with views, they are also abandoned by insight; thus, they are said to be abandoned by the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
This differs from what was stated previously.
This is the correct tenet of the Sarvāstivāda school.
Treatise.
Other schools say that it is better for attachment to arise [toward the object].
This records a divergent view.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
These are the proponents of conceptual differentiation (*vibhajyavādin*).
They maintain that perception (*saṃjñā*), mind (*citta*), and view (*dṛṣṭi*)—all three—are inverted;
yet they hold that there is no perception, mind, or inverted view that is not associated [with inversion].
According to the correct principle of the *Vibhāṣā*,
seeing what is inverted is also called an inversion.
Perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) are conventionally designated as "perversions," yet in reality they are not perversions.
Both perception and mind are actually associated with [the factor of] view (*dṛṣṭi*).
Among the twelve inversions postulated by that teacher, there are six inversions— namely, the notions of self,
permanence, pleasure, purity, mind, and view— as well as [the views of] pleasure and purity.
There are two views of inversion.
These eight are abandoned only by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*):
[the views of] pleasure and purity.
The four inversions of perception and mind are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation.
If one considers [suffering] as pleasure or [impurity] as purity,
these are perceptions and minds.
Regarding the four perversions that are not abandoned through cultivation but only through seeing:
for a noble one who has not yet abandoned desire,
[the perversions of] pleasure and purity have already been abandoned.
The second inversion:
for what reason does one perceive the mark of purity in an impure object,
and seek pleasure within that which lacks pleasure, thereby giving rise to craving?
Treatise:
The Vaibhāṣika masters do not accept this point.
Hereafter follows a threefold [explanation].
First, refuting and shattering the opposing schools;
second, providing a favorable explanation to establish one's own school;
third, correctly resolving the objections raised by the opposing schools.
Treatise:
If there is pleasure and purity up to the existence of arising desire and greed,
this first counter-objection refutes the other schools.
Treatise:
Based on the statement in the sūtra that "this is the inversion,
and nothing else," this second [section] provides a sequential explanation to establish our own school's position.
Commentary:
However, there are times when even the Noble Ones are confused by painted yakṣas.
This third point correctly addresses the objections raised by other schools.
This is because their objects are in reality neither pleasant nor pure,
yet they appear as if pleasant and pure; thus,
the noble ones suddenly give rise to craving toward those objects.
If one observes with discernment, one immediately knows that impurity and so forth are like a whirling firebrand or a painted yakṣa;
in reality, they are not a wheel or a ghost,
yet when seen abruptly, they are taken to be a wheel or a ghost.
If one observes carefully, one knows it is neither a wheel nor a ghost.
Treatise: If that is so, [then...]
Below are three sections:
first, the author of the treatise cites a verse by Ānanda to raise an objection;
second, he cites the explanation of another school.
In the third section, the preceding scriptural citations prove that the twelve inversions are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*).
Since the Master [Vasubandhu] does not accept the Sarvāstivāda position that these twelve inversions are abandoned solely by vision,
he does not attempt to defend it.
Treatise:
If this is so, for what reason does the mind become pure as soon as desire ceases?
To address this, the first verse cited states:
If the twelve inversions were to be abandoned solely by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), why did Ānanda speak this verse for the sake of Vibhajyavādin?
"Because of the inversion of perception and so forth... Since Vibhajyavādin was already an *ārya* (noble one), [how could he still possess these inversions?]
If there were no perversion of perception,
for what reason would you say that because of the confusion and perversion of perception,
your mind is scorched with fever and so forth?
The *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
"It is not that we claim perception is free from confusion and error because it is obscured by sensual desire;
rather, we simply state this:"
Not all forms of confusion are termed "perversion.
This is because only those instances of confusion involving perception and thought that accompany a perverted view are designated as "perverse."
If all forms of cognitive distortion were to constitute a "perversion," then all afflictions would necessarily be perversions;
[this would apply even when] Arhats are walking along a public road.

It is argued that while those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation do not function for an Noble One once they have been reached [and abandoned], there are also those which, though not yet abandoned, do not function. [The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "There are some defilements which, although not yet abandoned, do not manifest. This refers to those that do not arise even when one encounters their objects. For example, a person who has abandoned the desire realm may encounter objects belonging to the desire realm, yet because they have abandoned the defilements associated with that realm, those defilements do not manifest. Furthermore, even if a certain category of defilement has not yet been abandoned, it may not manifest due to the power of other counteractive factors, such as mindfulness or the presence of a superior path. Thus, the non-manifestation of a defilement does not necessarily imply its abandonment; rather, it depends on whether the conditions for its arising are present and whether counteractive forces are operative. This distinction clarifies the complex relationship between the state of abandonment and the actual functioning of the afflictions.

Treatise:
What dharma is it that reaches the name "non-existence" such that there is no craving for non-existence?
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 27, states:
"Non-existence" refers to the impermanence of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
The craving that arises with this as its object is called "craving for non-existence" (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*).

Therefore, this craving is abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is abandoned only through cultivation. The *Nyāyānusāra* asks:

For what reason are they said to be abandoned only by cultivation when, in reality, they are also abandoned by seeing?
For now, let us follow the Sūtra’s teaching;
that is, the Sūtra states that there are three types of craving.
The three types of craving: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
In this sutra, it is said that there is no craving which takes the impermanence of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) conditioned by grasping as its object;
this is because such craving seeks the cessation of the continuity of karmic maturation (*vipāka*).
As stated in the Sūtra:
"A certain class of beings, oppressed by suffering, thinks thus:
'May I, after death, be annihilated and cease to exist.'"
"How wonderful it is to be free from illness!
For now, let us rely on this teaching that [craving] is abandoned only through cultivation;
it is not the case that craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) is not abandoned through insight (*darśana*)."
Now, examining the correct principle:
this craving for non-existence universally takes all appropriated aggregates as its object;

the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*).
The treatise says: ...up to the point where they are called "conducive to the higher realms" (*ūrdhvagāmin*).
This is the explanation of the term.
These are called "fettering tendencies leading upward" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) because they do not transcend the higher realms and instead accord with and benefit them;
thus, the higher realms constitute the "upper portion."
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Thus, these five types consist of eight entities.

Because the three—restlessness (*auddhatya*) and so forth—are distinguished by their two realms, they form six [entities] when the upper two realms are distinguished. Only those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are termed 'conducive to the higher realms' (*ūrdhva-bhāgīya*)."
They are called "fettering bonds leading upward" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) because they accord with and benefit the higher realms;

for these fetters only manifest once those [defilements] to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) have been severed. This is because as long as the afflictions to be abandoned by insight have not been permanently eradicated, [these fetters do not arise].

Furthermore, they can also assist those [afflictions] so that they accord with the lower realm; therefore, as long as the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) have not yet been severed, the two types of craving in the upper realms, along with restlessness, pride, and ignorance, possess the power to assist them in causing one to fall back into the lower realm.

Thus, it is only when the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing have been permanently severed that those which manifest are called "factors conducive to the upper realm" (*ūrdhva-bhāgīya*). It is also said:
In some cases this is a fetter;
that is to say, for noble ones it is not a fetter,
whereas for ordinary worldlings it constitutes a state of being fettered.
That is to say, for one who has already become detached from sensual desire, there is a state that is not a fetter;
namely, for one who has not yet become detached from sensual desire. It further says:
Because restlessness disturbs and agitates meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
it is established as a fetter (*saṃyojana*) among the higher-tier fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
It is precisely for this reason that torpor (*styāna*) is not mentioned among the higher-tier fetters.
Regarding "conducive to meditative concentration," the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

Question: Why are only those [fetters] abandoned through cultivation established as the fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*)? Answer: That which causes one to proceed toward rebirth in the higher realms is called "conducive to the higher realms."
The fetters to be abandoned by insight also cause one to fall back to lower realms;
therefore, they are not established as the fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, that which is practiced by superior persons is called "conducive to the higher."
The "upper person" (ūrdhvaga) is an ārya, not an ordinary worldling (pṛthagjana).
Since the fetters to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya-saṃyojana) arise only in ordinary worldlings,
they are not established as the fetters conducive to the higher realms (ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana).
Among the noble ones, only those fetters that arise in a non-returner are established as the "factors conducive to the higher realms" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
From this inquiry, a further question arises: why is this so?
Why are the fetters (saṃyojana) arising in those who are stream-enterers (srotāpanna) and once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin) not "factors conducive to the higher realms" (ūrdhvabhāgīya)?
Answer: As for the factors conducive to the higher realms...
That is to say, while those who are heading toward higher rebirths [sever the fetters], the various fetters arising in stream-enterers and once-returners also cause them to be born in lower realms.
Therefore, they are not established as fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
[Question: Having already distinguished the fetters (*saṃyojana*), what are the bonds (*bandhana*)?
The following line clarifies the three bonds (*bandhana*).
The treatise states, up to this definitive explanation: [text].
This is the explanation.
That which binds sentient beings is called a "bond" (*bandhana*).
For what reason are these three alone designated as bonds?
Due to the three types of sensation,
[defilements] increase through association and by taking as an object with respect to one's own continuum;
if they belong to another continuum, they increase solely by taking as an object.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"It is designated as 'bond' (*bandhana*) because it is capable of binding;
that is to say, it has the sense of obstructing the approach to freedom from passion."
Although there is no difference between the characteristics of fetters (*saṃyojana*) and bonds (*bandhana*),
according to the *Mātṛkā*, there are three types of bonds:
first, the bond of greed (*lobha-bandhana*).
The second is the fetter of hatred;
the third is the fetter of delusion.
The remaining types of fetters are similar in their categories.
They are subsumed within three [categories]:
the five views and doubt are of the same class as delusion; the two fetters of pride and stinginess are of the same class as greed;
and the fetter of envy is of the same class as hatred.
All are subsumed within the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, the three bonds (*bandhana*) are taught in order to demonstrate what remains to be done by one who has already seen the truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*).
Because they bind the six groups of consciousness and place them within the prison of birth and death;

furthermore, because the Buddha specifically taught for those of inferior wisdom to reveal the coarse characteristics of the afflictions, he spoke only of the three bonds (*bandhana*). Other masters say:
Because they are induced by the power of the three types of feeling (*vedanā*),
it is said that there are three fetters (*bandhana*):
namely, attachment (*rāga*) for the most part toward one's own pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
The two types— by way of object and by way of association—
increase [the defilements] in part, even with respect to neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling],
as well as toward one's own suffering, others' suffering, and others' pleasure and equanimity.
There is only one type of object that increases [the defilement];
furthermore, hatred for the most part increases through both the object and the associated [mental factors] with respect to its own painful feeling.
To a small extent, it also [arises] with regard to neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling],
as well as toward one's own and others' pleasure and others' suffering;
in these cases, only one type of object of focus increases [in association].

Ignorance (*moha*) also predominantly increases in two ways— by way of its object (*ālambana*) and by way of association (*samprayoga*)— with respect to its own neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*); to a minor extent,
it also increases with respect to pleasant and painful feelings (*sukha-vedanā* and *duḥkha-vedanā*).
In all other feelings, there is only an increase in the objective condition (*ālambana*).
Therefore, the Blessed One, relying on the principle of the majority of cases,
taught that the three fetters (*bandhana*) are established in accordance with the three feelings.
What kind of greed and so forth are designated as "bonds" (bandhana) because they obstruct the departure from defilement?
They are those that exist only as active manifestations (samudācāra). If it were otherwise, all [defilements] would constitute the three [types of bonds].
Thus, one should ultimately preclude the pursuit of detachment from passion; the subsequent explanation is the same as in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Regarding the former explanation, the three bonds (*bandhana*) apply to all afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth;
yet they are specifically mentioned as three.
Because these are the fundamental matrices for all other defiled dharmas,
it is said that the three [categories] also subsume the rest.

The *Prakaraṇapāda* lists eight; the *Vibhāṣā*, ten;

They are called "envelopments" (*paryavasthāna*) because they cause one to be bound to the evil destinies.
Regarding the lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and the lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), they have already been explained as before.

"Envy (*īrṣyā*) refers to [the attitude] toward others... as has already been analyzed above.

Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) pertains to both the wholesome and the unwholesome, but here only the unwholesome is taken;

It causes the mind to become dull and contracted;
associated with lethargy, it is unable to sustain the body—
this is the characteristic of sleep.
Although sleep is indeed also dissociated from torpor (*styāna*),
this statement is made because the present discussion concerns only the *paryavasthānas* (envelopments). Furthermore,
it is said that sleep is not associated with the wholesome states of preparatory application (*prayoga-kuśala*), because their intrinsic natures (*dharmatā*) are mutually contradictory.
It is exclusively wholesome by birth (*upapattilābhika*), because its nature is weak and inferior. It also extends to the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Furthermore, it is said that the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) is exclusively born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Because the arising of minds such as those of craftsmanship would destroy that state of sleep.
Other masters say that even during the state of sleep, minds of deportment and craftsmanship may arise.
However, it cannot be practiced at the initial stage;
it can only be practiced later within a dream. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 37, states:

These are the deportment, the skillful, and the resultant types;
they are not the supernormal fruit type.
"Eportment" refers, for example, to one's own perception of walking and so forth within a dream.
That which arises from craftsmanship is like one’s own perception of painting and so forth within a dream.
That which arises from maturation is like the remaining neutral mental states that occur in a dream, excluding those previously mentioned.
Other masters say:
Only that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) among the states of sleep is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*);
because the mind is dull and obscured, it does not initiate bodily or vocal action,
and therefore lacks the nature of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).

When its manifestation is intense while its residual force is weak, it is called anger (*krodha*),
like the heat in a room during winter.
Its manifestation is subtle, yet its residual force is powerful; this is what is called resentment (*upanāha*).
For this reason, there are those who state the definition of resentment as follows:
When anger has subsided, that which continues to arise and causes the mind to become turbid is called *upanāha* (enmity). Furthermore, regarding the definition of *śāṭhya* (deceit):
it refers to first deliberating and employing such means so as to cause another to develop a perverted understanding at a later time; therefore, it is called deceit.
However, it is said in the world that one who displays signs for the sake of profit or fame in order to delude others is called a deceiver.

The bodily and vocal karmic actions induced by various forms of deception are designated by the name "deception" because they are the fruits of deception, just as one uses a general term to refer to things that are its general results.

Because I suffer, even those who hold to the view that the self is annihilated give rise to grief and distress;

When those of foolish nature perceive my teaching as annihilation, they give rise to fear and dread;
because those who cling to ascetic practices as pure and superior must harbor extreme sorrow and distress within their hearts.

that [opposing] view is incorrect,
because they arise from distinct moments of mind.

When the view of a self arises and manifests,
there must necessarily be the operation of joy toward that self;

One does not give rise to alarm or fear because of the characteristic of cessation.
Those who harbor the view of permanence feel terror toward cessation;
however, at the very moment such terror arises, they no longer conceive of permanence.

One who clings to ascetic practices as being pure and supreme will necessarily give rise to sorrow and distress within a different state of mind by taking as an object the various painful experiences they themselves undergo.
This occurs when one clings to ascetic practices as being pure and supreme.
One ought necessarily to give rise to joy because one perceives their virtue; yet,
you feel dejection when you are treated with contempt by others.

because both are equally quiescent,
