It clarifies that afflictions have attained permanent cessation;
therefore, it causes one to distance oneself from the object of focus,
so that they no longer arise with respect to that object.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 22,
states: "However, it is said herein that the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) can be abandoned with respect to their objects."
It is not in the sense of being associated [with the mind] that the term "possessing latent dispositions" (sānuśaya) is applied to the mind; rather,
it is spoken in terms of the meaning of "having latent dispositions increase therein" (anuśerate).
Because they can both be abandoned in the sense of "increasing along with" (anuśaya),
the treatise asks:
"When abandoning future afflictions, how can it be said that they are 'abandoned'?"
The master of the treatise raises an objection:
If that which is not produced is designated as "cessation," then cessation should apply only to the future.
How can it also be said that the past is abandoned?
The treatise says:
If one asks, "From what does the verse state that [the abandonment] reaches the dhyānas?"
This refutes the [opposing] interpretation.
The verse speaks of "from the object" (ālambana) in order to clarify that one who has fully understood the object abandons [the afflictions].
In accordance with the four preceding types of skillful means,
it is not only that the objects of cognition are fully known and abandoned,
but also that the cognizing subjects are abandoned.
Therefore, although there are three types of abandonment, such as the abandonment of the afflictions and so forth,
their status as being "unfixed" (aniyata) depends on the nature of their objects. Thus says the treatise:
Because it is ultimately severed within one's own continuum,
the author of the treatise himself explains for the sake of the Vaibhāṣikas from what the severance proceeds:
by the power of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
This causes the afflictions within one’s own continuum to be severed.
Because they have been severed,
[those afflictions] no longer exist with respect to their objects in the past or the future.
Lacking the power of subsequent increase,
they cannot bind their objects; thus,
the various afflictions within the mental continuums of others [do not bind].
Furthermore, all material forms and non-defiled phenomena are also termed "abandoned," because they are not bound by the afflictions within one's own continuum.
According to the *Nyāyānusāra*,
the abandonment of all afflictions occurs solely through the abandonment of the objects upon which those afflictions depend.
This is its root; the other three types of abandonment are its branches.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
The permanent abandonment of all afflictions necessarily proceeds from their objects;
for it is through the power of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) regarding the object that afflictions are made to be permanently abandoned.
As previously stated,
there are generally two kinds of objects for the afflictions:
namely, things that are bound [to the realms].
And as for unconditioned phenomena:
those afflictions that take conditioned phenomena as their objects,
and those [phenomena] produced by the power of such afflictions.
"Those afflictions that do not take this matter as their object. The commentary explains:

"Those that take what is bound [to a realm] as their object are those with objects within one's own realm (*svadhātu-ālambana*). Or, those that are produced through the power of attraction and do not take this matter as their object are those with objects in other realms (*paradhātu-ālambana*)."
In this way, these two afflictions give rise to various acquisitions (*prāpti*) within the manifest continuum of a single sentient being.
Even when an undefiled mind is present, this acquisition (prāpti) continues to function constantly without interruption.

It should be understood that it serves as the cause for the fruits of the various afflictions in the past and future, and as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for the fetters (saṃyojana) associated with existence. Thus it should be known.
The various afflictions that take as their object things not bound by the realms,
as well as those afflictions that subsequently manifest through the force induced by those [primary] afflictions,
even though they do not themselves take such things as their objects.

The categories of acquisitions (*prāpti*) induced by these are also the same as before. Those afflictions that take unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) as their objects are the afflictions that have the lower [stages] of the cessation (*nirodha*) and path (*mārga*) truths as their objects;
they are induced by the force of these afflictions.

...up to the statement that those afflictions which do not take this matter as their object are the [afflictions] associated with the outflows (sāsrava) regarding cessation and the path. As for the statement that they serve as the cause and fruit of past and future afflictions:
This means that when these various acquisitions (*prāpti*) exist in the present,
they are called "fruits" because they are of the nature of the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of past afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because it is the nature of the condition for the arising of future afflictions, it is called a "cause. When there is acquisition (*prāpti*), [the affliction] can arise;

when there is no acquisition, it does not arise. However, these various acquisitions are incompatible with the manifestation of the acquisitions that are the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) to abandonment.
Because it can maintain the abandonment of all afflictions pertaining to the past and future,
it causes the continuity of all afflictions that take this object as their basis, as well as those that take other objects, to proceed.
When the outflow of the various antidotes that abandon [the afflictions] regarding these objective conditions arises, the acquisition (prāpti) of the afflictions is immediately severed.
Although the substance of those acquired afflictions still exists with respect to their own objects of perception, [they are nonetheless abandoned].
Because causes and effects are thereby permanently severed,
it can be said that [the afflictions] are abandoned; since one knows the objects of the afflictions through the path that take one's own realm as their object,
those taking other realms as their objects are also abandoned.
Because one knows through the Path that the objects of the defilements are the untainted (anāsrava),
the tainted (sāsrava) objects are also abandoned; for as long as one has not fully understood even a small portion of an object,
the defilements that take that object as their condition will persist.
Furthermore, the afflictions that arise through the power of these delusions and take other objects as their conditions,
as well as the causes and acquisitions of the past and future afflictions they induce,
proceed without interruption within the present continuum.
When one attains thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) regarding even a limited object, the afflictions (*kleśa*) derived from it no longer arise;
therefore, it is known that the abandonment of afflictions definitely proceeds from their objects (*ālambana*). This is proven by the reasoning set forth above.
The abandonment of delusions is necessarily determined by their objects;
for it is by means of the Path seeing the object of these fundamental delusions that other delusions which take that same object are abandoned.

Furthermore, because the afflictions they induce are abandoned, it is known that the abandonment of afflictions necessarily proceeds from the abandonment of their objects (*ālambana*). Nevertheless, within this context, although there is no principle for an affliction and the path to coexist simultaneously.
However, because the Path perceives objects such as suffering and so forth,
the various afflictions are thereby severed;
this principle is difficult to comprehend.
This should be clarified by means of an analogy.
For example, suppose there is a person who has been bitten by a rat;
although he does not experience at that time any feverish distress, confusion, or the like.
However, because poison resides in the body due to causes such as fever and the like,
one is always designated as "one who has a disease," rather than being "one without a disease."
The Agada medicinal formula for counteracting the ingestion of poison is called "the healthy one" (*aroga*);
it is not for those who are already ill. Even though this Agada is administered for illnesses such as fever and the like, [it is so named because it restores health].
They do not function simultaneously within a single body; however,
by the power of the majesty and virtue of the agada, the poisons,
fevers, and other afflictions within the body are extinguished so that they do not arise.
It is said that agada can eliminate all diseases;
likewise, although the Noble Path does not coexist with the various afflictions within a single body at one time, [it nonetheless effects their removal].
However, by the power of the majesty and virtue arising from the Noble Path,
the fruits and causes of cessation prevent the various afflictions from arising;
it enables the practitioner’s physical vessel to become pure so that the afflictions do not continue.
It is said that they are "abandoned"; according to the aforementioned treatise,
one should understand that the various afflictions can be abandoned by means of their objects of perception (*ālambana*),
rather than through the fetters (*saṃyojana*) within one's own continuum.
And [the attainment of] the first fruit and so forth:
one attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) by severing the fetters that belong to the same category and the same grade.
This occurs because the objects of the afflictions of insight (*darśana-heya*) are severed through their antidotes, whereby their acquisition (*prāpti*) is eliminated.
It no longer manifests as a bondage toward its object,
and it also severs the functioning of the bonds of past and future natures.
According to this treatise:
This refers to the fetters within one's own continuum,
as well as those with a single fruit and so forth,
by virtue of the power of the Path.
It causes the fruit and the cause to be severed.
Because it lacks the power to bind with respect to the object of focus,
it is termed "severance."
It is not because they are not bound by other conditions that they are called "severed.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* is likewise.
This does not mean that one attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) by means of clearly discerning the objects of attachment.
For what reason have the masters of both past and present misunderstood this treatise?
Regarding the question, "How many kinds of remoteness (*dūratā*) are there?"—the following fourth section clarifies the four types of remoteness.
The treatise states: "That which is reached is also termed 'remote'."
This explains that they are distant in terms of their characteristics. Although they belong to the same aggregate and are situated in extreme proximity,
they are nonetheless called "distant" because their characteristics are different.
Treatise:
The nature of being distant through opposition (*pratipakṣa-dūratā*) is also termed "distant.
This explains the second type of distance.
For example, although the possession of ethical discipline and its violation coexist within the same body and are extremely close to one another—
being alike in their nature as unmanifest matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and not distant from each other—
they are nonetheless distinct because their natures as that which remedies and that which is remedied differ.
It is also called "remote.
The treatise states:
the remoteness of the three locations is also called "remote."
This explains the third point, remoteness by location (*deśa-viprakarṣa*).
For example, the eastern and western oceans,
though situated within the same world-system (*lokadhātu*), [are remote].
Since they are both water, their characteristics are not distant;
since they are both present, their time is not distant.
It is because the locations of east and west are separated that they are called distant.
Treatise:
The nature of distance in terms of the four times (*adhvan*) also constitutes "distance.
For example, although the past and future periods are both established upon the basis of a single dharma, they are nonetheless distant.
Characteristics are not distant,
nor is their location separated;
it is because they are separated by time that they are also called "distant."
Treatise:
In relation to what is it said to be "distant"?
This is the question posed by the Master of the Treatise.
Regarding the present world,
the Vaibhāṣika school replies:
How can that which has just ceased without interval and that which is currently arising— both being adjacent to the present— be called "distant"?
The author of the treatise raises an objection:
it is by virtue of the nature of worldly convention that something receives the designation "distant";
it is not the case that only what has been distant for a long time in the past or will be so in the future can be called distant.
This is the response of the Vaibhāṣika school.
[The opponent] objects: "If that were so, then the present should also receive the designation 'distant,' because its nature is distinct from the past and the future.
This is the objection of the Master (Vasubandhu). The commentary explains:
The natures of the past, future, and present are distinct.
The past and future are designated as "distant," while the present is likewise different from the past and future.
Present [dharmas] should likewise be designated as "distant.
The treatise states:
If it is argued that past and future dharmas are called "distant" because they lack functional activity (*kāritra*), [then present dharmas should also be so].
Since unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) lack any functional activity,
how can they be said to be "near"?
If it is argued that they are called "near" because one attains them universally through the present [moment], [then...]
The same principle should apply to the two periods of the past and future.
How can space and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) be called "near"? And so forth.
One should not categorically state that it is called "distant.
All of the above constitutes the Master of the Treatise’s refutation of alternative positions.
[End of] Treatise.
If one follows correct reasoning, once the past and future have been reached, the dharma has already abandoned its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, the Master [Vasubandhu], recounting the Sautrāntika position, explains that "time" refers to distance.
Treatise:
The word "etc. (ādi) is used to clarify that the examples cited are not exhaustive;
because these are merely briefly mentioned among the four types of distance, the full meaning is not yet complete.
The *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
"How can that which is adjacent to the present be called distant?
Because it is not the object of all five consciousnesses."
Furthermore, it is not because [the past and future] are objects of consciousness in part;
rather, that which possesses activity at a particular time is said to be "near.
Past and future [dharmas], however, definitely lack activity.
Therefore, it is called "distant.
One cannot object by saying that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), which eternally lack functional activity,
should also be called "distant," because the distinction between temporal distance and proximity is established based on time.
Therefore, regarding these three times,
if there is activity, it is said to be "near";
if there is no activity, it is said to be "distant."
Since all unconditioned phenomena transcend all time,
how can one argue that they are distant by means of time?
Just as spatial distance and proximity are established based on location, so too [is temporal distance].

This is not the case. If one were to object that because the characteristics of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) differ, they ought to be considered distant in terms of their characteristics, this is logically untenable;
for there is no denial that being distant in terms of characteristics applies universally to all phenomena.
If that is so, for what reason are unconditioned phenomena called "near"?
For instance, the essence of space pervades all places;
because its characteristic is non-obstruction, it is said to be "near."
The essence of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is called "proximate" because it can be attained with respect to all entities, in all places, and at all times,
without depending on effort.
For all those who practice with diligence and correctly cultivate the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
there is no distinction whatsoever among all its entities at the time they sever their afflictions.
Because it is swiftly realized,
it is called "proximate.
Since the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is thus designated by the term "proximate principle" (āsannayukti), yet the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) says:

The same principle should apply to the two periods of past and future; that is, meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and other such dharmas existing in the past and future should also be considered "near" because they are quickly attained,
just as with unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas and the like.
The previous explanation of the principle does not serve as a valid example,
because there is no such thing as many sentient beings collectively obtaining a single object without distinction across all its constituent parts.
Perhaps this analogy is likewise without fault. For example,
although all phenomena are termed "distant" because they differ from one another in their characteristics,
there is no error in permitting the designation of some as "near" based on other principles.
Thus, although the past and future are both termed "distant in time" because they lack functional activity with respect to temporal divisions,
there is no fault in permitting that a small portion of them be called "near" based on other principles.

It is not on the basis of some other principle that [the past and future] are called "distant," for that would contradict the meaning of being distant in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and temporal divisions (*adhvan*). Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati) states:
"According to correct reasoning, one should say that the past and future are called 'distant' because they are devoid of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of dharmas."
Because future phenomena have not yet acquired their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),
and past phenomena have already relinquished their own-characteristics, that [position] asserted by them contradicts the correct principle (*nyāya*):
all things lacking their own-characteristics are not distant by nature.
This established nature of distance must necessarily possess its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
because it is subsumed under the category of "distance," just like other instances of distance.
This means that other contrary natures and so forth are subsumed under the category of "remoteness" (dūratā).
Their specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) are not non-existent;
for it is already admitted that the past and future are subsumed under the category of remoteness.
One must necessarily admit that their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are not non-existent;
yet, to claim that they are "distant" while asserting that their specific characteristics do not exist is therefore in direct contradiction with correct reasoning (*nyāya*).
Treatise:
The preceding discussion stated that the abandonment of afflictions occurs through the arising of the counteractive path; does this abandonment involve "re-acquisition"?
The fifth section, consisting of one verse, clarifies the matter of re-acquisition.
The Commentary states: Regarding the phrase "attaining that superior attainment," this generally clarifies that while afflictions (*kleśa*) are not subject to repeated abandonment,
unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) can be attained repeatedly.
Treatise:
Regarding what was said about "repeated acquisition," how many times in total does it occur?
This question introduces the subject.
The treatise consists of six periods in total.
The answer "six" refers to the number.
The question "what are the six? refers to the six stages.
The treatise states:
"It refers to the arising of the path of remedy up until the attainment of the superior [state] upon its repeated arising.
The answer is: "In six stages."
There are four fruits of the path of cultivation;
when the faculties are refined, they become six.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Treatise on the Correct Principles) states:
If one refers to abiding in this [state] as being able to realize dissociation,
it denotes the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*); if one refers to abiding in this [state] as actually realizing dissociation, it denotes the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The path of liberation is explained in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*:
"However, all disconnections (visamyoga) possess only two moments."
This explains the differences.
Regarding the treatise, it says: "From those bound to the desire realm up to those who attain [the fruits] through all six periods."
This is explained according to the sequential [attainment]: the abandonment through the vision of the three truths occurs prior to the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*);
here, one's own realm is counted as one.
There are four [attainments] corresponding to the four fruits;
because of the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), there are six occasions.
Treatise.
The phrase "up to the form and formless realms, excluding the fruit of stream-entry" clarifies the five stages;
this is because at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna), one attains the fruit of stream-entry.
Subsequently, for one who attains the fruit through livelihood, there are only five occasions.
Even though livelihood may still exist after the fifth stage of the desire realm has been cultivated,
because the fruit lacks one [of these stages], it is considered to be attained in five occasions, just like the others.
Treatise:
The sixth [category], dissociation (*visamyoga*), refers to the attainment [of disjunction] at four times, because it excludes the first two [categories].
This clarifies the attainment [of results] during these four periods.
Treatise:

The ninth [category], "disjunction" (*visamyoga*), refers to the attainment [of disjunction] during the three periods of time, because it excludes the first three [categories]. This clarifies the attainment [of disjunction] across the three times.
Treatise:
From the ninth [dhyāna] of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) up to the attainment of the fruit itself,
this clarifies that [the fruit] is attained at two times.
Treatise:
Thus, regarding the statement "provisionally based on what is possible, up to excluding those such as stream-enterers," the six periods and so forth were previously explained.
This is stated according to those who possess dull faculties and proceed through the stages in succession;
if one speaks of those with sharp faculties,
the cultivation of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) is excluded.
Since one [category] is excluded from each of the preceding six, five, four, three,
and two positions, there are thus five, four, three, two, and one.
This applies if one transcends two fruits.
That is, excluding those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry. If one transcends three fruits,
then exclude those who have attained the fruits of stream-entry and once-returning.
If one of dull faculties follows the gradual path and attains it by means of the mundane path,
there are seven occasions.
If one of sharp faculties proceeds by way of gradual succession or by leaping over stages through the mundane path,
there are likewise six moments and so forth.
However, there are two types of cultivation for the sake of livelihood.
Mundane cultivation for livelihood is the correct abandonment of afflictions.
Uncontaminated cultivation for livelihood is of two kinds: first, the uninterrupted path and the path of liberation that abandon afflictions.
Second is the "repeated seal" (punar-mudrā).
Following the path of the repeated seal, it is also designated as "immediate" (ānantarya) and "liberation" (vimokṣa);
likewise, the "patience and knowledge of transcendence" (abhisamayakṣānti-jñāna) are also designated as "immediate" and "liberation."
The prior abandonment of afflictions is also termed "distant separation.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Whether one has abandoned few or many [afflictions], upon entering the Noble Path..."
He attains dissociation from the fetters;
according to what is appropriate for him, this occurs throughout all six periods, and so forth.
It is solely because of their sharp faculties. Furthermore, the sixty-first [treatise] states:
"Relying on the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*), one gives rise to the roots of goodness such as *uṣmagata* (heat) and so forth;
such a person will certainly attain the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) in this very life."
Because they possess sharp faculties and their revulsion toward existence is profound; according to the *Nyāyānusāra*, such transcendence belongs to those of sharp faculties.
Upon detailed examination, there are seventy-three individuals among those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) who enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Thus we know that although those who transcend [the stages] possess sharp faculties,
they do not belong to the category of the "sharp-seeded.
For this reason, they must again give rise to the uninterrupted path and the path of liberation.
Because those of the two vehicles are dull-witted,
when they wish to give rise to a subsequent path, they must necessarily do so by following the sequence of the preceding paths;
the Buddhas, however, transcend such sequence in their arising.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Among those who have previously abandoned the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and entered the Noble Path,
this excludes only the Bodhisattvas."
The others also definitely attain the acquisition of disjunction from all that is to be abandoned through cultivation in both realms by means of an untainted acquisition.
This is because they must all necessarily bring forth the superior path of fruition for the abandonment through cultivation in both realms.
By what evidence is this principle known?
It is because it is taught that when noble ones are born in the fourth dhyāna or in the stages above it, they necessarily possess the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*),
and because it is taught that when noble ones are born in the formless realms, they attain the full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the total abandonment of desire for the form realm.
For what reason does the bodhisattva not likewise [attain this] without relying on preparatory effort (*prayoga*),
since all meritorious qualities are able to manifest before them?

This is as in the case of the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and so forth. That is to say, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas lack the sovereign power to skip over and arise directly in various paths of antidote (*pratipakṣa-mārga*).
This is because, when they wish to realize a subsequent path, they must rely upon the preceding path as a preparatory application (*prayoga*) before they can realize it. According to this principle:
Re-cultivating the path of counteraction means further cultivating the seals (mudrā) to realize the paths of immediate succession and liberation.
It does not contradict the four paths.
According to one master in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*,
the Buddha Pralambabāhu was identical to a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, according to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*,
once one has reached the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), one no longer returns to cultivate the path leading toward that fruition (*phalaprāpti-mārga*).
This is as when one who has previously abandoned desire attains the fruit of *anāgāmin* by means of leaping over (*vyutkrāntaka*).
One does not again give rise to the antidote for abandoning desire, nor does one again attain the unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta*) of having abandoned desire;
and so on, until finally,
upon attaining the fruit of Arhatship, one never again attains it.
Because there was previously no acquisition (*prāpti*) of the untainted (*anāsrava*),
there is no acquisition to be relinquished;
furthermore, it cannot be acquired later either.
This is analogous to the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
The meaning of "leaping over" (*vyutkrāntaka*) regarding the *sakṛdāgāmin* is also to be understood accordingly.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
Regarding those who enter the vision of the truths after first abandoning six categories [of afflictions]:
their dissociation from the six categories abandoned by vision is also attained at five moments.
With the exception of one case as previously stated,
the disjunction from the six categories of defilements abandoned through cultivation is acquired solely at the time when the antidote arises via the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
One will certainly not give rise to that untainted counteractive path,
because it is comprised within the path directed toward the fruit of Once-returner;
one does not give rise to that path directed toward a fruit while abiding in the fruit itself.
Because one who abides in a superior fruit does not give rise to an inferior one, the Anāgāmin is understood by this same principle.
Subsequently, having given rise to the seal that certifies the realization of the Path of Seeing, one attains the six categories of the Path of Seeing;
because one does not give rise to the six categories of the Path of Cultivation.
One cannot attain the six grades of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) through the path of cultivation.
If one who is a leaper (pluta) toward the state of non-returner (anāgāmin) enters the vision of the truths (satyadarśana) based on the fundamental dhyānas,
they simultaneously attain the dissociation from the nine grades of defilements to be abandoned by vision in the desire realm.
It should be understood as before;
because the fundamental [dhyānas] are not the antidotes for abandoning desire,
if one relies on the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage].
If one relies on the fundamental [dhyāna],
the dissociation from the nine grades of what is to be abandoned by cultivation is also attained all at once.
It certainly does not give rise to that untainted counteractive [path],

because it is subsumed under the path directed toward the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala-pratipannaka-mārga*). Although the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) may arise in the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*), [it is still not the case here].
Because it is not an antidote, one does not obtain the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) of the desire realm. Furthermore, it says:

"Regarding the previous statement that those who enter the vision of the truths (darśanamārga) have abandoned six or nine grades of the desire realm, they previously cultivated the abandonment of the six or nine grades of disconnection (visamyoga), yet they do not possess the untainted acquisition (anāsrava-prāpti) thereof."
Is it that they will never attain it, or only temporarily not?
One should state with certainty that they will never attain it.
Is it not the case that at the time of realizing arhatship,
one necessarily attains all untainted acquisitions (*anāsrava-prāpti*) of dissociation from the defilements abandoned through both vision and cultivation during the preceding stages?
This would be so if those dissociations from the defilements previously abandoned possessed untainted acquisitions.
Now, at the time of relinquishing, one should obtain an untainted acquisition (*anāsrava-prāpti*) regarding that [state].
If it did not exist previously, it would likewise not exist now; thus, there would be no time for the attainment of dissociation (*visamyoga*).
It arises only from its own stage, and because it occurs when one abandons an inferior path to attain a superior one. Question: One attains the fundamental [dhyāna] through the abandonment of desire;
however, the fundamental dhyāna is not the antidote for the abandonment of desire.
When the Path of Seeing arises, one does not attain the unconditioned of the desire realm.
One attains the fourth dhyāna by becoming detached from the lower three dhyānas;
the fourth is not the antidote to those lower levels.

If one relies on the fourth dhyāna to give rise to the path of seeing (darśanamārga), one should likewise not attain the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) of the three lower stages. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* answers:
"That is to say, even if one has previously been free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana)."
Whenever one enters the vision of the truths (satyadarśana) based on any particular stage,
one necessarily attains the untainted antidote that abandons all views to be abandoned through vision within the two realms;
those [views] are what are abandoned through vision.
Because this is a single abandonment that is severed all at once,
when the path of seeing of a higher stage manifests,
one must necessarily cultivate the future path of the lower stages.
"Because the lower dhyānas are universally capable of serving as the antidote for the abandonment of the higher [stages]. The commentary explains:
"This is because the afflictions to be abandoned by the paths of the higher stages can be abandoned universally by the paths of the lower stages."
The afflictions to be abandoned by the path of a higher stage are precisely those that can be abandoned by the path of a lower stage.
One gives rise to the path of a higher stage while cultivating the path of a lower stage.
This is the cultivation of the same path;
the afflictions abandoned by a lower stage path cannot all be abandoned by a higher stage path.
Therefore, those on the lower paths do not cultivate the higher paths. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"Is it not already the case that one has abandoned the defilements of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) when, relying on the third dhyāna or other levels, one enters the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*)?"
One should cultivate the path of seeing of a future higher stage, because it serves as the antidote for abandoning the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). This is not so;
for one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of this stage [cannot do so].
That is to say, when one enters the vision of the truths (satyadarśana) based on this stage,

regarding those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of the truths— both those belonging to one's own stage and those of the higher stages— at the time of seeing each individual truth, [they are abandoned].
Because it can be abandoned instantaneously.
For example, when one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of the fourth dhyāna enters the vision of the truths (darśanamārga) while relying on the fourth dhyāna.
When one suddenly abandons the defilements to be abandoned through seeing on the five stages,
up until the point where one has not yet become free from the defilements of the first dhyāna,
and enters the vision of the truths (satyadarśana) based upon the first dhyāna.
One suddenly abandons the defilements to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) on the eight stages,
because it has never been the case that a higher stage abandons those of a lower stage;
thus, the fourth [dhyāna] and so forth do not [abandon what belongs to] the third and so forth.
All the factors to be counteracted are identical. Consequently,
having already abandoned the defilements of the third [dhyāna] and above,
when one enters the vision of the truths (darśanamārga) based on the third dhyāna and so forth, [the same applies].
Although a higher stage can counteract its own and the stages above it, it does not always share the same objects of abandonment as the lower stages;

therefore, when relying on a lower stage, one cannot cultivate the higher ones. Furthermore, it is said: "In the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), one attains the dissociation (*visamyoga*) from all [defilements] abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*)."
Only by the power of the path of seeing belonging to a lower stage do untainted states arise in one's own or higher stages; that is to say,
when the path of seeing belonging to a higher stage manifests before one.
One must necessarily cultivate the path of seeing of a lower stage in the future;
for by the power of that [cultivation], one attains the untainted acquisition (*anāsrava-prāpti*) of the dissociation from the lower [stage], but not [the dissociation] of a higher stage.
Therefore, in this stage of training (śaikṣa),

one must necessarily attain the untainted acquisition (anāsrava-prāpti) of the dissociation from what is to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya) throughout the realms of form (rūpa) and formlessness (ārūpya);
it cannot be established by reason that this applies to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).

The above explanation is because desire is abandoned only by the path of seeing belonging to the stage of *anāgamya*. One might object: "Should it not be the case that [the higher stages] do not serve as antidotes to lower stages, just as the fourth dhyāna and so forth do not serve as antidotes to the third dhyāna and below?"
However, when the fourth [moment of] the path of seeing (darśanamārga) manifests,
one is able to cultivate all future paths of seeing included within the lower stages. By the power of that path,
one attains the untainted acquisition (anāsrava-prāpti) of the disjunction from the defilements to be abandoned by seeing (darśana-heya) in all those lower stages.
Although these fundamental [stages] are not intended as antidotes for desire,
when the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) manifests in the fundamental stages,
one should cultivate all future paths of seeing subsumed under the *anāgamya* stage.

By the power of that path, one should attain the untainted acquisition (*anāsrava-prāpti*) of the dissociation from what is to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) within the desire realm; [this is the point of the preceding difficulty]. Since the fundamental [path] does not abandon the desire [realm], one cannot attain the abandonment of the desire realm [by means of it].
If one in a higher stage does not abandon the lower, how could there be abandonment of the lower? This analogy is not uniform;
for the path of seeing (darśanamārga) is twofold.
First, the antidote to the desire realm;
second, the antidote to the higher realms.
Regarding the antidotes to the desire realm, there are three.
Namely: the counteractive of abandonment,
the counteractive of revulsion,
and the counteractive of distancing.
The same applies to the three types of remedies for the form and formless realms.
Among the three remedies for the desire realm,
the first— the remedy of abandonment— is comprised solely of the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) stage.
The remaining [antidotes] pertain to six stages.
The higher [antidotes], which counteract the three types [of afflictions], all pertain to the six stages;
however, the antidotes for abandoning the [afflictions] of the two upper realms pertain to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It can only counteract the defilements of its own level and those of the levels above it.
Other antidotes on the Path of Seeing also counteract the defilements of the lower levels;
although the higher levels are not the specific antidotes for abandoning the lower levels, they nonetheless serve as such.
However, when the path of seeing belonging to a higher stage manifests in the present,
one universally cultivates the future paths of seeing of the lower stages,
because the objects to be abandoned by those lower stages are the same as those of the higher stage.
There is no path of seeing (darśanamārga) that serves as an antidote for the abandonment of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) which shares the same object of abandonment as the fundamental [path],
such that the path of seeing of the fundamental stage could manifest.

One is able to cultivate the path of seeing that serves as the antidote for abandoning the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned by seeing, which are subsumed under the stage of the "not-yet-reached" (anāgamya) and belong to the future;
by the power of that path,
one is able to attain the untainted acquisition (anāsrava-prāpti) of the dissociation from the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned by seeing.
Therefore, the examples cited by him are not analogous; this concludes the preceding explanation. Furthermore, it is said:
"The fundamental stages [of the form realm] constitute the antidote of aversion and the distant-separation antidote for the desire realm;
when the path of seeing is present, there are three kinds of antidotes for the form and formless realms."
Furthermore, one cultivates those belonging to the future stage of the "not-yet-reached" (anāgamya).
Thus, these two or three types of counteractive measures do not arise solely through the power of the future counteractive measure of aversion toward the distant realm of desire.
Thus, regarding the dissociation from the defilements abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) in the desire realm,
one attains an untainted possession (*anāsrava-prāpti*);
for it is only by the power of the abandonment-antidote (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*) that one can sever the possession of the fetters (*bandhana-prāpti*).
For those who have previously abandoned desire and enter the vision of the truths based on the *anāgamya* stage, the path of seeing—
which serves as the distant counteractive treatment (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*) for the weariness with the desire realm— becomes manifest.
One also cultivates the antidote for abandonment regarding the future,
because the path of the stage of the antidote for abandonment is now manifest.
It is by such reasoning that this is so.

Those who have not previously abandoned desire before entering the vision of the truths all obtain untainted acquisitions regarding the disjunction from the abandonments through vision in the desire realm.
For those who have previously abandoned desire and entered the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*),

there is absolutely no possibility for them to attain the untainted attainment (*anāsrava-prāpti*) of the dissociation (*visamyoga*) from the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the realm of desire. This is because the untainted path of cultivation (*anāsrava-bhāvanāmārga*), which is comprised by the *anāgamya* stage and functions as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) for abandoning what is to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, has not yet been attained.
It is unreasonable for [the path of cultivation] to be present in the body of one who has attained the fruit of non-returning, nor is it reasonable for it to be cultivated in the future;
for logically, it is impossible for the paths of both the once-returner and the non-returner to exist simultaneously within the body of one who has attained the fruit of non-returning.
For those who have previously abandoned the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and entered the noble path—
with the exception of Bodhisattvas—
others also certainly attain the untainted acquisition (*anāsrava-prāpti*) of the disjunction from all that is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in both realms.
They must all cultivate and abandon [defilements] in both realms,
because the path of their own superior fruits is universally present before them.
By what means is this principle proven?
It is taught that when noble ones are born in the stages from the fourth dhyāna upward, they necessarily possess the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya);
and it is taught that when noble ones are born in the formless realms (ārūpyadhātu),
they necessarily have the craving for form (rūparāga) completely abandoned.
Because they are attained through thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), the first abandonment— namely, that of desire— is not identical to the abandonment in the higher stages.
Although one relies on the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*) and practices the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage],
one practices both remaining types of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
Without cultivating the antidotes for abandonment,
one relies on the *anāgamya* (preparatory stage) and so forth to abandon the afflictions of the first dhyāna and above;
these must necessarily be abandoned by the same path as those of the higher stages.

For this reason, one cultivates the lower remedies based on the paths of the higher stages; for it is not appropriate to cultivate the abandonment of the two higher realms through the two [lower] paths.
Thus, based on the path of the second dhyāna and above, one attains the cultivation of the lower stages.
The path of abandonment and counteraction is not cultivated by those who leap over; however, in the path of the superior fruit, it must necessarily be cultivated,
because this is directed toward the subsequent fruit.

Because that path must necessarily be cultivated in successive stages: third, regarding the paths of subsequent fruits and those above them, one will certainly not again give rise to the preceding paths of approach, as they would serve no purpose.
By this principle,
those who leap over stages do not necessarily follow the sequential order;
they may also skip ahead to give rise to the higher paths.
Because one transcends the *anāgāmin* and others by means of the path of abandonment that treats [defilements] of the lower and middle stages as non-arising,
and because one initiates the path of abandonment that treats [defilements] of the first dhyāna and so forth.
Regarding this, some pose the following question and answer:
Since that which has already been abandoned and treated no longer manifests,
how can it be said that its own antidote has arisen? As stated previously,
the self-treatment consists exclusively of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The commentary explains:
It is called "self-treatment" (sva-pratikāra) because it resembles treating oneself;
or, it is so named because one attains its manifestation through self-interruption and treatment.
It is called "arising through its own counteractive" (*svapratipakṣaja*), not arising through the abandonment [of an affliction].
Alternatively, what is here referred to as "arising through its own counteractive" means:
It is not merely a matter of severing and treating;
rather, through the arising of distant aversion and treatment, self-governance also arises. Now, to examine the intent of this discussion in detail:
there are two types of the arising of self-governance.
First, the correct severance of delusions;
second, the non-severance of delusions.
Regarding the correct severance of delusions:
Regarding the four paths mentioned previously,
that which does not sever the afflictions refers to the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga).
It is modeled after the path of uninterrupted liberation;
it gives rise to the path of the supreme fruit,
following the same sequence as the paths that arose for the successive categories of afflictions previously abandoned.
This is called the path of self-mastery;
it is not the right abandonment itself,
yet it may be regarded as a "distant-part antidote" (prātipakṣika) insofar as it anticipates the right abandonment of afflictions.
It is modeled after the liberation of the Uninterrupted Path;
it is not like other paths of further progress,
and is thus called "self-governance of birth."

This refers to the fact that various disconnections (visamyoga) are designated by the name "cause" with respect to their results.
Below, the sixth section clarifies the thorough knowledge of abandonment (prahāṇa-parijñā).
First, it should be understood that there are two types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*). The first is thorough knowledge by wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*),
which refers to the uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) capable of thoroughly knowing the four noble truths, such as suffering and so forth.
Second, the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
Its essence is dissociation (*visamyoga*). Question: It is called "thorough knowledge" because it is capable of thoroughly knowing;
thus, it is a synonym for wisdom (*jñāna*).
How is it that [the cessation of the eye] is severed? Answer: Because it is the fruit of wisdom, just as karma is the fruit of understanding.
That is to say, a sutra states that the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are called "karma."
Because it is the fruit of that karma.
Furthermore, it is said that the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) fruit of arhatship is called "liberation" (vimukti), because it is the fruit of that liberation.
Thus, thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is established as being without fault in its cessation. Question: If that were so, the fruit of patience (*kṣānti*) would not be thorough knowledge. Answer:
Because all patiences are attendants of wisdom (*jñāna*), the name "wisdom" is applied to what is accomplished by patience.
What is accomplished by the minister is also called the work of the king;

or rather, it is because the power of untainted wisdom associated with meditative absorption such as the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) can collectively gather all the acquisitions of the untainted disjunction from defilements (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*).
At that time, the fruit of patience also becomes the fruit of knowledge.

Furthermore, when one gradually attains fruits such as those of the Once-returner and Non-returner, the untainted acquisition of disjunction (visaṃyoga-prāpti) resulting from the fruit of patience has already become the fruit of knowledge.
Treatise:
A single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is established for the abandonment of all [defilements].
Below this, the section on questions and answers divides abandonment into nine types.
The text contains six sections.
First, one part is divided into nine.
Second, it clarifies the results of the six pairs.
The third elucidates the conditions for establishment;
the fourth elucidates the stage of accomplishment;
the fifth elucidates the locus of total integration.

Sixth, the relinquishment through clear realization (*abhisamaya-prahāṇa*). This one and a half verses is divided into nine parts. The Treatise says, up to "establishing the three thorough knowledges" (*parijñā*): The Treatise says: Regarding the statement "up to establishing the three thorough knowledges," it means that from the point where the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) has been completed and one enters the first moment of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one abandons the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya-kleśa*). Because this is the first abandonment, it is established as the first thorough knowledge. Furthermore, when the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) of the desire realm have been completely eliminated, one attains the fruit of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin-phala*). Because this is the second abandonment, it is established as the second thorough knowledge. Furthermore, when the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation of the upper two realms (the form and formless realms) have been completely eliminated, one attains the fruit of the non-returner (*anāgāmin-phala*). Because this is the third abandonment, it is established as the third thorough knowledge. Thus, the three thorough knowledges are established based on these three types of abandonment. As for the phrase "up to establishing the three thorough knowledges," it indicates that there are other points of establishment beyond these. What are they? They are the four fruits of the śramaṇa (*śrāmaṇya-phala*). How are these established? It is because the four fruits of the śramaṇa are established based on the abandonment of the afflictions. What are those afflictions? They are the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing and the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation. How many are there? There are nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned by seeing and nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation, totaling eighteen. Among these, the first thorough knowledge is established based on the abandonment of the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned by seeing; the second thorough knowledge is established based on the abandonment of the first six grades of afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation; and the third thorough knowledge is established based on the abandonment of the remaining three grades of afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation. Therefore, although the four fruits of the śramaṇa are established based on the abandonment of the afflictions, they are not established based on all [eighteen] grades of abandonment. Why is that? This explains the first phrase, providing a general answer to the nine [categories]. That is to say:

Treatise:
Furthermore, regarding the bondage to the three realms up to the establishment of the six [faculties], how is this so?
First, let us inquire concerning those abandoned through vision (*darśana-prahātavya*).
Treatise:
This refers to the answer concerning how the three types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) are established, starting from those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This refers to the single full comprehension (*parijñā*) of the suffering and origin [truths] of the desire realm,
and one full comprehension each for the cessation and path [truths], totaling three.
Treatise:
Just as there are three to six types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) in the desire realm,
this serves as an analogy for explaining those in the two higher realms.
The two upper realms are also the same as the desire realm:
suffering and its origin are combined into one,
while cessation and the path each have one.

This constitutes the third synthesis. Thus, what are called the six kinds of universal knowledge (*parijñā*) regarding the abandonment of the dharmas of the three realms to be abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*) is a summary.
[End of] Treatise.
How is it that the remaining [fetters] bound to the three realms extend up to the third [dhyāna]?
Question: Regarding those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Treatise:
This refers to the inclusion of the factors bound to the desire realm along with the preceding ones;
this is the answer.
It means at the time of abandoning the ninth category of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm.
One complete knowledge is established,
called the "complete knowledge of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters.
For this reason, it is not termed the "exhaustion of sensual desire."
One is called "one who has exhausted the five lower fetters" because at that time one transcends the realm, attains the fruit, and realizes the full knowledge of the origin [of suffering];
for the dharma of the full knowledge of the origin is established together with the preceding [attainments].
Treatise:
Regarding the question of what is bound to the form realm up to the three types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), the answer is: the two upper realms.
The exhaustion of craving for form (*rūparāga-kṣaya*) refers to being free from the defilements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);

at that time, one does not accumulate a full comprehension (*parijñā*), because its essence consists solely of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) resulting from the abandonment [of defilements] through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the form realm. The exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana-kṣaya-parijñā*) refers to the exhaustion of the defilements of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
At that time, because one transcends the realms and attains the fruits [of the path], there is the accumulation of complete knowledge (*parijñā*).
As for the sequence at that time:
it takes as its essence the unconditioned state of cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding all things within the three realms.
This is called the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana-kṣaya*). The phrase "Thus it is called...
and what follows is the summary.
[End of] Treatise.
By what cause and condition does it reach the point of not being abandoned by insight?
This is the question.
For what reason are the abandonments-by-insight and the unconditioned established as three by combining the two realms?
The path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are each established as one for both realms.
The treatise states that this is because the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) for what is to be abandoned through cultivation differ.
Answer: When the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) are abandoned, those pertaining to the two realms are abandoned together.
This is because they are identical in employing a single path as their antidote.
When abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they are abandoned separately for each of the two realms;
because their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) differ, they are established individually.
Consequently, there are differences in whether thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is combined or separated.
Treatise:
Regarding the question of how far these established [categories] extend in terms of the paths and fruits,
the following two and a half verses [provide the answer].
The second section clarifies the differences between the six pairs of fruits.
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are eight pairs and sixteen gates;
the six pairs are as presented in this treatise.
Furthermore, there are two other remedies;
since this treatise has already discussed them extensively, they are not described here.
The Treatise says: "This is because it is the fruit of the path of cultivation."
This explains the number of fruits of patience (*kṣānti*) and wisdom (*jñāna*).
There are six fruits of patience;
there are three fruits of wisdom.

It should be said that they are like the fruits of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Regarding these two explanations, there is no formal evaluation. Sixth, according to the sequential order;

Those who are leapers (*pluta*) for the most part achieve only five types of full knowledge (*parijñā*).
Those who proceed by stages (*anupūrvaka*) for the most part achieve six types.
Because the two are combined, they constitute seven; however,
according to their sequential order,

If one includes both [the serial and the leaping], there are definitely seven;

at the time of reaching the knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna), [there would be only six].
What is the designation for the thorough knowledge (parijñā) thus obtained?
It cannot be said that one has attained the thorough knowledge of the lower realm through the path of the higher realm, because at that time,

The Master of Evaluation (*vibhāṣā-kāra*) says:

At that time, because one has attained the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*),

This is because Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas, relying on the fundamental dhyānas, attain the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).

Third, the clarification of the establishment of the objects of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*). Why is each [defilement] abandoned?
This refers to the eight truths of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the eighty-one categories of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The abandonment of each individual [defilement] does not establish a "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).
This does not mean that thorough knowledges are established according to the number of objects to which one is bound;
therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

For what reason is the abandonment attained through each individual path not established as a separate full knowledge (*parijñā*) for each? According to the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, and other texts,
there are four conditions for the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

There are five conditions for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). This treatise explains three conditions for the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and four conditions for the path of cultivation.

Because the simultaneous abandonment of the fetters is precisely the time when their simultaneous causes are extinguished. Question: For what reason are three conditions or four conditions established for the establishment of *parijñā* (thorough knowledge)? Answer: This is because it reveals the characteristic of permanent abandonment. As the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
For what reason is the abandonment obtained through each individual path not established as a separate full knowledge (*parijñā*)?
It is because full knowledge is predicated at the time of permanent abandonment.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"I shall now, for your sake, proclaim thorough knowledge," and so forth,
as explained at length.
In this context, what is called "thorough knowledge"?
It refers to the permanent abandonment of greed and the permanent abandonment of hatred.
"Delusion is eternally abandoned," and so forth, as explained at length.
This is what is meant by the expression "eternal abandonment."
It is only when the abandonment attained is entirely free from subsequent bondage that it is termed "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).
What is meant by abandonment with subsequent bondage?
And what is meant by abandonment without subsequent bondage?
When abandonment is complete through three or four conditions,
it is called "without subsequent bondage."
It is not called "existence" by way of its name; that is to say, there may be some [defilements] that have been severed,
even though one has attained the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
However, because other acquisitions (*prāpti*) are absent, it may not constitute a permanent abandonment; or rather,
there may still be a severance [of defilements],
even though other acquisitions have arisen.
The head of birth-and-death remains unsevered and firm,
because although one has repeatedly separated from the defilements of the eighth stage, one has not yet severed them; thus,
one falls back into the prisons of the evil destinies.
Or again, there may be those who have severed [the fetters];
although they are likewise deficient in that regard,
the remaining afflictions and bonds have not yet been eliminated.
The meaning of permanent abandonment has not yet been fully realized;
however, there may be an abandonment wherein other fetters are likewise eliminated.
Yet they are still unable to transcend their respective realms,
because the defilements of a similar class have not been abandoned without remainder,
and thus the sense of permanent abandonment is not yet perfected.
Such abandonments as these are termed "possessing residual bondage.
Therefore, universal knowledge (*parijñā*) is not established for them.
Only within nine stages—where three or four conditions are fulfilled and abandonment is free from residual bondage—is universal knowledge established.
The Treatise says: "Up to the point of being incomplete, it is not so.

This clarifies the three conditions for the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) to manifest the meaning of permanent abandonment. Although the dharmas with outflows (*sāsravadharma*) that are abandoned consist of many entities, [the path acts as their antidote].

this first one pertains to the stage of ordinary beings.

first, the untainted acquisition (*anāsrava-prāpti*) has not yet occurred;
second, the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) has not yet been severed. Regarding the phrase "severing the Peak of Existence":
In that stage, because one portion of the five classes of afflictions has not yet been abandoned, it is considered incomplete.
The treatise states:

Regarding the second case as well:

prior to the manifestation of the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayakṣānti*), although one has attained the untainted acquisition (*anāsravaprāpti*) and the acquisition of that acquisition (*prāptiprāpti*), as well as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

At that time, because the five categories of afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are all fully accomplished, it is not called "deficient. Regarding the term "double cause":
the cause belonging to its own category and its own stage is called the "self-cause."
One's own category within another stage, as well as all categories of other stages, are termed "other causes.
This is because the nine grades of afflictions abandoned through the vision of the truths are abandoned simultaneously in a single grade.
If one abandons a particular category within its own group,
one thereby abandons all other categories within that same group;
it is not the case that universal knowledge is not achieved unless one abandons every category within the group.
However, [an affliction] is not fully known by virtue of its belonging to another category;
those abandoned through the path of cultivation are not fully known by virtue of their own category but by virtue of other grades,
rather than by virtue of another category.
Because one must first sever the causes belonging to other categories,
for this reason the *Vibhāṣā* maintains that the path of seeing takes those of other categories as a single cause,
while the path of cultivation takes those of other stages as a single cause.
As for why only dual causes are established and not those bound by both [fetters],

Regarding the two causes and their simultaneous binding (*ubhayasaṃyojana*), although they both rely upon a single entity—and that "single entity" is established based on the abandonment [of defilements]—the meanings of "binding" (*saṃyojana*) and "cause" (*hetu*) differ.
That is to say, in relation to the five categories (*pañcanikāya*), that which causes them to arise is termed the "cause."

Within this context, that which can bind is called "bond" (*bandhana*); the distinction between "bond" and "cause of bondage" (*bandhanahetu*) lies in their specific meanings. For instance, when the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen, although the two categories lack the power to mutually induce the arising [of each other], [they remain bound].
Nevertheless, there exists a sequential capacity to function as a cause.

The meaning of the fetters abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) is as in the original [treatise]; however, the meaning of the fetters abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) is entirely absent [in this context].
It is not the cessation of both causes;
rather, it is the dissociation from both bonds.
Furthermore, one cannot say that the meaning of "cause" is identical to "bond."
Because afflictions that take uncontaminated objects do not bind other aggregates,
our own school maintains that both types [of binding] are taught;
that neither is mentioned here is for this reason.
One may simply say that this and that are established by themselves;
it cannot be said that they are not different,
because the substance and the meaning are broad.
Furthermore, regarding the term "broad in its essence" (*tattva-viśāla*):
this refers to [factors] such as the associated (*samprayukta*) and co-existent (*sahabhū*) dharmas. Regarding "broad in its meaning" (*artha-viśāla*):...
The treatise states: "The meanings of being of the same class (*sabhāga*), universal (*sarvatraga*), associated (*samprayukta*), and co-existent (*sahabhū*) are all [types of] causes."

Upon reaching the stage of the dharma-patience regarding the origin (samudaya-dharmakṣānti) within the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna), one reaches all the universal causes (sarvatraga-hetu).
This is the third stage.
At that time, possessing both [the cause and the abandonment] but lacking one [of the two conditions], it does not constitute full knowledge (parijñā).

Up to the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination, the subsequent knowledge regarding origination, and the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation.
The subsequent knowledge of cessation (nirodha-anvaya-jñāna), the dharma-knowledge of the path (mārga-dharma-jñāna), and the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna).

Question: For one who transcends [the stages], at the point of the fourth and fifth moments of mind, the two causes previously [mentioned] are extinguished.

At the stage of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna), one further eliminates the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra). Since these three conditions are thus fulfilled, [the attainment is established].
Why is "thorough knowledge" (parijñā) not established [for those who transcend]? Answer:
The establishment of thorough knowledge is based on the method of successive practice.
For those who transcend, the stage of thorough knowledge is established according to what would have been the successive order.
The state of complete knowledge (*parijñā*) is established only at this stage; although the three conditions were present in the preceding stages,
complete knowledge was not established there.

This clarifies the four conditions for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Question: For what reason are three established in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), but "transcending the realm" (*dhātusamatikrama*) is not established?
Is the establishment of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) for the purpose of transcending the realms?

Answer: Because the thorough knowledges (parijñā) of the path of seeing (darśanamārga) pertain only to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) state regarding defiled phenomena (kliṣṭadharma), it is only upon reaching the abandonment of both causes that the characteristic of permanent cessation becomes manifest.
Because those afflictions bound to that same level have all been abandoned,
and because the afflictions of the path of cultivation do not take this as their object,
the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the path of cultivation has both the defiled and the undefiled unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its essence.
Although one has severed both causes and so forth, because similar afflictions remain unsevered, the characteristic of severance is not yet manifest;

therefore, it is not established as "universal knowledge" (parijñā). Question: According to the following passage, one abandons five and attains one—namely, the universal knowledge of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters.
The *Nyāyānusāra* further states:
"Based on the fundamental dhyānas, one abandons two and attains one;
that is to say, the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañcāvara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*). According to this [passage].
The exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*) is also the fruit of patience (*kṣānti*).
Why, then, is it said that only three are the fruits of knowledge (*jñāna*)?
Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 63:
In the section on the accomplishment of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), it says:
"The fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) accomplishes one [thorough knowledge],

From the knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna),
or from the ninth path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) when free from the defilements of desire,
up until one has not yet produced the path of a superior fruit, it is called the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmi-phala).
He achieves the single full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, the Master of the Evaluation (*vibhajyavādin*) says: "It should be stated thus."

A Bodhisattva in the noble stages (āryabhūmi) definitely does not attain the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*) regarding the factors to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the form and formless realms, nor the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga-kṣaya-parijñā*).
This is because they possess the collective thorough knowledge (*saṃkalana-parijñā*).
Because it is impossible to cultivate those [lower stages] as antidotes for abandonment; based on this, the seventh [stage] also possesses the fruit of patience (*kṣānti*).
Why, then, is it said that there are only six fruits of patience? Answer: This is because the system of establishment (*vyavasthāna*) relies solely upon sequential order.
Regarding the three fruits of knowledge (*jñāna*) and the six fruits of patience (*kṣānti*). The treatise states:
Some maintain that [the fruits] can only be established once one has become detached from both fetters (*ubhaya-bandhana-vigata*).
This describes the commentaries on the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* and other works.
If one follows those [texts] for their establishment,
there are four conditions for the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and five conditions for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Commentary:
This [section on] "separation from both fetters" (*ubhayasaṃyojanaviyoga*) is not explained separately because it describes the author’s own position of non-establishment (*anabhyupagama*).
Although among the five conditions, the condition of dissociation from both fetters,
the condition of eliminating both causes, and the condition of transcending a realm differ in meaning, they are nevertheless established separately.
However, when it is said that these simultaneous causes are abandoned,
they immediately become the abandonment of simultaneous fetters and so forth; although there is a difference in meaning, [the underlying principle remains the same].
Because there is no distinction in their function, they are not explained separately. The treatise states:
although at the various stages of transcending the realms, the state of "thorough knowledge" (parijñā) has not yet been established.
This explains the resolution of doubts and difficulties.
If, at the time both causes cease, one must necessarily be separated from their simultaneous fetters (*paryavasthāna*),
then because their function is not distinct, only four conditions (*pratyaya*) are established.
At the moment of transcending a realm, one must necessarily be free from both causes.
Why, then, establish "transcending a realm" as something distinct from being free from both causes?
The answer states:
Although there must necessarily be simultaneous fetters at the time of transcending a realm,
this is not the case when one leaves the realms of form and formlessness, or when one abandons the afflictions of the lower three stages.
Although both causes have been extinguished,
one has not yet transcended the realm;
for this reason, a distinct condition for transcending the realm is established.
It is not the case that the absence of the two causes necessarily entails the absence of the conjunction;
rather, if there is the absence of the conjunction,
it necessarily entails the absence of the two causes.

That is to say, from the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) until the patience regarding the dharma of origin (*samudaya-dharma-kṣānti*), full knowledge (*parijñā*) is not accomplished. According to the treatise,

From the second half-verse below:
The fifth [section] clarifies the thorough knowledge of the origin (*samudaya-parijñā*).

The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 62, states:
Furthermore, it is essential to possess two conditions for the complete synthesis of universal knowledge (*parijñā*):
first, to transcend at least one of the three realms;
second, to exhaust at least one of the five destinies or four modes of birth.
Regarding the attainment of the first two fruits,
both meanings are absent at the time of becoming free from attachment to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
In one case there is a deficiency;
at the time of attaining the fruit of non-returning,
both meanings are complete without deficiency.
First, one transcends the desire realm;
second, when one exhausts the human destiny of womb-birth and attains the fruit of arhatship.
It also possesses two meanings:
first, it transcends the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
second, it exhausts the spontaneously born beings (*upapāduka*) within the celestial destinies. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
What is called "accumulation" (*samudaya*) has the meaning of "conjunction. If,
regarding the formless realm (*ārūpya*), one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) by abandoning defilements partially,
or attains the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*) by abandoning them completely— where "partial" refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The complete and partial cultivation of the path: if one becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm partially, one attains the fruit of once-returner;
if one becomes detached from them completely, one attains the fruit of non-returner.
This "partial detachment" refers to the six categories of the path of cultivation.
Complete detachment refers to the nine grades of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
This applies both to partial detachment and complete detachment within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
In both cases, the fruit is not obtained;
only in two instances are both conditions fulfilled,
namely, when the attainment of the fruit coincides with the transcendence of a realm.
Therefore, for the Arhat and the Anāgāmin, the abandonments attained through cultivation are established as a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*),
because at that time they arise collectively as a single-flavored attainment (*ekarasalābha*).
Although the other two fruits are attained at a time when they are of a single flavor,
one has not yet transcended the realm;
whereas at the time of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm, although one does indeed transcend the realm—
Because there is no attainment of a single flavor,
one does not accumulate full knowledge (*parijñā*) at that stage;
for it is only when two conditions are met that it is accumulated in its entirety.
Treatise:

The following half-line of verse [provides the answer].
The sixth [section] clarifies the thorough knowledge of relinquishment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
The treatise states: "Up to the point of falling away from the state of freedom from desire.
Within this, relinquishment is explained first.
The subsequent stage clarifies the attainment:
in the intermediate state, there is the relinquishing of one,
and the relinquishing of two.

one abandons six;
