Within this, there are three stages:
namely, when one falls back from the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one relinquishes the complete knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojanakṣayaparijñā*).
Upon falling away from the exhaustion of craving for the form realm, one relinquishes the full knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm;
upon falling away from the state of complete freedom from desire, one relinquishes the full knowledge of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters.
In these three instances, one relinquishes one [knowledge] in each case.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'abandoning two,' this clarifies that one abandons two upon attaining the state of an Arhat."
Within this, there are two categories:
first, those who are non-returners (anāgāmin) who have already abandoned craving for the form realm but fall back due to the arising of desire-entanglements and relinquish the two [attainments];
second, those who have exhausted craving for the form realm as well as those who have exhausted the five lower fetters (pañca-aṃga-hīnabhāgīya).
The second case refers to when one attains the fruit of arhatship; one also abandons two [factors], as previously explained.
This is according to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*.
Those who enter the path of seeing by relying on the fundamental dhyānas also abandon two:
namely, the single thorough knowledge of suffering and origin regarding the form and formless realms,
and the single thorough knowledge of cessation.
Because one fully comprehends the aggregates (*skandha*), one does not attain the lower comprehension of the path.
The treatise states that "one abandons five" because one abandons the aforementioned five.
This clarifies the abandonment of the five [fetters].
These belong to the three types of views in the desire realm and to those abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin in the formless realm.
Furthermore, because they are abandoned through the full comprehension (*parijñā*) of the origin (*samudaya*), they cannot be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Following the above principle, two are abandoned and five are abandoned.

Therefore, it is known that both treatises state that one transcends the fruit of patience and also attains the full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
As for the previous statement that "one attains six," [it refers to the following].
This indicates the sequence.
According to this text,
both the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Nyāyānusāra* state that five [faculties] are abandoned.
Some say that two are abandoned;
therefore, it is known that the fundamental fruits of dhyāna consist of two for the path of seeing and three for the path of cultivation as the correct [reckoning].
Commentary:
The statement "abandoning six" refers to the point when one attains the state of being free from desire;
this clarifies the abandonment of the six.
This refers to the six thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Regarding the statement in the treatise, "The attainment is likewise," this explains attainment starting from the phrase "except for the attainment of five" and below.
Because there are cases where one, two, or six [faculties] are acquired simultaneously with the acquisition of equanimity (upekṣā),
it is said that "it is likewise. This applies with the sole exception of the acquisition of five [faculties].
It is also because of many statements. Regarding the treatise:
it says that "attaining one" refers to falling back due to the arising of the fetters of form (*rūpa-rāga*).
"Clearly attaining one" means attaining what was not previously attained; that is,
for those who follow the gradual path, it refers to attaining the six universal knowledges (*parijñā*) by abandoning the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
and further, to gradually attaining one [knowledge] at each stage while progressing to abandon the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Furthermore, when one falls away from the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) due to the arising of the fetters of the form realm (rūpāvacara), one attains the full knowledge (parijñā) of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (pañcāvarabhāgīya-saṃyojana).
The treatise states that "one attains two" at the time of falling away due to the various fetters.
The second is the attainment of clarity.
This refers to two things: the exhaustion of craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga-kṣaya*), and the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana-kṣaya*).

because those faculties are dull, the afflictions are fierce and sharp and difficult to subdue;
they can only be subdued and treated by relying on the power of external conditions.
Therefore, one first clearly observes an external corpse in order to gradually subdue the afflictions of one's own mind.
That is to say, when one first wishes to observe an external corpse:
First, one should go to the place where the body is to be offered with a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
As the Blessed One said:
"A beginner who wishes to seek the skillful means for the swift cessation of sensual desire..."
One should diligently practice the tranquility of the path that gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness,
and so forth, as extensively explained.
Having reached that place...
In order to subdue and treat the four kinds of craving,
one should practice the contemplation of impurity by observing the external signs of corpses as described in the *Catuṣpādaka-vairāgya-mārga-sūtra*, using them as analogies for the internal body.
Since that characteristic is thus,
this should also be so. By means of this expedient,
one is gradually able to cause the mind to also give rise to a profound sense of weary aversion toward the internal body.
One is then able to subdue and treat the four types of greed previously mentioned;
because one perceives their intrinsic nature within one's own body,
the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-saṃjñā) swiftly reaches fulfillment.
One should cultivate the eight signs to subdue and treat the four types of craving.

In order to subdue and treat craving for color, one cultivates the sign of the livid corpse, as well as the yellow and red signs. In order to subdue and treat craving for shape, [one cultivates the remaining signs].

One cultivates the sign of being devoured and the sign of dismemberment in order to subdue and remedy greed for exquisite touch; one cultivates the sign of disintegration and the sign of skeletons in order to subdue and remedy greed for offerings and service.
One cultivates the sign of bloating and the sign of festering.
It is accepted that by taking a skeleton as the object, one can cultivate the meditation on impurity so as to generally subdue and treat these four types of craving;
for within a single skeleton, all objects for abandoning the four cravings are fully present.
Treatise: Therefore,
one should first distinguish how [the object] is brought to the point where it no longer manifests,
thereby explaining how the contemplation of impurity does not sever the afflictions.
The abandonment of afflictions is through attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*),
and afflictions are abandoned by taking a single location as a universal object (*ekadeśālambana*).
This is because the attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣamanasikāra*) in the contemplation of the skeleton (*asthisaṃkalā*) takes only a limited portion as its object.
One does not sever the afflictions;
one can only suppress them so that they do not manifest.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
One contemplates the thirty-six constituents within one's own body;
these are called the contemplation based on the reality of oneself,
as it is associated with attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇamanasikāra*).
Therefore, one cannot permanently sever the afflictions.
Relying on the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one conceptually contemplates various signs of impurity;
this is not subsumed under distorted attention (*viparyasta-manasikāra*).
Because it is diametrically opposed in nature to the afflictions (*kleśa*),
that which is inverted is fundamentally unable to accomplish what one intends to do.
If this [meditation] can subdue the afflictions according to one's desire, how could it be a distortion?
If you argue that this object is not actually bone, yet one perceives it as all being bone,
how could this not be a distortion?
This reasoning is also incorrect,
because it must be understood as follows:
that is to say, regarding those who perceive a person in what is actually a tree stump.
One does not form such an understanding.
Because I am now viewing a tree stump through the lens of the mark of a person, this is a perversion.
Now, the practitioner reflects in this way:
Although not everything within the various objective spheres consists of bone,
for the sake of subduing all afflictions,
I should now use resolute conviction to contemplate them everywhere as being bone.
Since one can subdue the afflictions by resolving them according to one's wishes as appropriate,
how could this be a perversion?
The power of this contemplation is able to subdue the afflictions so that they do not manifest for a time.
Since there exists such skillful means and power,
how could it not be wholesome?
Therefore, there is no loss as you have alleged.

That which is already matured is not autonomous or small.

That is to say, when one has already cultivated [the practice] to maturity, it takes one's own body as its object. There is that which possesses mastery but whose object is not small, meaning it has not yet been cultivated to maturity;

"already matured" refers to the first phrase;

One's own person is the first phrase;

its nature consists of four or five aggregates, including its attendants. As the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
If it were argued that the contemplation of impurity must be wisdom (*prajñā*),

This means that because the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) can directly counteract greed,
it should properly have non-greed (*alobha*) as its essential nature.
The appearance of purity, which is the cause of greed, is eliminated through the power of this contemplation.

All [contemplations] that accord with the various meditations on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) are indeed non-attachment;

Because it is only that which can suppress and remedy craving for visible forms (*varṇa*) and so forth that is designated as the essence of this contemplation;

If it includes the concomitant factors,

it does not take the various bases (āyatana) as its object,
because it takes only visible form (rūpa) as its object.
This refers to the meaning of the object, not the name.

If it is argued that the Venerable Aniruddha was unable to contemplate the heavens as impure,

This clarifies the basis of the body.

because the six desire-realm heavens lack such impure signs as the "bluish discoloration" (vinīlaka), it does not arise there at all. Regarding these two views in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there is no commentarial judgment.
The reasoning is the same as that of the former master, while this treatise agrees with the latter master.
Since the treatise also states that it is named "impure" solely because its aspect is that of impurity.
This clarifies the characteristics [of the knowledge].
According to the treatise, regardless of which time period one is in, it extends to taking all three periods of time as its object.
This clarifies that it takes the present world as its object.
Since attention through resolute conviction (adhimokṣa-manasikāra) takes only present objects as its conceptualized objects, it does not take the past or future as its objects.

if it is a dharma not destined to arise, it takes the three periods of time as its object.
Treatise:

this explains the reason why it is exclusively outflow-tainted.
The sixteen aspects of untainted practice (*anāsrava*) are not associated with attention through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*),
since they consist solely of [direct] realization.
The treatise states that it is not exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*),
because it is obtained through the departure from defilement (*vairāgya-lābhika*) and because it is attained for the first time.
This clarifies the two types of attainment (*prāpti*).
The *Nyāyabinduprakaraṇa* states:
"When one becomes free from the defilements (*kleśa*) of various respective stages and attains those respective meditative concentrations (*samādhi*)."
That is to say, one attains this contemplation of that stage;
having attained it through the abandonment of defilement, at subsequent times,
one also brings it into manifestation through application.
For those who have not yet abandoned the defilements, it is acquired solely through application.
Among these, all noble ones and ordinary beings in their final existence [acquire it].
All are attained through what has never been attained before; the others are attained only through what has been attained previously. The *Vibhāṣā* states:
"They are attained through preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and attained through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*)."
That which is obtained by birth may be obtained through application, or it may be obtained through the abandonment of defilements; it is not merely obtained by birth.
That which is obtained through the abandonment of defilements—
This means they are acquired through cultivation at the time of detachment from defilements and because the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is present; however,

Regarding ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), when the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is present, it applies to both what has been previously attained and what has not;

"Noble ones" refers to all noble beings (*ārya*).

first, those who are ordinary beings in their final existence as bodhisattvas.

first, the wind of inhalation (*āśvāsa*).
Second, the wind of exhalation;
third, the wind of speech;
fourth, the wind of elimination.

It arises from the region of the navel, flows upward, and strikes the throat.
It strikes the great elements (mahābhūta) that constitute the maturation-born and the development-nourished,

This exists within the mouth;

It should be understood that this arising has the mind as its cause;

Next, one contemplates arising and ceasing;
next, one contemplates dependent origination.
This is because the practitioner first contemplates how all conditioned phenomena arise and cease from causes.
This is because it is easy to enter the gateway of contemplating the interconnectedness of cause and effect;
alternatively, some may wish to first contemplate dependent origination.
Thereafter, one gives rise to the contemplation on the three meanings of dependent origination.
Immediately following this contemplation, one cultivates the skillfulness in the seven bases;
because of attaining skillfulness in these seven bases, [one proceeds further].
Having been able to establish the sequence of the truths of cause and effect regarding all previously perceived objects,
and having thus thoroughly cultivated wisdom and meditative concentration, [one proceeds].
One is then able to establish the truths that accord with clear realization (abhisamaya),
namely, the suffering of the desire realm and the higher realms, each distinct.
One contemplates these eight in their proper sequence.
One cultivates the sixteen aspects never before cultivated.
Through the wisdom derived from hearing, one first gives rise to such contemplation of the sixteen aspects within the eight truths.
Just as one perceives various colors through thin silk,
this is called the perfection of the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
The wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) should be explained accordingly.
Next, one develops a profound sense of weary aversion toward saṃsāra and takes delight in the merit of the tranquility of nirvāṇa;
thereafter, one frequently brings forth the contemplation of revulsion before the mind.
Through skillful means and diligent cultivation, these qualities gradually increase and become ever more excellent,
giving rise to such supreme roots of virtue comprised within the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), which are conducive to the stage of penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*).
Regarding the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) that takes the common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) of all objects as its object through combined cultivation:

according to the aforementioned treatise, this refers to the arising of the mindfulness of common characteristics after the three meanings and seven bases, whereby one enters the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata).
The contemplation of the three meanings refers to the three categories of aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu).
The seven points of proficiency are as follows:
One knows form as it truly is: form as suffering,
the origin of form,
and the way leading to the cessation of form.
The passing away of form,
the gratification of form,
and the peril of form.
And one knows, as it truly is, the renunciation of form;
the same applies to the seven [knowledges] regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
One knows form as it truly is through four knowledges.

"Knowledge" refers to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*). Regarding the question of why the first three are mentioned twice among the "seven points of proficiency":
the first [repetition] explains the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Furthermore, the three truths are stated twice because they are finite;
the truth of the path is not stated twice because it is infinite.
Furthermore, the preceding four sections provide an excellent exposition of the stage of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Because the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) necessarily involves the contemplation of the four truths,
all four are fully explained therein.
The latter three locations provide an excellent exposition of the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The noble path cultivated during the stage of the path of cultivation is itself the truth of the path;
it does not necessarily involve the contemplation of all four noble truths.
However, it speaks only of three. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 2, states:
"If one were to explain the virtues in their proper sequence, then the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) should be explained first herein."
Or [the practice of] mindfulness of breathing and so forth. Next, the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are explained;
next, the contemplation of the three meanings.
Next is proficiency in the seven bases (*saptasthānakauśalya*).
Next, the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) is explained;
the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) is explained next according to this treatise.
That is to say, immediately following the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna),
one contemplates the three meanings and the seven points of proficiency (saptasthānakauśalya) and thereby enters the stage of Heat (uṣmagata). Now, let us examine this in detail.
Regarding the differences between this treatise and the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*:
as for the sequence of entering into practice, it follows after the five stages of mental abiding (*pañca-vinīlaka-citta*).
Following the application of mindfulness with specific objects,
one gives rise to the application of mindfulness with general objects and enters the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*);
during this interval, one cultivates the contemplation of the three meanings.
Together with the seven points of proficiency and including dependent origination and so forth,
when about to enter the stage of "Heat," one enters from the perspective of general mindfulness.
The *Vibhāṣā* [treatise], because the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are of primary importance,
cites the former applications of mindfulness and does not cite the latter.
This treatise, being concise, does not describe the intermediate ones.
The *Nyāyānusāra* briefly sets forth all three stages;
therefore, the meanings of these three treatises do not contradict one another.
Treatise:
Having cultivated this contemplation, what roots of goodness arise?
Below, the fourth section clarifies the four roots of goodness, beginning with "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
These refer to the latter four of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*). Among them:
first, the essence of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and so forth is clarified;
second, the distinctions among the roots of goodness are clarified.
The three verses clarify the excellence of the three vidyās,
the transformation toward the four vidyās, and the duration of the cultivation of the fruits of the five vidyās;
these constitute the essence of the vidyās and so forth.
The Commentary states: "Reaching the name 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*) clarifies that the Heat-dharma arises from the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
This arises from either wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) or wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*)."
Therefore, the *Nyāyabindu* states:
"If there is one who has previously abandoned the defilements of the desire realm,
[they rely] upon the wisdom produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) subsumed under the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)."
Feeling revulsion for the places of birth and delighting in nirvāṇa,
one attends with a mental orientation accompanied by frequent practice of revulsion;
this gradually induces the arising of the distinct wholesome root of "heat" (uṣmagata).
There are those who, having previously not yet abandoned the defilement of desire,
give rise to the root of goodness known as "Heat" by relying on the wisdom derived from reflection.
Treatise:
This dharma is called "warmth" because it reaches the stage of warmth;
this explains the meaning of the term "warmth."
The untainted Truth of the Path is like fire;
it burns the fuel of the afflictions.
Because one first attains the precursor to this fire upon reaching this stage, it is called the "Heat" dharma (*uṣmagata*).
Treatise:
This root of merit of "Heat" extends to sixteen aspects,
clarifying the practice regarding the Truths.
Because the duration is long,
one is able to fully contemplate the objects of the Four Noble Truths as well as the sixteen aspects.
According to the section on the reduction of conditions,
this contemplation of the Four Truths proceeds by contemplating the four aspects of each individual truth before moving on to the next truth.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"This is a specific variety of the mindfulness-establishment on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that takes common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object; it is the mindfulness-establishment on common phenomena (*sādhāraṇadharmasmṛtyupasthāna*)."
Although one contemplates the contaminated as suffering, empty, impermanent, and non-self,
in the initial stage one first gives rise to the four aspects of suffering,
and subsequently contemplates the truth of origination.
This does not contradict reason.
As for the treatise’s observation of the Noble Truth of Suffering, it shall be analyzed later as appropriate.
This is the enumeration of the names of the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"However, although the various levels of 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*) take the Four Truths as their objects..."
However, it is said that for the most part, this is accompanied by the practice of revulsion (*nirveda*),
because at the time of its arising, the perception of the aggregates (*skandha-saṃjñā*) predominates. According to this treatise, during the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*),
one primarily contemplates suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).
Treatise:
This "heat" (ūṣmagata) root of goodness reaches the point where it receives a different name.
This clarifies the transition from the stage of heat into the stage of "summit" (mūrdhan).
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The practitioner cultivates these roots of goodness of 'heat' (*ūṣmagata*) in their inferior, medium, and superior grades,
gradually progressing through them."
Regarding the suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as taught by the Buddha,
he gave rise to compliant faith and observed that all states of existence are constantly being incinerated by fierce and blazing flames.
Among the three jewels, faith is preeminent.
When the subsequent roots of goodness produced through cultivation that accord with the stages of penetration arise,
they are called the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) stage.
This is the differentiation of the mindfulness-establishment (smṛtyupasthāna) that takes general and common characteristics as its object. Regarding the treatise:
among the moving roots of goodness, it reaches the point where they are called "Summits" (mūrdhan).
"Summit" (*mūrdhan*) is the name for this stage.

Within it, there are two meanings: first, it is called a "summit" because it is superior among the roots of goodness that are subject to regression and fluctuation, just as the head is the summit of a person;
second, it is called a "summit" because it marks the boundary between both progress and regression.
It is like the summit of a mountain;
therefore, it is called the "peak" (mūrdhan).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
The term "summit" (*mūrdhan*) indicates that this is the most excellent stage.
Just as when a matter of auspiciousness reaches its fulfillment,
people in the world say of such a person, "he has reached the summit."
It is called "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) because it is the most excellent among the moving virtues. The treatise states:
"This is also like the stage of 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*), extending up to sixteen aspects (*ākāra*)."
The clear observation of the aspects of the truths is the same as in the preceding stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*). The treatise states:
"In this way, from Heat through the Peak (*mūrdhan*) up to the application of mindfulness to phenomena alone (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*)."
This clearly explains the two types of wholesome states.
At the initial stage of establishing the foundation, the practice consists solely of the application of mindfulness to phenomena with mixed objects (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "At the initial stage of establishing the foundation, there is only the application of mindfulness to dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*); in the subsequent stage of progress, all four are present. Commentary: This means that when first entering the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), one practices only the application of mindfulness to dharmas; however, as one advances through the stages of cultivation, all four applications of mindfulness become manifest.
Because contemplation based on individual objects is inferior and cannot shift one's position,
whereas the power of collective contemplation is superior and can shift one's position, for this reason,
all [stages] in the initial position are the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Treatise:
For what reason does it reach the path of the Four Noble Truths?
This explains the initial establishment of the foundation.
Treatise:
At the subsequent stage of further progress, one possesses the four foundations of mindfulness;
this explains what follows the establishment [of the foundations].
Lower, middle, and upper-middle.
One may contemplate only form,
or contemplate only sensation.
Alternatively, if one observes them collectively,
there is nothing that is not subsumed.
Treatise.
Because of the profound respect for those [states] previously attained,
this explains that what has already been attained does not arise again.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Because these roots of goodness are induced by superior application,

one does not feel reverence for those already attained; nevertheless, although this stage of the Summits (mūrdhan) takes the Four Truths as its object, it is so called because it is on the verge of falling back.
The treatise states: "Faith directed toward the Three Jewels manifests predominantly;
this root of goodness of the 'Summit' stage reaches the point of being called the 'Dharma of Patience'."
This commentary explains that from the arising of the "summit" stage, one attains "patience. The treatise states:
regarding the principle of the Four Noble Truths, reaching this point is termed the "dharma of patience."
This explains the name "Patience" (kṣānti).
Although the roots of goodness in the preceding stages are also capable of patient acceptance regarding the principles of the Four Noble Truths,
because this stage is the most preeminent, it alone is specifically designated by the name "Patience."
Furthermore, although one may have attained conviction in the preceding stage,
there is still the possibility of falling back; however, in this [present] stage, there is no such falling back.
[It] is exclusively given the name "patience" (kṣānti). Question: If that is so, then the first [dharma] should also be called "patience.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Although the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) are also able to 'endure and accept' (*kṣamati*) the noble truths,"
Because one will necessarily enter the path of seeing immediately thereafter,
there is certainly no falling back;
yet, one does not fully contemplate the principles of the Four Noble Truths.
Because this possesses [complete] contemplation, it specifically receives the name "patience" (kṣānti).
Therefore, it is specifically designated as "patience in accordance with the truths" (satyānulomikī kṣāntiḥ).
Treatise.
This root of goodness of patience differs from the preceding one;
this clarifies the distinction between the universal and the specific regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
This is because it gradually resembles the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
for in the stage of the path of seeing, there is only the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
[Abhidharma] Śāstra.
However, because this stage of patience (*kṣānti*) reaches the point of immediate proximity [to the subsequent stage],
this clarifies that the objects of the three types of patience differ.
In the lower and middle patiences, one fully contemplates the eight truths— both superior and inferior— each possessing its four aspects (*ākāra*).
The highest patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) consists solely of one aspect of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) for one moment.
According to this principle, it is extended until there is no further distinction.
Commentary on the Categories:
The stages of Heat and Peak possess the contemplation of the eight truths and sixteen aspects,
because there is no distinction between these three positions.
Treatise:
This refers to the stage of medium patience within the designation [of the levels] attained by the yoga practitioner. Commentary: [End of section].
He gradually reduces his practice and reduces the objects of focus until he reaches the stage where he focuses on only one aspect of the Truth of Suffering within the Desire Realm for two moments.
This is called medium-grade patience (*madhyamā kṣānti*).

According to this treatise, it refers to each aspect (*ākāra*) and object (*ālambana*) of the noble truths, as well as the paths of antidote (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) for the realms of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
Because [the objects] are gradually reduced and abbreviated,
we know that while the lower patience (*kṣānti*) takes the upper [realms] as its object, each of the eight truths possesses four aspects (*ākāra*).
Once the Truth of the Noble Path (*mārga-satya*) pertaining to the form and formless realms has been reduced to one aspect or fewer, [the process continues].
This is called "intermediate patience.
When the practice of the path is reduced to its end, it is called "reducing the object of focus.
Next, one reduces the lower paths of the desire realm.
When one has thus reduced the objects and aspects of each of the three lower categories of suffering within the desire realm until only one aspect remains for two moments,
this is called "medium patience" (madhyā-kṣānti).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 5, states:
Furthermore, within the stage of patience (*kṣānti*),
one sometimes observes the noble truths through twelve aspects,
and at other times observes the noble truths through eight aspects.
Alternatively, it may be explained that at times one contemplates the Noble Truths by means of four aspects;
"at times twelve aspects" refers to excluding the four aspects of the Truth of the Path.
Sometimes there are eight aspects, consisting of four aspects each for the [truths of] Cessation and the Path;
sometimes there are four aspects. Regarding these aspects:
The aspects of cessation, abandonment, path, and origin each have four modes. Furthermore, it is explained that at times there are twelve modes, as one aspect is removed from each of the Four Truths;
or at times there are eight modes.
In each of the Four Truths, two modes of activity are excluded;
at times, four modes of activity are excluded;
in each of the Four Truths, three modes of activity are excluded.
Based on the second round of observation of form and so forth— excluding the Path—
in the *Saptasthāna-kuśala*,
this text serves as proof that the former interpretation is superior. If one relies on the latter explanation, there is no textual evidence to support it.
According to the text of the *Nyāyānusāra*,
the sevenfold skillfulness (*saptasthānakauśalya*) precedes the mindfulness of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛti*).
According to one master cited in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*:
In the paths of seeing and cultivation,
furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"In the contemplation of the seven bases, there are four knowledges regarding form."

The Dharma-knowledge and Subsequent-knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) regarding suffering are conventional (saṃvṛti). Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, impure knowledge (sāsrava-jñāna) that contemplates the truths is collectively termed conventional knowledge;
pure knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) that contemplates the truths is termed the knowledge of suffering, origination, and so forth.

According to the preceding text, proficiency in the seven points regarding the truths (*saptasthāna-kauśalya*) pertains to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 190, states:
"Question: What kind of person (*pudgala*), relying on the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā-carita*), enters the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*)?"
What kind of person enters the path of seeing by relying on the wishless?
Answer: It is one who practices according to the view who enters by practicing according to emptiness.
If one who practices through craving enters by means of wishlessness—
excluding only the Bodhisattvas—
it is explained that although they practice through craving, they enter by means of emptiness.
Because those whose conduct is dominated by views are attached to a self, they enter [the path] by means of emptiness;
because those whose conduct is dominated by craving are attached to existence, they enter by means of suffering and impermanence.
Because Bodhisattvas possess abundant compassion, they are said to be of "craving-conduct" (tṛṣṇā-carita).
In order to transform sentient beings, one does not weary of existence. Furthermore, there are two kinds of practitioners:
those who cling to the view of self enter by means of the practice of non-self, while those who cling to the view of "mine" enter by means of the aspect of emptiness.
Those who practice through craving are also of two kinds:

those in whom the conceit of "I am" (asmimāna) predominates enter by way of the aspect of impermanence, while those in whom indolence predominates enter by way of the aspect of suffering. Thus it is explained.
One discerns that the body is impermanent and does not give rise to pride out of self-reliance;
if one knows its characteristic of suffering, one applies diligence to seek liberation. — Master Guṇaprabha of the West.
Regarding the explanation of the reduction of the aspects:
for each of the eight truths, there are four aspects.
As their names indicate, they correspond in sequence and are mutually interconnected.
Just as one who is to enter the path of seeing at a later time by means of the aspect of impermanence under the truth of suffering of the desire realm,
first eliminates the aspect of non-self, proceeding from the end toward the beginning within its own truth.
Next is emptiness,
followed by suffering. If one intends to enter the path of vision through ascetic practices,
one must first eliminate the notion of non-self.
Next is emptiness,
followed by impermanence. If one intends to enter the path of seeing through the practice of emptiness,
one first eliminates the notion of non-self.
Next is suffering,
followed by impermanence. If one intends to enter the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) by means of "not-self," one first eliminates [the aspect of] emptiness.
Next is suffering,
and finally impermanence.
Since this is the case for the four aspects of the Truth of Suffering regarding the realm of desire, it is likewise so for the others.
The four aspects of the Truth of the Path mentioned above are likewise;
the remaining cases follow this same principle.
Fearing prolixity, they are not fully detailed here. The explanations provided by Guṇaprabha are excessively cumbersome and disorganized.
Since there is no scriptural evidence,
by what reasoning can it be known that they are necessarily interconnected? For example,
as in the case of the increase of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
Since one who practices the contemplation of non-self arises for the purpose of counteracting the notion of self,
what distinct reason is there for specifically arising the contemplations of detachment and so forth only with respect to cessation and the other [noble truths]?

Previously, was it not observed that the truths, such as cessation and so forth, are now explained as a single unit? When one contemplates the four truths through hearing and reflection, each individual truth possesses all four aspects (*ākāra*).
This follows the sequence of names, as in the case of the higher Truth of the Path and so forth.
That which arises later perishes first;
that which arises earlier diminishes later.
As for those whose view of self increases, they exclusively give rise to the notion of non-self.
The remaining three practices decrease accordingly;
the middle and superior levels of patience (*kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) follow this same single practice.
Thus, it is logically consistent that one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) by means of this very practice.
Commentary:
Because there is no interval from this stage and because it reaches the state of non-continuity,
it clarifies that one arises from Middle Patience (madhyakṣānti) to Superior Patience (adhimātrakṣānti).
The treatise states:
"Immediately following the highest degree of patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), it lasts for only a single moment;
this clarifies that the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) arises from the highest degree of patience."
Furthermore, it is explained that the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) and the superior patience (*adhimātrākṣānti*) share the same objects and modes of activity.
The treatise states: "Because this is contaminated (*sāsrava*), it reaches up to the supreme mundane dharma."
This is the explanation of the name. According to the treatise:
it is called "supreme" because one reaches it through the application of human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
This explains and resolves potential objections.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle three, states:
"Because this mind and its mental factors are preeminent over all other worldly phenomena, they are called 'foremost' (*agra*)."
Is it called "foremost" because it is superior to others?
If so, what is the fault?
If it were called "foremost" because it is superior to all [others], then...
How could this possibly surpass the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamaya*)?
However, the conventional knowledge cultivated at the conclusion of clear realization is an attendant of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
the wisdom of the path of seeing possesses particularly superior power.
This dharma is not like that.
Furthermore, how could this be superior to the mixed cultivation of the dhyānas?
Nevertheless, there are those meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the births they induce.
It is not shared with ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
whereas this dharma is not so.
Furthermore, how could this be superior to the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) cultivated at the time of the initial knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?
However, at the time of practicing that [other path], one is freed from all obstacles and the basis is purified;
this dharma is not like that.
Moreover, how could this possibly surpass the three samādhis— emptiness of emptiness, wishlessness of wishlessness, and signlessness of signlessness?
Yet even those [three] can still cause one to feel revulsion toward the Noble Path.
How much more so for that which is with outflows?
This dharma is not like that.
If it were called "foremost" merely because it is superior in certain respects, [then other dharmas would also deserve such a name].
The stages of Heat (ūṣmagata), Summits (mūrdhan), and Patience (kṣānti) should also be called "foremost," because each is superior to the wholesome roots of its respective lower stage.
Some have made this statement:
This dharma is called "foremost" because it is preeminent in every respect;
however, this is said in reference to its ability to open the gateway to the Noble Path,
and not with regard to everything.
This refers to conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) and so forth;
although they possess the superior qualities previously described,
they all lack the power to open the gateway to the Noble Path.
This dharma alone is capable;
therefore, it is entirely superior.
Some may say thus.
This dharma is called "foremost" because it excels all other matters;
that is to say, all superior matters, such as the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), are accomplished by means of this.
Why is this? If these sublime qualities did not exist, even the substance of the path that opens the gateway to the noble ones would not be cultivated,
let alone its superior function.
It is by means of this dharma that the gateway to the noble path is opened; only when one cultivates its essence does it possess superior efficacy.
Since all those excellent matters are accomplished through this, it is superior to all other things.
Other masters say:
"This dharma is called 'foremost' because it is superior in its division.
Question: If that were so, then *uṣmagata* and the others should also be called "foremost."
The answer is: because neither of those two parts is supreme.
That is to say, worldly wholesome dharmas generally comprise two parts:
first, those based on ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Second, regarding the noble ones:

although the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgra-dharma) are not called "supreme" with respect to the mundane conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and so forth of the noble ones, [they are so called in relation to other mundane states].

Because it is the most excellent among all the wholesome states attained by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is established as the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) alone. There is no commentary on this. Question: If that is so, regarding those who cultivate it in the future...
It cannot serve as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) to induce the arising of the Noble Path;
thus, it should not be considered primary. Answer: The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 2, states:
"Although it does not function as an equal-and-immediate condition..."
Because it is able to conform to and acquire what has already arisen;

for example, just as when a bhikṣu gives his consent (*chanda*) to the Saṃgha, other monastic affairs are also successfully established. Question: Do the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) conform to and transform matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*)?

Since that [state] does not function as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), how can it be designated as the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*)? The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, in its second response, states:
"Although it does not function as an equal-and-immediate condition..."
And it is able to conform [to them],
because that [object] arises simultaneously with this mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma).
One abiding,
one cessation,
and one fruit.
First, the outflow;
second, the maturation;
because of their proximity.
Treatise:
Thus, because [the factors] such as "Heat" (ūṣmagata) arise and manifest with increasing intensity,
this constitutes their essential nature (svabhāva).
It takes up co-existent dharmas,
excluding however their acquisitions (*prāpti*).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle three, states:
Question: Why is it that the fruits of śrāmaṇya are attained as the fruits of śrāmaṇya, yet the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgradharma) are not attained as the supreme mundane dharmas?
Answer: Because the fruits of śrāmaṇya are manifested through their actualization (pariniṣpatti).
The fruit of śrāmaṇya is attained as the fruit of śrāmaṇya because it is manifested by the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) of the "highest mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma).
Since that attainment (prāpti) is not itself an immediately preceding condition, [it does not constitute the fruit].
Furthermore, because they do not conform to those [stages] such as "arising" and so forth,
that attainment is not the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*);
likewise, the attainments of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), and Patience (*kṣānti*) are also not [the attainments of] Heat and so forth.
This is because one should not allow what has already been attained as noble to manifest again.
Some say that attainment (*prāpti*) is also the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). Other masters say:
Those acquisitions that arise simultaneously with it are the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*).
The critique states: whether they arise simultaneously with it or arise subsequently.
Because all [of these] are of the same nature as not being of the type of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*),
the same applies to Heat (*uṣmagata*) and the others.
Therefore, the initial explanation is correct.
Question: For what reason are arising and so forth [of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas] not themselves considered the Supreme Mundane Dharmas?
Answer: Because arising and so forth share the same fruit as those [Supreme Mundane Dharmas].
They proceed together without separation;
they are always in harmony, without priority or posteriority.
The characteristic and the characterized have never been separated from one another.
For this reason, it is also the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma);
yet it does not share the same fruit as that [supreme mundane] dharma,
nor does it function in association with it.
The nature and its characteristics are separate and do not coalesce;
whether preceding or following,
that which attains and that which is attained may at times be separated from one another.
For example, tree bark may sometimes be separated from the tree;

therefore, it is possible for [the stages of] Heat, Summits, and Patience to be attained even when they are not the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*). The *Nyāyānusāra* states: ...just as tree bark may at times be detached from the tree, so too it is possible for the attainments of Heat, Summits, and Patience to occur apart from the Supreme Mundane Dharmas. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* says:
However, since it is not admitted that the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and other stages can re-manifest once the Truths have been seen—
because for one who has already seen the Truths,
the manifestation of preparatory effort (*prayoga*) would be rendered useless— I shall now provide an explanation.
The preceding fruits are not subsumed under the subsequent paths of application (*prayoga-mārga*),
because there is no contradiction in principle regarding the attainment [of those fruits] arising after the path of application.
The stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth are the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for that noble path (*ārya-mārga*).
For it would contradict reason for the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and other stages to arise after the Path;
furthermore, one who has attained the Noble [Path] does not abandon the "Heat," which would entail the error of the "Heat" arising again after the fruit.
Upon attaining the fruit, one abandons the preceding stage; thereafter, there is no longer the attainment of the path of application.
Treatise:
herein, the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata) extends into the future.
Regarding the four clarities (*catvāri avabhāsāni*), at the initial stage of the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) one attains two aspects of cultivation;
because one advances the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) at this initial stage,
there is only the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that takes the three truths as its mixed object.
One cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness because one cultivates both general and specific contemplations of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Because one cultivates the aspects (*ākāra*) of one's own truths, they encompass all four aspects;
however, because there is no lateral cultivation, there are not sixteen aspects.
Regarding the Truth of Cessation, there is only the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that takes non-mixed objects as its focus,
because there is no [application of mindfulness] to the body, feelings, or mind.
Both types of cultivation consist solely of the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
Because one does not practice them incidentally, one does not cultivate the other truths or the four foundations of mindfulness.
The treatise states: "It is because one must reach this lineage before being able to cultivate them."
The commentary explains why [the term] "not cultivated alongside" is used, stating that "homogeneous" (sabhāga) means "identical in terms of the truths.
Treatise:
In the subsequent stage of advancement, one reaches the future sixteen [moments].
During the stages of advancement of Light (āloka) and Heat (uṣmagata), the formations are cultivated through practice.
This is because all three Truths possess form, sensation, mind, and mental factors.
It is not that one shifts from the initial stage;
rather, it is possible to manifest distinct contemplations of form, feeling, mind, and so forth.
Thus, it is said that one cultivates the present application of mindfulness in accordance with each moment.
Although one may concurrently cultivate the other truths and foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), they do not exceed four in number;

therefore, it says "four. Regarding the statement that when one aspect is cultivated in the present, sixteen aspects are cultivated in the future: this means that when any single aspect of the four foundations of mindfulness is currently being practiced, all sixteen aspects of the four truths are cultivated for the future.
This is because one practices the remaining truths concurrently.

Since there is no application of mindfulness other than that which takes the truth of cessation as its object, one cultivates the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna) in the present.
Because one cultivates the other truths as ancillaries, there are four future [applications of mindfulness].
Regarding the cultivation through practice, both the beginning and the end are identical to the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). Thus says the treatise.
Because one who possesses this lineage is also capable of cultivation,
this explains the reason for "attaining collateral cultivation" (*pārśva-bhāvanā*);
it may be understood according to the text.
Treatise:
From the initial placement of the feet at the summit (mūrdhan) up to the future sixteen [moments],
this clarifies the entry into the stage of the summit.
Because one first enters a distinct stage, the cultivation of practice consists solely of the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Since entering the stage does not differentiate among the modes of activity, one cultivates according to a single mode of activity. Regarding the statement "the four and sixteen of the future": [this refers to the fact that] while practicing one mode of activity, all four foundations of mindfulness and the sixteen aspects are cultivated as future attainments.
Because it permits concurrent cultivation,
and because the Four Truths are identical, they are explained together.
Treatise.
Later, when progressing to the future, there are sixteen;
it is permitted that these appear separately during the stage of progress.
Whichever single foundation of mindfulness is cultivated in the present, [it serves as the basis for all].
The four [immeasurables] of the future are explained as in the section on "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
They are explained separately because the three truths differ.
Treatise:
From the initial establishment of patience up to the future sixteen [moments],
this clarifies the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 188, states:
Question: Why is it that both the first and the last moments of *kṣānti* (receptivity) are all *dharmasmṛtyupasthāna* (application of mindfulness to phenomena)?
Answer: Because *kṣānti* is proximate to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), it resembles the Path of Seeing. [The commentary] states:
Indeed, all of them resemble the Path of Seeing.
Treatise:
However, regarding the advancement [of the path] until one no longer cultivates those aspects of practice—
within the stage of "clear" [insight], during the superior level of patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), one does not cultivate those aspects according to the reduction of the objects of focus.
The *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
that is to say, one who possesses the four conditions and fully cultivates the sixteen aspects.
If one takes three, two, or one as objects,
one cultivates twelve, eight, or four [factors] respectively.
Treatise.
Because the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) resemble the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*),
this clarifies the extent of the cultivation of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas;
for they resemble the Path of Seeing.
Because there is no cultivation of the distinct parts,
and because other practices are not cultivated.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says:
Question: Is it possible that while abiding for a single moment, one will attain the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) but not its object;

or will attain its object but not the Supreme Mundane Dharma; or will attain both the Supreme Mundane Dharma and its object; or will attain neither the Supreme Mundane Dharma nor its object? Answer: There is. When abiding in the stage of Superior Patience (*adhimātrākṣānti*), one should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*).
Furthermore, for one who enters the state of rightness and departure from birth by relying on the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-samādhi),

when abiding in superior patience (adhimātra-kṣānti), they shall attain the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgra-dharma). It is not the case that these [supreme mundane dharmas] do not have that same object of focus (ālambana).
This refers to those supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) included within the "not-yet-attained" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*).
Excluding those supreme mundane dharmas that take as their object the basis which is about to manifest,

all other supreme mundane dharmas that take remaining objects as their focus— these are the supreme mundane dharmas that will obtain as their objects things that are not themselves supreme mundane dharmas.
This refers to the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) subsumed within the five higher stages:
specifically, the supreme mundane dharmas that serve as the basis for what is about to manifest, as well as the supreme mundane dharmas that are about to be attained and their respective objects.

This refers to the case where, within the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgradharma) subsumed under the "not-yet-attained concentration" (anāgamya-samādhi), one takes as an object those supreme mundane dharmas that are about to manifest in the present; it does not refer to those supreme mundane dharmas that are not yet to be attained, nor to their objects.
This refers to those *agradharma*s (supreme mundane dharmas) subsumed under the five higher stages which take as their objects other domains,
excluding those *agradharma*s that serve as the basis for what is about to manifest immediately before one.
As it is with the *anāgamya* concentration, so it is with the other five stages. The commentary states:
This explains that when attaining the cultivation of the *laukikāgradharma*, there are differences regarding their objects of focus.
If one practices cultivation, it must take [the body] as its collective object.
As for "that which is relied upon," this refers to the body that serves as the basis for the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*);
since this is a body belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is also the object of focus.
It shall also be attained.
That which is the object of focus (*ālambana*) consists of all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Among these, that which serves as the basis (*āśraya*) is also that which shall be attained.

All other objects of focus are not attained [in this context], because all the *laukikāgradharmas* (supreme mundane dharmas) belonging to the same stage (*bhūmi*) and so forth can be cultivated, whereas those belonging to different stages and so forth are definitely not attained.
Question: Is it possible to possess the supreme mundane dharmas while not possessing the acquisition of their dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*)?

It can be answered in four propositions: 1. One who has accomplished the "highest mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) but has not accomplished the acquisition of its dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*).

This refers to one who, relying on a particular stage (*bhūmi*), has entered the state of rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) but has not yet abandoned the defilements (*kleśa*) of that stage. 2. One who has accomplished the acquisition of its dissociation but has not accomplished the "highest mundane dharma. This refers to one who has already abandoned the defilements of a stage but has not yet attained the "highest mundane dharma."

That is to say, if one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on a certain stage, and then, at the end of life, is born in a higher stage, they both accomplish the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgra-dharma) and accomplish the acquisition of the dissociation (visaṃyoga-prāpti) from that [stage].

That is to say: if one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on a particular stage, and having already become free from the defilements of that stage, dies and is reborn in a higher stage, then one neither possesses the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgra-dharma) nor possesses the acquisition of the dissociation from those [defilements].

That is to say, if one has not yet entered the stage of the certainty of correctness (samyaktva-niyāma) and still possesses the acquisition of the dissociation from outflows (āsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti) while remaining with a remainder of the basis (sopadhiśeṣa), one may speak as follows: Question: Is there any noble one (ārya)?

Is it possible to possess the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) while not possessing the acquisition of their dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*)? One should respond by establishing four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*). Regarding the case of possessing the supreme mundane dharmas but not possessing the acquisition of their dissociation: [this refers to one who has attained the first moment of the path of seeing but has not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm].

That is to say: if one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on a certain stage, yet has not yet abandoned the defilements of that stage, one possesses the acquisition of dissociation from them but does not possess the attainment of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgra-dharma).
That is to say, if one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on a particular stage,

and at the end of that life is reborn in the immediately higher stage, then while accomplishing the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgra-dharma), one also accomplishes the acquisition of the dissociation (visamyoga-prāpti) from those [defilements].
That is to say, if one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on a particular stage,

and having already become free from the defilements of that stage, dies without being reborn in a higher stage, then such a person neither possesses the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgra-dharma) nor possesses the acquisition of the dissociation (visamyoga-prāpti) from those defilements.
This refers to one who, relying on a particular stage (*bhūmi*), enters into the state of rightness and departure from corruption (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
and at the end of life, transcends the successive higher stages to be born in another higher stage;
such a person possesses all the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) with a remainder of the basis (*sopadhiśeṣa*).
And regarding all those acquisitions of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*), he spoke as follows:
"Is it possible that one who has attained the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*) might not have attained its acquisition of dissociation?"
It is answered in four statements. Regarding the first statement:
it refers to when one relies on the threshold concentration (anāgamya) or the first dhyāna.
One enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) in the intermediate dhyāna, yet has not yet abandoned the defilements of the first dhyāna. Regarding the second case:
it refers to when one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth by relying on this very stage.
The third case refers to one who, having passed away from that state, is reborn in a higher realm;

or one who, though not yet having attained the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), is reborn in the desire realm or the form realm after having already abandoned the defilements of the first *dhyāna*, or is reborn in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
This refers to one who, having entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on a particular stage,
leaves the defilements of the first dhyāna behind and dies without being reborn in a higher stage. As for the fourth alternative,
it refers to cases other than those previously described.
Treatise:
Having already distinguished the essential characteristics of the roots of goodness that have arisen,
the following three verses clarify the distinctions among those roots of goodness.
The Commentary says: "Up to the name 'Section on Ascertainment' (nirṇaya-bhāga)"—this is the first question.
[End of] Commentary.
"Decision" (nirṇaya) refers to the definitive determination of the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths;
this is the definition of the term "decisive analysis" (viniścaya).
Because the various noble paths are able to sever doubt, they are termed "definitive determination."
Because it is able to differentiate the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths, it is called "discrimination" (viveka).
This refers to the various paths of the noble ones (āryamārga), which are termed "thorough discernment" (nirṇaya). [Abhidharmakośabhāṣya]

"Stages" (bhūmi) refers to the names ranging from the stage of "provisioning" (sambhāra-bhūmi) to the stage of "definitive discernment" (nirvedha-bhāgīya). This explains the meaning of the term "stage.
All noble paths (āryamārga) are termed "definitive discernment" (nirvedha).
Since that which is conformed to here is exclusively the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), it is called a "part" (*bhāga*).
Therefore, these are named the "Aids to Penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Treatise:
These four serve as conditions leading up to the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*);
this explains the meaning of the term "conducive" (*anuloma*).
These four serve as conditions that induce a portion of discernment (*viniścaya*),
and because they can also be conducive to and beneficial for a portion of discernment,
these four types receive names corresponding to that [discernment].
Treatise:
Because these four types reach the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*),
this constitutes the second analysis of the three kinds of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because it is proximate to the Path of Seeing, it is neither hearing nor reflection. According to the treatise,
among the four [levels of application], the first two culminate specifically in the superior grade.
This is the third instance of dividing the chapters according to individual meanings;
it may be understood from the text as it stands. [End of] Treatise.
Because these four roots of goodness are abandoned through thorough knowledge (*parijñā*),
this constitutes the fourth clarification regarding their basis (*āśraya*).
These four roots of goodness have cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*) as their essential nature.
This is an attendant of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
for there is no cultivation (*bhāvanā*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
and there is no path of seeing in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Therefore, it does not extend to the desire realm or the formless realm;
furthermore, because the mind of the formless realm does not take the desire realm as its object, that which should first be fully known and abandoned in the desire realm [is not addressed there].
This further explains why the path of seeing does not exist in the formless realm.
Because desire must first be fully known and abandoned,
the path of seeing must necessarily take the desire realm as its object.
Since the formless realm does not take the desire realm as its object, there is no path of seeing therein.
Therefore, the desire realm is first fully known and abandoned.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Because it is the coarsest among the three realms."
Treatise:
These four roots of goodness reach the stage of "increasing the turning away from existence" (bhavavivardhana);
thus, the fifth [chapter] clarifies the fruit.
This section is not explicitly stated in the verse.
Regarding the basis for the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*), the treatise now explains *vipāka* (maturation). *Treatise:* [The text follows.]
The word "or" (*vā*) in the verse indicates that [the desire realm] reaches up to the seventh stage.
This explains the two characters "or seven" (*vā sapta*) in the verse.
[End of] Treatise.
These four roots of goodness extend up to the exclusion of Uttarakuru;
this sixth [section] clarifies the distinction of the physical bases upon which they rely.
Thus, the roots of goodness rely exclusively upon nine locations.
The *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
"It is based solely on the nine bodies of the desire realm,
for it is possible to enter the state of 'separation from birth' [the path of seeing] within them."
Treatise:
Because the first three roots of goodness last for only a single moment, this seventh [chapter] clarifies the initial and subsequent arising. As the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
Other masters say that if one has previously cultivated these four preparatory practices,
they will attain their first arising in all the heavenly realms; however, there is no formal evaluation [of this view].
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle seven, states:
Question: Why can [the path] not first arise among the gods?
Answer: Because in those realms there is no superior attention characterized by revulsion and so forth.

Question: Since there exist superior mental orientations such as revulsion and detachment within the intermediate state of the miserable realms (*apāya*), why do the roots of virtue not arise therein?
Answer: Because in the miserable realms, there is no superior physical basis (*āśraya*).
If there is a superior attention characterized by revulsion and so forth,
and if there is also a superior physical basis, then one is able to initiate it for the first time.
Because humans possess both, they are able to initiate it for the first time.
Treatise:
Because these four roots of goodness reach the state of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
this constitutes the eighth clarification regarding the distinct attainment [of the fruits] by men and women.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"These four roots of goodness depend exclusively upon males and females.
Regarding the first three, both males and females may attain both [the male and female forms]."
The fourth type of female body also attains two kinds [of roots].
This is so that it may not happen that, having later attained a male body, one fails to achieve the levels of heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth;
therefore, based on a male body, one attains only the wholesome roots of a male body.
Because a noble one does not become a woman again in subsequent lives,
whereas it is possible for those at the stages of Heat, Summits, and Patience to undergo a change of gender;
thus, these two bases serve as successive causes for the roots of goodness.
Regarding the fact that the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) based on a female body can serve as two causes:
this is because once a woman has attained the state of an Arya, there is the possibility of subsequently attaining a male body. As the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 7, states:
Question: Upon which body do these stages of Heat (uṣmagata), Peak (mūrdhan), Patience (kṣānti), and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) arise?
Answer: They arise upon the bodies of males and females.
Question: Can the Heat that arises upon a female body be attained by means of a female body?
Is it also the case that one attains the heat (*uṣmagata*) arising from the male body?
Answer: Yes, one does.
Just as one attains the heat [in general].
The same applies to the attainment of the Summits (*mūrdhan*) and Patience (*kṣānti*).
Question: Does one who, based on a male body, attains the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) arising from a male body, also attain the "Heat" arising from a female body?
Answer: Yes, it is attained.
Just as one attains *ūṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, so too does one attain *kṣānti*.
The warmth that arises in a female body with respect to a female body is also obtained;
it is both present in the body and accomplished,
and it is also manifested.
The heat obtained within a male body is not established within that body,
nor does it manifest.
As it is said regarding the stage of Heat (ūṣmagata),
so it is for the Summits (mūrdhan) and Patience (kṣānti). Heat that arises in a male body from a male body is both present in the body and accomplished.
It also manifests before one; however,
while the "heat" (ūṣmagata) attained regarding a female body arises,
it is not established within that body.
It does not manifest before one.
As it is said regarding "Heat" (ūṣmagata), so it is for "Summits" (mūrdhan) and "Patience" (kṣānti).
The "Heat" produced by a female body serves as the cause for the "Heat" produced by a female body.
The heat generated by a male body also serves as a cause for [the subsequent stages].
As it is said regarding heat, so it is for the summits and the patiences.
The heat generated by a male body serves as a cause for the heat generated by a male body.
It does not take as its cause the heat produced by a female body.
Why is this? Because that which is superior cannot have that which is inferior as its cause.
Because they are inferior.
As it is said regarding "Heat" (ūṣmagata), so it is for "Summit" (mūrdhan) and "Patience" (kṣānti). Now, examining the three treatises, these are the first three roots of goodness.
Both men and women each obtain two [results],
as their roots of goodness are identical.
This is according to the *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Abhidharmakośa*.
It is said that the fourth [type], the female body, also possesses two kinds;
thus we know this refers to those of many paths (*bahumārga*). If it were a single path (*ekamārga*), [it would not be so].
That path is one and the same.
Because it relies upon a male body, it is called the path relying upon a male body;
because it relies upon a female body, it is called the path relying upon a female body.
The "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma) attained based on a female body can only be attained based on a female body;
it cannot be attained based on a male body.
How can it be called "the path based on a male body"?
Since it is stated that both [genders] attain it,
we know that, like the *Vibhāṣā*, it is not a single path.
However, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* and the *Nyāyānusāra* differ regarding their causes;
their intentions are distinct.
This is because the *Nyāyānusāra* composes its treatise by taking the Noble Path and so forth as its primary cause.
This explains their mutual causality.
For example, the noble path serves as a mutual cause for both male and female,
as do other contaminated states such as the wisdoms arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Furthermore, innate wholesome states, defiled dharmas, and so forth,
all serve as mutual causes for both males and females;
it is not said that they depend on the inferiority of women.
For what reason are the four wholesome [roots] described as "inferior"?
Therefore, one does not adopt the interpretation of the *Vibhāṣā* regarding their being mutual causes.
The *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā* are not the only sources; some offer three interpretations that are unskillful and remain as if uncomprehended.
Fearing prolixity, I shall not describe them here—they can be understood by reading them side-by-side. However, according to the *Vibhāṣā*, [the author] mostly follows the Sautrāntika school.
Arhats and others generate the Path based on a single body;
they attain the cultivation of the Path in nine bodies of the desire realm.
Because the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding those bodies has not been attained, they do not cultivate the Path that depends upon them.
Now, since both treatises maintain that a sage does not perform the act of becoming a woman,
the implication that one cannot attain the "highest mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma) as a woman is difficult to understand.
Because Master Shen [Sengzhao] deviated from this principle,
he uses the term "attainment" (得) here rather than "cultivation" (修).

For what reason are the seven knowledges (*jñāna*) said to repeatedly perceive the principle of the truths (*satyadharma*), and why are they included within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) rather than the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?
