The Treatise says: Those who reach the highest point are called "Upstreamers" (ūrdhva-srotas).
There are seven types of Non-returners (anāgāmin).
For now, I shall list the five names and provide a brief explanation of these five names.
This can be understood according to the text.
The treatise states: "One who attains parinirvāṇa upon arrival" refers to one who attains parinirvāṇa as soon as they arrive [at the intermediate state].

This explains "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarāparinirvāyin*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "As for the term 'one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state'..."
This refers to a certain class of persons who have attained non-analytical cessation regarding the fetters of birth,
but not so regarding the fetters of arising.
When he is oppressed by the conditions of affliction within the desire realm,
he is able to exert himself to cultivate the superior application for abandoning the remaining fetters; however,
before his application is complete, he encounters the condition of death.
Thereupon, his life came to an end.

Due to the power of the active fetters (*saṃyojana*), he experienced the form-realm intermediate state (*rūpāntarābhava*); this was because he felt aversion toward the many sufferings [of that realm].
Relying on the path previously generated, they advance to sever the remaining fetters, become arhats, and attain parinirvāṇa.

... up to ... those who, upon passing away from the desire realm, undergo the intermediate existence of the form realm and then attain parinirvāṇa, receive the name "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyin).
It is not that they pass away from the form realm.
For what reason is it that a learner who has not yet abandoned sensual desire does not attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state?
The intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) in the desire realm has a body that is extremely weak;
because it lacks the capacity for manifold activities,
it is difficult even to transcend the phenomena of the desire realm while abiding in its state of fundamental existence (*pūrvakālabhava*).
How much more so for one who, while in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), can transcend the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to attain the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*);
such a person performs many deeds,
namely, transcending the three realms (*tridhātu*).
Furthermore, one can permanently sever the two kinds of afflictions and simultaneously attain the realization of the second or third fruit of śrāmaṇya;
however, while abiding in the intermediate state (antarābhava), such capacity does not exist. Moreover, in this intermediate state, one may attain parinirvāṇa.
Only the noble paths belonging to this specific stage arise;
for one who attains parinirvāṇa while in the state of the first dhyāna stage.
Only the fundamental dhyānas of their own respective stages give rise to the manifestation of the noble path;
it does not arise from the *anāgamya* or the intermediate (*dhyānāntara*) states, because it is difficult to bring [the noble path] into manifestation therein.

In the state of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), because the physical basis is extremely weak, only those [mental states] that are easily aroused can manifest. Furthermore, this applies only to the transition from death in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to birth in the intermediate existence of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
One who attains parinirvāṇa does not pass away from the form realm to be reborn in the form realm,
because within the form realm there are no calamities.
If one in the state of existence prior to birth cannot attain nirvana due to other obstructing conditions,
the same applies to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Treatise.

The term "attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (upapadyaparinirvāyin) refers to the state of having a remainder of the substratum of existence (sopadhiśeṣa); this explains attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth. Attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) includes both the state with a remainder of the substratum and the state without a remainder of the substratum (nirupadhiśeṣa).

According to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth possess only the remaining basis (nirmāṇakāya). Regarding those said to be "attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*):
This refers to a certain class of persons who,
due to having previously performed and accumulated karma conducive to rebirth, [attain existence].
Having passed away from the desire realm and taken birth in the form realm,
because he possesses the path of swift progress through diligent cultivation,
he becomes an arhat not long after being born.
One attains parinirvāṇa only at the exhaustion of one's lifespan;

it is in reference to this state of having a remainder of support (sopadhiśeṣa) that one is said to be "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (upapadyaparinirvāyin), rather than attaining parinirvāṇa without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa) immediately after being born.
Because he lacks mastery over the relinquishing of his life-span; according to this treatise,
a similar explanation is likewise provided for those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth.
Since this is not explained as "attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarāparinirvāyī*),

we know that one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state does so by attaining parinirvāṇa without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*) immediately after having attained existence with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*).
Treatise:
Other masters say that it is because [the mind] has not yet attained mastery;
this refutes the assertions of those other teachers.
Treatise:
There are those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion because they do not possess the path of swift progress;
this explains "with exertion."
Because one must practice the path with diligent effort for this reason, it is called "with exertion" (*sābhisaṃskāra*).
Furthermore, because there is no path of rapid progress, it follows after "attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarāparinirvāyin*) in the treatise.
The one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin) is so called because they proceed by means of the path of swift progress;
this explains "without exertion.
Although they lack swift progress, they are the same as those with exertion (sābhisamskāra).
Because there is no cultivation through effort, it follows after the stage of "with application.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"That is to say, if a certain class of person, while previously in the desire realm, relies on the power of samādhi through uninterrupted application..."
Having severed the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of non-returning,
they are subsequently reborn in the form realm; after spending a long period there,
they are further able to cultivate the path of the aforementioned type and attain arhatship.
One is called "attaining parinirvāṇa with exertion.
One who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion is the opposite of this.
The Treatise states: "Some say that because these two [extremes] lead to excessive faults,
[the author] refutes the divergent views."
Since all seven types of non-returners attain nirvana by taking those conditioned and unconditioned phenomena as their object,
they should all be designated as "with effort" (sābhisaṃskāra) and "without effort" (anabhisaṃskāra).
For this reason, it is said that there is the fault of over-extension.
However, in the sūtras, [the teachings] accord with reason.
This is an evaluation and adoption of the Sautrāntika school's position. The treatise states:
there is a path of swift progress that leads directly to parinirvāṇa.
To explain the meaning of the Sautrāntika school:
those with sharp faculties who practice without effort but possess a path of rapid progress should come first;
those with dull faculties who practice with effort but lack a path of rapid progress should come later.

Because those who attain [nirvana] without exertion or effort do so swiftly, they should come first; because those who attain it with exertion and great effort are dull-witted, they should come later.
Those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadya-parinirvāyin) attain the most rapid progress and the supreme grade of the path.

Prior to the "without exertion" (asaṃskāra-parinirvāyin), the "with exertion" (sasaṃskāra-parinirvāyin) was previously combined with the "attaining parinirvāṇa in this life" (upapadya-parinirvāyin) and placed later.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"However, there is a sūtra that says the 'without exertion' comes first."
Furthermore, there are also sutras that first state that conditioned formations exist;
since time itself is not distinct [from them],
there is no contradiction in whichever [explanation] is given.

Because there is practice that is worthy of honor, I have spoken of it first. According to this treatise, those with practice (*sābhisamskāra*) and those without practice (*anabhisamskāra*) follow after those who attain parinirvāṇa upon birth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*).
Thus, when these two are compared to one another, their sequence is not fixed.
Treatise:
To say "one who goes upstream" (ūrdhvasrotas) refers to one who attains parinirvāṇa only upon reaching [the highest realm];
this explains the one who goes upstream.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a general explanation;
second, a detailed explanation.
This passage provides a general explanation: the term "one who goes upstream" (ūrdhva-srotas) carries the meaning of "moving upward.
Although those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarā-parinirvāyin) are born in the higher realms, [they do not proceed further].
Since they attain parinirvāṇa in that very place of birth and do not ascend further,
according to the meaning of "upward movement" (ūrdhvasrotas), those such as the "one who attains nirvāṇa upon birth" (upapadyaparinirvāyin) are not called "upward-streamers."
If one born in the form realm necessarily transmigrates upward to higher levels,
they are all termed "Upstreamers" (ūrdhvasrotas),
because they possess an upward movement.
Commentary:
Because this very "one who flows upwards" (ūrdhvasrotas) reaches the ultimate limit,
it is divided into two types.
There are two types of those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*), distinguished by their causes and fruits.
That is to say, they differ because of distinctions in their meditative absorption (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and pleasure (*sukha*). Regarding the distinction by cause:
those who go upstream through pleasure and wisdom possess the mixed cultivation of meditative absorption (*vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna*).

Regarding the distinction by way of the fruit: those who proceed upward through delight and possess wisdom (prajñā) are born in Akaniṣṭha, but not in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu). Those who proceed upward through meditative concentration (samādhi) without having practiced the mixed cultivation of dhyāna (miśrabhāvanā) [are born in the formless realm].

Those who delight in meditative concentration are born in the higher realms as "upward-streamers" (ūrdhvasrotas) and reach the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), but they are not born in the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa).
This is because it is stated that those two heavens constitute the ultimate limit.
It is also possible to be reborn in the lower Pure Abodes or the Formless Realm;
for if it were not so, one could not be reborn in the four lower Pure Abodes or the three lower Formless Realms.
There should be no Arhat who is a "half-leaper.
The treatise states:
this refers to one who attains parinirvāṇa only after reaching a dhyāna.
This is the first explanation regarding those who ascend to the higher realms through the joy of wisdom (*prajñā*).
The treatise states: "Furthermore, there are differences based on whether they reach the 'pervasive exhaustion' (*sarvacyuta*)."
The opening of joy and wisdom constitutes the third [type of attainment].
This refers to the full leap, the half-leap, and the disappearance at every stage.
Treatise:
The term "complete transcendence" (sakṛd-utkrāntaka) refers to the meaning of complete transcendence;
this explains the first [type of non-returner] and is consistent with the *Nyāyānusāra*.
The treatise states: "Regarding 'half-leaping,' it refers to reaching the Single Guide.
This explains the second [type].
This is consistent with the *Nyāya*.
The treatise states that it is called "universal dissolution" (*saṃvarta*) because [the world] reaches [that state].
This concludes the third explanation,
which accords with the *Nyāyānusāra*.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 174, states:

Question: It is said that one who falls back from and dwells in the first dhyāna is born in the Brahmakāyika heaven, where they may become a "full-leaper," a "half-leaper," or one who "vanishes everywhere" and proceeds upstream.
If such a person falls back from and dwells in the second dhyāna, they are born in the Parīttābha heaven.
Falling back from the third dhyāna, one is reborn among the Śuddhāvāsa devas;
falling back from the fourth dhyāna, one is reborn among the Anabhraka devas and so forth.

Can such a person also become one who "leaps entirely" (aśakṣepaka), one who "leaps halfway" (ardhapluta), or one who "dies in all places" (sarvasthānacyuta) as an upstream-bounder (ūrdhvasrotas)? Some say that they cannot.
Because they are born in the Brahma-world,
and because there is no deficiency regarding the places where they should be reborn higher up without returning,
one establishes [the categories of] "complete leaping over," "half-leaping over," and "vanishing from all places" based upon that.
If one were to fall back and be reborn in a higher realm, the [leap-over] would be deficient;
therefore, the "complete leap-over" (*atyantātyaya*) and other such attainments are not established based on that.
Some say that it may also be called a "half-leap-over" (*ardhapluta*), because it leaps over a small portion of the intermediate realms. Others say it may also be fully designated by all three names.

That [text] states that when one passes away from the desire realm, wherever one is reborn, it can be designated as "complete leaping," "half-leaping," or "passing away in all places" with respect to that very place of rebirth above.
Question: If a non-returner passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the formless realm, [how is this categorized]?

Can one also achieve the "complete leap-over" (*atyantapluta*) and so forth? Some say it cannot; some say that it may also be called "half-leap-over" (*ardhapluta*); others say that it also possesses all three names.
The reasons for this are all as explained previously. Although there is no evaluative commentary [on these views],
the latter two explanations are correct,
because they encompass all persons.
Furthermore, those above that do not reach the Akaniṣṭha heaven and so forth are likewise subsumed within these three;
those below that do not originate from the First Dhyāna are likewise subsumed within these.
In this context, it is further stated that they "surpass" [the lower realms];
there is no logical error in this.
If one has already been reborn in a higher realm, then [surpassing] those below is possible.
Thus, it is simply called "half-leaping.
If one speaks only of being born in a higher place,
there is also the sense of "complete leaping."
Since there are those who undergo universal dissolution as well as those who leap over half,
we know that they must have previously attained the mixed cultivation within the desire realm.
Those born later in the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) may also attain it after six or seven births;
due to prior habituation, they subsequently initiate the mixed cultivation (*miśrabhāvanā*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
Regarding the term "pervasive dissolution" (sarvavyāpin):
it refers to being born in all places within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) because of the abundance of attachment to its sensory gratification (*āsvāda*).
Because throughout all sixteen locations within the four dhyāna stages,
each possesses an inferior degree of relish for the flavor [of meditative attainment],
which serves as the condition for the arising of rebirth.
Having passed away from each and every location among the Brahmakāyika devas,
they proceed until reaching the Akaniṣṭha heaven before finally attaining parinirvāṇa; therefore, this is called "universal passing away."
Based on this principle,
the abode of Mahābrahmā within the first dhyāna is not a separate location;
rather, it is subsumed under the second Brahmakāyika heaven.
If it were otherwise,
[the Brahma world] would be a place of biased views where Mahābrahmā resides,
and there would be only a single teacher.
There can certainly be no noble one (ārya) taking birth therein;
otherwise, there would be no distinction between those who pass away completely (sarvasthānacyuta) and those who leap over half (ardhapluta). [Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya] Commentary.
There are none who do not attain the stage of Non-returner, let alone those born in the lower realms.
This explanation of the meaning of "Non-returner" is the same as that in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Treatise:
It should be understood that this refers to those who have reached parinirvāṇa;
it is the conclusion regarding the wisdom of bliss.
The treatise states: Others attain parinirvāṇa only upon reaching dhyāna;
this explains the bliss of meditative concentration.
Treatise:
Because there is a distinction regarding the extent of their ascent among the two types of *ūrdhvasrotas*,
the two names are explained.
Treatise:
Regarding the two types of "Upstreamers" (ūrdhvasrotas), they reach at most seven more births.
This explains the two types of Upstreamers who have not yet reached Akaniṣṭha Heaven or the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
All of these include those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
For example, one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state after being born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna heavens is included within the category of "half-leapers" (ardhapluta).
Although there is no skipping of stages,
it is also called "half-leaping" because one transcends birth.
Treatise:
These five are called those who proceed to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
This concludes the summary of those who proceed to the form realm.
Treatise:
Because there are distinctions among those who practice the formless [attainments],
this explains the meditative absorptions of bliss.
There are four such distinctions.
That is to say: those who attain parinirvāṇa upon birth, those with effort, those without effort, and those who go upstream.
According to this treatise, there are two distinct types of those who proceed to the realm of form.
First, those who attain the mixed cultivation are born in the five Pure Abodes.
Second, those who do not attain the mixed cultivation are born in the Form Realm and subsequently take birth in the Formless Realm. Regarding those who practice the formless:
having already become free from attachment to form while within the Desire Realm, they are born in the Formless Realm.
This refers to two types of those who delight in meditative concentration:
first, those who, having been born in the form realm, are subsequently born in the formless realm;
second, those who, without being born in the form realm, are born directly in the formless realm.
Commentary:
This, together with the preceding five, makes six; together with the preceding six, they become seven.
This concludes the enumeration of the seven.
These are: first, one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; second, one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth;
and third, one who attains parinirvāṇa through application.
Fourth, those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion;
fifth, those who ascend through the form realm;
sixth, those who ascend through the formless realm.
There are seven types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*). If one adds those who undergo rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), there are eight kinds.
If one divides those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life into two, there are nine kinds.
If one is not reborn in the form realm, even though there is a subsequent birth, it is still called "attaining parinirvāṇa in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*).
Alternatively, it may be divided into two types. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Alternatively, one should establish nine types of non-returners in total;
that is, those who attain nirvana in the present life are divided into two kinds:
first, those who have already well-discerned the noble intent in a prior stage.
Second, being able to discern [the truth] well at the time of death; these constitute eight types in total.
Adding the case of rebirth, there are nine types. Regarding "rebirth," it refers to one who has already attained the stage of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) in a previous life.
Or, one who is a once-returner may only attain the fruit of non-returning within this very life;
the aforementioned term "parinirvāṇa in the present" refers exclusively to the present life.
Regarding those who first attain entry into the noble state and proceed to nirvāṇa:
the treatise states that among the five types of non-returners (anāgāmin) who practice within the form realm (rūpadhātu), [this refers to the first].
The following verse explains the second point:
the clarification of the nine types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
The treatise states: "...up to the point where there are distinctions."
This section distinguishes the non-returners (anāgāmin) into three types:

namely, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin), those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin), and those who ascend to higher realms (ūrdhvasrotas). Thus says the treatise.
How is it that these three types are distinguished by their manifestation through arrival at the encounter?
This section distinguishes the *antarāparinirvāyin* (one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state) into three varieties. Treatise.
From "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth" up to the term "birth-attainer" (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*),
this section divides the birth-attainers into three distinct types.
[End of] Treatise.
Because there are distinctions among those who proceed upward (*ūrdhvasrotas*),
this category of *ūrdhvasrotas* is divided into three types.
Treatise.
However, among these three types, there is no loss of non-confusion;
herein, "swift" refers to one who enters parinirvāṇa immediately upon birth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

"Not swift" refers to the intermediate [attainment], while "after a long duration" refers to the subsequent [attainment]. Among those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, attaining it immediately upon being born is "swift";
those who practice with effort are "intermediate."
The absence of practice is the last; among those who go upstream, the full-leaper is the fastest,
the half-leaper is next,
and the one who dies everywhere is the slowest.
Commentary:
These three types differ according to the duration they persist;
this clarifies the division into the nine causes.
Treatise:
Furthermore, they are collectively established as three because of the distinctions among the faculties (*indriya*).
This collective division into three is due to three causes.

Only those who initiate karma in this life attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*). Those who initiate both the karma for birth and the karma for existence attain parinirvāṇa upon being born (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*).

Those who initiate the karma for birth, the karma for existence, and subsequent karma are those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*). Furthermore, those whose afflictions are moderate attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Those with medium-level afflictions are those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth;

those with superior-level afflictions are those who go upstream. Furthermore, those with superior faculties are those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, while those with medium faculties are those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth.
Regarding those of dull faculties who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*):
the treatise states that these three [types] each reach nine distinct categories, totaling twenty-seven.
This clarifies the three groups of nine.
The intermediate parinirvāyins are divided into three based on differences in their faculties and afflictions.
Their karma is identical,
because that which is unarisen gives rise [to existence].
Furthermore, the three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) also possess three varieties based on their faculties and afflictions.
It is not due to karma alone,
because they equally possess arising, birth, and karma.
The latter three are fully possessed by afflictions, karma, and faculties.
The faculties (indriya) and afflictions (kleśa) may be understood as before.
Regarding the three types of karma,
the "complete leap" (atyantātyaya) involves only karma to be experienced in a subsequent life (aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karma) within a single lifetime.
In the case of "half-leapers," there is a greater proportion of karma to be experienced in subsequent lives;
in all cases of "falling from the summit," there is the greatest proportion of karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
Therefore, it is said that they are divided into three types based on the distinctions among karmas to be experienced in subsequent lives. The concluding summary is clear.
Treatise:
If that is so, for what reason do there appear even a single verse among the various sūtras?
Third, the explanation of the seven destinations of the noble person (*saptasatpuruṣagati*).
The treatise says: "Up to this point, they are established as one;
this enumerates the number seven."
Within the "born" category, there are two types, each with three sub-types, making six;
adding the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas) completes the previous total of seven.
[Abhidharma-kośa] Śāstra.
Why is it that [the discussion] relies solely on this up to the stage of the learner (śaikṣa)?
This is the question.
Why is it that only the non-returner (anāgāmin) is established as having seven destinations of the noble person (satpuruṣagati)?
The "path of the noble person" (satpuruṣagati) is not established based on prior fruits.
According to the treatise, "gati" has the meaning of "going"; it does not apply in the same way to merely reaching another state.
This is the first answer.
"Gati" (destiny) has the meaning of "going.
Because those who do not return (anāgāmin) practice only wholesome deeds, it is called the "destiny of the virtuous person" (satpuruṣagati).
Although those in the two preceding paths and fruits perform wholesome karma,
they also possess unwholesome states and are thus no different from ordinary worldlings;
for this reason, they do not receive the designation of "fortunate rebirths."
Treatise:
Furthermore, it is only up to the seven types that the "destinies of the superior person" (*satpuruṣagati*) are established;
this is the second interpretation.
The former refers to "good destinations" (*sugati*) in terms of practicing wholesome deeds;
this refers to "good destinations" in terms of upward progression.
Only those who have attained the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) proceed exclusively upward.
They no longer return to the lower realms;
those who previously headed toward the fruits of the path were all reborn here from the desire realm.
Although those who have only one interval remaining have only one more birth,
it may be either upward or downward;
it is not exclusively an upward rebirth.
Therefore, it is not called the "destination of the virtuous person" (*satpuruṣagati*). Of the two explanations, the latter is superior.
If merely practicing virtue were to constitute the "good destination," then those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) would also be [considered] as such, since they too practice only virtue.
Why is it not grasped?
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 175, states:
"Question: Just as arising and non-arising each have three types..."
The same applies to those who go upstream (ūrdhvasrotas), namely: those who leap entirely (pluta), those who leap halfway (ardhapluta), and those who vanish in every place (sarvasthānacyuta).
Why are they explained together as one? Answer: Birth and non-birth each constitute a single continuity of existence (bhava-saṃtati).
Within this, the distinctions between the various stages are difficult to discern;
therefore, three types are explained for each in order to make them known.
The three types of *ūrdhva-srotas* (those who ascend) are distinguished by their own respective numbers of births.
The distinctions are easy to understand;

therefore, following the superior meaning of the preceding [explanation], they are combined and explained as one type. Furthermore, since birth and non-birth are limited to a single brief period, regarding the meaning of their distinctions, there is only so much that can be easily established.
Therefore, it is divided into three;
as for those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*), there are many distinctions regarding their long duration,
making their boundaries difficult to discern.

that is to say, they previously resided in the lineage of those resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and practiced the meditative absorptions in a mixed manner (vyavakīrṇadhyāna).

they ride upon the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) that can be cultivated in a mixed sequence of preceding and succeeding stages;

Clarifying the Prior and Subsequent Arisings. Question: What dharma constitutes the essence of this mixed cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)? Answer: The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) constitute its essence.

this records a divergent opinion.

thus, up to the predominance of wisdom, one is reborn in the subsequent Pure Abodes.

Is the perception of the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens due to the power of karma,
or is it due to the power of mixed cultivation?
If it were due to the power of karma,
then the mixed cultivation of dhyāna would be in vain; if it were due to the power of mixed cultivation, [then karma would be irrelevant].
This contradicts what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*, which says:
"By means of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna and by means of karma."
One is born in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.

The treatise states: The Sūtra says that among the Non-returners (anāgāmin), there is one named "Body-witness" (kāyasākṣin).
The second half of the verse explains the seventh type: the body-witness non-returner (*kāyasākṣin anāgāmin*).
The treatise states: they are called "body-witnesses" because they have personally realized [the cessation of suffering].
That is to say, the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) is endowed with the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa).
Because one has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) within the body, one is further designated as "one who has realized through the body" (kāyasākṣin).
Because one realizes through the body a state resembling nirvana, one is called a "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin).
The treatise asks:
Why is it said that such a person is merely named a body-witness?
Question:
Why is it said that this is not called "realization by mind" (cittasākṣātkriyā),
but is instead called "realization by body" (kāyasākṣātkriyā)?
Treatise:
Because the mind does not exist [independently] and arises in dependence upon the body. Answer:
Because the mind does not exist [in this state], it is not called "realization by mind";
because the attainment of cessation arises based on the physical body, it is called "realization by body.
(Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra 53).
Question: For what reason is one called a "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin)?
Answer: Because one has personally realized the eight liberations with the body, yet has not exhausted all outflows (āsrava) through wisdom, one is called a body-witness.
Question: Why is one called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñā-vimukta)?
Answer: Because such a person has exhausted all outflows (āsrava) through wisdom, yet has not yet personally realized the eight liberations (aṣṭa-vimokṣa) with the body.
Treatise:
In truth, it should be stated that [it is so called] because the body reaches tranquility.
This is the Master’s correct preceding explanation.
In truth, it should be stated that when those non-returners emerge from the meditative attainment of cessation for the first time,
they attain a previously unattained state of mind consisting solely of consciousness, while the body remains tranquil.
He then reflects thus: "This meditative attainment of cessation is most tranquil;
it closely resembles nirvāṇa."
Thus, because one realizes the tranquility of the body through wisdom born of reflection and the body itself, it is called "bodily realization" (kāyasākṣin).
This is because one attains and realizes the tranquility of the body through its actualization.
Furthermore, because one realizes the tranquility of the body through the manifestation of wisdom,
it is called "bodily realization" (kāyasākṣin).
Treatise:
The Sūtra speaks of "attainment" (prāpti) but does not speak of "bodily realization" (kāyasākṣitva).
This is the question.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"It is said that the Blessed One addressed Anāthapiṇḍada, saying:

There are two kinds of fields of merit:
first, those in training (śaikṣa);
second, those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
There are eighteen types of those in training (*śaikṣa*), and only nine types of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). What are the eighteen? They are:

the four candidates for the fruits, the three who have attained the fruits, those practicing by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those practicing by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), those attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), those who go from family to family (*kulaṅkula*), those with only one interval remaining (*ekavīcika*), those attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), those attaining parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), those attaining parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), and those who ascend to the higher realms (*ūrdhvasrotas*). As for the nine types of those beyond training: [they are] the Arhat, the one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), the one liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), the body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*), the one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), the one attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), the one with few desires (*alpeccha*), the one contented (*saṃtuṣṭa*), and the forest-dweller (*āraṇyaka*).
The six types of lineage, those of non-retrogression, those liberated by wisdom, and those liberated both ways.
Treatise:
From the absence of causes up to the explanation of the distinctions among those in training (*śaikṣa*).

Answer: Based on the cause—the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*)—one establishes the persons who are in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). [This applies to] the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
It is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Because it is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), it is not a cause.
Although the "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*) is established as a distinct individual, [it is not a cause].
Because they lack a supporting cause,
the Buddha did not specifically designate them as fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
Because the Buddha perceives those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
and because they possess excellence through their abandonment [of defilements] and their faculties,
they are able to produce superior fruits and are thus called "fields of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*).
However, because the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) attained by non-returners (anāgāmin) is still with outflows (sāsrava),
it cannot be said to be "pure" on the basis of its being naturally liberated (svabhāva-vimukta);
for the physical body upon which it relies still possesses afflictions that have not been permanently severed.
One cannot say that they are called "pure" because of their liberation through the continuity [of the path];

therefore, the status of being a field of merit for those in training (*śaikṣa*) is not established based on the accomplishment of that [purity]. As for the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) merits existing in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), [they do not constitute such a field].
Although it is not subsumed under liberation by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vimukti*),
it is called "purified" because it is liberation through the continuity of the stream (*saṃtāna-vimukti*);
for this reason, it is also able to produce sublime fruits.

Therefore, based on convention and the distinctions among the faculties, it is said that all nine fruits of asceticism are called fields of merit. The commentary states: For this reason, those in training (śaikṣa) do not attain the realization through the body (kāyasākṣin), whereas those beyond training (aśaikṣa) attain both types of liberation (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).
The treatise states:

The Commentary states: "Up to the candidate for Arhatship" clarifies the fourth candidate.
From the abandonment of the afflictions of the first dhyāna up to the ninth uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,

the ninth uninterrupted path is specifically designated as the Diamond-like Samādhi (vajropama-samādhi).
This is why it is stated that [the path] reaches up to the eighth stage.

This explains the name of the concentration.
This concentration is firm and sharp;
it is likened to a vajra.
Because there is not a single latent tendency (*anuśaya*) that cannot be destroyed;
since they have already been destroyed previously, it is not the case that all are destroyed [simultaneously].
This is just as a great light can destroy subtle darkness.
It is also capable of destroying the coarse, not merely the subtle.
If it were a minor light, it would have already destroyed [the coarse] beforehand;
thus, it would destroy only the subtle and not the coarse.
Among all afflictions, the ninth grade of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation within the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the most subtle and difficult to sever.
Since this uninterrupted path has already severed these afflictions, [the subsequent path arises].

Therefore, it is known that among all paths of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*), this path of uninterrupted realization is called the most supreme. Question: Among the nine stages of the afflictions to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), these too are the most subtle.

The Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) is capable of severing [afflictions] and should be compared to a vajra. Answer: Since those nine grades of afflictions can be severed by a single grade [of the path], it is known that the power of those afflictions is weak and inferior.
Since the Path of Seeing serves as the antidote for such inferior afflictions, it is used as a metaphor.
One knows that this is not capable of destroying all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
If it possessed such power to destroy them, then at the moment the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) arises, [they would be destroyed].
Since what obstacle prevents it from destroying the remaining afflictions,
it does not receive the name "diamond-like" (vajropama).
Furthermore, among all the afflictions, there is none that is easily severed without an object.
The Path of Seeing counteracts those [defilements],
but it is known not to be the ultimate;
for this reason, the name "diamond-like" (vajropama) is not established for it.
Treatise:
The diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) extends through all nine stages;
this clarifies that there are many types of concentrations.
This concentration is attained through the four types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-dharma-jñāna*).
Among these six knowledges, any one may be present;
likewise, any one of the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) may be present.
However, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding the truths of suffering and origin takes only the aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its object;
the knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation and the path takes only the cessation and the path of the desire realm as their objects.

Regarding what has been stated above, there is no further dispute. Nevertheless, concerning the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) of cessation and the path, it is said that there are distinctions. One school asserts that the paths of all stages are only general and without distinction.

Cessation is exclusively an object of specific conditions and lacks any general condition. Regarding the paths of the various stages: according to one view, both the paths and cessation are exclusively objects of specific conditions; according to a second view, the paths of the various stages are objects of general conditions, while cessation is an object of both general and specific conditions.
Because of these differences, they constitute many varieties;
thus, the treatise states that this concentration reaches fifty-two types.
This concludes the first master’s enumeration of the stages (*bhūmi*).

Because the various stages [of existence] have been extinguished through abandonment;
because there is neither cause nor fruit;
as explained in the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa*.
For this reason, these stages consist only of particulars and not a generality; for, according to the treatise,

The Path of Release (*vimukti-mārga*) necessarily takes [the Path of Liberation] as its collective object (*ālambana*). Regarding the Path of the Eight Grounds, there are four types of objects; correspondingly, there are four aspects (*ākāra*).

This is because the paths belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) that counteract the eight grounds act as homogeneous causes for one another, and thus must necessarily take them collectively as their object.

The remaining five stages are explained by analogy because they are identical in their objective referents, and thus their numbers do not differ. According to the treatise,
from the twenty-eight [factors] of the Sphere of Infinite Space up to [the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception], they mutually serve as causes for one another.
This explains how the number [of knowledges] gradually decreases across the three higher stages.
Because the formless realm does not take the lower stages as its object,
there is no knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), and thus the eight modes of activity are excluded.
They do not take the four dhyānas as objects for cessation.
Furthermore, when the other sixteen aspects are combined and twenty-four aspects are excluded, there remain only twenty-eight.
In the sphere of infinite consciousness, four further modes of activity are subtracted, making twenty-four.
In the sphere of nothingness, four more are subtracted from the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Therefore, there are only twenty. According to the treatise,
some say that this meditative absorption extends up to twenty-eight.
The second master’s explanation consists of eighty types;
this is because this master distinguishes the paths according to the eight stages.
Adding the previous twenty-eight lines, there are eighty.
The Treatise says:
It should be understood that this is also the case for the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) stage.
This explains the remaining five stages by analogy. According to the treatise,
the forty [kalpas] of the Sphere of Infinite Space decrease to twenty-four.
It clarifies that in the formless realms there is a gradual decrease;
in the sphere of infinite space, there are no two types of dharma-knowledge,
and the four cessations and four paths are excluded.
Since each of the ten truths has four [aspects], forty are excluded.
In the sphere of consciousness, eight are reduced;
that is, since there are four for each of cessation and the path, thirty-two remain.
In the sphere of nothingness, eight more are further excluded;
thus, there are twenty-four.
[Treatise]
Furthermore, there is another who wishes to reach one hundred and twelve [stages].
This third master’s teaching on the elimination [of afflictions] is the same as that of the first master.
There is a difference in the conditions for cessation,
because one admits both general and specific conditions;
the specific conditions are as previously described.
Regarding the general conditions (*samantālambana*), two by two they form seven;
three by three they form six;
and four by four they form five.
Five times five combined produce four;
six times six combined produce three;
seven times seven combined produce two.
The eight stages combined with their objects form one;
in total, there are twenty-eight truths (*satya*).
Each truth has four aspects (*ākāra*).
The total is one hundred and twelve lines;
adding the initial fifty-two,
there are one hundred and sixty-four in all.
These one hundred and sixty-four [mental factors] will certainly not arise simultaneously; rather,
only one of them manifests at any given time.
Treatise:
Just as it should be understood that what is included in the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage] is likewise so for the others;
this serves as a categorical explanation for the remaining five stages.
Because the objects of focus are identical,
they are the same one hundred and sixty-four.
Treatise.
From fifty-two [minds] in the sphere of infinite space down to twenty-four in the sphere of nothingness—
this explains the formless realms.
In the sphere of infinite space, one takes only the cessation of the four stages as its object.
In total, there are ten truths and forty aspects;
four aspects for the path category,
and eight aspects for suffering and its origin.
In total there are fifty-two.
The sphere of consciousness takes the cessation of three stages as its object;
in total and in detail, these comprise six truths and twenty-four modes of activity.
The twelve modes of the classes of suffering, origin,
and the path comprise thirty-six in total.
The sphere of nothingness takes the cessation of two stages as its object.
In total, there are three truths and twelve aspects;
the twelve aspects of the categories of suffering, origin, and the path make twenty-four in all.
In total, across the nine stages, there are one thousand nine hundred and sixty distinct diamond-like concentrations (*vajropama-samādhi*).

Whichever one [of the three] is relied upon, all are capable of severing the ninth grade of afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Question: Among these three explanations, which one is correct? Answer: The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Both of those are unreasonable."
The Path necessarily takes [all] collectively as its object;
Cessation takes [only one] specifically as its object, as has already been explained. Therefore, the Path necessarily takes [all] collectively as its object.
The second master is refuted because [he asserts] that cessation is merely a distinct condition; thus, the third master is refuted.
This means that the first explanation is correct.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 28, states in its critique:
According to this explanation,
there are one hundred and sixty-four diamond-like concentrations (vajropamasamādhi) based on the threshold concentration (anāgamya);
by this standard, the third [position] is correct.
That is to say, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* permits both general and specific conditions for cessation,
whereas the *Nyāyānusāra* admits only specific conditions;
since the intent of these treatises differs, they cannot be reconciled.
Treatise:
If one proceeds according to the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), it should be considered as appropriate.
For now, let us distinguish this with reference to a single individual.
According to the latter explanation,
there are one thousand nine hundred and sixty diamond-like concentrations (*vajropama-samādhi*).
If categorized by spiritual lineage (*gotra*), this number further becomes sixfold.
The distinctions regarding the faculties and so forth should be considered accordingly as presented in the treatise.
This meditative absorption is capable of reaching the point where the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "The diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) induces the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna).
Because it reaches [the state of] the diamond-like concentration, it is called the knowledge of exhaustion."

Regarding the explanation of the name "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*): it is called knowledge of exhaustion because it arises for the first time simultaneously with the attainment (*prāpti*) of the exhaustion of all [defilements].
The treatise thus explains that through the attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), one obtains the name of "one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*);
this is the explanation of being "beyond training.
It is for the sake of attaining a distinct fruit.
Those who have training to undertake are called "those in training" (śaikṣa).
Although the Arhats have already attained [their goal], they still have training to undertake in order to acquire sharp faculties and various meritorious qualities.
However, because one must train for the sake of attaining a distinct fruit that is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
it is called "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).
This refers to one who abandons a dull fruit and attains a superior fruit.
This refers to attaining the fruit of what was previously relinquished;
it is not a distinct attainment of a different fruit,
and thus is not termed "training" (śaikṣa).
Treatise:
This very [title] should apply only up to the name "Arhat," which explains the term "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).
An Arhat is also called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat),
because that very knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) arises simultaneously with the attainment of the exhaustion of all [defilements].
It is called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Alternatively, this term 'exhaustion' (*kṣaya*) indicates the exhaustion of everything."

This means that because the ninth grade of afflictions as well as all remaining prior afflictions have attained cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
Furthermore, from the attainment of this knowledge of exhaustion onward, one no longer practices for the sake of any further distinct fruit of training (*śaikṣa-phala*).
Collectively termed "those beyond training" (aśaikṣa),
these individuals should perform services for others and should receive offerings.
Therefore, they are also called Arhats. According to the principles of this treatise,
it is already established that all [those up to this point] are designated as "those in training" (śaikṣa).
The explanation for those beyond training (aśaikṣa) applies analogously to those in training (śaikṣa).
The treatise asks:
For what reason do the first seven [stages] receive the name "those in training"?
He asked again:
"The treatise states that one studies for the sake of attaining the eternal bliss of the exhaustion of outflows."
Answer: It is for the sake of attaining the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) by means of refining the faculties (*indriya-pariśodhana*) and so forth.
Treatise.
The trainings have three essentials, which constitute the three bodies of training.
These define the nature of training;
those who are still in training rely upon these three types to seek the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Treatise:
If that were so, then ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) should be called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*).
This is the objection.
If ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) also sought the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) through morality, concentration, and wisdom,
they should be called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*). However, the treatise does not say so, because [such a status] would result in the loss of the true state of being in training.
This is an explanation.

There are two causes: first, "because one has not yet seen reality as it truly is. This means that although one perceives the principle of the truths within the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*), [one does not yet see them as they truly are].
Because they do not see things as they truly are and lack clarity; because there is the possibility of falling back prior to the stage of the two types of patience (*kṣānti*).
[From the] Treatise.
For this reason, the Sugata spoke the words concerning training with particular gravity;
by citing the sūtra and repeating the words concerning training,
he demonstrates that there is no falling back.
Treatise:
How can a noble one who abides in their fundamental nature be called "one in training" (*śaikṣa*)?
This is the question.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 176, states:
"Regarding those who abide in their original nature (*prakṛti-stha*), there are two causes and conditions for being called 'abiding in the original nature.
First, they maintain their noble and virtuous nature without falling back."
Second, guarding one's own virtues without further cultivation; herein, abiding in the original nature is the second [point].
Alternatively, it may be that these are not the two explanations found in the *Vibhāṣā*.
This abiding in its original nature is a mind with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Since that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) constitutes training (*śaikṣa*),
the noble one (*ārya*) abides in this mind of the original nature with outflows.
Since there is no untainted training (*anāsrava-śikṣā*),
how can one be called "in training" (*śaikṣa*)?
The treatise says:
The answer is: because the intention of training has not yet been fulfilled, and because one constantly follows [the path] accordingly.
There are two causes: first, although there may be a temporary absence of untainted (anāsrava) training...
One whose intention for training is not yet fulfilled is called "one in training" (śaikṣa).

This is like a traveler who, having briefly rested, is not said to have arrived at his destination but is still called a traveler; for the two types of untainted training (anāsrava-śikṣā) constantly follow him.
One is called a "learner" (śaikṣa) by virtue of attaining the dharmas of a learner.
What are these dharmas of a learner? This is the inquiry regarding the dharmas of a learner.
The treatise states:
"It refers to the untainted conditioned dharmas of those in training. The answer is: "They are the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*)."
Treatise:
What are the dharmas of one beyond training?
[This is] an inquiry concerning the dharmas of one beyond training.
Treatise:
It refers to the untainted conditioned dharmas of one beyond training.
Answer: The dharmas of one beyond training.
Treatise:
Why is nirvana not called "training" (śaikṣa)?
Question:
For what reason do the dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa) take only conditioned (saṃskṛta) untainted (anāsrava) phenomena,
excluding nirvāṇa? [The] Treatise [says]:
This is because both those beyond training (aśaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) likewise possess it.
This refers to the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
If they were those in training (śaikṣa),
why would both ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) be able to accomplish them?
If they were those in training, there would be confusion.
Treatise:
For what reason, furthermore, is this not called "beyond training" (aśaikṣa)?
This is the question.
This is the answer: because both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) also possess it.
Both those in training and ordinary worldlings achieve cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If it were the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there would be confusion. According to the treatise,
such a person in training (*śaikṣa*) proceeds until the fruit of arhatship.
Taken collectively, they are divided into eight persons by distinguishing between those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
because there are four for each stage of the path of application (*pratipannaka*) and the fruit (*phala*).
This is based on the distinction between the paths of application and the fruits of the dharmas to be accomplished.
This explains the distinctions between the individuals. According to the treatise,
although there are eight names, they do not deviate from the aforementioned fruits.
Commentary:
Although there are eight types of persons when categorized according to the dharmas they have accomplished,
in reality there are five kinds of persons who can achieve [the goal].
That is to say: there is one person each for the candidate for the first fruit and for the fourth fruit.
The candidate for the second fruit and the one abiding in the first fruit are the same person.
The one abiding in the second fruit and the candidate for the third fruit are likewise the same person.
One who abides in the third fruit and one who is a candidate for the fourth fruit are also the same person. Consequently,
there are only five distinct types of actual persons.
Treatise:
This is based on the gradual [attainment], which is not subsumed under the preceding fruits;
it explains that the "leap-over" [attainment] differs from the sequential [attainment].
If one were to leap over [stages],
the candidate for the second fruit would not be included within the first fruit,
and the candidate for the third fruit would not be included within the second fruit.
Treatise:
Regarding the two types of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) as previously explained, the second major section below analyzes the path through various gates. This section contains five parts.
First, detachment from a stage occurs by means of the path;
second, the acquisition of disjunction is induced by the path; third, regarding the detachment from stages, there is a distinction between universal and restricted application.
Fourth, the distinction of the paths included in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*);
fifth, the mundane path as its object of observation.
This concludes the first section of the half-verse.
The treatise says: "Because supreme governance is attained from its own stage.
Explanation:
The defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are abandoned solely by the untainted (*anāsrava*) path.
Now, those who sever afflictions through the path with outflows all do so by severing the afflictions of a lower stage by means of a higher stage.
Because that which belongs to its own level cannot counteract its own level,
and because the Peak of Existence has no higher level,
it is abandoned solely by the untainted [path].
Treatise:
From the afflictions of one’s own stage up to the point where they do not treat those of their own stage,
this explains why the path of a given stage cannot sever the delusions of that same stage.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
For what reason can the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) arising from a lower stage not counteract the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of a higher stage?
Because a higher stage is certainly not an object of focus for the path of abandonment consisting of the practice of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇākāra*) through a mundane path of a lower stage.
One cannot become detached from the defilements of a higher stage by means of revulsion toward a lower stage,
because the higher stage is infinitely more subtle than the lower one.
From this, it is proven.
Only the power of the untainted (anāsrava) can bring about detachment from the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra);
this principle is well-established.
Treatise.
"Because one is able to abandon all [afflictions] up to the eighth stage," this explains the remaining stages.
Treatise:
Since it is already established that one becomes free from the defilements of the eight stages by means of both [paths],
the second half of the verse explains how the path brings about the acquisition of the two types of disjunction (visamyoga-prāpti).

The Commentary states: "Up to 'because they have the same function' (tulyakṛtyatvāt), it clarifies that both paths of those in training (śaikṣa) induce two acquisitions. Regarding the phrase "because the two kinds of paths have the same function," this refers to the cause for cultivating the two paths. As for "having the same function": *Note: This passage explains that the path of seeing (darśanamārga) and the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) for a practitioner in training both result in the acquisition of two types of fruits—the fruit of the path itself and the fruit of the abandonment of defilements.*
This is the same as [the explanation in] the *Tongzhi* (Compendium).
It is explained in detail in the "Chapter on Inferior Wisdom" (*Hīnajñāna-varga*). Treatise:
Other masters explain that [the path] does not lead to the non-attainment of afflictions;
this records a divergent view.
This master does not establish the cultivation of causes.
It is merely realized that [the abandonment] exists;
that is to say, it is established that there is no acquisition of outflow-free states (*anāsrava-prāpti*) without the existence [of abandonment].
Therefore, one knows that it is by means of the acquisition of outflowing states (*sāsrava-prāpti*) that the abandonment is maintained.
The treatise states: "When a noble one in training reaches the point of accomplishing those afflictions.
This is an explanation by way of citing specific instances.
For example, a noble one in training first abandons the afflictions of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Subsequently, relying on the four dhyānas, one refines the faculties until reaching the path of liberation; at this point,
one abandons the previous dull fruits and their corresponding paths,
and attains only the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmin) from the fourth dhyāna downward, as well as the three higher formless attainments above it.
If one who has not previously cultivated the contaminated path attains the unconditioned,
then the acquisition of the uncontaminated would entail the relinquishing of the acquisition of the contaminated,
and thus it would follow that they are free from afflictions.
Since afflictions themselves are not established [as entities],
it is clearly known that there exists the acquisition (prāpti) of outflows (sāsrava).
Treatise:
"This proof is irrational because it fails to establish the object of doubt," thus the Master [Vasubandhu] refutes it;
this reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, it is commonly accepted that when there are no two acquisitions (*prāpti*), afflictions do not arise.
The treatise states: "For instance, because they are separated [from the object], their arrival does not constitute proof."
This points out the refutation.

It is commonly accepted that the afflictions of the sphere of non-perception (asaṃjñisattva) lack the acquisition of outflow (sāsrava-prāpti). Although there is no twofold acquisition at the time of relinquishing [afflictions] through the refinement of the faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti), [the point remains].
It is commonly accepted that when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is born into a higher plane of existence,
the acquisition of the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the lower planes is entirely absent, and those lower-plane afflictions cannot arise either.
Therefore, it does not constitute proof. The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Although these two lack the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the abandonment of afflictions..."
Furthermore, because they are superior and progressive, they prevent the arising of afflictions;
the same should apply to those [other factors].
Therefore, the proof [of your position] is irrational.
Therefore, one can only say this: because the function performed by the two paths within that state is identical,
the manifestation of either one induces the arising of both acquisitions (*prāpti*).
It cannot be said that [this is] for the sake of establishing abandonment. The treatise states:
"Since it is said that the noble ones reach the attainment of the abandonment of the untainted, the explanation may be inferred accordingly."
Ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) possess only contaminated acquisitions (sāsrava-prāpti) for the abandonment of afflictions.

Noble ones (ārya) possess only uncontaminated acquisitions (anāsrava-prāpti) for the abandonment [of afflictions] through the path of seeing (darśanamārga) and the peak of existence (bhavāgra). The term "noble" excludes ordinary beings.
This is distinct from the eight [types of acquisition].

Regarding the exclusion of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the distinction between cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) and the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*): by which path does one become detached from the defilements of which stage?
This is explained in the following verse.
Third, the clarification of the path’s transcendence of stages and its specific application.
The treatise states: "Because it has already transcended [the lower stages].
This clarifies that all untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) pertain exclusively to the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) concentration.
It is able to abandon the defilements of its own stage, the lower stages, and the higher stages.
All other stages abandon only the defilements of their own stage and the higher stages.
Because there is no Path in the Desire Realm, it relies on the Higher Unattained (anāgamya) to effect abandonment.
The remaining untainted [paths] exist only in the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*) and not in the threshold stage (*anāgamya*),
because one attains a higher stage only after having abandoned the defilements of the lower stage;
for this reason, a higher stage cannot abandon the defilements of a lower stage.
Treatise:
Because all contaminated paths have already been abandoned [upon reaching the fundamental dhyānas],
it is clear that only the contaminated paths of the *sāmantaka* (preparatory stages) can sever the afflictions of the lower stages.
It cannot abandon the afflictions of its own level or those of higher levels,
because it is itself increased by the latent tendencies of the afflictions of its own level; thus,
it cannot abandon the afflictions of its own level.
Because its power is inferior, it cannot abandon the higher [stages].
Since one has already become detached from the lower [stage] once the fundamental dhyāna of a higher stage has arisen,
only the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) can effect abandonment.
Treatise:

Regarding the various [attainments] based on the *sāmantaka* that separate one from the defilements of the lower stages, the following verse states: [The verse begins: "Having separated from the defilements of the lower stage... and so forth.
The fourth section clarifies the specific paths included within the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
The treatise states: "Regarding 'reaching' (*prāpta*), this refers to the eight concentrations of the desire realm;
it clarifies that there are eight [paths] capable of severing [the afflictions]."
These are the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments.
There are nine [realms] from which one is separated, namely:
the desire realm and the eight meditative absorptions.
Treatise:
The first three access concentrations (*sāmantaka*) do not necessarily constitute the access concentrations themselves;
this clarifies whether they belong to the first, second, or third dhyāna, and whether they are determinate or indeterminate.
Regarding the upper five dhyānas, one enters the fundamental [attainments]. According to the treatise,
when reaching the access concentrations (sāmantaka), one necessarily enters the fundamental [dhyānas].
This explains the reason.
It is because the experience differs between the three lower stages— the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) and the fundamental stage (*maula*).
Because transitioning into a different feeling involves some slight difficulty:
if the aspiration for the superior mind is strong, one enters the fundamental [dhyāna];

if the aspiration is inferior, one cannot enter it. In the fourth dhyāna and the four formless attainments, the preparatory (anāgamya) and the fundamental stages share the same neutral feeling (upekṣā-vedanā).
Because one who is free from the defilements of a lower stage must necessarily aspire to the higher stage,
the meditative absorption of the higher stage necessarily enters the fundamental state (*maula*). Thus says the treatise.
Regarding the "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) and "liberation" (*vimukti*) moments of all supramundane paths,
the following single line of verse clarifies the fifth point: the practice of mundane paths with conventional objects.
The Commentary states: From "up to one aspect" through "one aspect," it clarifies the six aspects of the uninterrupted path and the path of liberation.
The upper and lower objects of focus differ; this is stated according to each individual case.

This reveals that at the time of abandoning the afflictions, there are the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), but it does not necessarily imply the arising of all three.
Whichever single aspect arises, it is capable of severing the afflictions.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 64, asks:
"In the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*), which aspect follows [the previous one]?"
What is the characteristic mode of activity of the path of liberation that arises?
The assessment states: this matter is not fixed;
it proceeds from the coarse mode of activity of the uninterrupted path.
Subsequently, one may give rise to the three types of contemplative aspects—such as tranquility (*śānta*) and so forth—as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The same applies to [the aspects of] suffering (*duḥkha*) and the rest. By means of these six types of contaminated (*sāsrava*) contemplative aspects, [one proceeds].
Because they arise according to the inclinations of those who have become free from defilement.

Question: When one becomes free from various defilements by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), what stage (*bhūmi*) do the immediate concentration (*ānantaryasamādhi*) and the liberation concentration (*vimuktisamādhi*) each take as their object?
The critique states: Although each of these various explanations can give rise to the wisdom of the disciples,
the initial explanation is superior in terms of its underlying principle.
This means that all nine paths of uninterrupted transition take the desire realm as their object, while all nine paths of liberation take the first dhyāna as their object. Why is this?
Because when one becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm by means of the mundane path, [these are the respective objects].
Because one can only become detached by feeling weary of the lower realms and aspiring toward the higher realms,
it should be understood that the same applies to becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm and the defilements of the seven higher stages.
Question: Within the mundane paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), how many types of aspects (*ākāra*) can each cultivate?
Answer: When ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) become free from the defilements of desire (*kāma-rāga*).
Within the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), one cultivates the three aspects (*ākāra*) of suffering and so forth;
within the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one fully cultivates all six aspects;
and within the subsequent paths of liberation, one likewise cultivates these same six aspects.
He also cultivates the infinite aspects of the first dhyāna stage in the future,
and so on, until he is free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness.
It should be understood that the same applies accordingly to each case.
If the noble ones cultivate the six aspects of practice as described for ordinary beings,
they further add the sixteen aspects, both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
If a noble one is separated from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness,
they cultivate only the sixteen aspects of the untainted;
the rest is as previously explained.
Question: Why is it that the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna cultivates both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) sixteen aspects (*ākāra*),
whereas the preparatory stages of the higher levels cultivate only the uncontaminated?

Answer: Because the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna possesses the aspects of the noble path (*āryākāra*), it is able to cultivate both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) sixteen noble aspects.
This is because the preparatory stages of the higher levels lack the aspects of the noble path.
One can cultivate only the aspects of untainted practice (*anāsrava*).
Question: As previously explained for the present, what is the object of focus (*ālambana*) for those cultivated in the future?
Answer: At the time of becoming free from the defilements of desire,
the three modes of activity— coarseness and so forth— which are cultivated in the nine paths of uninterrupted transition,
take only the desire realm as their object.

[Abhidharma] Śāstra.

Second, the explanation of the six kinds of learners (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).

The Commentary says: Because they take those as their antecedents, it is clarified that both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) also possess six types of spiritual lineage (*gotra*).

Treatise: However,

There is no refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) on the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Refinement of the faculties occurs in both the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*),
just as it does for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle seven, states:
"The factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) are also of six kinds, namely: those of the nature of regression (*parihāṇadharman*), and so forth."
The transformation of the lineage of retrogression toward liberation, such as the arising of the mental application (manasikāra) and other factors,
and likewise the transformation of the nature of mental application and so forth;
the transformation from the Śrāvaka [lineage] to arise as a Pratyekabuddha or a Buddha.
One may transform from the lineage of a Pratyekabuddha to that of a Śrāvaka or a Buddha;
however, if one belonging to the Buddha-lineage has already attained the stage conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), it can no longer be transformed,
because it is extremely intense.
It is also said that there are six types of natures within the *nirvedhabhāgīya* (stages conducive to penetration).
As the treatise states, in accordance with what is taught in the Sūtra: "I have declared four kinds of *adhicitta* (higher mental states) by means of which one proceeds."
The following single line of verse explains the third point:
the differences among the three types of regression regarding the four kinds of *adhicitta* (higher mental states).
This refers to the four dhyānas. The intent of this question is as follows:

the Sūtra states that there is a regression from the immovable liberation of mind (akopya-cetovimukti) and from the dwelling in happiness in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra), which is the fruit of the immovable nature (akopyadharman).
Now, it is asked: for what reason does one not waver from or fall away from the dwelling in happiness in the present life?
It is answered by means of the three types of falling away.
The treatise says: "It reaches the point where [the defilements] do not manifest."
This explains the three types of falling back.
It can be understood according to the text.
Treatise:
Because one has reached the stage of "already attained" within these three categories,
the descriptions of individuals differ according to the extent of their retrogression;
