Treatise:

Regarding the fault of contradiction from the perspective of falling back from enjoyment up to the signless state, this explains the consistency of the "immovable" [attainment]. As for the statement that there is falling back from the bliss of the present life:
According to the explanation based on falling away from enjoyment (*parihāṇi*),
the proponents of non-falling away (*aparihāṇivādin*) should not be subject to such criticism. As for these proponents of non-falling away:
This refers to the Sautrāntikas and others who maintain that all untainted liberations (anāsrava-vimukti) are termed "non-retrogressive" (avivartika).
How then is it stated in the sūtras that there are six spiritual lineages (gotra)?
As previously stated in the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā*,
this is based on the discourse concerning the blissful experience of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha-vedanīya*) associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Since it is admitted that all Arhats may fall back from their fruit,
the following single verse-line,
the fourth, clarifies the timing of such a fall from the fruit and so forth.
The Commentary states: "Up to the point where one reaches a state worthy of full trust" clarifies that one who has regressed from a fruit does not die.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 61, says:
Furthermore, the fundamental stage of fruition possesses five causal conditions:
first, relinquishing the path previously attained;
second, attaining the path never before attained.
Third, the realization of the severance of fetters through a single taste;
fourth, the simultaneous attainment of the eight knowledges;
fifth, the simultaneous cultivation of the sixteen aspects.
Therefore, when one falls back from the fruit, it has not yet been reacquired;
there is no principle for death [in that state]. This is not the case for those who are heading toward [the fruit].
Therefore, although one has not yet regained [the state] at the time of falling back, there is the possibility of passing away. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* asks:
"Who undergoes falling back?"
Who is it that does not fall back? One who enters the Noble Path by practicing the contemplation of impurity may still experience falling away;
however, one who enters the Noble Path by practicing mindfulness of breathing [is not subject to such].
There is necessarily no falling away.

Respect for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, as well as the increase of non-greed and non-delusion, should be understood respectively as having falling away and not having falling away. In which realm and which destiny is falling away possible? Only in the three continents of the desire realm is there falling away.

Regarding those who attain the fruits of sanctity within the six heavens of the desire realm (*ṣaḍ-kāmāvacara-deva*), some say that because they possess sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*), there is no falling away;

for they possess superior wisdom capable of subduing the mind, turning their backs on the objects of exquisite desire and entering the Noble Path (*āryamārga*). Others say that those who do fall away do so due to a deficiency in the necessary conditions (*sambhāra*).
Alternatively, it is because the physical basis (āśraya) is not in equilibrium.

In the abodes of the six desire-realm heavens (*ṣaḍ-kāmāvacara-deva*), both of these conditions are absent; those of dull faculties belonging to the lineage of followers by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) who are born there attain the state of an Arya and have no possibility of falling away. Furthermore, it says:

Regarding those who undergo retrogression, does it occur because they give rise to afflictions, or because they have already retrogressed previously and [the afflictions] now manifest? The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states that afflictions arise due to three causes, namely:
not having been abandoned, and so forth. The general explanation says: this is based on the presence of all necessary conditions.
Furthermore, regarding those who have deficiencies: with what kind of mind does one give rise to afflictions and fall away from the state of non-interruption?
Specifically, concerning those who fall away from the state of no-more-learning by giving rise to afflictions:
if they fall away by giving rise to the fetters of the form realm or the formless realm.
It arises immediately after a wholesome mind associated with the stage of meditative concentration conducive to retrogression belonging to its own level;
it does not occur when an unobscured-neutral mind subsumed under a higher level is present while one dwells in the desire realm.
This excludes only the fruition-attainment (phala-prāpti),
yet there is no falling away from that state.
Is it not the case that the factors conducive to decline (hāna-bhāgīya) are each abandoned at the time of becoming free from passion (vairāgya) within their own respective stages?
How is it that for one who is no longer in training (aśaikṣa), when they have not yet fallen away but give rise to afflictions, those [afflictions] manifest before their mind? In reality, this is so.
However, there are three types within the category of the "portion conducive to maintenance" (sthity-anukūla-bhāga):
first, that which slightly favors falling away (parihāṇi).
Second, slightly conforming to progress;
third, maintaining one's own station.
The aforementioned "conformity to retrogression" refers to the meditative absorption of one's own level.
This refers to a small portion within the state conducive to abiding (*sthity-anuloma*).
That which is conducive to decline (*hāny-anuloma*) receives the name "conducive to decline" because it slightly inclines toward decline;
however, this concentrated mind largely overlaps with that which maintains its own position.
It is subsumed under the stage conducive to stability.
For those who have not yet lost the stage conducive to decline,
afflictions manifest immediately after their minds [have reached that state].
If one abandons that mind and falls from the state of being gathered by conformity to a minor degree of conformity to decline,
then one gives rise to a decline through the conditions of affliction;
therefore, there is no contradiction between the text and its meaning.
If one falls away due to the arising of the fetters of desire,
then from the two minds of one’s own stage— the wholesome and the non-obscured-neutral— either may immediately manifest.
This applies to all those who fall away from the knowledge and the afflictions of the stage of training (śaikṣa).
When the defilements of the form and formless realms arise,
if at the time of falling away one has previously completely abandoned the defilements of this stage,
they arise immediately after a wholesome mind associated with the dhyāna of the stage of retrogression belonging to that very stage.
If one has not yet completely abandoned the defilements of this stage,
then from this stage, both wholesome and defiled minds arise immediately after one another.
All [the factors] are capable of manifesting.
Regarding those who arise from the desire realm and then fall away:
this refers to one who has previously completely abandoned the defilements bound to the desire realm.
From the two minds of its own level— the wholesome and the unobscured-neutral— either may immediately arise.
If one has not yet completely abandoned the defilements of the desire realm,
all three minds of the desire realm— the wholesome, the defiled, and the unobscured-neutral— may immediately arise.
If one has not yet attained pure dhyāna or the formless attainments (*ārūpya*),
it is impossible for one to fall away from what has been attained through the arising of fetters belonging to the realm of form or the formless realm.
However, such a person may fall away from what has been attained through the immediate arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
If one has attained pure dhyāna in the present,
yet has not yet attained pure formless attainment (ārūpya) in the present,
it is impossible for one to fall away due to the arising of formless fetters (ārūpya-saṃyojana).
One who falls away from what has been attained due to the fetters of the desire realm or the form realm loses what was acquired.
If one has already manifested and attained pure dhyāna or the formless attainments,
one may fall away from what was acquired through the simultaneous arising of the fetters of the desire, form, or formless realms.
When one undergoes a fall from what has previously been attained,
if superior fetters arise and manifest such that one falls away without generating lower wholesome states,
the lower afflictions are not established.
If the lower fetters arise and manifest, one falls from meditative absorption and loses the higher wholesome states;
thus, the absorption becomes a state of higher affliction.
Furthermore, there are those who maintain that one must first fall away [from the fruit] before [the defilements] can arise.
At a later time, when encountering an object, the affliction manifests. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 61, asks:
"Does one who has fallen back give rise to afflictions?
One school of thought says that one does give rise to afflictions.
One school asserts that [the mind] does not arise.
The critique states:
Of these two assertions, the former is superior.
Since one only incurs the loss of superior qualities when afflictions actually manifest,
this explains the state of regression.
If one is of a nature subject to regression,
it is not necessary that defilements must manifest for them to regress;
this is because there are those in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) who are of a regressive nature.
The Commentary states: Furthermore, one who abides in the stage of fruition may stumble but does not fall.
This clarifies that while there may be regression from the fruition, one does not perform actions that lead to such regression.
Treatise:
Regarding what was stated above concerning the attainment [of fruits] through the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), there are two verses below.
The fifth section clarifies the differences in the refinement of the faculties (*indriya*).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 67, states:
"If the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) is attained based on a particular stage (*bhūmi*)," [the faculties are refined accordingly].
One then transforms the faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) based on that very stage, or alternatively based on another stage;
however, it must be a superior stage and not an inferior one. Furthermore, the *Sixty-eighth [Fascicle]* states:
Is there a case where one falls away from the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) yet does not [re]establish the fetters to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya-saṃyojana)?
Answer: There is.
That is to say, when one falls away from the superior spiritual lineage (viśiṣṭa-gotra). Furthermore, it says:
The stages of Heat, Peak, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma constitute the proximate preparatory application for the Noble Path,
because they take the Truths as their object and resemble the Noble Path in their mode of activity.

Because they share the same basis of existence (*āśraya*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and because they perceive the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) identically, whereas in the preceding stage this is not the case,
the six types of spiritual lineage (*ṣadgotra*) are not established [at that point].
There is also the meaning of the transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*).

That is to say, transforming the faculty of the *parihāṇadharman* lineage so that the warmth (*uṣmagata*) of the *cetanādharman* arises; and so on, up to transforming the faculty of the *prativedhanādharman* so that the warmth of the *akopyadharman* lineage arises.
One transforms the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) of a śrāvaka into the "heat" of a pratyekabuddha;
one transforms the "heat" of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha into the lineage-root of the "heat" of a Buddha.
As it is said regarding the stage of heat, so it is for the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*).

There is a distinction regarding the stage of patience (*kṣānti*). That is to say, one who possesses the lineage of the *parihāṇadharman* (one subject to falling away) transforms it and gives rise to the patience of the *cetanādharman* (one capable of volition),
proceeding gradually until—
One transforms the faculty of the lineage of *kṣānti* capable of progress and gives rise to the faculty of the lineage of the immovable *kṣānti*;
one transforms the *kṣānti* of a śrāvaka and gives rise to the *kṣānti* of a pratyekabuddha.
There is no sense in which the lineage and faculties of the patience of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas could give rise to the patience of a Buddha. Why is this?
Because patience transcends the evil destinies.
Those who have attained forbearance (*kṣānti*) attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the miserable destinies (*apāya*).
However, at times, Bodhisattvas, by the power of their great vows,
take birth in the miserable destinies to benefit sentient beings.
Therefore, there is no principle for those in the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) of the two vehicles to turn toward the Buddha vehicle.
Some say that even for Pratyekabuddhas in the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*),
there is no turning toward the Buddha vehicle.
The commentary states:
Regarding the "those who practice in groups" (vargacārin),
they are those who, while in the stages of *ūṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, turn toward and enter the Buddha Vehicle.
Because it does not contradict reason,
what was stated previously is correct in principle.
This refers to the paths of preparation for the transformation of faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) in the stages of training (śaikṣa) and beyond-training (aśaikṣa).
It applies to both what has been previously attained and what has not yet been attained.
Although the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) have not been previously attained,
the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) applies to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The same applies to future cultivation.
The paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*);
those cultivated for the future are likewise exclusively untainted.

The ninth liberation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*), because at that time one cultivates the wholesome roots of the three realms as appropriate.
The treatise says: "Because it reaches the point where what has been accomplished becomes firm."

This clarifies the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). The treatise states that this is because, within the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), one has reached the highest degree of opposition [to the defilements].

The explanation of the training of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) for those in training (śaikṣa) states that "the opposite of the above" refers to being sustained by both the paths of those in training and those beyond training (aśaikṣa). [Abhidharmakośabhāṣya] Commentary.
The various stages of the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga) are designated as one;
likewise, there is one for the path of preparation of those in training (śaikṣa) and one for those beyond training (aśaikṣa). Thus says the treatise.
Thus, because there is no interval [between them] and they do not constitute a superior [path],
the liberation immediately following the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-viśeṣa*) employs exclusively the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

The various great masters from whom I have received instruction all maintain that the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) is entirely for the purpose of eliminating the manifestation of non-obscured, neutral ignorance (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-ajñāna*) which is induced by the power of the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and meditation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*).
The cultivation of the faculties during the stage of training (śaikṣa) is specifically for the purpose of eliminating the afflictions arising from views;
as for the cultivation of the faculties during the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa)...

This is precisely for the purpose of refuting [the view that] [the path] is produced by the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Just as when those afflictions capable of producing [the path] are severed,
there arise various numbers of uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) and liberation (*vimukti*) paths.
It is so, it is so. The number of paths for severing the manifestation of that ignorance which has arisen is likewise the same.
Therefore, when one beyond training (aśaikṣa) cultivates the faculties (indriya),
nine paths of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) and nine paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga) are employed;
for one in training (śaikṣa), each of the two types of cultivation of the faculties requires one path of each.
However, the ignorance produced by the afflictions of the paths of seeing and cultivation has many categories according to the specific differences in what they obstruct; therefore,
when [the mind] transforms from states such as regression into states such as reflection, [it arises].
As each of the various paths manifests, it has its own specific result to bring about;
therefore, there is no such thing as attaining a superior state by skipping over stages. Furthermore, it is asked:
for what reason is this called "refining the faculties" (*indriya-saṃcāra*)?
Because it disciplines and causes the faculties to increase;
that is to say, by the power of the Path, it causes the faculties to continue in succession,
whereby one abandons the inferior and attains the intermediate.
Abandoning the intermediate [faculties] and attaining the superior ones,
gradually increasing and excelling, is called "refining the faculties" (*indriya-saṃvara*). Therefore,
the term "refining the faculties" signifies the meaning of "transforming the faculties" (*indriya-parāvṛtti*).
Although one gradually attains superior faculties through the eight liberations,
because the fundamental mind seeks a superior nature,
one does not fall into inferiority until that superior nature has been attained.
Just as one abandons a previous orientation only upon attaining a subsequent fruit,
so too within the noble stages, if one attains a superior lineage,
one must necessarily abandon the previously inferior one.
When one cultivates the faculties (indriya) during the stages of "Heat" (uṣmagata) and so forth,
merely attaining a superior nature while the inferior nature ceases to function is termed the transformation of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra).
It is not attained by abandoning the inferior.
The *Śāstra* states:
"The basis refers to the body; 'reaching' refers to excluding the final three."
This clarifies the basis (*āśraya*).
There are two kinds of bases:
first, the physical body (*deha*).
Those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) alike depend upon the bodies of the three continents,
because there is no falling away elsewhere; for wherever there is a possibility of falling away, [those two types of persons do not abide].
There may be the refinement of faculties (indriya-saṃcāra).
In other places, because there is no falling back, there is no refinement of faculties.
This also depends on the stage (bhūmi).
The one beyond training relies on nine;
the one in training relies on six.
[Abhidharma] Śāstra.
Why is this so? It is because [the training] culminates in relying solely on the six stages;
this explains the reason. The refinement of the faculties by one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is like the attainment of the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*).
Therefore, it extends across nine stages.
When those in training (śaikṣa) refine their faculties, they abandon the dull fruits and their corresponding paths of approach,
retaining only the sharp fruits.
The prior fruits for those in training depend exclusively on the *anāgamya* stage.
The third fruit, that of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), depends on all six stages but not on the formless realms,
because it is like the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
In this regard, for one who cultivates the faculties during the stage of training (śaikṣa),
if they abide in the path of fruition (phalamārga),
then all three— preparatory application (prayoga) and so forth— are subsumed within the path of fruition.
If one abides in the path of the superior fruit,
it is subsumed under the preparatory, uninterrupted, and superior-fruit paths;
the path of liberation is subsumed under the fruit.
For one who dwells in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and cultivates the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*),
the three paths— preparatory (*prayoga*) and so forth— are subsumed solely within the path of fruition (*phala-mārga*).
This is because when one dwelling in the stage of fruition cultivates the refinement of the faculties...
When one abandons a fruit and attains a fruit while abiding in the stage of a superior fruit and cultivating the refinement of the faculties,
one abandons two [factors] and attains a fruit.
Furthermore, when those in the various noble stages cultivate and refine their faculties,
they may be identical to the stage of the fruit originally attained.
Alternatively, there is a distinction:
for the first and second fruits, the stage (*bhūmi*) upon which they rely must necessarily be the same;
for the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and the arhat (*arhat*), the stage upon which they rely is not fixed.
Regarding the distinctions of whether one relies on the original stage, or on a higher or lower stage:
if those who are non-returners (anāgāmin) refine their faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) based on a lower stage.
One cannot attain the fruits [of the path].
An Arhat is not like this, because he has already attained the fruits as originally described. According to this treatise:
Those who enter the path of seeing based on the fundamental stage also cultivate the faculties (indriya).
Those who attain the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmin) based on a higher stage likewise do so.
Because one cultivates the faculties (indriya) based on the lower stage,
the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 67, states that the master of the final assessment (*pūrvapakṣa*) should say: "It should be stated thus."
If one has already attained mastery over a higher stage,
yet relies upon a lower stage to train in the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) and so forth,
one may likewise attain the untainted path of the fruit (*anāsrava-phalamārga*) of that higher stage.
However, at the time of the transformation of the faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti), one cannot attain the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu),
because there is certainly no non-returner fruit (anāgāmi-phala) therein.
The *Nyāyānusāra* bases its argument on those who lack mastery over the higher stages.
Regarding those who have attained the superior fruits as described in the *Vibhāṣā*,
this is stated from the perspective of mastery;
thus, there is no contradiction.
Treatise:
Regarding the individuals (*pudgala*) of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*),
the following half-verse [is stated].
The sixth [section] clarifies the nine kinds of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

This answers the preceding enumeration.

By means of the attainments of the lowest-of-the-low and so forth, nine distinct types are established.
Answer: What was previously meant by "by what"?
Treatise:
There are seven noble persons belonging to the stages of training and beyond training.
The following is one verse in a single line.
The second major section clarifies the inclusion of all noble ones (*ārya*). Within this, there are three parts:
first, the establishment of the names of the seven types of persons;
second, the names of those liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*) and those liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*).
The three trainings and the state beyond training are called "fulfilled.
This is the first section of the single verse.
The treatise says, up to the term "follower by dharma" (*dharmanusārin*).
Regarding the two types of individuals on the path of seeing, based on their previous stage of application (*prayoga*),
they are called "followers by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*) because they rely on the faith of others,
and "followers by dharma" (*dharmānusārin*) because they rely on the teachings of the Dharma.
The Commentary states: Based on the differences in their faculties, from the stage of "one liberated by faith" (śraddhādhimukta) up to "one who has attained vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
it clarifies the two types of persons in the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
Those in whom the faculty of faith is predominant are called "liberated by faith" (śraddhādhimukta);
those in whom the faculty of wisdom is predominant are designated as "attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta). [Abhidharma-kośa] Bhāṣya.
Because one attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and proceeds up to the attainment of the final cessation (*nirodha-āyatana*),
one who has attained the absorption of cessation within the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) is given the specific name "Body-Witness" (*kāyasākṣin*).
Treatise:
Based on the difference in liberation (*vimukti*), the designation "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) is established.
This clarifies that the two types of persons in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) are divided into two according to their differing degrees of liberation.
Commentary:
Although these names number seven, extending up to "one liberated at any time," their essential substance consists of only six.
These are the two types of individuals: those of sharp and dull faculties.

Since there are two for each of the three stages, their substance consists of only six. The *kāyasākṣin* (body-witness) is identical to the *śraddhādhimukta* (one liberated through faith) and the *dṛṣṭiprāpta* (one who has attained vision). *Prajñāvimukti* (liberation through wisdom) and *ubhayatobhāgavimukti* (double liberation) are identical to the *samayavimukta* (occasional liberation) and the *akopyadharman* (one of immovable nature), respectively.
Treatise:
It should be understood that herein [the analysis] extends as far as it is appropriate to contemplate according to reason;
from here on, the sequence of the text may be understood through the verses.
Treatise:
What are called "both-ways liberated" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) and "liberated by wisdom" (prajñāvimukta)?
[The answer is given in] the second half of the verse.
The second section provides a further explanation of the two liberations (*vimukti*).
The treatise states: "Because one attains liberation.
This explains the alternative names for the two liberations.
Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, fascicle 54.
Question: Is there one who first attains the fruit of arhatship and subsequently attains the meditative absorption of cessation?
Regarding the obstacles to liberation, is there a fulfillment of liberation of mind for such a person?
Is it untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Some say it is tainted (*sāsrava*),
because when one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) with an untainted mind, one has already been liberated.
The critique states that one should say this:
both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) attain liberation. Why is this so?
There are two kinds of liberation:
first, liberation while in the world;
second, liberation within the body.
When that person has not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), the minds entering and emerging from it cannot function in the world;
because they do not function in the world, they do not abide in the body.
When they have attained the meditative absorption of cessation, the minds entering and emerging from that absorption function in the world and abide in the body.

Just as the name "liberated in both ways" (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta) is established based on its meaning, the names of the preceding five [types of arhats] should likewise be established based on their meanings. The *Nyāyānusāra* asks:
"What is the essential nature of the obstacle to liberation?"
The minds of all Arhats are already liberated;
yet they further seek liberation in order to liberate themselves from those obstacles.
This refers to that which exists within the various liberations that are obstructed:
an inferior, non-cognizant, and unobscured-neutral nature capable of obstructing liberation;
this constitutes the essence of the obstacle to liberation.
When one attains freedom from defilement regarding various realms,
although there is already no further abandonment remaining, liberation arises;
it is only when those [defilements] do not function that one is said to be liberated from them.
Other masters say that this obstacle to liberation has as its essence the lack of mastery over the various meditative absorptions (dhyāna).
Other masters say that this obstacle to liberation has as its essence the non-attainment of the various meditative concentrations.
Other masters say: it is because they do not diligently seek out the preparatory practices for them,
and because they do not hear them.
Because it has not been repeatedly practiced,
liberation does not arise;
this very state is termed the essence of the obstacle to liberation.
The first explanation is the reasonable one.
Why is this? Because there must certainly be some slight power of dharmas capable of acting as an obstruction.
This causes them to lack mastery over meditative concentration. If it were not so,
for what reason would they be unable to attain mastery within those various concentrations?
That which fails to attain certainty must necessarily have a cause.
One cannot say that the very failure to attain certainty is itself the cause,
for a self-nature cannot logically take itself as its own cause.

Alternatively, one might also say that the obstacle of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa) should likewise be defined as having the non-attainment of the fruit of arhatship as its nature; however, since that is not the case,
[the former position holds].
How is this so? Even the fruit of arhatship cannot arise if one does not diligently seek it through application;
how then could there not be a distinct entity for the afflictive hindrance?
Therefore, the latter three explanations are all unreasonable.
Furthermore, even uncontaminated minds are said to attain liberation from this [bondage],
because liberation is spoken of in terms of being "in the body" and in terms of "functioning in the world."
This means that it is only when one is liberated from the obstacles to liberation that [the path] arises within the body and functions in the world.
Treatise.
As the Blessed One said regarding the abandonment of the five afflictions,
the following verse-line clarifies the fulfillment of the stages of training and beyond-training (śaikṣa and aśaikṣa).

The Treatise says: Up to the point of not yet being free from the defilement of desire, it clarifies the three fulfillments (*paripūri*) in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), as well as their deficiencies. Regarding the three fulfillments:
first, the fulfillment of the faculty (*indriya-paripūri*), which refers to possessing sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*).

Second, fulfillment of the fruit refers to attaining the state of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*). Third, fulfillment of meditative concentration refers to attaining the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Fulfillment of the faculties occurs because one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) possesses sharp faculties.
Because he has not yet attained the stage of non-returner, his fruition is not complete;
because he has not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation, his concentration is not complete.
Treatise:
There are those who are trainees (śaikṣa) up to those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti);
this may be understood according to the text.
Treatise:
There is no case where a learner (śaikṣa) attains the designation "perfected" (*paripūrṇa*).

This clarifies that among learners, there is none who attains perfection of the faculties (*indriya*) through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) without also attaining perfection of the fruit (*phala*).
Because one who has attained fulfillment in meditative concentration will necessarily attain fulfillment in the fruit;
as well as those who have attained fulfillment in both faculties and concentration.
This is also explained as above. The treatise states:
"All those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa) are also designated by the name 'perfected' (paripūrṇa)."
The commentary states that the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is not explained separately as the fulfillment of the fruit, because all [of them] are the fulfillment of the fruit.
There are those who, by means of their faculties alone, have already attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*);
thus, it is through the faculties and the absorption that the designation "perfected" (*paripūrṇa*) is obtained.
Within this, there are three propositions.
The first phrase is due to the faculties alone;
the second phrase is due to meditative concentration alone;
the third phrase is due to both the faculties and meditative concentration.
This can be understood according to the text.
The treatise explains at length that the distinctions among the various paths are immeasurable.
The following third major section clarifies the distinctions among the various paths; therein,
first, the distinctions among the paths are clarified,
and second, the four types of practice (*pratipad*) are clarified.
Third, it elucidates the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
Fourth, it elucidates the four kinds of verified confidence (avetyaprasāda).
Fifth, it elucidates right liberation and right knowledge.
Sixth, the clarification of the pervasiveness and limitation of wearying detachment (*nirveda*). This single verse first clarifies the four paths.
The treatise says: "Up to" refers to the three remaining paths.
A Brief Exposition of the Essence of the Path.
Treatise:
What is the meaning of the "path"?
This refers to the meaning of the Path (*mārga*).
The treatise states that it is so called because it is the path leading to the fruit of Nirvana.
There are two interpretations of the meaning of "path" (*mārga*). "Path" is a name for a road;
the path leading toward *nirvāṇa* is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*).
This is the sense of being the basis for movement.
Whatever one pursues must necessarily depend upon the path.
Because one seeks nirvāṇa by means of these four paths,
the treatise asks:
how can liberation and superior progress be called "paths"?
Question: The preparatory stage (*prayoga*), the immediate stage (*ānantarya*), and the stage leading toward nirvāṇa may be called the "path" (*mārga*);
however, the stage of liberation (*vimukti*) has already been reached.
Since it has already transcended superior progress,
how can it be called the "path"?
The treatise provides three explanations.
The first [explanation] says:
Because it is of the same category as the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*) and so forth,
and because this path has progressed to a superior degree (*adhimātra*).
Treatise:
Alternatively, because the power of each preceding stage reaches each succeeding stage,
this is the second explanation.
The preceding stages lead up to the subsequent ones, all of which possess the meaning of the Path (*mārga*).
According to the treatise, this is because they are able to lead one toward entry into the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
This is the third interpretation.
Liberation (*vimukti*) and supreme progress (*viśeṣagamana*) are also designated by the term "path" (*mārga*),
because they have already entered into the state of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"The noble ones of the three vehicles traverse this level path and swiftly reach the two kinds of nirvāṇa realms."
Treatise:
Elsewhere, the path is established under the name "effective practice" (pratipad).
The following verse in one line [states]:
Second, the explanation of the practice leading to penetration (*pratipad*).
The treatise states: "Because it proceeds spontaneously.
This explains the "pleasant" penetration. "Penetration" (*prativedha*) is a specific name for the Path (*mārga*).
The name "bliss" (*sukha*) is explained by the fact that it functions spontaneously without much hardship.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Because it functions spontaneously, it is like riding in a boat or raft."
Treatise:
The path relies on the formless realms; as it reaches the contemplation of increasing tranquility and decreasing insight, this explains the path of difficult progress.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Although the Path is not suffering,
it is also called suffering because it proceeds with difficulty in association with painful sensation."
Just as traveling by land on horseback and so forth involves hardship when one moves slowly,
because in this stage both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) increase and decrease [alternately], the names "suffering" and "pleasure" are established based on these stages.
Commentary:
This very pleasure and suffering, when reversed, are termed "swift.
This explains "slow" and "swift."
These names, "slow" and "quick," are established based on the faculties (*indriya*).
Regarding these aforementioned terms "slow" and "quick," they apply to the path and not to the person. This is discussed in the treatise.
Alternatively, for those who are dull-witted, the attainment is extremely rapid;
this is the opposite [of the former case]. This explanation—that the names "slow" and "rapid" refer to the person and not the path—is stated in the *Nyāyānusāra* (*Abhidharmanyāyānusāra-śāstra*).
This practice consists of five aggregates, yet its nature comprises four aggregates;
it is distinguished by the meditative absorptions of the form realm and the formless realm,
though the name applies to both.
Because its wisdom is preeminent,
it is specifically designated by the name "view" (*dṛṣṭi*),
such as the various conventional knowledges at the edge of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*).
Furthermore, it is established that its essence consists of five aggregates or four aggregates;
this is the definition and name set forth in the treatise.
The Path is also termed the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
The third section below clarifies the factors of enlightenment in verse; therein are six parts.
First, enumerating and explaining the names;
second, establishing their essential nature;
third, explaining the foundations of mindfulness and so forth.
Fourth, it clarifies the sequence of the stages of increase;
fifth, it clarifies the distinction between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*);
sixth, it clarifies the differences according to the levels (*bhūmi*) upon which they rely.
This single verse first cites the number and explains the names.
The *Śāstra* states: "Up to the eight branches of the noble path" (*aṣṭāṅgika-āryamārga*), which cites the number and explains the names.
Treatise:
From the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) up to these two, they are called "awakening" (*bodhi*). This explains the term *bodhi*.
This is called awakening (bodhi).
It has two meanings:
first, because it is like waking from sleep.
"Because of awakening through twofold realization" and "because ignorance and sleep are forever severed" mean that it is like waking from sleep;

"and because of knowing things as they truly are, having done what was to be done" means that through the awakening of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), one no longer has further tasks to perform.
The Treatise on the Knowledge of Non-arising and the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment leading to Bodhi.
An explanation of the reason why thirty-seven factors are called "aids to enlightenment" (bodhipakṣa).
Treatise:
Are the entities of these thirty-seven factors each distinct?
The following single line of verse constitutes the second [section], which establishes the essential nature (*svabhāva*).
The Commentary states: "Up to 'the other nine are the same as before.'"
It clarifies that ten dharmas constitute its essence;
this is the definition of its substance.
In the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 95, there are three explanations.
One tradition holds that it is identical to this treatise;
another tradition divides the precepts into two parts,
taking eleven factors as its essence.
One teacher divides [the path] into three:
namely, right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
This treatise, however, explains them by combining them into ten constituent factors.

Although their formulations differ, they do not contradict the underlying principle. Question: Why are there only ten [factors] as the essential body? [Answer: This is according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*’s criteria for inclusion and exclusion. Question: Why, among all forms (*rūpa*), is it only non-informative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) that is established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), and not other forms? Answer: Because right speech, right action, and right livelihood accord with the power and function of the Noble Path, their influence is particularly predominant; therefore, they are established as factors of enlightenment.
Other forms are not like this. Furthermore, ethical discipline can serve as grain, whereas other forms cannot.
Moreover, the *Nyāya* asks: "For what reason is manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)?"

The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) consist exclusively of wholesome states conducive to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which possess a superior capacity for conformity when associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta-avijñapti*).
Manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) is not so;
therefore, it is not established [as such]. Question: Why is the mind (*citta*) itself not established as a factor of enlightenment?
Furthermore, the mind possesses equal functional power regarding both the categories of affliction and purification;
however, the factors of enlightenment pertain specifically to the category of purification.
Because their functional power increases disproportionately, they are not established [as such].
Furthermore, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) assist and support enlightenment.
The mind-king (*cittarāja*) should not be assisted by awakening (*bodhi*), just as a king has no logical necessity for ministerial assistants. Question:

Among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), why are only mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and feeling (*vedanā*) established as factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*)?
Answer: Mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom possess a predominant power and function conducive to purification;
the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) are likewise.
Therefore, these three are included.
Because their functional power is superior among both the defiled and purified categories,
they are also established as factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma). Other masters say:
Although the power and function of what is afflicted are superior,
they perform beneficial work for the pure category;
it is like a caṇḍāla, whose nature is base and inferior.
Yet, because they perform beneficial functions for the noble lineages,
they are likewise established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and desire (*chanda*) belong to the category of defilement (*saṃkleśapakṣa*).
Because its functional power increases disproportionately,
it is not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
In the contemplation of mental images (*saṃjñāmanasikāra*), resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) increases disproportionately.
The factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) accord with the contemplation of reality;
therefore, resolute belief (adhimukti) is not included among them. Other masters say that the factors conducive to enlightenment predominate during the stage of training (śaikṣa).
In the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) is finally superior;
therefore, it is not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
Mental attention (*manasikāra*) is also inconsistent with the meaning of the object.
Therefore, this is not established either. Other masters say:
"At the initial moment of grasping an object, the power of attention (*manasikāra*) is predominant;
as the continuity of the object proceeds, that power gradually diminishes."

The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) do not establish [a specific object] because it would be inconsistent with the meaning that they only arise after the object has been apprehended for a long time. Question: Why are all three types of feeling (*vedanā*) common to the untainted (*anāsrava*)?
Only joy (*prīti*) is established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Answer: Because the two feelings of pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) lack that characteristic.
Furthermore, the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the factors of enlightenment is sharp and intense.

Pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are not established [as factors] because they are dull; furthermore, untainted pleasant feeling (*anāsrava-sukha-vedanā*) is obscured and impaired by the pleasure of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*), and equanimity is obscured and impaired by the equanimity of mental formation (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*).

Because their characteristics are not clearly defined, they are not established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Question: Among the great wholesome mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharmas*), why are only these four—faith, diligence, pliancy, equanimity, and heedfulness—established [as such]?

Are they the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)? Answer: Because these four are preeminent in accordance with enlightenment, they are specifically established as the factors conducive to enlightenment;
that is to say, faith is the foremost [factor] for proceeding toward enlightenment.
As one is about to give rise to the manifold practices, faith serves as the primary foundation;
therefore, faith is established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Diligence universally exerts itself toward the practice leading to enlightenment.
Because it causes one to swiftly advance toward the enlightenment of the three vehicles,
it is also a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and composure serve as the antidote to lethargy (*styāna*).
The excellence of the factor that assists insight is equanimity of application, which counteracts restlessness;
it is superior as an assistant to the category of tranquility.
The factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) have calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) as their primary elements;
therefore, they are all established together as factors conducive to enlightenment.
These include the six factors such as shame (hrī) and dread of blame (apatrāpya).

Although the power and function of the wholesome dharmas of the category of scattering are superior [to those of the unwholesome], they are weak and inferior in strength compared to the wholesome dharmas of meditative concentration; therefore,
they are not established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Because they are properly subsumed within the meditative concentrations of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma),
the remaining two universal unwholesome mental factors (akuśalamahābhūmika) and the six universal afflictive mental factors (kleśamahābhūmika) [are excluded].
The ten minor afflictive mental factors (parīttakleśabhūmika),
as well as greed, hatred, pride, and doubt among the indeterminate mental factors (aniyata-bhūmika),
are all not established [as universal] because they accord with defilement (saṃkleśa).
Although sleep (*middha*) and remorse (*kaukṛtya*) are also associated with the wholesome, they are exclusively *upapattiprātilambhika* (innate).
The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), however, are *prāyogika* (cultivated through application). Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra* states:

For what reason are the dissociated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) not established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)? Because, being dissociated, they lack any distinct or superior capacity to assist in enlightenment,
unlike the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), which, though dissociated, does possess such a capacity.

However, because the wheel of the Path takes the conditioned as its hub, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) do not establish them separately. Question: Why are the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharmas) not established [among the factors of enlightenment]? Answer: That which accords with the factors of enlightenment must necessarily give rise to functional activity.
Being unconditioned and without function,
they are not established as such.
Because of this principle of exclusion and establishment, only ten types are the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
All others are not established [as such].
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* asks:
"For what reason is faith (*śraddhā*) not established as a member of the path of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*)?"
At the time of first setting out, faith is predominant;
once one has entered the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*) within the factors of enlightenment and the path (*bodhipakṣadharma*),
the power and function of faith gradually diminish at that time.
Therefore, they are not established among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) or the path-factors (*mārgāṅga*).
For what reason are joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) established among the factors of enlightenment,
yet not likewise established among those path-factors?
That is exclusively in accordance with awakening,
not in accordance with the path.
What is meant by "in accordance with awakening"?
Furthermore, within the path of cultivation, one cultivates nine grades of superior awakening in each stage.
Just as one repeatedly awakens to the truths again and again,
so too does one give rise to ever-increasing superior joy.
Because one subsequently contemplates the truths with noble and supreme joy,
just as a person who digs the earth finds treasure and feels joy,
they subsequently take pleasure in digging further.
Therefore, joy increases through the power of conforming to awakening;
it is essential that one rests all activities through the power of lightness and tranquility,
and brings the mind to equanimity through the power of relinquishment.
Only then can one discern objects with precise awareness;
therefore, tranquility (praśrabdhi) and equanimity (upekṣā) are established among the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga).
Why, then, are these three not conducive to the Path?
Swift movement is the meaning of the Noble Path;
this [term] is slightly inconsistent with "swift movement," because both [terms] enable the mind to abide in tranquility.
For what reason are vitarka and śīla established as factors of the path,
yet not likewise established among the factors of enlightenment?
Because they accord specifically with the path and do not accord with enlightenment.
What is the path of conformity?
First, within the path of seeing, one employs vitarka to spur right view,
[directing it] toward the objects of the eight truths, both superior and inferior.
Observe with swift agility:
let morality be the hub that forms the wheel of the path of vision,
causing it to revolve rapidly toward the truths.
Therefore, both vitarka and śīla are established as factors of the path.
Why, then, would these not be conducive to awakening?
For instance, vitarka functions without tranquility regarding the truths.

regarding the dharmas one has faith in, upon reaching the point where one attains the verified confidence (*dharma-avetyaprasāda*) in all of them,
this clarifies the general and specific dharmas.
The three truths (trīṇi satyāni) pertain exclusively to the Path (mārga), both collectively and individually.
Consequently, when one contemplates the four truths (catvāri satyāni), there is in every case the "pure confidence in the Dharma" (dharme 'vetyaprasāda). [Abhidharmakośabhāṣya] states:
The commentary states: One also attains the precepts beloved by the Noble Ones;
the clear precepts and the verified purity regarding the Four Truths are all present.
Because they reach their respective objects of faith differently, there are only two;
however, by clarifying the differences among the three types of clarity regarding faith, faith is divided into three.
Faith alone constitutes one essence;
precepts likewise constitute another.
Therefore, there are only two essences in total.
Commentary:
Since these four kinds of "arrivals" (prāpti) are not [yet] verified purities (avetyaprasāda),
it is clarified that they are exclusively untainted (anāsrava).
Treatise:
Based on what meaning is the name "clear confidence" (avetyaprasāda) established?
This is a question concerning the establishment of the name.
Treatise:
From "realizing things as they truly are" up to "all are called pure.
This is the answer.
To realize the principle of the Four Noble Truths as they truly are is the explanation of "realization.
To have faith that sublime ethical discipline (*śīla*) is purity is the answer regarding "purity."
Treatise:
Because it is free from the defilement of lack of faith and the defilement of breaking the precepts,
this explains the reason for the two names "attainment" and "purity."
Treatise:
Because they are established through the attainment of purity, they are designated by the name "clear confidence" (avetyaprasāda).
This is the combined explanation of the term "clear confidence."
The term "verified purity" (*avetyaprasāda*) refers to the pure faith and pure ethical discipline attained through the realization of the truths by means of wisdom.
As stated in the *Śāstra*: "It is just as when one emerges from meditative absorption and reaches the subsequent stages."
The treatise explains the fourfold sequence.
How does the sequence of manifestation occur at the time of emergence?
Question: Regarding the sequence of emergence.
Treatise:
This refers to the stage of emerging from meditative absorption until one attains right faith in the Triple Gem.
The treatise explains the sequence of present knowledge through the stages of contemplation, stating:
"It is like a skilled physician who arrives when the illness has been eliminated."
This is presented by means of an illustration to clarify the point.
The treatise mentions four types [of vehicles], up to and including the vehicle that is mounted;
this is the second illustration.
Treatise:
The Sūtra states that those in training (śaikṣa) accomplish the eight branches.
Below this, the fifth section clarifies right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and liberation (*vimukti*). This section contains four parts.
First, the time of clarifying right knowledge;
second, the time of clarifying liberation;
third, the time of clarifying the severance of obstacles by the Path.
The fourth elucidates the meaning of abandonment and detachment.
This constitutes the first section of these two verses. The treatise states:
"...up to the point where the wisdom of liberation can be established."
The explanation for establishing the names "liberation" (vimukti) and "knowledge" (jñāna) is as follows:
although many ropes may be untied,
if there remains even a single bond, it is not called liberation.
This clarifies that the name "perfect liberation" is obtained;
it is not the case that there is no essence of liberation such that one could speak of "knowledge of liberation.
This clarifies the knowledge of liberation.
Treatise:
Because the one beyond training (aśaikṣa) has already attained liberation, they possess only eight [factors].
When including the one beyond training, there are ten members.
The Śrāvakabhūmi states: "For those in training, there are only eight branches.
This is because the essence of liberation consists of both attainment and its basis, which are conditioned phenomena."
The treatise explains that the liberation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Within this liberation, it is by means of resolute confidence (*adhimokṣa*) that the factors of conditioned liberation are established. Thus says the treatise.
The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* includes liberation within this aggregate of liberation (*vimukti-skandha*).
Furthermore, it divides the factors of liberation into two: liberation of mind (*citta-vimukti*) and liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* likewise divides them into liberation at times (*sāmaya-vimukti*) and liberation independent of time (*asāmaya-vimukti*).
This is the aggregate of liberation (*vimukti-skandha*) among the two liberations and the five aggregates of the Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya-skandha*).
The two kinds of liberation explained above both have meditative resolve (*adhimokṣa*)—
both moderate and superior— as their essential nature.
This is the position of the Sarvāstivāda school. The treatise states:
"If that were so, it would not be the case that [the object] is reached through mere resolute conviction (adhimukti) alone."
The Sautrāntika school cites a sūtra to challenge the Vaibhāṣika position.
Since the sūtra states that the mind is separated from greed,
it is known that [this state] is not merely a matter of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
Treatise:
If that is so, what is it? This is the question posed by the Sarvāstivādins.
Treatise:
Other masters state that "attainment" (prāpti) is called the aggregate of liberation (vimukti-skandha).
Another master from the Sautrāntika school explains it thus.
Thus, the name "mind-king" (cittarāja) is taken as the essence of liberation.
The *Nyāya* school offers this defense:
"This does not constitute a valid proof."
It is also stated in the Sūtra:
"What is the most excellent purification of the mind?
It is the departure from all sensual desires and unwholesome, unvirtuous states."
...up to: abiding in the fourth dhyāna, so that the aggregate of meditative concentration (samādhi-skandha), which was not yet fulfilled, may become fulfilled.
That which is already fulfilled is "cultivation for the sake of inclusion," which is precisely what is called meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Just as various meditative concentrations arise and reach fulfillment through the functional power of various practices such as desire and so forth.
Samādhi perfected is called "mind"; desire, effort, and so forth are not the mind, yet they are the purification that removes stains.
Samādhi causes the mind to be free from turbidity;
it is not that the mind itself is removed from stains that is called samādhi. Thus, by the power of desire and the other factors, [the mind becomes purified].
It causes the aggregate of liberation to arise in its perfection;
this perfection is called the liberation of the mind.
Liberation causes the mind to be free from defilement.
Therefore, it is not the case that being free from defilement is itself called liberation.
Thus, the system established here does not contradict the sūtras.
Treatise.
Thus has been explained the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising,
which is the second correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
This correct knowledge is precisely what was previously described as the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising.
Because one knows correctly and as it truly is that "my births have been exhausted," and so forth.
[The] Treatise [asks]: In which time-period does the mind clearly manifest liberation?
The second half of the verse explains the time of liberation.
The treatise states: "Because at this point the mind arises."
This clarifies that liberation is attained at the moment the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) arises.
Previously, due to the afflictions, the obstruction prevented [the mind] from arising;
now, because correct abandonment (*samyak-prahāṇa*) has been attained, it arises.
This is stated explicitly regarding the acquisition (*prāpti*) of afflictions;
however, in principle, it also extends to the karma of the form and formless realms.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
When it is said that the obstacle to liberation is not merely the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
this is because the karma that produces the results of cessation and birth in the form and formless realms is also an obstacle to be abandoned at that time.
This karma also obstructs the attainment of arhatship;

for this reason, the great masters of old all said: "Karma [acts as an obstacle] to the attainment of the stage of patience (kṣānti), the non-returner (anāgāmin), and the fruit of arhatship (arhattva-phala)."
This is an extreme hindrance. The treatise states:

from the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) up to what is called "already liberated," it clarifies that obstacles have been correctly abandoned and that obstacles have already been severed.
Regarding the discussion on the time of attaining right liberation and having already been liberated:
it is because one has not yet given rise to the state of an Aśaikṣa (one beyond training) within the world of the body and its movements.
It is because all those in the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) attain liberation simultaneously at that very moment;
the *Mūla-śāstra* mentions only those who are "born" [into that state].
Question: When the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) of one in training (*śaikṣa*) reaches the time of birth...
Is it not also by means of the obstacles that one attains liberation?
Why does the fundamental treatise (*mūla-śāstra*) not mention this? The *Nyāyānusāra* answers:
[as stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*].
Although all minds in training are also liberated from obstacles at the moment of their arising,
the treatise speaks only of the first mind of one beyond training being liberated at its arising;
this is because it refers to liberation through the realization of abandonment without remainder.
Furthermore, because this refers exclusively to pure liberation,
herein the mind possesses liberation by its very nature (*svabhāva-vimukti*),
rather than liberation through a continuous succession (*saṃtati-vimukti*).
The four lines are easily understood.
The treatise asks: "From what are all conventional minds liberated?"
Question: This refers to the time when the mundane mind is liberated.
Treatise:
It also means that from that [liberation], the obstacles to the arising of the mind are likewise removed.

Answer: When all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena within the body of one who has attained the fruit (*phala*) obtain liberation, there is simultaneously liberation from the obstacles that hinder the arising of the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Another explanation states:
That is to say, from this point on, one attains liberation from the obstacles that hinder the arising of tainted minds;
just as in the case of cultivated dhyānas and other such tainted minds,
which attain liberation from their respective meditative hindrances.
The treatise asks:
"In the state prior to liberation, does this [nature] not arise?
This is the question.
Since this impure mind has not yet reached the state of liberation, how could it not arise?
For what reason, then, is it said that it is liberated from obstructions? [The Treatise says:]
Although there are cases where that which has already arisen is not similar to the present,
the answer is:
before one has abandoned the obstructions.
Although there are instances where tainted minds have already arisen,
they do not resemble those that have now become free from hindrances.
Treatise.
What is the reason for this?
What is being asked? This is the treatise.
If it arises subsequently together with the acquisition of afflictions, does it not then arise without the acquisition of afflictions?
The answer is:
that which has already arisen previously does arise together with the acquisition of afflictions.
Now, regarding those who are currently born, they lack such delusion and attainment.
The treatise asks:
at what stage does the path cause the obstructions to birth to be severed?
This refers to the latter half of the verse.
Regarding the third path, when abandoning the hindrances, the treatise states:
"Because it reaches the state of being identical to the freedom from hindrances."
Although the liberation from hindrances and the abandonment [of defilements] may differ, regarding the departure from hindrances,
both the arisen and the unarisen are free from hindrances.
Because the obstruction is equally non-existent.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"As is commonly seen in the world when a waterway is being cleared..."
Just as both near water and distant water are freed from their respective obstructions,
so too, once the path capable of severing the afflictions is seen to have arisen within one’s continuum,
it should likewise be said that both the proximate mind and the remote mind attain liberation.
Treatise:
The Sūtra speaks of the three realms;
the following one-line verse [explains this].

The fourth section clarifies the distinctions between the unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), detachment (*virāga*), and cessation (*nirodha*) within the three realms.
The treatise states: "Regarding 'up to unconditioned liberation'":
this explains the three realms mentioned in the Sūtra.
This refers to the unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*) among the two aforementioned liberations.
Its essence is a single unconditioned reality;
it is given three distinct names based on three different meanings.
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 72, states:
"Regarding the substance of the three realms, there are differences in terms of conventional designation;
however, in terms of ultimate reality, there is no distinction."
What is meant by "difference based on conventional designation"?
It refers to designating the separation from the fetter of greed as the "element of separation" (vairāgyadhātu),
and the severance of the remaining eight fetters as the "element of abandonment" (prahāṇadhātu).
The cessation of all other entities bound by fetters such as craving and so forth is called the element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*).
For what reason are the three elements distinguished in this way?
It is because contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are, in brief, of three kinds.
The first are those that can bind but cannot defile;
the second are those that both bind and defile;
the third are those that are neither, as they are factors conducive to binding and defilement.

The unconditioned states realized through the abandonment of these three are, respectively, called the realms of abandonment and so forth. [The commentary] states: "Regarding the term 'fetters' (*saṃyojana*):"

The unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta*) consisting of the detachment from greed for the pervasive, the single fruit, and so forth, as well as the intrinsic nature of greed and other such factors, are called the "realm of detachment" (*virāga-dhātu*).

The remaining eight [realms] are likewise so; however, the unconditioned states consisting of the intrinsic nature of phenomena and the abandonment of fetters (*saṃyojana*) are called the "realm of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-dhātu*).
When the fetters directed toward other objects are severed, this is called the "element of the cessation of the remainder.
That is to say, these nine fetters and the single fruit, etc., are "cessation" in relation to others,
while they are "separation" in relation to themselves.
The statement that "form is a non-defiled dharma, being exclusively cessation rather than a comprehensive, fixed, or distinct entity," is therefore termed "provisional.
Now, examining the correct principles, both [previous views] fail to exhaust the full meaning.

These three entities are each distinct and do not intermingle or defile one another; as for the dharma being "exclusively" [cessation], this refers to the eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) themselves, which are designated as "abandoned."
"Greed" refers to detachment.
Among the remaining dharmas and various fetters, there is not even one that is extinguished.
This explains the distinction between the three.
This is superior from the perspective of principle; otherwise,
the three would become confused.
However, regarding what is called "provisional," these three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) have no difference in their intrinsic nature;
they are all designated by the name "cessation" (*prahāṇa*).
This name is provisional and not ultimate reality.
Regarding the section on detachment and cessation within the three outflows (*āsrava*),
the treatise asks:
"If one is able to feel revulsion toward an object, is one necessarily able to become detached from it?"
The following single line of verse constitutes the sixth major section, which clarifies weary detachment (*nirveda*).
The treatise says: [This applies] up to the others, but it is not so for the rest.
This explains "disgust" (*nirveda*). According to the treatise,
within the objective sphere of the Four Noble Truths, one attains the name "detachment" (*vairāgya*) upon reaching each stage.
The commentary explains that because there is a distinction between breadth and narrowness, four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) are established.
The universal nature of *nirveda* (disgust) regarding both the severance and non-severance of afflictions is broad;
its restriction to taking only suffering (*duḥkha*) and origination (*samudaya*) as objects is narrow.
Its universal nature regarding all four truths is broad.
It is narrow because it consists solely in the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*). Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra*:
"There is disenchantment that is not detachment, up to [the point where] there is no detachment from defilement":
This is the first phrase.
It refers to the wisdom that transcends the patience and knowledge regarding suffering and its origin pertaining to the human realm,
as well as all wisdom belonging to the paths of preparation, liberation, and advancement.
Treatise:
There is detachment that is not preceded by revulsion, because it is capable of abandoning defilements;
this is the second phrase.
Third, the four lines should be understood according to their respective applications.
As for what was previously stated regarding "aversion and non-aversion," this refers to the *dharmakṣānti* of transcendence (*abhisamaya*).
And as for the various views,
they are comprised within the wisdom of the paths of preparation, liberation, and advancement during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
This is because those who practice "leap-over" (*vyutkrāntaka*) do not possess, nor have they abandoned, nor have they already abandoned [the afflictions] associated with them.
Because the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*) are not antidotes through abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*).
