Chapter Seven: The Analysis of Knowledge (Vijñāna-vibhaṅga). Part One of the Seventh Chapter on the Analysis of Knowledge.
Regarding the "Analysis of Knowledge": [it is as follows].
Wisdom (*jñāna*) is defined as the discernment that has already seen [the object].
Alternatively, wisdom is said to be the state in which the intention to seek to see the object has ceased and the application of effort has become relaxed.
The categories of wisdom do not exceed ten types;
because this chapter explains them extensively, it is titled "Discrimination" (Vibhaṅga).
Wisdom itself is the Path.
The Path is the cause of cessation.
The former sages and saints clearly understood the person perfected by the Path.
This chapter elucidates the person’s reliance upon the Path through clear wisdom.
The effect precedes the cause;
therefore, this is the clear wisdom.
Treatise.
At the beginning of the preceding chapter, it was stated: "Is there that which is wisdom but not vision?
This concludes the previous section and introduces the subsequent one;
the response in verse may be understood accordingly.
From this point downward, all subsequent sections follow this principle and are not individually described. Within this chapter, the main text is divided into two parts:
first, the discernment of wisdom;
second, the virtues perfected by wisdom. Within the former section, it is further divided into seven parts.
1. Clarifying the distinctions between patience (*kṣānti*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and vision (*darśana*).

2. Clarifying the differing characteristics of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*). 3. Clarifying the establishment of the ten knowledges. 4. Clarifying the distinctions between the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the abandonment of defilements (*prahāṇa*).
The fifth [section] explains the modes of activity of the five sciences and ten knowledges;
the sixth, the analytical exposition according to the six categories of meaning;
and the seventh, the detailed elucidation of the cultivation of knowledge.
This first verse clarifies the distinctions between patience (*kṣānti*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and vision (*darśana*).
The commentary states: "Up to the point of having the nature of deliberation (*tarka*).
This clarifies that noble patience (*ārya-kṣānti*) is not subsumed under knowledge.

The term "sage" (ārya) is established to distinguish it from contaminated patience (*sāsrava-kṣānti*); "doubt regarding what one has abandoned oneself" distinguishes it from the doubts of other schools.
Because it coexists with the acquisition of doubt (*vicikitsā-prāpti*), it is not called "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
The *Nyāyabindu* states: "Alternatively,
when the intention to perceive an object has ceased and the application of effort has become lax, this is termed wisdom (*jñāna*)."

Because the various patiences (*kṣānti*) arise with an intense application of the mental state of deliberation (*tulanā*), they are not subsumed under "knowledge" (*jñāna*); this is according to the aforementioned treatise.
Furthermore, because the "exhaustion of outflows" (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*) do not involve such deliberation, they are [classified as knowledge].
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) do not have the nature of viewing (*darśana*).
This is because all remaining [knowledges] universally involve the nature of inferential deliberation (*tarka*).
It is explained that all remaining knowledges are both knowledge (*jñāna*) and vision (*darśana*).
Because they have already abandoned their own doubt, they are subsumed under knowledge;
because they possess the nature of inferential deliberation, they are called vision.
Because it is not the first seeing, it is not called "patience" (kṣānti). According to the treatise,
all contaminated wisdom up to worldly right view constitutes six [types].
It is explained that all contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) may be termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*),
because within the objects perceived, it is not a first-time perception.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 44, states:
"There is not a single sentient being who, regarding any object, has not repeatedly contemplated it with tainted wisdom since beginningless time;
therefore, all tainted wisdom is subsumed under *jñāna* (knowledge). This concludes the treatise. This [passage] refers to the inclusion of all tainted wisdoms, both defiled and undefiled.
All are termed "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
Although the five consciousnesses differ from moment to moment in their objects,
they are also termed "wisdom" because they take similar types of objects as their conditions.
Furthermore, regarding the objects of apprehension,
because one has repeatedly observed them with outflow-tainted wisdom since beginningless time—
excluding the wisdom associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness— [the latent tendencies are removed].
All remaining wholesome wisdoms are termed "view" (dṛṣṭi),
which are subsumed under mundane right view (laukika-samyagdṛṣṭi).
Among all defiled wisdoms, only five are termed "view."
All that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is not view (*dṛṣṭi*).
Treatise:
As has been explained thus, [these] are all subsumed under the nature of wisdom (*prajñā-svabhāva*).
This clarifies that both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) wisdom (*prajñā*) are designated as "wisdom" in all instances,
because both are capable of discerning phenomena (*dharmas*).
Treatise:
How many kinds of characteristics does wisdom have, and what are they?
Hereafter, the second section clarifies the distinctions between the ten types of wisdom; this passage is further divided into four parts.
First, it clarifies the names and distinct natures of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*).
Second, it clarifies how the three knowledges constitute the nine knowledges.
Third, it clarifies how the nine knowledges constitute the ten knowledges.
The fourth [section] clarifies the distinctions between the characteristics of exhaustion and non-arising.
These two verses clarify the names and essential natures of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*).
The treatise states: "up to the distinction of their intrinsic natures."
This is the enumeration of the names of the knowledges.
First, they are grouped into two categories. The treatise states:
"These two knowledges, up to their differentiation of phenomena, are classified as follows."
This explains the opening of two knowledges into three. Regarding these three,
conventional knowledge takes the Four Noble Truths as its object.
This clarifies that the objects of the three types of knowledge are each distinct.
The *Nyāya* commentary explains:
"The aforementioned contaminated knowledges are collectively termed 'conventional' (*saṃvṛti*)."
Objects such as jars and garments have destructible natures;
because they are manifest according to worldly convention, they are called "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*).
This cognition mostly takes conventional objects as its domain.
Because it functions predominantly in accordance with worldly conventional matters,
it is established by name as "conventional knowledge" (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*);
it is not that it lacks the apprehension of the ultimate, for it does function in accordance with ultimate matters.
However, because this object of craving lacks the superior capacity to pacify the various internal afflictions, it is not untainted (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, it is asked:
what is the distinction between tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) wisdom?
The untainted [wisdom] is clear and sharp in its activity toward its object;
that tainted wisdom is the opposite of this.
It is like the charcoal of *khadira* wood and other woods, which differ in their efficacy for burning and smelting, and differ in their capacity to perfume as superior or inferior incense.
The thermal power of flaming iron and grass fire differs;
likewise, the distinction between these two types of wisdom when compared to one another is also such.
The treatise [proceeds] precisely within these three kinds of wisdom.
The next verse [explains] this.
Second, it opens up [the discussion] to form nine knowledges.
The Treatise says: ...up to the four knowledges of cessation and the path.
These—the dharma-knowledge and the subsequent knowledge—constitute four [knowledges] based on their objects;
together with the preceding dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge, they further constitute six knowledges.
If conventional knowledge is added, there are seven knowledges in total.
Treatise:
Thus, these six knowledges extend to being called "exhaustion" and "non-arising.
This clarifies that the six knowledges reach the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) together constitute nine knowledges in total.
According to the treatise, this is because these two initially arise taking [the aforementioned objects] as their cognitive domain.
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) take only the four aggregates of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as their object.
Only these two knowledges extend across multiple moments.
The first moment of thought takes as its object only the suffering and origin of the Peak of Existence;
the subsequent moments take other objects.
Otherwise, [it would not be so].
For what reason does the first [moment] exclude subsequent births?
The treatise asks:
Is the object of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) the same as this?
Question: The treatise states that while [the mind] takes suffering and its origin as objects in the same way, it differs in taking cessation and the path as objects.
Answer: According to this treatise, it is the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi).
It takes only the four aggregates of non-perception as its object,
because it is identical to the first [attainment] in its exhaustion. — Treatise.
Regarding the nine types of knowledge previously mentioned,
the final two verses open up the third [type] to constitute ten knowledges.
The treatise states: "It is not so for the others.

This clarifies that among the dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, path-knowledge, and conventional knowledge, the knowledge of others' minds is excluded from the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, exhaustion, and non-arising.
Treatise:
This knowledge [perceives] the present object as well as past and future minds.
This clarifies the three determinate characteristics of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Treatise:
Regarding the three types of superior minds, those that have reached the state of supremacy are minds that cannot be known through the three conditions of clarity.
This is because [the latter] is known only as equal or inferior.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"However, since the knowledge of others' minds and its object differ in terms of faculty (*indriya*) and stage (*bhūmi*)."
It should also be known that there are differences:
the objects of knowledge consist of contaminated minds and mental factors,
whether they have been previously attained or not yet attained.
There are fifteen types in each case;
that is, the desire realm and the four dhyānas each have the lower, middle, and superior faculties.
These can know [the objects] except for the three grades of the desire realm.
There are twelve each for those previously attained and those never before attained.
Regarding the objects to be known and the untainted [cognitions] that know them,
all are excluded from the three [realms] of desire.
Each has twelve [types]. Furthermore,
regarding the arising of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)— which is comprised of inferior faculties and has been or has not yet been attained among the various contaminated states—
it occurs according to its respective correspondence.
One can know the three grades of mental states (mūla-citta-varga) of the lower stages;
one also knows the lower and middle grades of one’s own stage,
and fully comprehends all three grades of one’s own and lower stages.
When the untainted knowledge of others' minds arises with a lower faculty,
it knows only those of its own stage, lower stages, and lower faculties; likewise, when it has a middle faculty, it also knows those of the middle.
The superior [knowledge] further knows the superior.
For what reason do the tainted and untainted knowledges arise?
There are differences in the extent to which they know the minds of lower stages.
The three grades of contaminated [faculties] can be perfected within a single lifetime;
however, the distinction between noble ones is established according to their uncontaminated faculties.
Indeed, there is not even one who perfects two grades of faculties.
Moreover, since there is the establishment of three [categories], there is a distinction;
how then can it be said that there is only one *pudgala*?
The nine grades of the path bring about the abandonment of the nine grades of afflictions;
this differentiation of the paths is not due to differences in the faculties,
but rather because the subsequent paths increase as the causal conditions gradually develop.
In this sequence, they enable the abandonment of multiple grades of afflictions;
alternatively, each spiritual lineage (gotra) possesses nine grades,
such that once one set of nine grades is accomplished, another cannot be.
Therefore, there is no contradiction between the preceding and following statements.
Consequently, while a mind with lower faculties may arise based on a higher stage,
a mind with higher faculties arising based on a lower stage— where stage and faculty mutually differ in excellence— will necessarily not cognize one another.
The same applies to the relative positions of the stages (*bhūmi*) and the faculties (*indriya*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Question: Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) in the first dhyāna, how many types of minds and mental factors from the desire realm and the four dhyānas—specifically those resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*)—can it cognize?"
Some say that one can know four kinds. Why is this?
Because all [of these] are subsumed within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that [the supernormal power] can only know the *abhijñā-phala* (result of superknowledge) of the first dhyāna, but not that of the other three.
Why is this? Because as it is with the cause, so it is with the fruit. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "Regarding the mind and mental factors of the intermediate dhyāna..."
By what level of meditative concentration can this knowledge be known?
Some say it can be known by the superior knowledge of the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, there are those who say that it can be known by the inferior grade of wisdom of the second dhyāna.
The critique states: one should speak thus.
The three grades of knowledge of the first dhyāna can all be known.
Why is this? Because they are subsumed within a single stage (*bhūmi*). This is as stated in the treatise above.
Treatise:
Because this wisdom does not take the ultimate as its object,
it clarifies that it does not know the causes of the past and future.
Treatise:
Furthermore, because the categories of Dharma-knowledge and Subsequent-knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) take [their respective objects] as their cognitive objects (ālambana),
it is clarified that Dharma-knowledge and Subsequent-knowledge do not take one another as cognitive objects.
Because the knowledge of categories (anvaya-jñāna) does not pertain to the path of desire,
it does not take [the desire realm] as its object; because the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) does not pertain to the higher paths, it does not take [the upper realms] as its object.
Inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) does not take these as its objects.
Although the dharma-knowledges of cessation and the path also counteract the afflictions of the higher realms that are to be abandoned by cultivation, they do not do so completely;
therefore, inferential knowledge does not take them as its objects.
Treatise:
This knowledge of others' minds extends to the objects of this [present] knowledge;
it clarifies that within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), there is no knowledge of others' minds.
The path of seeing can also serve as the object of another's mind.
The treatise states: "If the minds of sentient beings reach the stage of the path of seeing..."
This is a general indication that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have already cultivated preparatory practice and possess the knowledge and vision of the path of seeing.
According to the treatise, those sentient beings reach the first and second moments of mind.
This section specifically clarifies the stage of the śrāvaka’s knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*). The treatise states:
"If one seeks further knowledge up until the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which is not yet [fully] realized..."
This clarifies that because the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of the Śrāvaka is inferior,
it only becomes perfected after many moments (*kṣaṇa*).
Although he is also able to know the sixteenth moment of mind, [the process is protracted].
The sixteenth moment of mind is not included within the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

According to the treatises, this is because the "Rhinoceros-like" (*khadgaviṣāṇakalpa*) and those of the "Dharma-follower" (*dharmānusārin*) types have already reached the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the subsequent [Path of Meditation].
This section specifically clarifies the Pratyekabuddha’s knowledge of the minds of the dharma- and anvaya-kṣāntis.
Some say that he knows the first two and the fifteenth mind.
Regarding the statement that other masters explain the Pratyekabuddha’s mind-knowledge,
the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* says:
"Some say that the Rṣabha-like [Pratyekabuddha] knows four moments."
This refers to the first two moments of mind, the eighth, and the fourteenth;
this statement is logical. Why is that?
Having permitted that one knows the first two moments of mind through cognition,
one knows the eighth mind by skipping over five moments.
If one further cultivates the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for a duration of five moments, the application should be perfected.
Why not allow that the fourteenth moment is known?
Others also say that four moments are known.
This refers to the first two moments of mind and the eleventh and twelfth [moments], as stated in the treatise.
The treatise says:
"The World-Honored One, desiring to know, attains the capacity to know all."
It clarifies that the Buddha possesses the capacity to know all things without the need for preparatory application (*prayoga*). Question:

For what reason is the essence of the untainted knowledge of others' minds (*anāsrava-paracittajñāna*) exclusively the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) and not any other type of knowledge? Answer: The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Because uncontaminated knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is definitively unable to know the contaminated minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of others, it is stated:
"This is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*), yet it cannot know the uncontaminated minds and mental factors of another's body."
Because it is subtle and superior,
it is not the object of the knowledge of others' minds that pertains to those already possessed of outflows.
That principle may indeed be so.
For what reason, then, can one’s own untainted knowledge of others' minds not know another's tainted mind and mental factors?
Regarding the mode of activity (*ākāra*) and the object (*ālambana*) of the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that arises toward tainted objects: because this knowledge differs from them,
when untainted knowledge takes a tainted object as its focus,
it necessarily takes it as a collective object with a mode of activity characterized by aversion.
Therefore, it is certain that one cannot produce the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) by taking the minds and mental factors of others as distinct objects.
This is because when the various noble wisdoms take contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) as their objects,
they necessarily give rise to a profound sense of revulsion toward those objects.
One delights in relinquishing them as a whole rather than observing them individually,
because joy arises when taking the untainted (*anāsrava*) as an object; yet,
once they have been observed as a whole, one also delights in observing them individually.
If one sees or hears something unpleasant,
one abandons it by taking it as a whole object and takes no pleasure in focusing on its particulars;
this is not the case with regard to what is pleasant.
Having already seen and heard them collectively, one also delights in regarding them individually;
therefore, with respect to the tainted minds and so forth of others,
there is certainly no noble wisdom that takes them as objects through individual, distinct observation.
The untainted knowledge of others' minds is determined by the knowledge of others' minds, because it knows the various mental states and mental factors of others individually.
Is it not also the case that there are three applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) which include the receptivities and knowledges regarding suffering and its origin? [The author] replies: No.

If untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) cannot take [the mind] as a distinct object, for what reason are the knowledges of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) included within the three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), since they do indeed take the mind, feelings, and mental factors as distinct objects? Although this is so...
It does not, however, take only a single dharma as its object; rather,
because it takes multiple entities as its objects,
it is stated that when the knowledge of others' minds arises, it takes one dharma as its object but cannot take two or three minds, and so forth.
The three applications of mindfulness subsume the objects of many minds and so forth; therefore, they are subsumed by taking many [objects] collectively rather than by taking them individually.
Treatise:
What is the difference between the two knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising?
The following single line of verse clarifies the distinction between the characteristics of the two knowledges.
The treatise says: ...up to this point, it is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).

This clarifies the characteristics of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*). Knowledge, vision, clarity, awakening, understanding, wisdom, radiance, and contemplation—these are collectively enumerated as synonyms for knowledge. To decisively resolve is called knowledge;
to investigate is called vision.
Being free from darkness is called clarity;
awakening to principle is called enlightenment;
thorough comprehension is called understanding.
The discernment of phenomena is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
"Light" refers to manifest illumination;
"contemplation" refers to investigative observation.
Thus, although their names differ,
their essence is one. Therefore,
the *Nyāyabindu* states:
Is it not the case that the two types of knowledge (jñāna) are not subsumed under the nature of vision (darśana)?
How, then, can one speak of them as "knowledge," "vision," "clarity" (vidyā), and so forth?
To this, some offer the following explanation:
This is done for the sake of convenience in expression.
However, in reality, these two types of knowledge are also called "vision" because they serve as the cause for the arising of vision at a later time.
That is to say, after the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) has ceased, when one emerges from meditative absorption.
This is because the analytical insight (*pratyavekṣaṇā-darśana*) does not manifest [in these states].
Furthermore, at the time when one first attains the immovable nature (*akopyadharman*) and later attains the immovable state through the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*),
even after the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), the analytical insight likewise does not manifest.
Therefore, this "view" (dṛṣṭi) is named after its fruit;
or, because it resembles a view, it is metaphorically designated as such.
It is like establishing the name "light" because it functions as manifest illumination.
Light itself is not the essence of the cognition of the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*);
however, there is no error in calling it "light" because its function of illumination is like that of light.
Likewise, these two types of cognition are in reality not the essence of seeing (*darśana*).
"Manifestly illuminating as if seeing, established with the name 'seeing'"—the above is from the treatise (*śāstra*). The treatise asks:
"What is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)? ... up to: this is called the knowledge of non-arising.
This clarifies the practice of the knowledge of non-arising.
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) knows: "Suffering has been known; the origin has been abandoned; cessation has been realized; the path has been cultivated.
The knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) knows that there is no further falling back.
Therefore, it is said: "It has been known," and so forth.
"One should not further know," and so forth.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* asks:
"For what reason does the treatise, within the context of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), again state this?"
"I have already known suffering and so forth.
Logically, one should only say this and not "I know [it] again" and so forth,
because two mental applications cannot operate simultaneously.
If they were to arise in succession,
there would be no distinction between the preceding [moment] and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and thus it should not be stated again.
One should understand that the intent of this statement is to dispel doubt.
Lest there arise doubts:
just as one liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) first gives rise to the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and subsequently attains the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna),
so too should it be admitted that one liberated at any time (asamayavimukta) first gives rise to the knowledge of non-arising and subsequently attains the knowledge of exhaustion.
In order to manifest that all *kṣayajñāna* (knowledge of exhaustion) arises preceded by this,
he further first speaks the words "already known" (*ājñāta*) and so forth;
or alternatively, he first simply says, "I have already known," and so on.
This shows that for those liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta), there is only the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna);
subsequently, they again declare, "I have already known," and so forth.
This shows that for those not liberated by occasion (asamaya-vimukta), the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) arises after the knowledge of exhaustion.
Therefore, although it is stated repeatedly,
there is no fault. As for the one who possesses the wisdom of non-arising:
What is meant by "non-arising"?
The Master of Right Reasoning says:
it is because non-analytical cessation possesses non-arising.
This wisdom arises by taking non-arising as its object; thus it is called "wisdom of non-arising.
Although cessation is ever-present, it does not attain the state of permanence.
This wisdom only arises when that [object] has ceased;
for it is only by virtue of its arising that one speaks of its cessation.
It is at the stage of its cessation that this wisdom is produced.
Alternatively, the term "non-arising" (anutpāda) refers to the attainment of cessation (nirodha-prāpti).
As the treatise states: "The attainment of nirvāṇa is also called 'nirvāṇa' itself. End of the treatise.
"How can untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) produce such a cognition?
This is the question.
All untainted knowledges do not exceed the sixteen aspects (ṣoḍaśākāra).

I have already known that suffering and the other [truths] do not consist of sixteen aspects. How, then, can one produce such knowledge? [The Treatise says: I have already known that suffering and the other [truths] do not consist of sixteen aspects. How, then, can one produce such knowledge? [The Treatise says: I have already known that suffering and the other [truths] do not consist of sixteen aspects. How, then, can one produce such knowledge? [The Treatise says:]
Regarding the distinction between the two knowledges from Kaśmīra,
the Master of the Treatise cites the *Vibhāṣā* as an explanation;

the intended meaning of the root treatise is that [the subsequent knowledge] arises from within the subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) following the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
One is able to know, "I have already known suffering," and so forth,
when emerging from subsequent-to-arising knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) into subsequently attained knowledge (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
One can immediately know that one no longer further knows suffering and so forth;
by this it is proven that the functions of the two types of untainted knowledge-power (anāsrava-jñānabala) are distinct.
Treatise.
Some say that untainted subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is also a vision (*darśana*).
This is a statement of a divergent interpretation. [End of] Treatise.
Thus, the ten knowledges (daśajñāna) encompass [the others] up to six partial portions.
To clarify the mutual inclusion of the ten knowledges: conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) constitutes one whole;
that is, conventional knowledge itself.

One partial portion, namely the knowledge of others' minds; two entire [knowledges], namely the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*); and seven partial portions.

That is to say, the knowledge of the extinction and non-arising of the four truths each comprises one whole [category] and a small portion of four others— namely, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origination, and the knowledge of cessation— which are each their own respective knowledge, as well as the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*),

subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of extinction (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). The knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) comprises one whole [category].
That is to say, five partial portions of one's own knowledge,
plus the knowledge of others' minds; [the latter] consists of one full portion of the knowledge of others' minds,
and four partial portions of one's own knowledge.
That is to say: the conventional, path, dharma, and subsequent knowledges; the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising, each constituting one whole;
and six partial portions of their own respective knowledges—namely, the four truths, the dharma-knowledge, and the subsequent-knowledge.
Treatise:
For what reason are the two knowledges established as ten?
[The following] one verse [provides the answer].
The fourth [section] establishes the ten knowledges (*jñāna*).
The treatise says: "Because it has reaching as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)," the first establishes conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Because its nature as conventional wisdom can be destroyed and because it cognizes many worldly truths (saṃvṛti-satya),
it is called "conventional wisdom" (saṃvṛti-jñāna) with respect to its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
[End of] Treatise.
Because they serve as antidotes to two [levels]— namely, the desire realm and the higher realms—
the second [set] serves as an antidote, and thus the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) are established.
Because it serves as an antidote to what is not the Dharma in the desire realm, it is called the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
The antidote to the non-dharma of the higher realms should also be called "dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna); however,
it is not permissible to apply the name "dharma-knowledge" twice over, but rather it may be designated as a "subsequent knowledge" (anvayajñāna).
This is because it serves as an antidote to the category of non-dharma (*adharma*).
According to the treatise, this is due to the three aspects (*ākāra*), up to the fact that there is no distinction in their essence (*svabhāva*).
Third is the establishment of the knowledge of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-jñāna*).
This is distinguished by the single function of the categories of suffering and its origin,
rather than by a difference in their objective spheres.
The treatise states: These two wisdoms are distinguished solely on the basis of their differing modes of activity.
Because the objects of the four aspects differ, and because their co-existent factors differ,
the fourth [knowledge] establishes the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path.
Regarding the two truths of cessation and the path, both their essential natures and their aspects differ.
Based on these differences in objective referents and mental aspects,
the two types of knowledge are distinguished.
Treatise.
Due to five preparatory applications (*prayoga*), it receives the name "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*);
this is the fifth establishment of the knowledge of others' minds.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* further cites the explanation of the Venerable Pārśva.
This wisdom arises by way of induction.
One must first know the mind [of another] before subsequently knowing its object.
Therefore, from the beginning, it is designated simply as the "knowledge of others' minds" (paracittajñāna).
When inducing this wisdom, what preparatory application (*prayoga*) should be cultivated?
First, one should observe the color and shape of forms,
as well as the distinctions of mental states expressed through desired sounds and speech.
That is to say, when that practitioner first begins their training,
desiring to thoroughly discern the distinctions within the minds of others,
they first carefully observe the manifest forms of their own body.
He considers why there are differences in the vocal sounds one enjoys,
thereby realizing that distinctions such as clarity and so forth depend upon the mind.
Next, he further examines the clarity and other qualities of another’s body.
Furthermore, differences arise due to the diversity of the mind;
consequently, at a later time, through mindfulness of the body free from desire,
it becomes pliant, pure, and induces the arising of superior meditative concentration.
Based on meditative concentration, there arises powerful knowledge and wisdom;
this wisdom truly perceives the minds of others,
as clearly as within a bright pearl.
The distinct characteristics of various colored threads can be clearly perceived;
this is called the preparatory practice for cultivating conventional knowledge of others' minds.
When one cultivates the untainted knowledge of others' minds,
one takes the knowledge that contemplates impermanence and so forth as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
In this stage of preparation, it takes both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) as its objects.
Regarding the passage from the treatise stating, "At the time of fulfillment, it takes as its object the mind and not form," and so forth:
[it is said] because the six matters have been accomplished and because it has reached the initial arising.
Sixth is the establishment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*):
regarding the seeing of suffering and the abandoning of its origin.
It is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) because it arises for the first time within the body when the task of realizing cessation and cultivating the path has been accomplished.
Treatise:
From "because the seven causes are perfected" up to "because it arises as a cause," this clarifies the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
All the noble paths within oneself,
when taken as causes for this [knowledge], are called the perfection of causes.
Because the causes are perfected, the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) is established separately.
Treatise:
Regarding the aforementioned dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge (anvaya-jñāna),
the following verse states:
The fourth clarifies that the antidotes for the dharmas and their categories differ.
The treatise states: "Up to the point where there is nothing capable of counteracting desire.
This explains the meaning of the verse.
The *Nyāyānusāra* asks:
"For what reason do only the dharma-knowledges of cessation and the path treat the higher realms,
while those of suffering and origin do not?"
Because their objects, tranquility, renunciation, and antidotes are identical—
namely, desire, the higher realms, cessation,
and the path that acts as the antidote.
Because they are mutually related and their characteristics are indistinguishable;
for all analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are wholesome and eternal,
and all noble paths (*āryamārga*) are capable of leading to liberation.
The objects of focus— suffering and its origin—
and the realms of desire and the higher realms differ because of distinctions such as small and great, subtle and coarse, and lower and upper.
Furthermore, the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origination take as their objects those states that are to be reviled;

it is impossible to feel revulsion toward those [objects] while being free from craving for these [states]. This continues until the two knowledges of cessation and the path, which do not take reviled objects as their objects.
There is likewise no fault in using a lower object as the condition for treating a higher one,
just as in the case of the contemplation of impurity or the aspiration for Nirvana.
That is to say, the contemplation of impurity takes the objects of the desire realm as its focus;
it can only cause the mind to feel revulsion toward the desire realm.
When the aspiration for nirvana manifests before one, [this contemplation serves as the basis].
It is universally able to cause the mind to feel revulsion toward and turn away from the three realms.
Such knowledge of the suffering and origin of desire arises;
it is capable only of causing the mind to become detached from the defilements of the desire realm.
When the phenomena of the desire realm cease, the knowledge of the path arises.
Because it causes the mind to become universally detached from the defilements of the three realms,
it is held that the category of the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path increases.
This continues until the attainment of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Based on this, the Great Sage, having perfectly and excellently understood it,
establishes the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) by way of complete antidotes.
Treatise:
Among these ten knowledges (*jñāna*), which possesses which aspect (*ākāra*)?
Below, the fifth section clarifies the aspects of the ten knowledges; this passage contains three parts.
First, the aspects of the ten knowledges are clarified;
second, the aspects of the untainted (anāsrava) are clarified;
third, the essence and objects of the aspects are clarified.
These one and a half verses constitute the first section.
The Commentary states that this will be explained in detail later.
This clarifies that the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) possess sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).
Because there are four dharmas and four types of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The treatise states: "Conventional knowledge possesses these [objects], up to their specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)."
Regarding the characteristics of clear worldly knowledge (*laukikī prajñā*):
those who possess these refer to these sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).
That is to say, the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), and Patience (*kṣānti*) each possess these sixteen aspects.

The "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma) has only the aspect of suffering and so forth; furthermore, there are others capable of taking all phenomena as their objects, such as their specific and general characteristics (svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa), namely, the five contemplations for settling the mind (pañca-vastu-sthāpana).
The general and specific mindfulnesses,
the twelve links of dependent origination,
the contemplation of the eighteen elements as selfless, and so forth.
Regarding the characteristics of the general and the specific,
the treatise states that the four knowledges, such as the knowledge of suffering, possess four types of cognitive aspects (*ākāra*).
The wisdoms that clearly realize the four truths each possess four aspects (ākāra) pertaining to their respective truths. According to the treatise,
within the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), these are subsumed up to sixteen [aspects].
The aspect of the knowledge of others' minds is explained as follows:
uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) knowledge of others' minds is described in the same manner as the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*); as for contaminated (*sāsrava*) knowledge of others' minds—
Just as the mind and mental factors have their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their objects,
so too are their modes of activity (*ākāra*);
they are not subsumed under the sixteen modes of activity.
Commentary:
These two types [of mental factors], up to "not taking ideation as an object" and so forth,
clarify the grasping of distinct objects.
Whether they are untainted (*anāsrava*) or tainted (*sāsrava*),
there are two kinds of knowledge of others' minds.
All [of these] take only a single dharma as their object.
[Question:
If that is so, why [does the text speak of] "greedy minds" and so forth?
This is difficult.
If one were to take only the mind and not the mental factors,
why would the Sūtra state that there exists a "mind with desire"?
Greed is a mental factor (caitta), while the mind is the sovereign mind (cittarāja). Is it not, therefore,
that two things are being grasped?
Treatise:
It is not that [the robe] is grasped simultaneously with the reaching for it; rather, it is grasped together with the cloth and the impurities—this is the general rule.
The mind and greed are distinct; the mind takes [the object] by means of a separate cognition.
It is like when one takes a garment, one does not simultaneously take its stains.
Commentary.
Regarding those with minds possessed by craving (*sarāga-citta*), it extends from [the state] up to being bound solely by craving.
Generally speaking, there are two types of minds possessed by craving.
A mind associated with craving is called a "mind possessed by craving."
Both the abandoned and the unabandoned are called "minds with greed.
Other tainted minds that are bound by greed are also called "minds with greed."
"If one has severed craving, one is no longer called 'possessing craving'.
