It does not manifest before one because of attachment to a self. Regarding the fifth point, the distinction between universal and restricted objects of focus:
the question is asked, "How does the aspect of non-self arise?"
Answer: If one is born in the desire realm and gives rise to the aspect of non-self regarding the desire and form realms, one is able to take all phenomena as objects.
If one is born in the first dhyāna and gives rise to the aspect of non-self regarding the first dhyāna, [one is likewise able to take all phenomena as objects].
Those who are not in meditative concentration can take all phenomena as their objects;
those who are in concentration take as their objects only that which ranges from the first dhyāna up to the peak of existence.
The same applies to the aspect of non-self (*anātman*) when arising in the three higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
The principle for birth in the second meditative absorption and so forth may be understood by analogy.
Question: Between the two realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and form (*rūpadhātu*), which has more objects of focus (*ālambana*) for the aspect of non-self?
Answer: If the aspect of non-self in the form realm were indeterminate, its objects would be equal to those of the desire realm and so forth;
if it were determinate, then the dharmas that serve as its objects would be fewer than those in the desire realm.
This means that they cannot take as their object the matter that arises concomitantly with themselves. Now, upon closer examination:
in the desire realm and the first dhyāna, etc., the aspect of non-self (*anātman*) is scattered;
it takes as its object a small portion of the dharmas, whereas from the second dhyāna upwards, it is otherwise.
Because it cannot take as its object the vitarka and vicāra associated with itself, nor their arising and so forth—thus, the sixth question-and-answer analysis. Question:
Is this not the aspect of "non-self" (anātman)?
If it is associated with an attention of delight,
how can it take a dharma that is to be reviled as its object?
If it is associated with an attention of revulsion...
What is the object-condition for phenomena that are to be welcomed?
It should be stated as follows:
it is accompanied by a mental orientation of welcome.
Question: If that is so, how can one take as an object a phenomenon that is to be loathed?
Answer: Because that practitioner of yoga generates a sense of delight toward this phenomenon that is to be rejoiced in, even amidst an immeasurable mass of phenomena that are to be loathed.
If there is even one thing worthy of delight, joy arises;
how much more so when there are many?
It is like placing a single gold coin upon a heap of copper coins.
Thus, one generates a collective sense of delight toward this collection;
this case is likewise,
and therefore there is no fault.

Question: Since the faculties of joy (*saumanasya*) and sorrow (*daurmanasya*) are also able to take all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-dharma*) as their objects, why is this aspect (*ākāra*) not associated with them?
Answer: Because they are mutually contradictory.
That is to say, this [aspect] proceeds as an aspect of delight (*prīti*).
Because that [feeling] operates with a mode of activity characterized by distress,
it is not associated [with the mind]. Thus says the Treatise.
The objects of focus have already been explained.
Below this, the sixth section clarifies the number of wisdoms that are accomplished.
The treatise says: "Up to [the stage of] 'arrival,' one will certainly accomplish seven."
The clarification of the stages of accomplishment consists of three sections: first, the stage of gradual increase;
second, the stage of freedom from desire;
and third, the stage of no-more-learning.
This is the first [point]: all ordinary persons and noble ones (ārya) alike possess conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Ordinary persons who have not yet abandoned desire possess only conventional knowledge;
as do noble persons who have not yet abandoned desire while abiding in the stage of receptivity toward suffering (*duḥkhe kṣānti*).
It is the same as that of ordinary worldlings;
although one has attained untainted discernment (*anāsrava-prajñā*), it is not yet called "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Upon reaching the second moment, the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) is added.
Thus, by adding the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna),
three knowledges are established.
In the fourth moment, furthermore, the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) is added.
In the sixth moment, the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna) is further added;
in the tenth moment, the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) is further added;
and in the fourteenth moment, the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) is further added.
Up until the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), prior to being free from desire,
one accomplishes all seven knowledges (jñāna) as previously described.
[Treatise]
Thus, for those who reach the state of being born in the formless realm,
this is the second stage of detachment from desire.
Within this stage, the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) is added to each of the respective stages.
This refers to when one was an ordinary person and at the very beginning of being a noble one;
previously there was one, and now there are two.
Up until the stage of cultivation,
there were previously seven [abodes] and now there are eight.
However, as for ordinary beings born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu):
Although one who is free from the defilement of desire does not achieve the knowledge of others' minds,
this is because tainted (sāsrava) thoughts of others arise as equanimity (upekṣā) in the higher realms.
As for noble ones (ārya) born in the higher realms who do achieve the knowledge of others' minds:
Because one who possesses untainted knowledge of others' minds does not relinquish it when born into a higher realm,
there are two types of knowledge of others' minds established according to the differences in their respective stages:
namely, that of the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) and that of the fifteen moments of mind [of the path of seeing].
One only accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds with outflows; however,
at the moment of transcending the path-knowledge of the category of dharma (mārga-jñāna-dharmajñāna) of an Anāgāmin,
one fully accomplishes both types.
Because the untainted Path Truth (mārgasatya) of the fundamental stage is taken as the essence of the fruit,
both [the path and its fruit] are fully accomplished during all other stages of cultivation while one is free from the defilements of the desire realm.
The noble ones born in the formless realm immediately abandon the mundane [attainments].
Regarding the discussion on those liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*), it extends up to the increase of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
This clarifies the third stage, the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Within the stage of no-more-learning, there are nine for those of dull faculties and ten for those of sharp faculties;
these are explained in the same manner as previously interpreted.
Treatise:
In which stage are how many wisdoms cultivated simultaneously?
Below, the seventh major section clarifies the cultivation of wisdom.
Within this, there are six [sections]:
first, clarifying the path of seeing;
second, clarifying the path of cultivation.

1. The three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) on the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). 2. The four types of clear knowledge regarding the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) and so forth. 3. The five types of clear knowledge concerning the specific limitations of the stages (*bhūmi*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Sixth, the explanation of the four kinds of cultivation.
Below, these two lines of verse first clarify the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Now, I shall explain cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
One must understand the meaning of "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). The *Nyāyabindu* states:
"Furthermore, one should investigate what is meant by cultivation."

This means that practicing wholesome conditioned phenomena so as to bring them to perfection and mastery is the meaning of "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). It does not apply to defiled or neutral states, because they lack superior and desirable fruits;
nor does it apply to unconditioned wholesome states.
Because it does not exist within a continuum, and furthermore, because the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) has no fruit. Now, I shall offer an alternative explanation:
because the unconditioned is devoid of increase or decrease.
The Commentary states: Up to the "mindfulness foundation of formations" (*saṃskāra-smṛtyupasthāna*), it clarifies the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
This refers to the time when the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and seven knowledges (*jñāna*) manifest.
One cultivates only the mindfulness foundations (smṛtyupasthāna) regarding one’s own truth and the four aspects (ākāra).
If one takes the three truths as objects, one cultivates the four mindfulness foundations;

if one takes the truth of cessation (nirodhasatya) as the object, one cultivates only the mindfulness foundation of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna), because it is cultivated through its own specific nature (svabhāva).
Treatise:
For what reason is the path of seeing cultivated only as a homogeneous cultivation?
This is the question.

For what reason is it that the path of seeing (darśanamārga) consists only of cultivation of the same kind (*sabhāga-bhāvanā*), whereas the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and so forth do not? The treatise states:
Because [the former] has never been attained before and its arrival is certain.
Answer: There are two meanings.
First, because one has not yet attained this untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). Second, because both the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) and its object (*ālambana*) are determined.
During the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) definitely take the eight truths as their objects and abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*) associated with those eight truths.
The path of cultivation does not function in this manner; when abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation,
it takes as its object either the truth of suffering or even the truth of the path.
Furthermore, because the objects of focus are not the Truths and are intermingled and indeterminate,
the treatise states that one can only practice [the contemplation of] suffering, its origin, and its cessation until one is able to cultivate them concurrently.
It clarifies the cultivation of conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). Because it is cultivated at the conclusion of each individual Truth (*satya*),
it is called "conventional wisdom at the edge of clear realization" (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Because the knowledge of these truths is attained in its full perfection at that final stage,
it is cultivated at the end;
for at the stage of the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), it is not yet perfected.
Therefore, one cannot cultivate it at this stage.
[Question:
Why is this not cultivated at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna)?
Question: Why is this path not cultivated? Treatise: [The following is provided].
Regarding the question of whether conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) can ever be cultivated extensively throughout the course of the Path,
there are two explanations provided in response.
First, according to the explanation of what has been experienced and what has not:
since beginningless time, one has already known suffering and abandoned its origin.
It is the realization of cessation. Because it is known, abandoned, and realized by means of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*),
one cultivates that conventional knowledge through these three aspects.
Since beginningless time, one has never cultivated the untainted path;
consequently, one cannot cultivate that conventional knowledge, because it is absolutely impossible to have a clear realization (abhisamaya) regarding the universal aspects of the path.
The actualization through the object refers to seeing suffering and abandoning the origin.
Realizing cessation and cultivating the path may allow a single sentient being to fully comprehend the exhaustion of suffering.
One may completely sever the origin [of suffering] and bring it to an end, and completely realize its cessation;
yet, there is necessarily no one who can cultivate the path to completion.
Consequently, regarding the side of the truth of the path,
one cannot cultivate that conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). Thus says the treatise.
Although the limits of accumulation and cessation are reached, because there are many lineages (*gotra*),
this explains away the contradiction.
That is to say, a single sentient being, during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), realizes all suffering.
Because one has not yet abandoned all origins nor realized all cessations,
whereas in the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), these must necessarily be abandoned and realized.
The Path is not like that;
it is not only that one does not cultivate all paths during the Path of Seeing,
but even upon reaching the Stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa), one is still unable to cultivate them.
Because the three vehicles and six lineages have distinct paths and do not cultivate them equally,
[this is] discussed in the treatise.
Some say that because this [knowledge] is ultimate, it cannot be cultivated;
this is an alternative explanation.
Since the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna) belongs to the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), it does not cultivate the limits of vision (darśana-anta).
The author of the treatise refutes this, stating that what is not universally established through logic should not be used as proof.

Although the Sautrāntika school claims that the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna) belongs to the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), the Vaibhāṣika school asserts that it is [the path of seeing].
Since other schools do not accept that this is the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga),
it is not universally established and should not be used as proof.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Why is this not cultivated at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*)?
This knowledge belongs exclusively to the retinue of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)."
Because it is subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one cannot cultivate it [at that time].
This means that because the cultivation of the seven points of excellence (*saptasthānakauśalya*) serves as the seed, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) arises;
therefore, at the moment the path of seeing arises—
They are described as being its retinue,
and so forth; it is for this reason that the Blessed One spoke of the "limit" (*anta*) with respect to the three truths.
As stated in the Sūtra: there is the extreme of the view of a self-identity, and there is the extreme of the origin of the view of a self-identity.
There is a limit to the destruction of the body (*kāya-nirodha-anta*), but there has never been a sūtra stating that there is a limit to the path of the body (*kāya-mārga-anta*).
This is because no one is able to cultivate the path to its ultimate limit. Question: Among the three stages, which cultivation is superior and which is inferior?
The *Nyāyānusāra* replies:
"If one considers the continuum, the subsequent is superior to the preceding because the cause increases the body and brings about its attainment."
If one speaks in terms of the realms (*dhātu*), all that is above is superior to what is below.
Therefore, regarding those previously cultivated which are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
the realm is superior while the body is inferior.
Regarding those cultivated in the subsequent stage that are bound to the desire realm:
the realm is inferior while the body is superior.
This consists of four permutations.
This should be reflected upon according to reason.
The treatise states: "Because this conventional knowledge reaches a point where its arising is no longer possible."
This clarifies that [the defilements] do not arise.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 36, states:
Question: If this is so, why do they not manifest before one?

Answer: Because this wisdom contradicts the actual manifestation of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and because there is no possibility for it to arise once one has passed beyond the stage of the path of seeing;
even if it were during the stage of the path of seeing—
When the path of seeing (darśanamārga) does not manifest for even a moment,
this knowledge arises;
for the path of seeing has no sense of being interrupted by moments.
Therefore, it is impossible for this knowledge to manifest.

Question: If it does not manifest, how can it be said that this [knowledge] relies upon the bodies of those who practice through faith (śraddhānusārin) or those who practice through dharma (dharmānusārin)?
The answer is that his body is of two kinds:
first, that which is the basis for the path of seeing;
second, that which is the basis for the conventional wisdom at the conclusion of clear realization.
The path of seeing is acquired in the body that serves as its basis;
it is both possessed within that body and manifested therein.
The conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization is acquired in that body,
yet it is not accomplished within that body.
It is not manifest. It is the conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*),
which is acquired in the body that serves as the basis for that conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization.
It is also accomplished within that body and is manifested therein;
the vision of the path is attained in that very body.
Yet it is not accomplished within the body,
nor is it manifest; even at the stage of the Path of Vision (darśanamārga).
When the body upon which this conventional knowledge relies is present before one,
then that very knowledge is also accomplished and present before one.
The path of seeing (darśanamārga) is accomplished only in the future;
however, at the stage of the path of seeing,
one necessarily gives rise to the body that serves as the basis for the path of seeing.
The realization of the path of seeing is also manifested in the present;
this knowledge is realized only in the future.
If, at the stage of the path of seeing,
one does not give rise to the body that serves as the basis for the path of seeing,
then there would be no sense of "seeing the noble truths" through the path of seeing.
Consequently, they would no longer be noble ones (*ārya*). Therefore, the basis for the arising of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) must necessarily occur;
by this means, that body attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Therefore, this knowledge never arises at all. Furthermore, the *Nyāya* states:

"Because this knowledge certainly does not arise based on the bodies [of those who follow by faith or follow by dharma]. That is to say, it refers to the bodies of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
It is possible for it to arise based on a conditioned basis;
however, during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), its arising is impossible.
Therefore, this body remains in a state where it is subject to non-arising (*anutpattidharman*).
Based on the principle that because [dharmas] are unarisen, they are necessarily not produced— this being the treatise’s argument— the treatise asks:
"If this is so, for what reason is it called 'cultivation' (bhāvanā)?"
It is difficult. According to the treatise,
it is because that which was previously unattained is now for the first time attained.
This is a general principle.
According to the explanation of cultivation,
if the conditions are lacking, [the defilement] will not arise.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"It means that at that time, although one has attained mastery [over it],
its substance does not manifest before one due to the obstruction of other conditions."
It is precisely for this reason that it is called "attainment" (*prāpti*);
because by means of it, one realizes those phenomena and gains mastery over their arising.
This is because when there is the attainment of various phenomena, they immediately manifest before one.
As with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth: there are some dharmas that are first acquired and later manifested, such as the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*);

for those of sharp faculties, the knowledge of non-arising is acquired simultaneously with the knowledge of exhaustion. There are also some dharmas whose acquisition is such that they never manifest again.
Regarding such wisdom and other phenomena,
there are certain dharmas that appear before one without being apprehended,
such as external forms and the like.
Therefore, although it is unarisen, there is still the sense of "cultivation.
As for the objection in the treatise— “Since it cannot give rise to the sense of attainment, upon what does it depend?”— this is the difficulty raised.
Treatise:
It is simply because of the attainment [of the dharma] that it is called "attainment.
This is the answer.
Commentary:
Because [the attainment] is already attained, the thesis that one "attains" the ultimate principle is not established.
This concludes the refutation.
Treatise:
As the ancient masters explained up to their dissatisfaction with this interpretation,
[the author] here sets forth the Sautrāntika explanation.
The *Nyāyabindu* (or *Nyāya-vidūṣaṇā*) refutes this, saying:
How could this wisdom not be present before one?
To say that it "arises" based on its support is merely a figurative way of speaking about its attainment.
One cannot say that this [attainment] is present simply because its basis has been acquired;
for it must not be the case that the basis is identical to the essence of the attainment itself.
This concludes the extensive refutation found in the treatise.
Treatise:
Following the basis of each stage up to the seventh stage, this section describes the specific applications and limitations of the cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Accordingly, those in the higher stages also cultivate the lower contaminated [states].
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 36, states:
Question: Is it possible for two noble beings born in the same stage to both possess the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization?
Is there one who does not achieve [it]? Answer: Yes.
That is, one who relies on the first dhyāna to enter into the state of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma).
First, one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on the second dhyāna;
upon the end of that life, one is reborn together with the second dhyāna.
One who relies on the first dhyāna does not achieve this knowledge.
Because it transcends the ground of abandonment,
one who relies on the second dhyāna accomplishes this knowledge;
because when born in its own ground, it is not abandoned.
Is it possible for two Arhats dwelling in the same stage to have one of them achieve conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realizations?
Is there one who does not achieve it?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, there was previously one who, relying on the first dhyāna, entered the path of seeing.
First, one enters the path of vision based on the second dhyāna;
at the moment of death, one is reborn in the second dhyāna,
and while abiding in the intermediate state (antarābhava), one attains the fruit of arhatship.
One who relies on the first dhyāna does not accomplish this,
because it is abandoned by transcending that stage.
One who relies on the second dhyāna accomplishes this knowledge.
"Because that which arises from its own stage is not abandoned"—this is the treatise. The treatise states:
"At the limit of the cultivation of suffering and origin, one reaches [the stage] where these truths serve as the object."
This clarifies the distinctions between the aspects of abiding and practicing mindfulness and their respective objects.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"That is to say, if one practices at the conclusion of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Truth of Suffering..."
One employs the four aspects of the contemplation of suffering:
if it is bound to the desire realm, one contemplates the suffering of the desire realm;
if it is bound to the form realm, one contemplates the truth of suffering of the higher realms.

The cultivation of the truths of origination and cessation follows this same principle. Regarding the truth of suffering: if it is bound to the desire realm, it takes the origination and cessation of the desire realm as its object;
if it is bound to the form realm, it takes the origination and cessation of the two upper realms as its object.
The treatise states:
Because it is obtained through the power of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is obtained solely through application (*prayoga*).
This clarifies that between the two types of acquisition, it is acquired solely through application.
Because they are acquired through the preparatory stage of the path of vision (*darśanamārga-prayoga*),
those included in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are produced by reflection (*cintāmayī*),
while those included in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are produced by cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*).
It is not that which is produced by hearing (*śrutamaya*), because that is subtle and inferior.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 36, states:
"Question: For what reason is the conventional knowledge at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*) not that which is produced by hearing?"
Are there roots of goodness cultivated at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that consist of what is accomplished through hearing (*śrutamaya*)?
Answer: No; because those [roots] are exclusively the attendants of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), being cultivated by a path that is intensely sharp and swift.

It is not a member of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) consisting in what is heard, because the knowledge of exhaustion seeks cessation and is thus a path of leisure; it is able to cultivate [the factors] generally throughout the stages above. Thus says the treatise.
The treatise states:
Because wisdom increases, it constitutes its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
this clarifies the essence.
Thus the ancient masters explained it.
Conventional knowledge is identical in its contemplative cultivation,
because it contemplates the truths in the same manner as the path of seeing.
The contemplation of the truths during the path of seeing causes that knowledge which contemplates the truths to increase.
Because it subsequently arises from that attainment, it is called "cultivation through concordant observation.
By this standard,

within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are concordant knowledges (*anvayajñāna*) which take the path of seeing as their object for the purpose of observing the principles of the truths (*satyadharma*).
Furthermore, it does not serve to abandon afflictions;
nor does contaminated wisdom (sāsrava-jñāna) separately abandon the afflictions of views (dṛṣṭi-heya).
For these reasons, they are not a common antidote (samapratipakṣa).
Treatise:
Next, regarding the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), although it occurs within the state of defilement,
there are the following two lines of verse.
The second [section] clarifies the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The treatise states: "Up to the actual cultivation of the two knowledges" clarifies the first moment of the sixteenth [moment of the path], which is the path of cultivation.
Cultivation is of two kinds:
namely, the cultivation of practice and the cultivation of attainment.
Practice refers to actual manifestation.
"Attainment" refers to cultivation in the future.
At the first moment of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), one cultivates two knowledges: namely, the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
This essence consists of one [entity] having two aspects.
Both the sequential and the leap-over [attainments] are likewise these two. If they are cultivated in the future, the two stages differ.
Treatise:
From "one who has not yet abandoned desire" up to "not cultivating the mundane," it clarifies cultivation in the future.

Because the supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds belongs to the four fundamental dhyānas: if one has not yet abandoned desire, one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds, but cultivates only the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), and the knowledges of the Four Truths; if one has already abandoned desire, the knowledge of others' minds is added.
One does not cultivate the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising, because these belong to the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
Nor does one cultivate conventional knowledge, because it is not an antidote to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"For one who has previously abandoned desire and entered the Noble Path,
for what reason is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) not cultivated during the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*)?"

The cultivation [of the path] occurs only by relying on the path of preparation (*anāgamya-mārga*), which is comprised of the qualities of contemplation through the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). This is because, during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*),
one is occupied with contemplating the principles of the truths (*satya*).
Because the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is extremely rapid, it cannot be cultivated;
the same principle applies to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Now, at the time of the sixteenth moment, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), it is subsumed under the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), as there is sufficient leisure for cultivation.
Having cultivated this wisdom—[as stated] in the aforementioned treatise—this above clarifies the cultivation while abiding in the fruit.
Subsequently, regarding the stage of advancement (*prasthāna*), there are three types of abandonment:
first, the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm.
Second, the abandonment of the seven upper stages;
third, the abandonment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Among these three categories:
In severing each individual affliction, there are further four paths:
namely, the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
In these various stages, one practices and attains the two types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
There are similarities and differences.
However, those of the same class are clarified in a single location;
it is due to this sequence of before and after that distinctions arise.
Treatise:

From the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) up to their respective actual cultivation, this clarifies the distinctions in the practice of the three types of practitioners. Regarding the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*anantarya-mārga*) for abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm:
Regarding the eight paths of liberation:
because these abandon the afflictions of the desire realm, they do not employ the four subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*), nor the knowledge of others' minds,
the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Because it cuts off both the mundane and supramundane paths,
there is conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
Thus, there are six knowledges in total.

This refers to the knowledge of the four truths, the dharma-knowledge, and the conventional knowledge. It is also the same as the six knowledges regarding the cultivation of the ninth path of liberation.
Because it involves distinct future cultivation, it is not explained here; it severs [the afflictions] of the upper seven stages.
Because they employ subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), there are four subsequent knowledges.
Since the dharma-knowledges of cessation and the path can sever the higher realms, they include both types of dharma-knowledge;

and since [the path] does not pertain to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it includes conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). Question: For what reason are the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of the desire realm explained as being in the same location?

This clarifies the distinctions regarding the abandonment of the seven higher stages. Answer: In the nine paths of uninterrupted activity and eight paths of liberation for abandoning desire, one cultivates the future [states] of these;
however, in both cases, one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds.
Therefore, by means of the "same place" (samānabhūmika) illumination, one abandons the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) and the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) of the upper seven stages.

Regarding their common practice, one cultivates four types of knowledge: the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), the two dharma-knowledges (dharmajñāna and anvayajñāna), and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), totaling seven knowledges.
Because there is a specific reason for cultivating [the knowledge of others' minds] in the future, it is explained separately;

for one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds within the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), whereas one does cultivate it within the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Therefore, as previously stated in the treatise,
one practices the application of effort for the abandonment of desire according to what is appropriate for the present cultivation.
In the case of abandoning the afflictions of the desire realm, the uninterrupted path and the path of liberation do not employ subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
This does not contradict the meaning of the preparatory and superior paths;
therefore, four types of subsequent knowledge are added herein.
Commentary:
From this point upward, up to the addition of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*),
it clarifies that the three aforementioned cases involve future cultivation (*anāgata-bhāvanā*).
Because they have not yet abandoned desire and because they are on the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), they do not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds;

furthermore, this is because they have not yet attained the knowledges of exhaustion (*kṣaya*) and non-arising (*anutpāda*). Regarding the mutual cultivation of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*): [they are cultivated together].
It is cultivated because the power of the causes mutually support one another;
the lower stages are explained by analogy to this. To abandon the stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one adds the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*);
this clarifies the Peak of Existence.
Therefore, the first eight liberations are identical in their cultivation with uninterrupted practice (*ānantarya-prayoga*).
That which is not identical in its clarity is due to the distinctness of future cultivation.
In the eight paths of liberation, one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds in the immediate succession;
in the ninth path of liberation, one may cultivate either nine or ten [knowledges].
This is why they are explained separately.
Excluding the mundane [knowledges],
because they are the antidotes to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
Adding the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna),...
Because it is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). The treatise states:
"It abandons the six [defilements] of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) regarding suffering, origin, cessation, and the path."
Because it is an uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds;
because it is the antidote to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one does not cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). Thus says the treatise.
The abandonment of desire through cultivation up to its application according to circumstances;
this explains the cultivation of the conduct of desire and so forth.
Within the text there are four [sections]: the ninth liberation, which is the abandonment of desire through cultivation.
The first example: the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that abandons [defilements] of the upper seven stages.

The second example: the path of further progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) of the ninth [moment] that abandons the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm, and the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) that abandons [defilements] of the upper eight stages.
This is the third example.

Since the practice and cultivation here are identical, they are likewise explained together. The path of superior progress that abandons the seven stages above and the eight categories of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is the fourth example.

Because the cultivation of others' minds (paracittajñāna) may manifest first, the knowledge of others' minds is added. The differences in the modes of cultivation for these four types above can be understood accordingly.
[End of] Treatise.
From this point upward, up to the future [cultivation] of the four truths and the knowledge of others' minds,
the cultivation of the "attainment of clarity" (vidyā-lābha) follows these same four preceding cases; in all such instances, one cultivates eight knowledges in the future,
excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).
Because these are for those in training (*śaikṣa*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"The four [formless] attainments cannot sever the defilements of the desire realm;
the two dharmas of suffering and origin are not the antidotes for the higher [realms]."
For what reason does that antidote arise?
This wisdom is cultivated in the future.
If one were to allow that it is not an antidote for that [object], then...
The objection that one should also cultivate conventional knowledge when abandoning the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and so forth is irrational;
for it is not accepted that only the antidote is cultivated in the future.
This means that cultivation is also admitted because there is a relationship [between them],
such as the cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*);
or it is cultivated because they mutually support one another through the power of their causes.

Just as when abandoning desire one simultaneously cultivates the four types [of knowledge], so too at the stage of abandoning the defilements of the higher realms, one cultivates the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin.
If one abandons the defilements of the desire realm without cultivating the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
then when abandoning the higher realms, one does not cultivate these two knowledges— suffering and origin.
In that case, for one who gradually attains the fruit of non-returning,
there would be no possibility for the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) to arise and manifest;
likewise, an arhat would have no occasion for the dharma-knowledges of suffering and its origin to arise.
This is because that which was previously attained has already been relinquished,
and that which was not previously attained is not what is being cultivated;
this is according to their respective categories.
If one has previously attained [a wisdom] that serves as the power of a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) to draw forth the arising of a subsequent wisdom of similar outflow (niṣyanda),
then this wisdom arises because it was drawn forth by that prior wisdom.
Because that [subsequent] knowledge can act as the cause for that [prior] knowledge, the power of the cause for the arising of this knowledge supports it;
thus, although they do not share the same antidote, the future [knowledge] is cultivated. This is based on the aforementioned treatise.
Cultivating conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) at the conclusion of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is called "cultivation by connection" (*sambandhabhāvanā*).
However, it is not contrary to reason that this is also termed "cultivation by simultaneous observation" (*samānakālīnabhāvanā*).
This involves the preparatory (*prayoga*) and subsequent (*viśeṣamārga*) stages for abandoning the defilements (*kleśa*) of the nine stages.
All cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), though the specific points of their discernment have not yet been clarified.
For now, let us examine these in relation to one another: although they are not causes of the same kind (*sabhāgahetu*), they nonetheless possess the functional power to mutually induce one another.
By means of this, one cultivates them in mutual relation with untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
[The] treatise [now] proceeds to distinguish the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) attained through the separation from defilements.
The following single line of verse clarifies the third [category], the one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The Commentary states: "up to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)."

Regarding the explanation of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) and so forth: at the initial moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), it takes only the four aggregates of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as its object.
Therefore, the cultivation of practice consists only of the knowledges of suffering (*duḥkha*), origin (*samudaya*), subsequent (*anvaya*), and exhaustion (*kṣaya*).
Although there are four names,
three are fixed and identical in essence;
suffering and its origin are not fixed.
Because all categories are definitively identical within a single moment of thought. [The] Treatise [continues]:
Next, it distinguishes the quantity of wisdom cultivated in the remaining stages.
The following three lines of verse clarify the fourth point:
the cultivation of other stages, such as the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).
The treatise says: "Up to the point where one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*)."

This clarifies the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) by those still in training (*śaikṣa*). Because there are five distinct natures (*gotra*) within the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*), the term "various" (*sarva*) is used.
Since these are states of one still in training, they are neither "exhausted" (*kṣaya*) nor "unborn" (*anutpāda*).
Because it resembles the Path of Seeing, there is no conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*);
because it is an uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*), one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). Therefore, there are only six.
Treatise:
Regarding the various paths of liberation, up to the inclusion of the knowledge of others' minds,
this clarifies the paths of liberation.
Regarding the four dharmas, the cultivation of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is the same as before.
Within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), there is no severing of hindrances.
For those who have already abandoned desire, they cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
This is also as previously stated.

Other masters claim that the attainment (*prāpti*) also cultivates the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
This describes an alternative explanation. Regarding the discussion:
from the various paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) up to what is called "knowing the minds of others" (*paracitta-jñāna*).
This clarifies the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*). Its cultivation of practice is the same as that of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*),

In the future [moment], conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is added;

Treatise:
All paths of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*) up to the future also number eight.
This explains the path of superior progress.
For one who has not yet abandoned [the defilements], there is the cultivation of the practice of detachment.
In the future, seven or eight [factors] are cultivated together.
Treatise.
Because the training of the faculties by one beyond training (aśaikṣa) proceeds up to the subduing of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra),
this clarifies that it pertains to the state beyond training. Since it is an uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga), the knowledge of others' minds is not cultivated therein.
Because one practices cultivation, one does not cultivate the exhaustion [of outflows].

This refers to the ninth liberation of one who sharpens their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) within the fifth lineage.
The practice and cultivation are the same as before;
because they already possess sharp faculties, they cultivate ten [paths] in the future.
Treatise:
All paths of preparation (prayoga-mārga), up to and including the future [state], are also ten.
However, there is a difference in the cultivation of the path of clear realization (abhisamaya-prayoga) and the path of superior progress (viśeṣa-gati).
This can be understood from the text. According to the treatise:
for those in the stage of training (śaikṣa) who practice mixed cultivation, there are eight [types] up to the future [life].
This clarifies the mixed cultivation within the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).

Because the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) consists of both untainted (*anāsrava*) and tainted (*sāsrava*) moments of mind, its practice of cultivation encompasses both the supramundane and the mundane.
Because within the path of liberation there is only a single moment of untainted mind, the cultivation of practice consists of only four [moments]:

the Dharma-knowledge and Subsequent-knowledge paths. As for the statement that "the preparatory stage increases the conventional," it means that within the preparatory mind, there are many untainted moments of mind.

Because they are interspersed with one another, the various paths of further progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) additionally include the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), since it is possible for that knowledge to arise beforehand. As for the future [paths], there are only eight, because these belong to those still in training (*śaikṣa*).
Based on the fundamental [meditation],
the treatise states that the mixed cultivation of the stage of no-more-learning is the same as the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*).

This clarifies the mixed cultivation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Regarding the statement that in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), eight [minds] are future for the dull-witted and nine for the sharp-witted:

this is because they do not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*). In the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), nine are future for the dull-witted and ten for the sharp-witted.
Because one cultivates the knowledge of others' minds. According to the treatise,
in the stage of training, when cultivating the supernormal powers, one cultivates all eight knowledges.

The "clear knowledge" (*vidyā*) refers to the cultivation of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*). Because the five paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) do not involve correct contemplation (*yoniśomanasikāra*), one cultivates conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) in the present;
because they mutually induce one another, one cultivates seven knowledges in the future.
Excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising.

Regarding the five paths of liberation, two are indeterminate and thus are not termed "cultivation. These are the two paths of liberation for the knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of supernormal power.

The five paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) are all mundane (*saṃvṛti*) because they consist of non-rational contemplation (*ayoniśomanasikāra*). The path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of the knowledge of others' minds is untainted (*anāsrava*), and thus consists of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
And the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) arises accordingly. All superior progress is like the knowledge of others' minds;

however, it is said "and" because one additionally practices the contemplation of suffering, origin, and cessation as appropriate. Among the supernormal powers practiced by those in training (śaikṣa), the five types of immediate succession (ānantarya) are excluded.
All others in the future cultivate all eight knowledges,
excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising because they have not yet attained them.
[End of] Treatise.
The cultivation of supernormal powers by one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is the same as that for the refinement of the faculties;
this clarifies the cultivation of supernormal powers by one beyond training. Regarding immediate cultivation, it is like that of one in training (śaikṣa), because the objects of focus are identical.
The future cultivation differs:

for those of dull faculties, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is added; for those of sharp faculties, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is further included. Regarding the application of liberation (*vimuktimārga-prayoga*), the present cultivation is like that of a learner (*śaikṣa*).
Whether they be those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa),
none take the exhaustion [of outflows] or the non-arising [of further afflictions] as a preparatory application for liberation.
There is a difference regarding the future [attainments]:
for those of dull faculties, the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) is added; for those of sharp faculties, it is accompanied by the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Excellence in progress (*viśeṣagamana*) is the same as the refinement of faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*) for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Regarding the divine eye and divine ear, they are not even termed 'cultivation' (*bhāvanā*)."
Because these two liberations are indeterminate (avyākṛta),
neither those in training (śaikṣa) nor those beyond training (aśaikṣa) cultivate them.
Treatise.
Because the noble ones give rise to the remaining [attainments] up to and including the Peak of Existence solely through the cultivation of the conventional,
this clarifies that all noble ones cultivate contaminated (*sāsrava*) qualities;
since these are contaminated, they all practice the cultivation of the conventional.
In the future, those in training who have not yet abandoned desire will cultivate seven [paths];
those who have already abandoned desire will cultivate eight.
This may be understood by analogy with what preceded.

For those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the dull-witted have nine [factors] and the sharp-witted have ten, as previously explained. Regarding the statement "excluding the extremely subtle mind (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma-citta*), for this [state] one cultivates only the conventional [knowledge] in the future": [This means that] at the moment of the extremely subtle mind, one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) because it is not cultivated in the future; nor does one cultivate the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) because they have already been attained.
