Because of the aforementioned causes conducive to meditative concentration (*samāpatti-hetu*), one does not emerge from that concentration. The treatise states:
If it is argued that there is no fault in allowing [the mind] to arise based on the support [of the body], [we reply as follows].
Furthermore, this also resolves the objection.
According to this treatise, the Sautrāntika school [holds as follows].
It is admitted that body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) can function while one is in meditative absorption,
and that body-consciousness of the form realm may arise based on a body of the desire realm, taking contact of the form realm as its object; however,
it is admitted only that it takes the wind of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) as its object.
Treatise:
If that were so, it would entail the fault of contradicting reason regarding one who is currently in meditative absorption.
This is the objection raised by the Vaibhāṣikas.
While one is in an untainted meditative absorption (anāsrava-samādhi),
the contact and body-consciousness (kāya-vijñāna) should likewise become untainted,
because at the time when the untainted first dhyāna is present before one, [these factors arise].
That is to say, that pliancy-contact is itself a factor of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga),
while the pleasure within body-consciousness constitutes the factor of pleasure (sukha-aṅga).
It cannot be equated with the joy (prīti) among the five factors [of dhyāna], because that joy is untainted (anāsrava), whereas this pleasure is tainted (sāsrava).
[The opponent claims] there is the fault of contradicting reason. [The respondent says: There is no fault of contradicting reason in this treatise.
The Sautrāntika replies:
Why is this so? [End of] treatise.
This is a challenge from the Vaibhāṣika school. The treatise [responds]:
We accept that physical pliancy (*kāya-praśrabdhi*) is included within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
This is the Sautrāntika response by citing an example from the sūtras.
For the sūtras state that bodily pliancy (*kāyapraśrabdhi*) is a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
[Abhidharma] Treatise.

If you claim that [the term "limb"] is applied to those [factors] in accordance with their conformity [to awakening], we grant that such a statement was made; however, this serves as an example to refute your position.
Do you not yourself say that what conforms to the factors of awakening is called a "factor of awakening"?
In our school, body-consciousness is also called "untainted" (anāsrava) because it conforms to the untainted;
thus, there is no fault of contradicting reason. Treatise.
If it is argued that [the Vaibhāṣikas] admit that contact (*sparśa*) is always with-outflows (*sāsrava*),
the Vaibhāṣika school cites a sūtra to challenge this: since the sūtra states that fifteen elements (*dhātu*) are with-outflows,
how can there be contact of serenity (*praśrabdhi-sparśa*)?
And as for body-consciousness,
that which accords with the outflow-free (anāsrava) is called "outflow-free.
Treatise.
This is because there is no contradiction with the sūtras, as they were spoken with an underlying intention (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
This is the Sautrāntika interpretation of the sūtras;
it refers here to other types of contact and other body-consciousnesses.
Only names are said to be with outflows (*sāsrava*).
According to the intent of this treatise,
the Sautrāntikas maintain that because the wind of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and bodily consciousness are conducive to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), they are so designated.
The treatise states: "Provisionally designated as untainted.
How is it that the untainted reaches the minor untainted factors?
This is the objection from the Sarvāstivādins:
"The wind of pliancy (praśrabdhi) is indeed actually with-outflows (sāsrava);
it is called 'without-outflows' (anāsrava) only because it is conducive to the state without-outflows."
How can an untainted meditative absorption (anāsrava-samādhi) be directly present such that some of its factors (aṅga) are tainted (sāsrava) and some are untainted (anāsrava)?
The Sautrāntika school responds: "What fault is there in their arising not being simultaneous?
This is the Sautrāntika explanation.
When the consciousness of the body arises, the feeling of joy does not arise;
when the feeling of joy arises, the consciousness of the body does not arise.
What fault is there in this?
According to this principle,
it is not stated that body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) are truly untainted (*anāsrava*).
[End of] Treatise.
"If one says that the principle of joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and the four factors (*aṅga*) applies"—
this is the statement of the Vaibhāṣika objection. The treatise [continues]:
This also entails no fault, just as in the case of [the presence of] vitarka and vicāra;
this is the Sautrāntika response.
The Sautrāntikas cite what they themselves accept as an analogy.
That school admits that vitarka and vicāra do not arise simultaneously,
yet they establish both as factors [of the first dhyāna],
such that the first dhyāna possesses five factors.
Commentary:
If it is argued that the application of vitarka and vicāra as an analogy is unestablished,
this restates the objection of the Sarvāstivādins.
Now, as for the method of employing an analogy:
for an analogy to be valid, it must be accepted by both parties.
My school does not accept that two things arise sequentially.
The analogy is not established. The treatise states:
"This is not unestablished, because it is impossible to state a fault [against it]."
The Sautrāntika school also maintains this.
In my previous *Indriya-pāda*,
I established the reason that because the coarseness and subtlety of the mind are mutually contradictory, they cannot exist simultaneously.
Furthermore, the reasons you have stated before me cannot refute my position;
therefore, the analogy is established.
Now, regarding the principles of Hetuvidyā (Logic):
If a thesis has already been established and refuted even though it was not mutually accepted,
that lack of acceptance does not constitute a failure of proof.
Treatise.
From this, one may say that [the Sautrāntikas] do not assert the perception of [the factors] such as vitarka and vicāra.
This is the explanation according to the Sautrāntika school’s own tenet:
because in the first dhyāna, the factors of vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and vedanā are established.
The subsequent dhyānas are established by way of the reduction of preceding factors;
it is for this reason that five factors are first mentioned.
By reducing the initial vitarka and vicāra, the second dhyāna is established.
By diminishing the feeling of joy (*prīti*) along with vitarka and vicāra, the third dhyāna is established.
By diminishing the feeling of pleasure (*sukha*) along with the [remaining] three factors, the fourth dhyāna is established.
Since perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth are not diminished, they are not established as factors [of these dhyānas].
Treatise: Or one should explain why, at the outset, only five factors are established.
This is the Sautrāntika’s counter-interrogation.
If it is not as I have explained, you must provide an explanation.
Why is it that only five factors are established for the first dhyāna?
The treatise states: If it is argued that these five are established as factors because they reach [the object], [then...]
This restates the tenet of the Sarvāstivāda school. The treatise states:
"This is not reasonable, up to the point that it would entail superior vitarka and vicāra."
This is the Sautrāntika refutation.
The treatise states:
"Although there is one class [of people]... up to... because it is a common designation."
Although certain masters of the Vaibhāṣika school explain that the five factors are established for the first dhyāna because they serve as its requisites,
this is not because it was so designated by the ancient masters of the Sautrāntika school.
Treatise:
One should carefully examine and discern [the stages] up to what is called "internal serenity.
This concludes the initial dispute between the two schools regarding the factor of bliss in the first two dhyānas.
Next, we shall together examine the factor of "purity" (*prasrabdhi*) within the second dhyāna.
This is for the Vaibhāṣikas to cause the Sautrāntikas to reflect carefully upon.
Treatise:
"This concentration is free from [distraction] to the extent that it is like a river with waves"—
this is the explanation of the Sautrāntika school.
That is to say, this second dhyāna is free from the agitation caused by *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought).
The transformation of the continuity [of the mind] into purity is termed "internal serenity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).
The treatise says:
If that is so, this [serenity] should be identified here as the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
The Sarvāstivādins and Sautrāntikas raise this objection:
if it is claimed that it is called "inner serenity" (adhyātmasamprasāda) because it is devoid of vitarka and vicāra,
then this inner serenity would have no substantial reality.
How can it be said that the eleven real entities are refuted? Therefore, one should state that this is precisely the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*);
this is the correct tenet of the Sarvāstivāda school. Thus says the treatise.
This means that when one attains the state designated as "internal serenity" (adhyātmasamprasāda),
this is its detailed explanation.
In the first dhyāna mentioned previously, one has already departed from the realm of distraction.
Now, the second dhyāna is separated from its own level;
since it has already attained the second dhyāna and is separated from the first dhyāna,
it may likewise be separated within its own level.
There arises deep faith;
this faith that has arisen is called internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).
Treatise.
"Faith is the characteristic of purity," which leads to the establishment of the name "internal serenity";
this explains the meaning of the name. "Faith is the characteristic of purity," which explains the meaning of "purity.
"Free from externals. This explains the meaning of "internal."
"Explaining 'internal'" (*nai*) is the analysis of the term.

"Evenly flowing" (*samatā*) explains "equal" (*sam-*). To establish the name "internal equanimity and purity" (*adhyātmasamprasāda*) because it is pure and internally equal is the synthesis of the explanation.
The Commentary states: "Other masters say that [the *prāptis*] have no distinct substantial entities (*svabhāva*).
This describes the interpretation of other Sautrāntika masters.
Treatise:
If there were no separate entity [for mental factors], then mental concomitants (caitta) would be untenable.
This is the objection of the Sarvāstivādins.
Treatise:
Distinct states of mind may also be termed mental factors (*caitta*).
This is the position accepted by the Sautrāntika school.
Commentary:
Although this principle exists, it is not our own tenet;
the Master’s intention is to accept the principles of the Sautrāntika school.
This refers to what is called the Sarvāstivāda school. The treatise states:
"As stated above, up to the point where it is known for certain that [the three times] exist."
The outsider asks the Sarvāstivādins:
"In your treatise,
do you not say that joy (*prīti*) is not the feeling of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*)?"
The Sarvāstivādins ask those of other schools:
"As you accept it, so do we. (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya)
The opponent replies:
"As the Sthaviras admit, so do I also admit. [End of] Treatise.
How do other schools [maintain that] it reaches the point of being admitted as not being a pleasant feeling (*saumanasya*)?
The Sarvāstivādins interrogate the outsiders.
Treatise.
This means that joy exists separately and its substance is distinct [from pleasure];
this is the response of the opponent.
That is to say, the Sthavira school maintains that joy is a separate mental factor (*caitta-dharma*).
It is not feeling (*vedanā*).
In the three meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), all pleasure (*sukha*) is the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*);
therefore, it is joy.
The sensation of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*): their essential natures are each distinct.
Treatise.
Because the bliss of the three dhyānas has not yet reached the point of clear and distinct realization.
This is not the position of the outsiders (bāhya), as it contradicts two Āgamas. Thus, the Āgama says:
This is called the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary).
As explained in the *Vibhaṅga-viparyāsa*, up to the bliss of cessation without remainder.
This cites the first sutra.
The sutra states that in the three dhyānas, joy (*prīti*) is extinguished without remainder;
therefore, we know that there is no feeling of joy (*prītivedanā*) in these three dhyānas.
The Commentary states: Furthermore, another sutra says that up to this point it is joy (*prīti*) and not pleasure (*sukha*).
This cites the second sutra as proof.
Since it is stated that in the fourth dhyāna there is the abandonment of pleasure and pain, preceded by the disappearance of joy and sorrow,
and since joy occurs after pleasure,
we know that the faculty of joy does not exist within the third dhyāna.
The Sūtra states: "Having abandoned pleasure and abandoned pain, with prior joy and sorrow having subsided.
This means that in the first dhyāna, sorrow and pain are abandoned;
in the third dhyāna, joy is abandoned.
The bliss of the four dhyānas is abandoned because it is contrasted with suffering; therefore, the Sūtra mentions it first.
As for joy and grief, they are not so contrasted, and thus their prior disappearance is not mentioned.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 81, states:
"Regarding the statement that the fourth dhyāna abandons suffering,
the term 'abandonment' is spoken of in reference to the exhaustion of both factors [pleasure and pain] together."
Regarding what is called the "pair of dharmas," it refers to suffering and pleasure.
At the time of becoming free from the defilement of desire, although suffering has already been exhausted, pleasure has not yet been exhausted.
Now, having become free from the defilements of the third dhyāna,
both suffering and pleasure have come to an end;
thus, it is said that both are abandoned.
When one is free from the defilements of the three dhyānas, pleasure and the other [feelings] are all abandoned.
Why, then, is it said specifically that the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is abandoned?
Answer: Because at that time, pleasure has reached its cessation.
One knows that the defilements of the desire realm and the first dhyāna have been abandoned,
as well as the joy (*prīti*) and other factors;
however, because these have not yet been completely exhausted, they are not mentioned.
Furthermore, the Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, fascicle 81, states:
"As the sūtra says, in the first dhyāna the faculty of sorrow (daurmanasya) ceases;
in the second dhyāna the faculty of suffering (duḥkha) ceases."
Question: When one is detached from the defilements of desire, one abandons sorrow and suffering;
why does the Sūtra make this statement? Answer:
It makes this statement based on the overcoming of their respective antidotes.
This means that although the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is abandoned during the stage of detachment from desire,
it is not yet called "transcending the remedy for suffering.
This occurs at the time one attains detachment from the first dhyāna.
Because it is the antidote that transcends suffering.
The antidote to suffering refers to the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, this statement is made because it transcends the category [of suffering] and because it is the basis for the cessation of suffering.
This means that although the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is abandoned during the stage of detachment from sensual desire,
one has not yet transcended the basis and the lineage (*gotra*) of suffering;
this occurs at the time of attaining detachment from the first dhyāna.
It is called the cessation of suffering because it is the basis for transcending suffering and because it is the nature of the lineage of suffering;
[the term "cessation"] refers to both the basis and the nature of the lineage.

This refers to the various groups of consciousness. Question: Although the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is abandoned at the stage of detachment from desire, one has not yet transcended its antidote, its basis, and its lineage.
One should not say that sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is extinguished in the first dhyāna.

Answer: The antidote to the faculty of sorrow, its basis, and its lineage all reside in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Since it shares the same locus as the faculty of sorrow—namely, the mental consciousness—[it cannot be said to be extinguished there].
Therefore, at the very moment of right abandonment, that cessation is spoken of.
The basis of the faculty of suffering and the nature of the class of suffering do not coexist in the same consciousness with their antidote.
Therefore, it is only after [the afflictions] have been overcome, their basis [eliminated], and their lineage [extinguished] that the cessation of suffering is declared.
Some say that the faculty of pain (duḥkhendriya) is extinguished in the second dhyāna.
This refers to the cessation of vitarka and vicāra.
For the noble ones conceive the notion of suffering regarding vitarka and vicāra,
surpassing even the ordinary worldlings' revulsion for the sufferings of hell.
Because it can give rise to the perception of suffering, it is called the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
The above is from the treatise. Question: When the four dhyānas arise, there are the universal wholesome mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*).
It comprises the ten universal mental factors,
the two non-universal factors of vitarka and vicāra,
and the mind-king (citta).
Twenty-three factors arise in association [with dhyāna].
Why, then, are only nine factors employed as the branches of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*)?
Among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), they are mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and feeling (*vedanā*).
Equanimity, pliancy, and faith among the wholesome universal mental factors (mahābhūmika),
along with the indeterminate vitarka and vicāra, are established as the factors of concentration (samādyaṅga).
The remaining fourteen dharmas are not included within the factors of concentration.
Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 80, states in its refutation of the [opposing] position:
"The mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is the sovereign; it is not a subordinate factor of the mental concomitants (*caitta*).
Among the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), three—mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)—" [are the sovereigns].
Because it is preeminent in accordance with purity, it is established as a limb;
because its functional power is equally preeminent within both the defiled and pure portions, feeling is likewise established [as a limb].
However, among the five feelings, sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*) are not invariably associated [with the mind];

therefore, they are not established as factors [of dependent origination]. Perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and desire (*chanda*) predominantly conform to the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*) and do not lead toward its cessation (*nivṛtti*).
Therefore, it is not established as a factor (*aṅga*).

Attention (*manasikāra*) is not established as a factor because its function is preeminent only in the realm of desire and the distracted stages when confronting objects, and not in the various meditative stages (*samāpatti-bhūmi*).
Resolution (*adhimokṣa*) is preeminent only in the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is superior across all stages;
therefore, it is not established [as a separate faculty].
Among the wholesome factors, faith (*śraddhā*) is the primary foundation for all practices.
Just as a water-purifying gem makes the mind clear and pure,
it is established as a factor [of enlightenment].
Excitement is an obstacle to concentration, and equanimity is its antidote.
Lethargy is an obstacle to wisdom, while pliancy is its antidote;
therefore, [pliancy] is established as a factor.
Because shame, embarrassment, non-attachment, non-hatred, heedfulness, and non-harming do not accord as closely with the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) as these do, they are not so established.
This dharma serves as a proximate antidote primarily for the unwholesome dharmas of the distracted stage within the desire realm;
its power is thus more intense there than it is in the meditative stages.
Therefore, it is not established [as a fruit].
Diligence brings much suffering to body and mind;
concentration causes much happiness to body and mind.
Because they do not accord perfectly with one another, they are not established as factors [of enlightenment].
However, those that accord with bodhi are established as the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma).
Among these, vitarka and vicāra are included within the indeterminate [factors].
When the factor of serenity (praśrabdhi) is particularly strong, it can assist meditative concentration (samādhi) by exerting control over the mind,
causing it to abandon grossness and subtlety and counteract desire and evil.
Therefore, the factors [of dhyāna] are established as branches;
as for the remaining mental concomitants, they are not established as branches because they do not correspond with meditative concentration.
Treatise:
Regarding the factors of the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) thus described,
there is the following verse:
The second [section] clarifies that there are no members in the defiled [state].
The Treatise says: "up to being defiled. This describes one class of teachers who explain according to the characteristics [of the members].
This can be understood according to the text. Regarding the treatise:
other masters say that it is because [the mind] reaches the inclusion within the great wholesome [roots].
This describes an alternative explanation.
While defiled concentration is not wholesome and is therefore excluded,
the remaining [types] are not excluded because they can be associated with both the wholesome and the defiled.
Therefore, the preceding text states that they do not all possess [these qualities].
The treatise says: The sūtras state that the three meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are subject to movement (*iñjita*).
The following single line of verse constitutes the third major section, which explains the "immovable" (*āniñjya*) as taught in the Sūtra. The Treatise says:
up to the point where it mentions that there are eight types of calamities and misfortunes.
This explains the preceding sutra.
It is called "Immovable" because it is free from the eight kinds of calamities.
Treatise:
What are these eight? They are:
questioning, and treatise.
The answer is that from vitarka and vicāra through the four types of sensation, it is said to be "immovable.
[End of] Treatise.
However, the sutras state that [the breath] is moved by joy and bliss;
this explains the differences from other sutras.
If one takes a comprehensive view including the desire realm, it refers to both the breath and the wind.
There are thus eight afflictions.
If one considers only the internal mental states of the form realm,
they are free from applied thought (vitarka), sustained thought (vicāra), joy (prīti), and bliss (sukha).
Treatise:
Other masters say that it reaches and illuminates but does not move;
this describes a divergent interpretation.
Treatise:
As for all the feelings associated with the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*),
the following single verse states:
The fourth [section] clarifies the arising of the dhyānas.
The treatise says: "Up to the association with the four consciousnesses."
This describes the initial arising of dhyāna. The treatise states:
"The second [dhyāna] has two [factors], because [the first] is coarse up to the level of mental joy."
This describes the second dhyāna.
Because there is no remaining consciousness, there is no pleasure associated with the three [sensory] consciousnesses.
Because mental joy is coarse, there is no pleasure associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Treatise:
The third [section] contains two parts up to the distinction regarding the experience of existence (*bhavopaga*);
this describes the latter two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
In the third dhyāna, because mental joy (*saumanasya*) is subtle, there is the pleasure (*sukha*) of the mental level (*manobhūmika*).
In the fourth dhyāna, because the mind becomes even more tranquil, there is only the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣāvedanā*).
This is what is meant by the distinction among the feelings born of meditative concentration (*dhyānajā vedanā*).
This is the summary. According to the treatise,
the three consciousness-bodies do not exist in the three higher dhyānas.
The following single line of verse explains the fifth point, the borrowing of consciousness (*vijñapti*).
The Treatise says: "Up to contact and the manifestation of expression."
It is stated that the higher stages are without vitarka and vicāra,
lack the three bodies of consciousness and the mind that initiates expression,
and borrow the mind of the first dhyāna.
Because the five bodies of consciousness and the mind that initiates expression are necessarily associated with vitarka and vicāra; thus says the treatise.
These four [minds] are exclusively *anivṛtāvyākṛta* (unobstructed-indeterminate) because they are inferior;
they do not borrow from the defiled or the wholesome. Once one has been born in a higher realm, one has already abandoned the defilements of the lower realms.

Furthermore, because they do not give rise to inferior wholesome states: [Question] When one born in the three higher meditative absorptions (dhyāna) gives rise to the two supernormal powers (abhijñā) of the eye and ear belonging to the lower levels, what is their moral quality?
Some say that these are exclusively minds of deportment (īryāpatha-citta).
Or [it might be argued that] it is conditioned by a mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*), or a mind resembling a mind of deportment; in all such cases, this is not so.
Ear-consciousness cannot be a mind of deportment.
The vocal informative karma is also not to be described as a mind of deportment,
for that would contradict the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
If it is claimed that the vocal informative action (*vāgvijñapti-karman*) arises [directly from the mind], this refers to the second master;
according to him, a mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises from the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika-citta*).
Because it takes the twelve bases as its object and is also called a "mind of deportment" (īryāpatha-citta),
this mind that initiates vocal intimation is termed a "mind of deportment."
This too is unreasonable.
How could it be that the minds which produce vocal informative karma from the second dhyāna upward all arise only after a mind of deportment?
According to the interpretation of the first master,
how can this be a mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*)?
The first master maintains that only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that initiates deportment is a mind of deportment.
Since speech is not itself a deportment,
how could it be considered one?
For this reason, it is known.

If the four types of indeterminate mind do not exhaustively encompass the mind, and since indeterminate matter likewise does not exhaustively encompass matter, what prevents the four types of indeterminate [matter] from also failing to exhaustively encompass the mind? Question: You have already stated that the four types of indeterminate [matter] do not exhaustively encompass the indeterminate mind.
It is not yet known what kind of indeterminate state this borrowed consciousness is. Answer: This borrowed consciousness is indeterminate by its own nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*).
It is neither vocal or physical deportment (*airyāpathika*) nor indeterminate as that which is other than deportment (*anairyāpathika*).
In the higher stages, there is no neutral [state] that is either craft (*śailpasthānika*) or non-craft;
transformation (*nairmāṇika*) exists only in the mental consciousness and is not a neutral state of transformation;
and maturation (*vipākaja*) does not arise in a different stage and is not a neutral state of maturation.
For this reason, it is known that it is solely the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
[End of] Treatise.
Having thus explained the matter of dhyāna individually,
the following single verse-line clarifies the initial attainment of the meditative absorptions (samāpatti).

The Treatise says: "When one is born into one's own level, it is stated that the pure fundamental attainments (*mauladhyāna*) are entirely not accomplished because they are acquired through two means.
The Treatise continues:
The same applies to the seven lower stages up to the Uncaused Realm (*anabhisamskāra-parinirvāṇa*), because they possess higher stages.
Thus, it is stated that all seven lower stages are fully endowed with both detachment from defilements (*vairāgya*) and rebirth (*upapatti*).
This is because they have higher stages above them.
The Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is unique;
because it is the unsurpassed stage, it cannot be said that one is "born" there.
[End of] Treatise.
[The opponent] asks: For what reason is the term "entirely unestablished" (sarvathā-asiddha) stated? [The author] replies:
The verse begins by stating that it is "obtained while entirely unestablished."
To what does this negation refer? The treatise states:

Explaining the second liberation: regarding the statement "perceiving internal non-materiality while observing external forms," this refers to the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*),
wherein one perceives one's own internal body as being devoured by worms and so forth.
Not perceiving the characteristics of the body,
one perceives only the insects and so forth;
therefore, it is called "the liberation consisting of the perception of external forms while having no perception of internal form."
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The practitioner who cultivates contemplation subsequently gradually eliminates the perception of internal forms."
That is to say, through the power of resolute conviction, one brings about one's own death;
the physical remains are then carried on a litter and placed in a charnel ground,
where various birds and beasts vie with one another to devour them.
In a brief moment, the body is entirely consumed and one sees only birds and beasts;
or else, one is burned by fire in that place until nothing remains but ashes scattered and driven away by the wind.
In a brief moment, the body vanishes and one perceives only the realm of space.
Or, one imagines one's own body as being like ghee or salt, being dissolved and consumed by fire, water, and so forth,
until the body is no more and one perceives only the fire and other elements.
This is called the liberation consisting of the perception of external forms while being internally without the perception of form.
Because the power of this resolute conviction (adhimukti) eliminates the perception of form,
although it arises in relation to the body, one does not perceive the body.
Once the perception of internal forms has been eliminated,
the mental continuum proceeds without further activity,
and a superior pliancy and bliss spontaneously manifest.
In this stage, repeatedly cultivating the aspect of aversion toward the objective sphere of visible forms is called the fulfillment of the second liberation;
it is also like the first liberation regarding desire and greed.
Although one may have previously cultivated the perception of impurity and attained liberation,

Therefore, he subsequently cultivates the internal perception of formlessness and the contemplation of revulsion toward forms;

[Treatise: The Sūtra says: "To regard what is not-self as self is a perversion of perception, conception, thought, and view. Why is this so? Because it is by means of these four—perception, conception, thought, and view—that one regards what is not-self as self. Therefore, these four are collectively termed "perversion" (*viparyāsa*). What are these four? They are: 1. Perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*); 2. Perversion of conception (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*); 3. Perversion of thought (*citta-viparyāsa*); and 4. Perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*). What is meant by "perversion"? It refers to being contrary to reality. That is to say, because these four are contrary to the true nature of things, they are called "perversions. Furthermore, because they cause sentient beings to fall into ruin, they are called "perversions. Moreover, because they lead sentient beings to wander through the three realms of existence, they are called "perversions. Finally, because they obstruct the attainment of nirvāṇa, they are called "perversions. Thus, for these reasons, the Sūtra speaks of "perversion. Regarding the specific distinctions among them: The perversion of perception is the grasping of a self within the five aggregates based on false conceptualization. The perversion of conception is the mental construction of a self within the five aggregates based on false conceptualization. The perversion of thought is the mind’s adherence to a self within the five aggregates based on false conceptualization. The perversion of view is the wrong view that clings to a self within the five aggregates based on false conceptualization. In this context, "perception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to the act of perceiving; "conception" (*dṛṣṭi*) refers to the act of viewing; "thought" (*citta*) refers to the mind itself; and "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) refers to the specific mental factor of wrong view. Since these four function together to produce the error of regarding what is not-self as self, they are collectively designated as "perversion. Thus, the Sūtra establishes that regarding what is not-self as self is indeed a perversion of perception, conception, thought, and view. This concludes the explanation.

Furthermore, all those who grasp the aggregates as a self claim it to be a real self and not a conventional one. The treatise states:
"If it is admitted that [the mind] arises based on one's own body and reaches another body as its object..."
This is a challenge from the non-Buddhists:
"The body is truly not the self;
it is in dependence upon the body that the grasping at a self arises."
Another's body is not the self;
how could there not be attachment to a self arising in relation to another's body?
Treatise.
"Because he has cultivated such attachment to the self-grasping [ego-clinging]," the Master of the Treatise replies.
"This is because the personal body is connected with the mind that grasps."
One reckons one's own body as the self;
because the bodies of others are not connected to the grasping mind,
they are not reckoned as the self.
Treatise:
What is meant by "mutual connection"?
This is a question from the non-Buddhists. As for the term "mutual connection":
What is the meaning? The treatise states:
it refers to the nature of cause and effect.
This is the master of the treatise’s response.
The mutual relationship between the body and the grasping at a self as being cause and effect is termed "association.
Treatise:
"If there is no self-entity, whose is this grasping at a self?
This is the objection of the non-Buddhists.
"If there is a self-entity..."
The grasping at a self belongs to the self;
names and characteristics belong to the attributes. If there were no substantial entity of a self, [these would not exist].
To whom does the grasping at a self belong? It belongs to name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
Regarding this, the treatise states: "As previously explained, it belongs to that which serves as the fruit."
The Master of the Treatise points back to the previous answer.
The treatise asks:
"If that is so, what is the cause of the grasping at a self?"
The non-Buddhists ask about the cause of the grasping at a self.
The treatise states:
it refers to that which has existed from beginningless time up until the defiled mind.
The master of the treatise answers regarding the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*). The treatise states:
"If my substance (*ātman*) does not exist, who would possess suffering and pleasure?"
This is a question posed by a non-Buddhist (tīrthika). The treatise states:
"If one relies on this [tree], up to the point where there are flowers upon the tree..."
This is the Master of the Treatise’s response.
The dharma and the analogy are understandable.
Now, upon what do suffering and pleasure depend?
This is a question from a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).
The treatise states that [the six internal bases] are explained as their support.
The Master of the Treatise replies:
It is precisely within the six internal bases that, according to their arising,
they are designated as the bases for the suffering and pleasure that arise at those times.
Treatise:
"If the self truly does not exist, who is it that performs actions and undergoes their results?
This is the question of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
Since there is neither an agent nor an experiencer,
who is able to perform an action,
and who is able to experience its result?
Treatise: What is the meaning of "acting" and "experiencing"?
This is the question posed by the author of the treatise.
The treatise states:
"Action" refers to that which performs the action, and "experiencer" refers to the one who undergoes the experience;
this is the response of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
The Commentary states: "This merely changes the name without clarifying its meaning.
This is the Master of the Treatise’s censure.

Regarding the commentary: "As for the phrase 'those who debate the characteristics of phenomena' up to 'conventional names and so forth,' this is an explanation by those who cite non-Buddhists to debate the characteristics of non-Buddhist phenomena."
Commentary:
Herein, the Master of the Treatise refutes [the opponent] by means of two alternatives regarding the claim that "you have reached the status of an independent creator."
If one speaks of a real self as Devadatta,
the analogy is not universally established;
if one speaks of the aggregates as Devadatta, it follows that they are not an independent agent.
Treatise:
Regarding the three types of karma up to their belonging to causes and conditions,
it is explained in detail that all phenomena depend upon causes and conditions and are not independent.
Treatise:
Because the self you maintain is subject to movement, it is not sovereign.
The Master of the Treatise refutes the existence of a real, sovereign self.
In reality, although the self does not depend on causes,
it is also not sovereign because it performs no action.
Treatise.
From this point onward, it is stated that "characteristics are unobtainable," which summarizes the refutation.
Treatise:
However, regarding all phenomena, the term "agent" is employed.
The Master himself explains this "agent" as being for the purpose of refuting a self that acts as an agent.
Treatise:
What is the superior cause capable of producing bodily action?
This is a question posed by the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
Treatise:
This refers to everything from recollection up to "one should contemplate in this manner.
Thus the Master of the Treatise explains.
The successive arising of the functions of the supreme causes is designated as the "agent.
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cling to a self,
yet in this context, such a self has no functional utility.
Therefore, it is not the agent.
[The opponent asks:
"How, then, can the self experience the fruits of karma?"
The Master of the Treatise previously refuted the agent.
This refutation of the experiencer of the fruit now begins with a question.
The Treatise says:
If it is argued that [the self] has already been refuted regarding its arrival at the fruit,
the Master [Vasubandhu], even granting this assumption, points back to the previous refutation:
"Since I have already established that the mind of consciousness possesses no functional capacity..."
Regarding the experience of suffering and pleasure, there is likewise no capacity [for agency].
Treatise:
If, in reality, there were no self, how could sin and merit arise and grow?
This is a challenge posed by the non-Buddhists: "If there is no self,
then the aggregates alone must be the cause of birth."
Regarding that which is called "karmic action":
those who experience pleasure and pain,
as well as insentient things, also possess matters such as harm and benefit.
Question: Why is it not said that demerit and merit increase?
Treatise:
That is because they do not experience meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), as has already been explained above.
The Master of the Treatise explains this objection while simultaneously refuting [wrong] attachments:
it is solely the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*),
because they are the locus upon which mental factors such as sensation (*vedanā*) depend.
All insentient phenomena are not the basis for feeling and so forth,
nor are they the basis upon which demerit or merit arise.
I am not the basis for sensation and so forth,
as has already been explained previously.
[Treatise]
If it were truly the case that a non-existent self produces future fruits,
this would be an objection from the non-Buddhists (tīrthika). [The] Treatise [says]:
Suppose there were a real self that reaches the point of producing future fruits.
This is the master of the treatise’s counter-objection and challenge. The Treatise states:
"It arises based on my doctrine and non-dharma.
This is the reply of the non-Buddhist. "I am the basis."
Dharma and adharma are the bases;
from dharma and adharma, future fruits arise. Thus says the treatise.

As for the statement, "Whoever relies on whom should not rely on me," this refers to the previously refuted point that phenomena (*dharma*) and non-phenomena (*adharma*) do not rely upon a referent (*artha*).
Treatise.
However, within the sacred teachings, until the future fruit arises,
the Master explains this according to the Sautrāntika tenet;
whereas the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that it arises from an action that has already perished.
The Sautrāntikas [hold that it] arises from the seeds impressed by karma.
[The Vaibhāṣika] asks: "If that is so, from what [do they arise]?"
This is the response of the non-Buddhist.
The treatise states that the continuity of karma reaches the point of immediate succession, at which it is born.
The Master of the Treatise explains this according to the Sautrāntika doctrine,
further clarifying it through an analogy.
The Treatise states:
If that is so, from what [does it arise]?
This is an external question regarding the analogy.
The treatise says:
"From the continuity of the seed until it eventually draws forth the arising of the fruit"—
this is the Master’s response.
If this is so, why does the treatise say that "the seed produces the fruit"?
The non-Buddhists ask:
"If [the fruit] arises successively from the flower,
why do you say that the fruit arises from the seed?"
Treatise:
"By means of the seed, [the result] reaches the point of being distinct from what should yield its fruit.
This is the Master’s explanation.
First, there is the exegesis following the sequence; second, there is the exegesis by means of counter-objection.
These may be understood according to the text.
Treatise:
Although it is thus stated that [the fruit] arises through differentiation upon reaching [the cause],
this explains how karma produces its fruit at the time of its arising.
It does not arise immediately [after the action],
nor does it arise apart from the action;
rather, it arises from a specific transformation within the continuum of that action.
Treatise:
What is meant by "the transformation and differentiation of the continuum"?
This is a question from the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
The treatise states that "differentiation" (viśeṣa) refers to reaching [a state] preceded by karma.
The Master of the Treatise explains the differentiation of transformation (pariṇāma-viśeṣa).
This can be understood according to the text. The treatise states:
"As there is consciousness accompanied by grasping, it revolves within birth and death."
The master of the treatise explains by citing specific instances and also quotes verses as proof.
The treatise states:
Regarding this point, because it leads to ultimate cessation,
the Master of the Treatise explains that all causes produce effects.
The differences in their destruction are as can be understood from the text.
Treatise:
"For what reason does a distinct fruit arise once the fruition-fruit has reached its completion?
This is an external objection,
[suggesting] that just as an externally ripened fruit can serve as the cause for a subsequent fruit.
Why is the fruit of maturation not itself the cause of maturation?
[The] treatise says:
Furthermore, it is not the case that a distinct fruit arises until the end of the analogy.

The Master of the Treatise explains the preceding objection and simultaneously refutes the arising of a fruit. First, he states that it is not the case that all things used as analogies are identical in nature;
this explains the preceding objection. However, from a seed, no distinct fruit arises.
This refutes the previous [position] by establishing that the fruit becomes the cause once again.
The treatise asks: "If that is so, from what is the subsequent fruit produced?"
This is an external inquiry.
The treatise states: from the subsequent transformation through maturation up to what is conventionally termed a "seed" (*bīja*).
The Master of the Treatise explains the cause for subsequent arising. The treatise states:
"This is also like this," up to "therefore the analogy is of the same nature."
The Master of the Treatise [explains] the correspondence of the principles. The treatise states:
"Alternatively, by means of a distinct calculation, one reaches another rebirth from a previous maturation."
The commentary explains that dependent origination through specific conditions is likewise synonymous with maturation (*vipāka*). The treatise states:
"Up to this point, we have merely followed what has been reached; apart from the Buddha, there is no one capable of knowing it."
The Master of the Treatise subtly investigates and concludes that this is known by the Buddha;
he provides a verse as proof,
which may be understood according to the text.
From here below are three verses.
This constitutes the second major section: the exhortation to study and the circulation [of this teaching] within the present chapter.
The first verse exhorts the study of the wisdom of hearing;
the next verse exhorts the study of the wisdom of reflection;
and the final verse exhorts the study of the wisdom of cultivation. Thus has this path of the cause of purity been well expounded.
"Purity" refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*).

"Cause" refers to the Buddha’s teaching. This means that the Buddha’s supreme words are the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which emerges as the essence of the path of pure causes. One should abandon the blind attachments of all outsiders.
This causes one to abandon the teaching of a self; it is the result of evil views.
It clarifies the cause for the teaching of a self.
It seeks the eye of wisdom and exhorts one to hear the teaching of non-self. The second verse says: "This is the single broad path to the palace of Nirvāṇa."

Contemplating the principle of non-self is the broad path leading to nirvana. That the nature of non-self is traversed by a thousand sages means that the manifest path traversed by a thousand sages is vast.
The nature of selflessness is the essence of the path to liberation. Regarding that which is illuminated by the light of the words of the Buddhas, the Sun:
the Buddha’s speech is like the sun shining upon the nature of selflessness; although it opens the eyes of the dim-sighted, they are still unable to perceive it.
This is the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
Because the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) has not yet abandoned the teachings while seeking direct vision,
the eye has not yet opened.

Although the wisdom born of reflection opens the way, if one reflects on the meaning while remaining obscured by the teachings, one cannot perceive it clearly. This brief explanation has been given regarding this particular point;
it refers back to what was previously stated.
Thirdly, there is the exhortation to cultivate the wisdom of meditation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*), which serves as the gateway to opening the poison-removing door of the wise person’s wisdom.
This clearly explains the meaning.
Untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is able to destroy the afflictions;
therefore, the afflictions are termed "poisons."
The four types of well-cultivated wisdom capable of serving as preparatory application are called "gates.
This is intended so that each may act according to their own capacity and strength;
this refers to the differences in spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and training. To universally awaken to all that is knowable and accomplish supreme activity—this is the result.
To fully realize that among all phenomena known,
there is no self whatsoever,
is to accomplish the supreme karma of nirvana.

The Commentary on the Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya, Fascicle Thirty: From last autumn until this winter, the task of punctuating this entire work from beginning to end has been completed. Now, upon examining its fundamental substance, it is evident that between the original manuscript and the subsequent transcriptions, numerous errors have become compounded. Whenever I open the text, I am inevitably confused by the lack of sequence from beginning to end; thus, I have extensively collated the original and added some critical analysis, reaching approximately half of the work. Although I have altered the previous draft, I fear I may be contradicting the profound deliberations of the former sages; yet, for the sake of encouraging the understanding and resolution of future students, there remain here and there omissions and repetitions that require correction.

Recorded by the former Junior Sōjō, Kakujū (in another hand), on the third day of the twelfth month in the third year of Hōen, by lamp-light. One copy was transcribed from the original text held at Jion-in in Kōfuku-ji. Although the original text by Shūkai contains deletions that are difficult to read, it has been recorded here so that future students may derive some benefit from it.
Completed on August 2, 1927 (Shōwa 2). Recorded by the Editor.
